greek_from_text: Athenian possession under Miltiades by c. 500-493 BC; Athenian cleruchy (re)organised c. 450 BC
pre_greek_note: Herodotus (5.26) says Imbros was inhabited by 'Pelasgians' when Otanes took it c. 511 BC; no native name attested. The text refers to the island, not specifically to the Kastro site.
status_evidence: IACP (Imbros); ATL (Imbrioi); own coins (Hermes Imbramos) 4th c. BC; medieval Roman bishopric (later metropolis of Imbros)
note: The ancient and medieval town was at Kastro/Kaleköy on the N coast. The island was surrendered to Mehmed II through Kritoboulos of Imbros, 1455/56.

greek_from_text: Archaic colony, c. 600 BC (necropolis excavated 1915-23 is Archaic); founders disputed
founder: Athenians under Phorbas (Ps.-Scymnus); Teos or an Ephesian, Hegesistratus, in other sources
pre_detail: The town (Eski Hisarlık) has yielded only an Archaic-Hellenistic necropolis (French excavations 1915, 1920-23). The so-called tumulus of Protesilaos at Karaağaç Tepe is a Chalcolithic/EBA/LBA settlement mound (Demangel 1926; Özdoğan 1993), but it lies c. 2.5 km W of the town near Seddülbahir, beyond the same-site test.
pre_sources: Demangel, Le tumulus dit de Protésilas (1926); DEFC site 747; LuwianSiteAtlas site 87 (Özdoğan, IstMitt 43, 1993); Waiblinger, CRAI 1978; Pleiades 501411
pre_greek_note: An Early Bronze Age (Troy I–II period) settlement mound lies under the so-called tumulus of Protesilaos at Karaağaç Tepe near Elaious (Schliemann; Demangel 1926); it is next to the Greek town rather than under it, so pre_settlement stays 'unknown'.
status_evidence: IACP (Thracian Chersonese); ATL; Hellenistic coins; Roman provincial coins (Commodus); fortified by Justinian
note: The mother city is disputed: Athens (Ps.-Scymnus), Teos, or an Ephesian founder (Plutarch). The Protesilaos sanctuary was in its territory.
sources: IACP (Thracian Chersonese); Hdt. 9.116-120; Pleiades 501411; Wikipedia: Elaeus

site: near Anafarta harbour / Suvla bay (Eceabat, Çanakkale)
greek_from_text: Aeolian colony of Archaic date (7th-6th c. BC); exact date unrecorded
pre_detail: Site unlocated; no evidence either way.
status_evidence: IACP (Thracian Chersonese); ATL (Delian League member); own coins 4th c. BC
note: The site is placed at Anafarta harbour on the Aegean side of the peninsula, which is uncertain. Its colonists are also said to have taken part in founding Ainos.

site: W side of the peninsula N of Eceabat (Eceabat, Çanakkale)
greek_from_text: Milesian colony of Archaic date; exact date unrecorded
pre_detail: Site unlocated; no evidence either way.
status_evidence: IACP (Thracian Chersonese); ATL (Limnaioi)
note: Strabo (7 fr.) calls it a Milesian foundation. The site is not identified; the Barrington Atlas places it approximately.

greek_from_text: Aeolian (Lesbian) colony, 7th c. BC
pre_greek_note: The Madytos mound excavations at Eceabat found Early, Middle and Late Bronze Age levels below the Greek town; no pre-Greek name is attested.
status_evidence: IACP (Thracian Chersonese); ATL 445/4-421/0; own bronze coins 4th c. BC (ΜΑΔΥ); bishopric (787 'Madyta or Koila'; Notitiae 10th-14th c.)
note: Ottoman Maydos continued the Greek name until 1928, when it was renamed Eceabat. Some sources add later Milesian/Klazomenian settlers.
sources: IACP (Thracian Chersonese); Pleiades 501503; Wikipedia: Madytus; TIB 12

site: Kilye bay N of Eceabat (Eceabat, Çanakkale)
greek_from_text: made a Roman municipium by Hadrian (coins: Aelium Coela); bishop 431
pre_detail: Site at Kilye bay not identified on the ground. The large Bronze Age mound of Maydos Kilisetepe lies in Eceabat itself, c. 3 km to the S, and belongs to Madytos, not Koila.
status_evidence: Roman provincial coins with Latin legends (Hadrian to 3rd c.); Hierocles (Europa); bishops 431, 458, 787
lang_later: Latin was the official language of the municipium (coins); Greek-speaking see by the 5th c.
note: It was a harbour of the Chersonese before it became a municipium. In 787 the see is called 'Madyta or Koila', and from the 10th c. it is listed as Madytos.
sources: Pleiades 501471; Wikipedia: Coela; TIB 12 (Külzer 2008); Le Quien, Oriens Christianus

greek_from_text: Aeolian (Lesbian) colony, 7th c. BC
pre_detail: Rejected the proposed 'yes'. The LBA claim comes from a Turkish surface survey (Körpe, AST 33, 2016), relayed by the LuwianSiteAtlas, which does not count as evidence. Surface sherds are not stratified, and the city's location is itself uncertain (Barrington: 'Yalıkabat?'; Akbaş castle per others). Homer's listing of Sestos among the Trojan allies (Il. 2.836), which Isaac 1986 and Der Kleine Pauly take as a 'Thracian' Sestos, is epic tradition and not enough on its own (rule 5). I found no excavation evidence of pre-colonial levels in non-Turkish literature.
pre_sources: en./de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sestos (citing Isaac 1986, 159-60; von Bredow, BNP; Danoff, KlP); Pleiades 501609 (BAtlas 51 G4, 'Yalikabat?'); Hom. Il. 2.835-6; Körpe 2016 not accessible (surface survey)
status_evidence: IACP (Thracian Chersonese); ATL; decree for Menas (OGIS 339, late 2nd c. BC); coins Hellenistic-Roman
note: It was the main crossing point of the Hellespont (Xerxes' bridge, siege of 479 BC). Justinian fortified it, but it was not a late Roman see.

greek_from_text: attested as a polis at the battle of 405 BC; own coins 4th c. BC
pre_detail: Site unlocated; no evidence either way.
status_evidence: IACP (Thracian Chersonese); Ps.-Skylax 67; own coins 4th c. BC (goat type)
note: It is known mainly for Lysander's victory of 405 BC. The town's site at the mouth of the 'Goat River' is not precisely located.

greek_from_text: Athenian foundation of Miltiades the Elder, c. 560-550 BC (Ps.-Scymnus)
pre_detail: Site unlocated; no evidence either way.
status_evidence: IACP (Thracian Chersonese); ATL
note: Ps.-Scymnus gives Miltiades as founder of Krithote and Paktye. The site is placed only approximately.

greek_from_text: first attested 200 BC, surrendering to Philip V with Madytos (Livy 31.16.5); bishop 431
pre_detail: No excavation of early levels at Gelibolu; Pleiades' 'founded by the Macedonians in the 5th c.' is unsourced, and no native predecessor is recorded.
status_evidence: Hierocles (Europa); bishops 431, 536, 787; Latin see from 1208; medieval Roman naval base
note: Pleiades says it was 'founded by the Macedonians in the 5th c. BC', a claim with no clear source. It is not in IACP. It was taken by the Ottomans in 1354, their first base in Europe.

site: c. 3 km S of Bolayır (Gelibolu, Çanakkale)
greek_from_text: Athenian foundation of Miltiades the Elder, c. 560-550 BC
pre_detail: Bektaş (2025) places Paktye at Maltepe Höyük near Bolayır. The 'höyük' name suggests a mound, but no pre-Greek levels have been published.
status_evidence: IACP pp. 907-908; ATL
note: It marked the Propontic end of Miltiades' wall across the isthmus from Kardia (Hdt. 6.36). Pliny says it was later merged into Lysimacheia.
sources: IACP pp. 907-908; Hdt. 6.36; Pleiades 501546; Wikipedia: Pactya

greek_from_text: Athenian colony under Miltiades the Elder, c. 561-556 BC
pre_detail: Bektaş (2025) identifies Agora with Bolayır, where surface pottery 'from the Bronze Age' onward is reported (jointly with Bakla Burnu), but there is no site-specific publication; earlier Pleiades placement only tentative.
pre_sources: Bektaş, Anadolu Araştırmaları 32 (2025); Koçel Erdem 2023 (Thrace through the Ages); Pleiades 501332
status_evidence: IACP p. 905; Hdt. 7.58; ATL (Chersonesitai); lion-type 'ΧΕΡ' coinage (4th c. BC) probably of the Chersonesite state
note: It may be the 'Chersonesos' of the sources; the site is only tentatively placed near Bolayır. A medieval Roman see 'Chersonesos' (Europa) may continue the name, but this is uncertain.
sources: IACP p. 905; Hdt. 7.58; Pleiades 501332; Wikipedia: Agora (Thrace)

site: head of the Gulf of Saros near Bolayır (Gelibolu, Çanakkale)
greek_from_text: Milesian-Klazomenian colony, probably 7th c. BC; Athenian settlers under Miltiades c. 560 BC
founder: Milesians and Klazomenians (oikist Hermochares, local tradition); later Athenians
pre_detail: Located by recent survey at Bakla Burnu. Surface pottery 'from the Bronze Age to the Byzantine period' is reported from Bakla Burnu and Bolayır together, without detail per site, so pre-Greek occupation at Kardia itself is not established.
pre_sources: Koçel Erdem 2023 (Thrace through the Ages, Archaeopress) citing Bektaş 2021; Bektaş, Anadolu Araştırmaları 32 (2025); Pleiades 501458
status_evidence: IACP (Thracian Chersonese); Hdt. 6.33, 6.36, 7.58; own coins 4th c. BC
note: It was the home of Eumenes and Hieronymus of Kardia. Lysimachus destroyed it c. 309 BC and moved its people to Lysimacheia. Pleiades 501458 combines Kardia and Lysimacheia, so the coordinates are approximate.

other_names: Hexamilion (medieval Roman fortress and see); Eksemil (Ottoman)
greek_from_text: founded by Lysimachus in 309 BC, with the people of Kardia and other Chersonesite towns
pre_detail: Previously 'no known'. Ancient sources present it as Lysimachus' new city of 309 BC, with Kardia's people moved in (Paus. 1.9.8; Diod. 20.29). Recent survey work (M. H. Sayar; Bektaş 2021) treats it as a synoecism of existing Kardia (Bakla Burnu), Agora (Bolayır) and Paktye, with the city at Bolayır. Surface pottery 'from the Bronze Age to the Byzantine period' is reported from the Bolayır (Lysimacheia) and Bakla Burnu (Kardia) settlements together, so the new-ground claim no longer holds. The Bronze Age material is not published in enough detail for a 'yes'.
pre_sources: Paus. 1.9.8; Diod. 20.29.1; Koçel Erdem in Erdem & Şahin (eds.), Thrace through the Ages (Archaeopress 2023) ch. 1, citing Bektaş 2021 (PhD, İstanbul Univ.); Bektaş, Anadolu Araştırmaları 32 (2025) 138-176
status_evidence: Diodorus 20.29; Lysimachus' capital; coins 3rd-2nd c. BC; refounded by Antiochus III 196 BC; see of Hexamilion (bishop 787)
note: The site was formerly placed at Hexamili; it is now placed near Bolayır, with most ruins at Ortaköy. The medieval Roman see 'Hexamilion' (787) is taken as its continuation (seed row 'Hexamilion' merged here).
sources: Diod. 20.29; Livy 33.38-41; Cohen 1995; Pleiades 501458; Wikipedia: Lysimachia (Thrace)
refoundations: Lysimacheia (Lysimachus 309 BC) → damaged 287 BC → destroyed by Thracians c. 198/7 BC → restored by Antiochus III 196 BC → Justinianic fortress Hexamilion (6th c.)

greek_from_text: town attested from the Hellenistic period; city status as a Flavian colonia (Flaviopolis), 1st c. AD; city in Hierocles
pre_detail: Site unlocated; no evidence either way.
status_evidence: Hierocles (Europa); Barrington 'Aphrodisias/Col. Flaviopolis'
lang_later: Latin colonists in the 1st-3rd c. AD; Greek by late antiquity
note: Equating the Flavian colony with Aphrodisias follows the Barrington Atlas; the site is unlocated.
sources: Pleiades 501352; Jones 1971, 17; RE Aphrodisias 4; Wikipedia: Aphrodisias (Thrace)

other_names: Poltyobria / Poltymbria (earlier Thracian name, Strabo); Apsinthos (?)
greek_from_text: Aeolian colony, 7th c. BC (from Mytilene and Kyme; Alopekonnesians also named)
pre_greek_note: Strabo (7 fr.) gives the earlier name Poltyobria, a Thracian name preserved only in Greek, so it is not entered as a pre-Greek name. The Apsinthian Thracians held the region.
status_evidence: IACP (Ainos); Hdt. 7.58; abundant Classical coinage; Hierocles (Rhodope); bishops 451, 553; autocephalous archbishopric; Gattilusi lordship 1384-1456
note: It lies on the E (Turkish) bank of the Hebrus mouth. The Ottomans took it in 1456.
sources: IACP (Ainos); Hdt. 7.58; Pleiades 501337; TIB 6 (Soustal 1991); Wikipedia: Aenus

greek_from_text: Thracian town with its own coinage with Greek legend (ΚΥΨΕ), c. 400 BC
pre_greek_note: A Thracian town before it issued Greek coins; no native-script name exists.
status_evidence: IACP (cited, Thrace); own coins 5th-4th c. BC; Livy (Macedonian/Seleucid campaigns); Via Egnatia station; bishops 553, 787 (Rhodope)
lang_later: Thracian was probably still widely spoken until the Roman period (uncertain)
note: The name has the form of the Greek word κυψέλη ('beehive'), possibly a reinterpretation of a Thracian name. It is unclear when it became a polis; the coinage is the earliest evidence.

greek_from_text: bishopric attested by 1170 (later Peristasis and Myriophyton)
pre_detail: Identification with Tyrodiza (Hdt. 7.25) via Pleiades; no excavation at Şarköy and no native predecessor recorded.
status_evidence: medieval Roman bishopric by 1170 (suffragan of Herakleia)
note: Pleiades equates Roman Tiristasis with Herodotus' Tyrodiza, a dependent town of Perinthos. Whether Classical Tyrodiza had polis status (IACP) is unverified.

greek_from_text: as Serreion Teichos, a tribute-paying Greek community 428/7-418/7 BC (ATL); Ganos a fort by the 4th c. BC; city in Hierocles
founder: unknown Greek settlers (legend: companions of Byzas)
pre_detail: Ganos was a stronghold of the Odrysian kings in the 4th c. BC (Aeschin. 2.90, 3.82) and one of the coastal places Seuthes offered Xenophon (Anab. 7.5.8), but nothing shows a native settlement before the Greek community. The Ganos survey (Işıklar Dağı) has published Classical and later pottery and an Iron Age-to-Roman cult place, with no pre-Greek settlement levels.
pre_sources: Aeschin. 2.90, 3.82; Xen. Anab. 7.5.8; Şahin and Bülbül in Thrace through the Ages (Archaeopress 2023); Pleiades 511415
status_evidence: IACP p. 922 (Serreion Teichos); ATL; Hierocles 633.1 (Gannos); bishopric, archbishopric 1324, metropolis 1329
note: Equating Serreion Teichos with Ganos follows Pleiades and the Barrington Atlas. Mount Ganos was a major medieval Roman monastic and wine centre. The mother city is unrecorded.
sources: IACP p. 922; ATL I 545-46; Pleiades 511415; Wikipedia: Ganos; TIB 12

greek_from_text: city in Hierocles (c. 527); earlier a fortified place of Alcibiades (c. 405 BC)
pre_detail: Site unlocated; no evidence either way.
status_evidence: Hierocles 632.6 (Europa); Nepos, Alc. 7.4
note: C. Foss (Barrington Atlas) places it tentatively S of İnecik.

other_names: Aproi; Colonia Claudia Aprensis; Theodosiopolis (Theodosius I or II); Naples (Frankish)
greek_from_text: Roman colony founded by Claudius (Colonia Claudia Aprensis), c. AD 46-54
pre_detail: Apros existed before the Claudian veteran colony: Theopompus (4th c. BC, cited by Steph. Byz.) names it, and the name is Thracian. The colony (Colonia Claudia Aprensis) took the name of this inland Thracian town. This is a refoundation of a native town on textual grounds; no pre-Roman levels have been reported at Kermeyan.
pre_sources: Steph. Byz. s.v. Ἄπρος (Theopompus); Plin. NH 4.47; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aproi; Pleiades 511153
status_evidence: Pliny NH 4.47 (colonia); Ptolemy; Hierocles (Europa); bishops 431 (council list), 458, 536, 787, 878; archbishopric by 640, metropolis 1179
lang_later: Latin-speaking veteran colony at first; Greek-speaking by late antiquity
note: The site at Kermeyan follows the Barrington Atlas/Pleiades; the council seed placed it at Malkara. The Bulgarians destroyed it in 1205.
sources: Pleiades 511153; Pliny NH 4.47; Catholic Encyclopedia: Theodosiopolis; TIB 12
refoundations: Apros → Colonia Claudia Aprensis (Claudius) → Theodosiopolis (late 4th/5th c.)

greek_from_text: walls restored 383-403 and renamed Theodosiopolis; city in Hierocles; bishop 536
pre_detail: At Barbaros, surveys found Classical (5th c. BC) black-glaze pottery and 4th c. BC Greek inscriptions; no pre-Greek levels reported.
status_evidence: Hierocles (Europa); bishops 536, 680, 787, 14th c.
note: Pleiades records a Classical settlement 'Paniai', whose status is unknown. Some Turkish scholars place Bisanthe at Barbaros instead. Home of the historian Priscus of Panium.
sources: Pleiades 511351; Wikipedia: Panion; Jones 1971, 381 n. 37; TIB 12

other_names: Rhaidestos / Rhaedestus (from Roman times); Rodosto / Rodoscuk (Ottoman)
greek_from_text: Samian colony, Archaic (c. 600 BC; the Samian Propontic colonies date from c. 600)
pre_detail: TDV İslâm Ansiklopedisi suggests that Thracians (Bistones) first settled the site and that the name Bisanthe is Thracian, but this is inference; no pre-Greek levels have been reported at Tekirdağ (finds there are 4th c. BC Thracian gravestones).
status_evidence: IACP (Propontic Thrace); Hdt. 7.137; Xen. Anab. 7 (offered by Seuthes); ATL; bishopric Rhaidestos (787), later metropolis
note: Equating Bisanthe with Rhaidestos (Tekirdağ) follows Pleiades/Barrington; some Turkish scholars put Bisanthe at Barbaros. The Ottoman name Rodosto continues Rhaidestos; Tekirdağ is a separate Turkish name.

site: coast E of Tekirdağ (Süleymanpaşa, Tekirdağ), exact site unknown
greek_from_text: Samian colony c. 600 BC
pre_detail: Rejected the proposed 'yes'. The only source is the Turkish excavator's own summary (N. Atik, Arkeoloji ve Sanat 152, 2016). It calls Karaevlialtı a 'Thracian settlement mound' whose 'earliest finds were terracotta pieces dating back to 3000 BC', but the earliest architecture is 6th c. BC, and it reports no stratified pre-colonial level. Menekşe Çatağı is only 'nearby' (rule 8), and kureansiklopedi does not count. No non-Turkish corroboration found; the IACP and Barrington give no prehistoric data, and Barrington places Heraion at 'Aytepe'. This could become 'yes' if the KST reports show a stratified EBA level under the acropolis.
pre_sources: Atik 2016, record and abstract at acikerisim.nku.edu.tr/xmlui/handle/20.500.11776/6787; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heraion_Teichos (IACP p. 918; Hdt. 4.90); Pleiades 511271
status_evidence: IACP p. 918; besieged by Philip II 352 BC (Dem. 3.4)
note: It lay a little E of Bisanthe; the site is not identified (Wikipedia gives c. 41.02 N 27.74 E).
sources: IACP p. 918; Suda / Harpokration s.v.; Pleiades 511271; Wikipedia: Heraion Teichos

other_names: Herakleia / Heraclea (Thraciae), from the 3rd c. AD
greek_from_text: Samian colony, 602/1 BC (Eusebius/Jerome)
pre_detail: Rejected the proposed 'yes'. The Bronze Age claim rests only on press reports (Milliyet 2022; turkisharchaeonews/Hürriyet Nov. 2021: 'ceramics, spoon pieces, cooking utensils and animal bones believed to be 5,000 years old'). These announce unpublished finds from the Koçel Erdem excavations, with no stratigraphy or exact findspot (rule 4). The early name 'Mygdonia' comes only from Tzetzes, a late source and not a good one (rule 6). The standard works (Sayar 1998; Schönert-Geiß 1965; BNP) report no pre-Samian levels.
pre_sources: turkisharchaeonews.net/node/1042; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perinthus (Sayar 1998, 2021; von Bredow BNP); Pleiades 511357
status_evidence: IACP (Propontic Thrace); ATL; coins; Roman neokoros city and capital of Thracia; Hierocles (Europa; metropolis); bishops from 325
note: Turkish Ereğli comes from Herakleia, not Perinthos. Philip II besieged it in 340 BC.
refoundations: Perinthos → Herakleia (3rd c. AD), metropolis of Europa

other_names: Daunion Teichos; Daunium; possibly medieval Roman see Daonion
greek_from_text: tribute-paying Greek community 454/3-418/7 BC (ATL)
pre_detail: Site unlocated (near Gümüşyaka?); no evidence either way.
status_evidence: IACP p. 918; ATL 454/3-418/7; Ps.-Skylax (between Perinthos and Selymbria)
note: The mother city is unrecorded (probably Samian/Perinthian sphere). The medieval Roman see Daonion (suffragan of Herakleia) may be the same place, which is unverified.
sources: IACP p. 918; ATL; Pleiades 511227; Wikipedia: Daminon Teichos

greek_from_text: Megarian colony, founded before Byzantium (Ps.-Scymnus), i.e. before c. 667-659 BC
pre_greek_note: The name is Thracian, 'town of Selys' (-bria = town, Strabo 7.6.1), which implies a Thracian place; it is known only through Greek, so not entered as a pre-Greek name.
status_evidence: IACP (Propontic Thrace); ATL; coins; Hierocles (Europa, as Eudoxiopolis); bishops 451, 680-81; archbishopric; surrendered to the Ottomans 1453
note: Silivri continues the Thracian name Selymbria.
refoundations: Selymbria → Eudoxiopolis (Arcadius, c. 400; old name persisted)

greek_from_text: see of Athyra in the medieval Roman Notitiae (c. 10th c.); a settlement since the Hellenistic period
pre_detail: Athyras is attested in Hellenistic-Roman sources; no pre-Greek levels are reported at Büyükçekmece.
status_evidence: medieval Roman bishopric (suffragan of Herakleia), Catholic titular see Athyra
note: The date of the first bishop is not verified; the date given is the earliest Notitia listing I could confirm.
sources: Pleiades 511172; TIB 12 (Külzer 2008); Le Quien, Oriens Christianus

other_names: Constantinople / Κωνσταντινούπολις, Nova Roma (Constantine 330); Antonina / Augusta Antonina (Septimius Severus, briefly); hē Polis
greek_from_text: Megarian colony, c. 668-659 BC (Hdt. 4.144: 17 years after Chalcedon; Eusebius 659/8); Greek pottery from the 7th c. BC
pre_greek_note: Pliny (NH 4.46) says the place was earlier called Lygos, a Thracian name known only from Latin, so not entered as a pre-Greek name. Neolithic-Chalcolithic remains exist within the later city (Yenikapı).
status_evidence: IACP (Propontic Thrace); ATL; coins from late 5th c. BC; Roman provincial coins; imperial capital 330-1453; patriarchate (councils 381, 553, 680-81)
note: One entry for Byzantium and Constantinople (refoundation 330). Turkish İstanbul comes from Greek εἰς τὴν Πόλιν. The Ottomans took it in 1453. Justinian's 'city' of Sykai/Ioustinianai (later Galata) is treated as part of it.
refoundations: Byzantion → Antonina (Septimius Severus, briefly) → Constantinopolis / Nova Roma (Constantine I, 324-330)

greek_from_text: first bishop at Nicaea II (787)
pre_detail: Identification with Çatalca rests on the council seed; no excavation and no native predecessor recorded.
status_evidence: bishop 787; suffragan of Herakleia (still listed in modern times)
note: Identification with Çatalca is the modern view given in the council seed.
sources: Council seed (Nicaea 787); TIB 12 (Külzer 2008); Catholic Encyclopedia: Heraclea

greek_from_text: first bishop at Nicaea II (787); later archbishopric/metropolis
pre_detail: In antiquity a village (Delkos) in Byzantion's territory by the lagoon; no earlier settlement reported at Durusu.
status_evidence: bishop 787; later archbishopric and metropolis of Derkos
note: It was a Roman station (Delkos); Durusu was called Terkos until the 20th c. The council seed point lies c. 9 km from Durusu; the Pleiades point is used here.

greek_from_text: walls built under Justinian; archbishopric (later metropolis) in the Notitiae from c. 900
pre_greek_note: Salmydessos was a coast and town of the Thracian Thynoi (Hdt. 4.93; Xen. Anab. 7.5); no native-script name.
status_evidence: medieval Roman archbishopric, later metropolis; Catholic titular see Medea; Justinianic fortifications
note: The medieval Roman name Medeia continues in Midye. The date of the first see is not exactly verified. It submitted to the Ottomans in 1453.

greek_from_text: civic coins with Greek legends from the 2nd c. AD (Hadrian to Philip); earlier the seat of the Thracian (Astaean) kings, 1st c. BC-AD 46
pre_greek_note: Thracian royal residence (Pliny: 'arx regum Thraciae'); Thracian royal tumuli at Vize; the name is Thracian but has no native-script attestation.
status_evidence: Roman provincial coins; Hierocles (Europa); bishops 431-787; autocephalous archbishopric; Hagia Sophia church
note: The Thracian kings used Greek in their inscriptions before AD 46. The start date of the coinage (Trajan or Hadrian) is approximate.

greek_from_text: archbishop John at Nicaea II (787)
pre_detail: Turkish sources date the town to Theodosius II; the castle is early Byzantine and no Thracian or earlier settlement is reported at Pınarhisar.
status_evidence: bishops 787, 879, 1027, 1315-31; archbishopric in Notitia of Leo VI
note: Turkish Pınar ('spring') translates Greek βρύσις. Turkish sources say it was founded under Theodosius II, which is unverified. The Ottomans took it in 1368.
sources: Wikipedia: Pınarhisar; TIB 12 (Külzer 2008); Le Quien, Oriens Christianus

greek_from_text: Roman station (Tzirallum, 313); fortified by Justinian; first bishop at Nicaea II (787)
pre_greek_note: The name is probably Thracian (Tzirallum/Syrallum), known only from Latin and Greek sources.
status_evidence: bishop 787; later metropolis; major medieval Roman fortress town (Pecheneg siege 1090)
note: The Thracian origin of the name is likely but unproven. The Ottomans took it in the 1350s/60s under Murad I.

greek_from_text: Thracian-named town (Ptolemy, itineraries); first bishop attested 553
pre_greek_note: Thracian name (-para 'village'), known only from Greek and Latin sources.
status_evidence: bishops 553, 787; later autocephalous archbishopric (as Mesene); shrine of St Alexander
note: The see may date from the 4th c., but 553 is the first certain bishop. The Avars sacked it in 591. Misinli continues the medieval name Mesene.

greek_from_text: first bishop at Nicaea II (787)
pre_detail: Nothing is known of an ancient predecessor at Hayrabolu; the district has Thracian dolmens and tumuli, but no settlement under the town is reported.
status_evidence: bishops 787-1351 (suffragan of Herakleia)
note: Nothing is known of an ancient predecessor. It was sacked by the Pechenegs in 1087.

greek_from_text: Thracian Bergule raised to city status and renamed for Arcadius by Theodosius I (or Arcadius), c. 390s
pre_greek_note: Bergule, a town of the Thracian Astai (Ptolemy, itineraries); the name has no native-script attestation.
status_evidence: Hierocles (Europa); bishops 553, 787; archbishopric
note: It was briefly the capital of Europa. The medieval Romans defeated the Rus' here in 970.

greek_from_text: bishop at Nicaea II (787) per council list; earlier the Thracian-named station Bourtoudizos, fortified by Justinian
pre_greek_note: Roman station Burtudizon/Bourdizos with a Thracian name; no native-script attestation.
status_evidence: bishop 787 (council seed); see in the Notitiae; Catholic titular see Bulgarophygum
note: The council seed records a bishop in 787; the name Bulgarophygon is otherwise first known from the battle of 896.

other_names: Adrianople; Uskudama / Uscudama (earlier Thracian town); Orestias (learned medieval Roman name)
greek_from_text: founded by Hadrian c. AD 124/125 on the site of Thracian Uskudama
pre_greek_note: Uskudama/Uscudama, a town of the Bessi or Odrysae (Ammianus, Eutropius); known only from Latin, so not entered as a pre-Greek name.
status_evidence: Roman provincial coins (Greek legends); Hierocles (Haemimontus, metropolis); bishops 553, 787; medieval Roman metropolis
note: Scene of the Gothic victory of 378. Taken by the Ottomans c. 1369 (dates 1361-1371 are debated) and their capital until 1453.

greek_from_text: Megarian colony, 685/4 BC (Eusebius); 17 years before Byzantium (Hdt. 4.144)
pre_detail: Excavations in Kadıköy (Haydarpaşa, Altıyol) go back only to Classical/Hellenistic levels, and no pre-Greek level is reported on the city site. The Neolithic-Chalcolithic Fikirtepe mound lies c. 2 km east, across the Kurbağalıdere. There is no positive evidence of new ground either, so the 'no known' value is changed.
pre_sources: Hürriyet Daily News 145537 & 152786; Habertürk 2509981 (Haydarpaşa); en.wikipedia Fikirtepe; Hdt. 4.144
status_evidence: IACP (Chalkedon); ATL; coins Classical-Roman; Hierocles (Bithynia); metropolitan see; Council of Chalcedon 451
note: The Neolithic Fikirtepe mound lies c. 2 km away in Kadıköy but not on the city site. The Ottomans took it in the mid-14th c. (Orhan).

other_names: Brylleion? (earlier or neighbouring town, Pliny); Apameia (Prusias I, after Queen Apama, c. 202 BC); Colonia Iulia Concordia Apamea (Caesar or Augustus)
site: Mudanya (Bursa); ruins at and just south of the town
greek_from_text: Colophonian colony (Pliny NH 5.143; Steph. Byz.); foundation date unknown (probably Archaic); attested as a Greek city by the Classical period
pre_detail: Not excavated. Barrington gives the Classical name Brylleion for the same site, but its origin (Greek or native) is unknown; the eponym Myrlos is legendary.
pre_sources: Pleiades 511194; RE s.v. Bryllion; Plin. NH 5.143
status_evidence: Coins (Myrleia; Apameia Myrleanon; C.I.C.A. colonial issues); Hierocles; bishops 431, 451, 787; later autocephalous archbishopric
note: Given by Philip V to Prusias I (202 BC) and renamed Apameia; Roman colony under Caesar or Augustus. Turkish Mudanya continues medieval Roman Moudania, not Myrleia/Apamea.
sources: Pliny NH 5.143; Pleiades 511194; IK 32 (Apameia); Wikipedia: Apamea Myrlea
refoundations: Myrleia → Apameia (Prusias I, c. 202 BC) → Colonia Iulia Concordia Apamea (Caesar/Augustus)

other_names: Cius; Prusias pros thalassei (Prusias I, 202 BC); Kios again under Claudius, Prusias again Flavian (coins, Sommer)
greek_from_text: Milesian colony (Pliny NH 5.144); founded as an emporion at the end of the 7th c. BC (pottery from rescue excavations)
pre_detail: Rescue excavations give nothing before the late 7th-c. BC emporion. A tradition attributed to Aristotle's Constitution of the Kianoi (schol. Ap. Rhod. 1.1177) says Mysians, then Carians, lived there before the Milesians. This is a succession legend, not counted alone.
pre_sources: Plin. NH 5.144; knowledge: Arist. fr. 514 Rose ap. schol. Ap. Rhod. 1.1177; en.wikipedia Cius
status_evidence: IACP (Propontic coast); Athenian tribute lists; Classical silver coins; Hellenistic & Roman coins; Hierocles; bishops 325–787; later archbishopric
note: Razed by Philip V (202 BC) and refounded by Prusias I as Prusias ad Mare. Gemlik is thought to derive from Turkish gemi ('ship'), not from Kios.
sources: IACP (Avram); IK 29 (Kios, Corsten 1985); Pleiades 511385; Wikipedia: Cius
refoundations: Kios → Prusias ad Mare (Prusias I, 202 BC) → Kios (Claudius) → Prusias (Flavian) → medieval Roman Kios

site: Armutlu peninsula, perhaps near Arnaköy (Armutlu, Yalova)
greek_from_text: city of Bithynia in Hierocles (c. 527); later a see under Nicomedia
pre_detail: Unlocated.
status_evidence: Hierocles; Notitiae (suffragan of Nicomedia); titular see
note: Location unknown; the Catholic titular-see register (GCatholic) places it at Arnaköy on the Armutlu peninsula. Date and founder of the 'Neo-Caesarea' are not documented, so founder_group is a guess from the name.
sources: Hierocles 691; GCatholic: Neocaesarea in Bithynia; TIB 13 (Belke 2020)

other_names: Drepanon/Drepana (earlier village); Kibotos/Civetot fort nearby (Alexios I)
greek_from_text: village Drepanon raised to city and renamed Helenopolis by Constantine, c. 327 (in honour of his mother Helena)
pre_detail: The earlier village Drepanon has a Greek name. Surface work and underwater survey at Hersek report nothing before the Roman period.
pre_sources: Pleiades 511240; Hürriyet Daily News 188429 (georadar 2023-24); en.wikipedia Hersek Headland
status_evidence: Socrates HE 1.17; Procopius Aed. 5.2 (Justinian's works); Hierocles; bishops 553–879; Notitiae to 12th–13th c.
note: Earlier village Drepanon, traditionally Helena's birthplace. Justinian added an aqueduct and baths; the town stayed small.
sources: Socrates HE 1.17; Procopius Aed. 5.2; Pleiades 511240; Wikipedia: Helenopolis (Bithynia)

greek_from_text: city in Hierocles (c. 527); mentioned c. 400 (Palladius, Socrates); bishops 553–787
founder: unknown (Phoenician foundation per Steph. Byz., legendary)
pre_detail: Stephanus' Phoenician foundation is legendary; no archaeology at Karamürsel.
status_evidence: Hierocles; bishops 553, 680–81, 787; Notitiae
note: Late-attested coastal town on the south shore of the Gulf of Nicomedia; date of city status unknown.

greek_from_text: Megarian colony founded 712/11 BC (Memnon: Ol. 17.1); Athenian colonists added 435/4 BC (Diodorus 12.34)
pre_detail: The site is unlocated and unexcavated. Its eponym (Astakos son of Poseidon and the nymph Olbia) is mythical.
status_evidence: IACP (Propontic coast); Athenian tribute lists; Classical coins
note: Destroyed by Lysimachus (c. 301 BC); its people were moved to the new Nicomedia (264 BC). Exact site unlocated; placed near Başiskele at the head of the gulf.
sources: Memnon FGrH 434 F 12; Strabo 12.4.2; Diodorus 12.34.5; Pleiades 511169; Wikipedia: Astacus (Bithynia)
refoundations: succeeded by Nicomedia (264 BC) on a nearby site

other_names: Nikomedeia; medieval Roman Nikomedeia; Ottoman İznikmid/İzmid, Kocaeli
greek_from_text: founded by Nicomedes I in 264 BC as the new royal capital, opposite the destroyed Astakos
pre_detail: A new royal capital founded by Nicomedes I (264 BC) 'opposite' the destroyed Megarian Astakos, with Astakos' people moved in. No native settlement is known at İzmit, and the Çukurbağ excavations report Roman levels. (Pausanias 5.12.7 equates it with Astakos, which would be Greek occupation in any case.)
pre_sources: Memnon FGrH 434 F 12.1; Strabo 12.4.2; Paus. 5.12.7; Journal of Urban Archaeology (Brepols), Çukurbağ excavations
status_evidence: royal capital; Hellenistic & Roman coins; metropolis of Bithynia; Diocletian's capital; Hierocles; bishops 325–787
note: Synoecism of the people of Astakos (Megarian colony, 712/11 BC), which is listed separately. Ottoman conquest 1337.
sources: Memnon FGrH 434 F 12; Strabo 12.4.2; Pleiades 511337; Wikipedia: Nicomedia

greek_from_text: island fortress-town made a bishopric in the 9th c.: bishop Leo at the council of 869, Antonius 879; see in the Notitia of Leo VI (c. 901–907)
pre_detail: Earlier occupation of the island was Greek (Thynias/Apollonia, Heraclea's dependency). The island's name evokes the Thracian Thynoi, but no Thracian settlement is attested there.
status_evidence: bishops 869, 879; Notitiae from Leo VI; titular see
note: Ancient Thynias/Apollonia was a dependency of Heraclea, not a polis. Counted only by the medieval-see rule; the settlement stayed small (fortress besieged by the Latins in 1261).

greek_from_text: civic bronze coins inscribed ΔΙΑΣ, of the Mithradatic series (c. 95–70 BC)
pre_detail: No archaeological or textual evidence for a pre-Greek settlement at Akçakoca has been reported.
status_evidence: coins (ΔΙΑΣ, Mithradates VI era); Pliny; Ptolemy (Diospolis); Marcian of Heraclea
note: Port 60 stadia east of the Hypios mouth. City status rests on the small coinage; not in Hierocles.
sources: Marcian, Peripl. 2.8; Ptol. 5.1.3; TIB 9 (Belke 1996); Pleiades 844907; Wikipedia: Dia (Bithynia)

site: Tahtalı/Çalı area (Nilüfer, Bursa); alt. Kapanca harbour (Şahin 2011)
greek_from_text: town Helge renamed Kaisareia Germanike in honour of Germanicus; coins with Germanicus' portrait (Tiberian/Caligulan)
pre_detail: Pliny (NH 5.143) names the earlier town Helge alias Booskoite, so a settlement preceded the renaming. Its ethnicity is unknown (Booskoite is Greek) and the site is disputed.
status_evidence: Roman provincial coins (RPC city 49); Hierocles (Kaisareia); bishops 325–879
note: Pliny NH 5.143 calls the earlier town Helge alias Booskoite; its people's language is unknown. Site disputed between Tahtalı/Çalı west of Bursa and a coastal harbour at Kapanca.
sources: Pliny NH 5.143; RPC I 2017; Pleiades 511267; Şahin, Olba 19 (2011); Wikipedia: Germanicopolis (Bithynia)

other_names: Prusa ad Olympum; medieval Roman Prousa
greek_from_text: founded by Prusias I, traditionally with Hannibal's advice (Pliny NH 5.148), i.e. c. 186–183 BC
pre_detail: Downgraded from 'yes'. The Classical plates and bowls from the Tophane rescue excavations (Şahin & Gülsefa 2017, a Turkish academic ceramic study I could not re-read) show pottery of pre-Prusias date on the citadel. No stratified pre-186 BC occupation level is documented, and calling it a native settlement is an inference. Strabo 12.4.3 ('Prusias who fought Croesus') is a recognised garble, not a reliable report of a pre-Hellenistic town, and Pliny NH 5.148 gives Prusias I and Hannibal as founders. This is a real lead, but it falls short under rule 3.
pre_sources: Strabo 12.4.3; Pliny NH 5.148; Şahin & Gülsefa, Uludağ Üniv. FEF Sos. Bil. Derg. 18/32 (2017) 77–104 (first-pass ref, not accessible here); Pleiades 511384 (not retrievable)
status_evidence: Roman provincial coins; Dio Chrysostom; Hierocles; bishops 325–787; later metropolis
note: Strabo 12.4.3 confuses the founder; a minority attributes the foundation to Prusias II. Ottoman capital after the conquest of 1326.
sources: Pliny NH 5.148; Strabo 12.4.3; IK 39–40 (Prusa); Pleiades 511384; Wikipedia: Prusa (Bithynia)

other_names: Ankore/Helikore (earlier settlement, Steph. Byz.); Antigoneia (Antigonus I, c. 315 BC); Nikaia (Lysimachus, c. 301 BC)
greek_from_text: founded as Antigoneia by Antigonus I c. 315 BC (after Eumenes' defeat); renamed Nicaea by Lysimachus c. 301 BC
founder: Antigonus I Monophthalmus; refounded/renamed by Lysimachus
pre_detail: Antigonus' Antigoneia replaced an earlier Ankore/Helikore. The tradition calls it a Bottiaean (i.e. Greek-type) colony destroyed by Mysians. No pre-Greek name or prehistoric level is known at İznik.
pre_sources: Steph. Byz. s.v. Nikaia; Pleiades 511268 (Helikore); en.wikipedia Nicaea
pre_greek_note: Steph. Byz. records an earlier settlement Ankore/Helikore, said to be a Bottiaean colony destroyed by the Mysians; no native-script name attested.
status_evidence: Hellenistic & Roman coins; rival metropolis of Bithynia; Hierocles; bishops 325–787 (councils of 325 and 787); capital of the Empire of Nicaea 1204–1261
note: Ottoman conquest 1331.
sources: Steph. Byz. s.v. Νίκαια; Strabo 12.4.7; IK 9–10 (Nikaia, Şahin); Pleiades 511268; Cohen 1995

site: near Yalakdere (Kocaeli); alt. Pazarköy (Orhangazi, Bursa) per Ramsay
greek_from_text: district (regio) of Nicaea raised to city rank under, or shortly before, Julian and named after his mother Basilina (c. 361–363)
founder: Julian (or Constantius II), named after Basilina
pre_detail: Unlocated (Yalakdere vs Pazarköy).
status_evidence: Council of Chalcedon 451 (dispute Nicaea/Nicomedia); Hierocles; bishops c. 400–879
note: Site not securely located; Pleiades/modern view near Yalakdere, Ramsay on the west shore of Lake Askania.
sources: ACO II (Chalcedon, session 13); Hierocles 691; Pleiades 511180; Wikipedia: Basilinopolis

greek_from_text: see under Nicaea: bishop Anastasius at the Council in Trullo (692); Leo 787; two bishops 879
pre_detail: Unlocated; known only from church lists.
status_evidence: bishops 692, 787, 879; Notitiae (suffragan of Nicaea) to the 12th–13th c.
note: Known only from church lists. The identification with Bilecik (Catholic Encyclopedia) is old and unproven; coordinates are a regional placeholder.
sources: Le Quien, Oriens Christianus I 657; Catholic Encyclopedia: Linoe; TIB 13 (Belke 2020)

other_names: Justinianopolis Nova (Justinian); Malagina/Melangeia (medieval Roman); Modrene? (equated in 12th-c. Notitiae)
site: Metabole castle above Paşalar (Pamukova, Sakarya); alt. Günüören (Osmaneli, Bilecik)
greek_from_text: refounded by Justinian as Justinianopolis Nova; bishop Macedonius at the council of 553; Theodorus of 'Justinianopolis Nova or Mela' 680
pre_detail: The location (Metabole/Paşalar vs Günüören) is uncertain and unexcavated.
status_evidence: bishops 553, 680, 787, 869, 879; Malagina archbishopric, later metropolis (13th c.); aplekton and imperial stud
note: Mela is identified with the army base Malagina by Pétridès and others (not certain). The seed's unnamed council row (553; 680–81; 787) fits this see. Ottoman conquest 1306.
sources: Foss, AnatSt 40 (1990); Ramsay, HGAM; Wikipedia: Mela (Bithynia); Wikipedia: Malagina; TIB 13 (Belke 2020)

greek_from_text: see under Nicaea in the Ecthesis of Ps.-Epiphanius (c. 640); bishop Isidore at the Council in Trullo (692)
pre_detail: Unlocated; known only from bishop lists.
status_evidence: Ps.-Epiphanius (c. 640); bishop 692; later Notitiae
lang_later: possibly settled by Slavs (Serbs) in the 7th c., if the name reflects that; no Slavic bishops' names
note: Site unknown; the coordinates are only a placeholder in the lower Sangarius region, and the province is unknown. The Serb-origin theory conflicts with the c. 640 date.

other_names: Modrene (medieval Roman see and district); Modrina
greek_from_text: Modra a town at the source of the Gallos (Strabo 12.3.7); attested as a see under Nicaea only in the Notitiae, securely in the 12th c. ('Modrene, that is Mela')
pre_greek_note: Modra is a non-Greek (probably Phrygian/Bithynian) name known only from Greek sources.
status_evidence: Notitiae (Modrene, suffragan of Nicaea); titular see Modra
note: May be the same see as Mela (12th-c. Notitiae: 'Modrene, that is Mela'), which would make it a double count; the Annuario Pontificio treats them as separate. The see may be older than the 12th c.
sources: Strabo 12.3.7; Pleiades 845022; Wikipedia: Modra (Bithynia); Wikipedia: Mela (Bithynia)

other_names: Kieros (earlier town, Heracleote possession); Ottoman Üskübü
greek_from_text: Kieros taken from Heraclea by Prusias I and refounded as Prusias, c. 190–185 BC (Memnon)
pre_greek_note: Kieros/Kios (named after its river) is known only from Greek sources (Memnon, Photius).
status_evidence: Roman provincial coins; Greek civic inscriptions (IK 27); Hierocles; bishops 325–879
note: Kieros belonged to Heraclea Pontica before its capture; whether it was then a polis is unclear. Prusias' date is approximate.
sources: Memnon FGrH 434 F 19; IK 27 (Prusias ad Hypium, Ameling 1985); Pleiades 845049; Wikipedia: Prusias ad Hypium; TIB 9 (Belke 1996)

other_names: Claudiopolis (Claudius); Hadriana (Hadrian); medieval Roman Klaudioupolis, Boli
greek_from_text: Bithynian town that was a city of the Roman province by Pompey's organisation (64/63 BC) at the latest; Strabo 12.4.7 gives it the Salon district; claimed Mantinean (Arcadian) origin (Paus. 8.9.7)
pre_greek_note: Name 'town of the Bithynians' (Thracian-speaking Bithynoi); no native-script form attested.
status_evidence: Roman provincial coins (Claudiopolis, Hadriana); Pliny Ep. 10.39; Hierocles (metropolis of Honorias); bishops 431–787
note: Birthplace of Antinous. The city's start date is approximate: the Mantinean link is a later kinship claim, and no pre-Roman coinage is known. Bolu comes from (Klaudiou)polis.
sources: Strabo 12.4.7; Paus. 8.9.7; IK 31 (Klaudiupolis, Becker-Bertau 1986); Pleiades 844879; TIB 9 (Belke 1996)

greek_from_text: raised to city status as Flaviopolis, probably under Vespasian (69–79); imperial coins from Antoninus Pius to Gallienus
pre_detail: No pre-Hellenistic material is reported at Gerede. The recent study of Krateia and Keçi Kalesi gives the Hellenistic (Bithynian) period as the earliest and notes Hıdırlık Tepesi as the probable acropolis, which is undated.
status_evidence: Roman provincial coins (Antoninus Pius–Gallienus); Greek civic inscriptions; Hierocles; bishops 431–787
note: A small autonomous coin with ΚΡΗ is attributed to it, which would suggest earlier civic status. The origin of the name Krateia (Greek or native) is unclear.
sources: TIB 9 (Belke 1996, Paphlagonien und Honorias); Pleiades 844991; Wikipedia: Cratia (Bithynia)

other_names: Herakleia en Pontoi; Pontoherakleia (medieval Roman); Penderaklia (medieval Italian)
greek_from_text: c. 560 BC (Ps.-Scymnus: founded 'when Cyrus took Media', i.e. c. 560/554 BC) by Megarians and Boeotians of Tanagra; no earlier Greek material known
pre_detail: Founded in Mariandynian territory and the Mariandynoi were reduced to dependants, but no native settlement on the site is attested archaeologically or textually. The Lykos/Herakles stories are myth, and it is even unclear whether the Roman city overlies the colony.
pre_greek_note: Built in the land of the Mariandynoi, who were reduced to dependent status; no pre-Greek settlement known at the site itself.
status_evidence: IACP (Pontos); coins from 5th c. BC; tyrants and Hellenistic decrees; Hierocles; bishops 431–787; medieval Roman metropolis
note: The Mariandynoi became dependent labourers. Herakleia founded Kallatis and Chersonesos (outside Turkey).
sources: IACP (Pontos), Herakleia; Burstein 1976, Outpost of Hellenism; Ps.-Scymnus; Pleiades 844944; Wikipedia: Heraclea Pontica

greek_from_text: Aeolian polis; tradition of settlement by Penthilos' Aeolians after the Trojan War (Strabo); excavated Iron Age (Archaic) necropolis from c. 7th c. BC
pre_greek_note: Early Bronze Age (EBA II, c. 3000-2700 BC) settlement and cemetery on the island; no pre-Greek name attested in native sources.
status_evidence: IACP (Aeolian islands/Troas); Hdt. 1.151; Archaic and later coins; Hierocles (Insulae); medieval Roman bishopric, later metropolis (14th c.)
note: The excavators note that early Iron Age burial customs look Anatolian rather than mainland Greek, so the date of Aeolian settlement is uncertain. The island was evacuated by treaty in 1383 and found empty by the Ottomans in 1455.

greek_from_text: coastal Greek town paying tribute to Athens in the mid-5th c. BC (Athenian tribute lists)
pre_detail: Coastal Daskyleion near Eşkel is known only from the tribute lists and later texts; no excavation, and no native predecessor is recorded.
status_evidence: Athenian tribute lists (Daskyleion on the Propontis); IACP (Propontic coast); Steph. Byz.
note: Distinct from the Persian satrapal seat Daskyleion at Ergili (Balıkesir, TRO batch). The Athenian tribute-list entry is usually referred to this coastal town; the medieval Roman see 'Daskylion' is placed at Ergili by the council seeds but may have been this town. Mother city unknown.
sources: IACP (Avram, Propontic coast); Pleiades 511226; Barrington 52 D4; Wikipedia: Dascylium (Bithynia)

greek_from_text: Milesian foundation (name; 'Milesian colony' in later sources); first civic coins 4th c. BC
pre_detail: Located at Melde Bayırı/Üç Kurnalı near Mustafakemalpaşa after a 1975 Bursa Museum rescue excavation; published evidence (coins 4th c. BC onward, stelae) is Greek and later, and no pre-Greek levels are reported.
pre_sources: Güzelsoy, Yazıtlar ve sikkeler ışığında Miletopolis kenti (MA, ÇOMÜ 2014); Pleiades 511318
status_evidence: 4th-c. BC and Roman provincial coins; Strabo 12.8.10–11; Hierocles; bishops 680–81, 787
note: Possibly the successor of Miletouteichos (attested 410–330 BC); some scholars identify the two. Site at the Makestos–Rhyndakos confluence; Wikipedia gives coordinates nearer Karacabey.
sources: Strabo 12.8.10; Pleiades 511318; IK 26 (Kyzikos II, Miletupolis); Wikipedia: Miletopolis

other_names: Miletoteichos; Lopadion (medieval fortress town; archbishopric from 1178)
greek_from_text: 'Wall of the Milesians', named in an Athenian decree of 410/09 BC; attacked unsuccessfully by Agesilaus in 395 BC (Hell. Oxy. 25.3); theorodokos c. 330 BC
pre_detail: Site uncertain (Uluabat/Lopadion vs. Miletopolis vs. Dedebayırı Tepe); nothing pre-Classical reported at any candidate.
status_evidence: Athenian decree 410/09 BC; Hell. Oxy. 25.3; theorodokoi list c. 330 BC; IACP (Propontic coast)
note: Pleiades places Miletouteichos at Uluabat, the site of the medieval fortress town of Lopadion (fortified by John II Komnenos, c. 1130); others identify it with Miletopolis or put it at Dedebayırı Tepe.
sources: Hell. Oxy. 25.3; IACP (Avram); Pleiades 511320; Wikipedia: Miletouteichos

greek_from_text: claimed to be a Milesian colony under Apollo of Didyma (kinship decree with Miletus, 2nd c. BC); first coins Hellenistic; foundation date unknown
pre_detail: Gölyazı has a Hellenistic-Roman necropolis and walls; the settlement is dated from the 6th c. BC at the earliest, and no prehistoric or native levels are reported on the lake peninsula.
status_evidence: Hellenistic & Roman provincial coins; decree on kinship with Miletus; Strabo 12.8.11; Hierocles (Apollonias); bishops 325, 787
note: Milesian origin rests on the city's Hellenistic claim; some scholars suspect an Attalid-era foundation. greek_from is therefore only a terminus ante quem. Village of Gölyazı (formerly Apolyont) on the lake peninsula.
sources: Strabo 12.8.11; Robert 1980; Pleiades 511151; Wikipedia: Apollonia ad Rhyndacum

site: Orhaneli (Bursa); ruins at the edge of the town
greek_from_text: founded by Hadrian (c. AD 124–131) on the Rhyndakos below Mysian Olympus
pre_detail: Hadrianic foundation (c. AD 123-131) where excavations by the Bursa Museum have recently begun. Reports describe only Roman and later remains. They do not say the site was new ground, and no earlier settlement is reported either.
status_evidence: Roman provincial coins; Greek civic inscriptions (IK 33); Hierocles; bishops 451–787
note: The Ottoman name Adranos continued Hadrianoi; the modern name Orhaneli does not.
sources: IK 33 (Hadrianoi, Schwertheim 1987); Pleiades 609396; Wikipedia: Hadriani ad Olympum

other_names: Elaphonnesos / Neuris (older names of the island, Strabo, Pliny); Marmara (medieval Roman name of island and town)
greek_from_text: Milesian colony, early 7th c. BC (traditionally contemporary with Abydos, c. 680-670 BC); home of Aristeas of Proconnesus
pre_detail: No pre-Greek settlement known at the town of Proconnesus (Marmara town); the island's alternative names (Elaphonnesos/Neuris) are not attested as a native town.
status_evidence: IACP (Propontic coast); Athenian tribute lists; coins; Hierocles; bishops 431, 787; autocephalous archbishopric (Notitiae)
note: Turkish Marmara continues the medieval Roman Greek name of the island (from marmaron, 'marble'), not the ancient city name. Exact centre of the ancient town at modern Marmara is approximate.
sources: Strabo 13.1.12-16; Hdt. 4.14; IACP (Propontic coast); Pleiades 511378; TIB 13

greek_from_text: Archaic Milesian colony (Strabo 14.1.6); already mentioned in the Aristeas story (Hdt. 4.14); burnt by the Phoenician fleet 493 BC (Hdt. 6.33)
pre_detail: Erdek is unexcavated for early levels. The name Artake may be pre-Greek (Homer's spring Artakie, Od. 10.108), but it is not attested as the name of a native town at the site, and the Odyssey setting is legendary.
status_evidence: IACP (Propontic coast); Athenian tribute lists; later a dependency of Cyzicus; medieval town that received the population of Cyzicus
note: Origin of the name Artake is unclear (possibly non-Greek); 'Greek name' used as instructed for uncertain cases. In the Middle Ages the population of Cyzicus moved to Artake, later seat of the metropolitans of Cyzicus.
sources: Strabo 14.1.6; Hdt. 4.14; 6.33; IACP (Propontic coast); Pleiades 511158; TIB 13
refoundations: Absorbed into the territory of Cyzicus (Hellenistic-Roman); medieval successor town of Cyzicus

greek_from_text: Milesian colony 679 BC (Eusebius' second foundation date); Eusebius also gives an earlier foundation in 756 BC
pre_detail: Tradition makes the Doliones (said to come from Thessaly) the first inhabitants and Pliny gives older island names (Arctonnesus, Dolionis), but no pre-Milesian levels have been found in the Belkıs excavations; legendary traditions alone.
status_evidence: IACP (Propontic coast); electrum and silver coinage from the Archaic period; Roman free city and assize centre; Hierocles; metropolis of Hellespontus; bishops 325-787
note: Eusebius gives two foundations (756 and 679 BC); the later, Milesian one fits the archaeological evidence better. Myth places the Doliones (a pre-Greek people) here, but there is no archaeological proof of a native town at the site.
sources: Eusebius, Chron.; Strabo 12.8.11; 14.1.6; IACP (Propontic coast); Pleiades 511218; Wikipedia: Cyzicus
refoundations: City ruined by earthquakes (443-1063 AD); population moved to Artake (Erdek) before the 13th c.

other_names: Pegai (Πηγαί, medieval Roman town and bishopric at the same site)
greek_from_text: Archaic colony of Miletus (or of Cyzicus), Strabo 13.1.12; no foundation date; attested in the Athenian tribute lists and Thuc. 8.107
pre_detail: Karabiga castle hill unexcavated for early levels; no native predecessor or pre-Greek name recorded.
status_evidence: IACP (Propontic coast); Athenian tribute lists; coins; medieval Pegai a bishopric/archbishopric, united with Parion in the 14th c.
note: Karabiga ('Black Biga') continues the medieval Greek name Pegai, not Priapos. Metropolis disputed: Strabo gives Miletus or Cyzicus.
sources: Strabo 13.1.12; Thuc. 8.107; IACP (Propontic coast); Pleiades 511375; TIB 13 (Pegai)
refoundations: Priapos -> Pegai (medieval Roman fortress town, Latin base 1204-1225)

site: near Dimetoka village, north of Biga (Biga, Çanakkale)
greek_from_text: first attested in the Athenian tribute lists, 454/3 BC (to 418/7)
pre_detail: Known only from the tribute lists; site at Dimetoka unexcavated; no native predecessor recorded.
status_evidence: IACP (p. 979); Athenian tribute lists 454/3-418/7 BC; Polybius 5.77.8 (taken by Attalus I)
note: Site identified by L. Robert (1937) at Dimetoka, a village name that preserves 'Didymoteichos'. Origin of the community unknown.
sources: IACP p. 979; Polyb. 5.77.8; Robert 1937; Pleiades 511235; Wikipedia: Didymateiche

other_names: Parion; Colonia Pariana Iulia Augusta (Caesar/Augustus); Colonia Gemella Iulia Hadriana Pariana (Hadrian)
greek_from_text: colony of Paros, Erythrae and Miletus, 709 BC (Eusebius)
pre_detail: Excavations since 2005 (Başaran) report Archaic and later material only; no prehistoric levels have been published. Pleiades' Neolithic/Iron Age tags come from an automated OSM location and are not backed by a publication. The foundation legend (Parion son of Jason) is mythical.
pre_sources: turkisharchaeonews.net/node/190; ark-itbf.omu.edu.tr Parion kazıları page; Pleiades 511354
status_evidence: IACP (Propontic coast); Athenian tribute lists; coins Archaic-Roman; Roman colony; Hierocles; bishops 431, 451, 787; autocephalous archbishopric, metropolis in the 14th c.
note: Pleiades lists prehistoric periods for the site, but no pre-Greek town is documented; left 'unknown'.
sources: Strabo 13.1.14; Eusebius, Chron.; IACP (Propontic coast); Pleiades 511354; Wikipedia: Parium
refoundations: Roman colony under Caesar/Augustus; renewed by Hadrian (Colonia Gemella Iulia Hadriana)

site: c. 9 km NE of Çardak (Lapseki, Çanakkale)
greek_from_text: Archaic Milesian colony (Strabo 13.1.19; 14.1.6); taken by the Persians 497 BC (Hdt. 5.117); no foundation date
pre_detail: Survey pottery from Adatepe (Paisos) in the northern Troad is 'probably Troy VI/VII' (Late Bronze Age), and two NAA samples match Troy fabrics. This archaeological evidence is independent of the doubtful 'Apaššawa' identification.
pre_sources: Pavúk & Schubert 2014, Studia Troica Monogr. 5 (hdl.handle.net/10900/73590); LuwianSiteAtlas site 33 'Apaisos' (zenodo.org/records/17128262)
status_evidence: IACP (p. 991); Athenian tribute lists 453/2-430/29 BC; Hdt. 5.117
note: Abandoned before Strabo's time; its people moved to Lampsacus. A Hittite form 'Apaššawa' proposed by Zangger & Woudhuizen (2018) rests on the doubtful Beyköy 2 text and is not used here.

greek_from_text: Phocaean colony, 654/3 BC (Eusebius); Strabo implies Milesian participation
founder: Phocaeans (Phobos; Charon ap. Plutarch, Mul. virt. 18)
status_evidence: IACP (Propontic coast); Athenian tribute lists (12 talents); gold and silver coinage; Hierocles; bishops 4th c., 451, 680, 787
note: Tradition (Charon ap. Plutarch) has the Phocaeans received at Pityoussa by Mandron, king of the Bebrykes, so a native settlement is implied; no archaeology. The origin of the name Lampsakos is unclear; 'Greek name' used as instructed for uncertain cases.
sources: Plutarch, Mul. virt. 18; Strabo 13.1.18-19; IACP (Propontic coast); Pleiades 501570; Wikipedia: Lampsacus

greek_from_text: first attested as a tribute-paying community in the Athenian tribute lists (mid-5th c. BC)
pre_detail: Site and its relation to Perkote uncertain; no archaeological data.
status_evidence: IACP (Troas); Athenian tribute lists (Palaiperkosioi)
note: Small community near Perkote ('Old Perkote'); its relationship to Perkote and the exact site are uncertain.

greek_from_text: first attested as a town taken by Daurises in 497 BC (Hdt. 5.117); later given to Themistocles
pre_detail: Site only approximately located (east of Umurbey); no archaeological data. Homeric Perkote (Il. 2.835) is epic only.
status_evidence: IACP (Troas); Hdt. 5.117; Xen. Hell. 5.1.25
note: Homeric Perkote (Il. 2.835) suggests an older settlement, but there is no archaeological evidence. Origin of the Greek community unrecorded.

greek_from_text: Archaic Milesian colony (Anaximenes of Lampsacus ap. Strabo 14.1.6); no foundation date
pre_detail: The Musaköy identification is tentative and no pre-Greek finds are reported. Homeric Arisbe (Il. 2.836) is epic, not evidence.
status_evidence: IACP (Troas); Alexander's muster point 334 BC (Arrian 1.12.6)
note: In ruins by Strabo's time. Site identification (Musaköy) is tentative.

greek_from_text: Milesian colony c. 680-670 BC, with the consent of Gyges of Lydia (Strabo 13.1.22)
status_evidence: IACP (Troas); Athenian tribute lists; coins Archaic-Roman; Hierocles; bishops 451 (seed)/458, 680, 787; metropolis from 1084
note: Homer lists Abydos among Trojan allies and Strabo says Thracians held it before the Milesians (text only). Major medieval Roman customs port; abandoned c. 1304-1318.
sources: Strabo 13.1.22; IACP (Troas); Pleiades 501325; Wikipedia: Abydos, Hellespont; TIB 13

greek_from_text: first attested 497 BC, taken by Daurises (Hdt. 5.117); Aeolian city (Strabo)
pre_detail: Cook reported grey ware of supposed 2nd-millennium date on the Dardanos hill, but its Bronze Age date has since been doubted (it may be Archaic Aeolic grey ware). A 2001 rescue dig on the disturbed bastion found nothing before the mid-7th c. BC. Homeric Dardanos/Dardanoi is legend only.
pre_sources: Cook 1973, 60 (cited by R. Körpe, Çanakkale Araştırmaları Türk Yıllığı, cdn.comu.edu.tr/cms/ckalearastirma/files/411-dardanos-tabyasinda-savas-alani-arkeolojisi-ve-son.pdf); Pavúk & Schubert 2014, Studia Troica Monogr. 5
status_evidence: IACP (Troas); Athenian tribute lists; coins 5th c. BC-3rd c. AD; Roman free city (peace of Dardanus 85 BC); Hierocles; bishops 451, 787
note: The Dardanoi of Homer and the Drdny of Egyptian Kadesh texts are a people, not this town; no pre-Greek town is attested at the site.

site: c. 1.5 km NE of İntepe (Merkez, Çanakkale)
greek_from_text: first attested c. 400 BC (Xen. Anab. 7.8.5); coins 4th c. BC; Archaic-Classical necropolis
pre_detail: Cook's survey found nothing earlier than the 6th c. BC on the Ophryneion hill. The Troia-area Bronze Age surveys record sites at neighbouring Rhoiteion and Işıldak Tepe but none here. The Akamas foundation legend is myth.
pre_sources: Cook 1973, The Troad, 77; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ophryneion; Pavúk & Schubert 2014, 'Die Troas in der Mittel- und Spätbronzezeit', Studia Troica Monogr. 5 (hdl.handle.net/10900/73590)
status_evidence: IACP (Troas); coins 4th c. BC; member of the Ilian koinon
note: Absorbed by Ilion in the Hellenistic period. Necropolis finds may push the Greek settlement into the 6th c. BC.

greek_from_text: first attested 480 BC on Xerxes' route (Hdt. 7.43); Aeolian town
pre_detail: Survey sherds of middle/late Troy VI date (2nd millennium BC) come from Eski Kale/Baba Kale, the Rhoiteion site; the Greek town is attested from the late 8th c. BC. The evidence is small: three sherds.
pre_sources: Pavúk & Schubert 2014, Studia Troica Monogr. 5 (hdl.handle.net/10900/73590); Aslan & Polat 2012; Cook 1973, 77-90; LuwianSiteAtlas site 111 (zenodo.org/records/17128262)
status_evidence: IACP (Troas); Athenian tribute lists; coins; member of the Ilian koinon
note: Later absorbed by Ilion.

other_names: Ilios / Troia (Homer); Troy; Wilusa (Hittite, Bronze Age city)
greek_from_text: Greek (Aeolian) resettlement of Hisarlık c. 700 BC (Troy VIII); sparse occupation continued after Troy VIIb (ended c. 950 BC)
pre_greek_note: Hittite Wilusa (Alaksandu treaty, Manapa-Tarhunta and Milawata letters, from c. 1400 BC) = Greek (W)ilios; widely accepted since Forrer 1924 (Starke, Hawkins, Latacz), not by all. Taruisa (Annals of Tudhaliya I) is sometimes equated with Troia.
status_evidence: IACP (Troas); coins from 4th c. BC; head of the Ilian koinon; Roman free city; Hierocles; bishops 325, 451, 553, 787
note: Troy VI-VIIb was an Anatolian (probably Luwian-speaking) city; Mycenaean pottery there is imported or imitated, so it was not a Greek city. Protogeometric pottery appears in VIIb3 (10th c. BC), but Greek settlement proper starts c. 700 BC.
sources: Wikipedia: Troy; Rose 2014; Latacz 2004; IACP (Troas); Pleiades 550595
refoundations: Enlarged by Lysimachus (c. 300 BC); sacked by Fimbria 85 BC; rebuilt (Troy IX); in decline after earthquakes c. 500 AD

greek_from_text: Mytilenaean fortified town (Archeanax), late 7th c. BC; captured by Athens under Phrynon c. 607 BC
pre_detail: No pre-Greek finds are reported from the Yenişehir ridge itself. The Chalcolithic-EBA mound of Kumtepe, with one Troy VI sherd, lies c. 1.8 km E on the Scamander plain, but it is a separate site rather than the same nucleus. Epic and Athenian Trojan-war claims are legend.
pre_sources: LuwianSiteAtlas site 85 Kumtepe; Pavúk & Schubert 2014, 'Die Troas in der Mittel- und Spätbronzezeit', Studia Troica Monogr. 5 (hdl.handle.net/10900/73590); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sigeion
status_evidence: IACP (Troas); Athenian tribute lists; coins 4th c. BC; Athenian decree for Sigeion (IG I³ 17, 451/0 BC)
note: Fought over by Mytilene and Athens c. 607-530 BC; Peisistratus installed his son Hegesistratus. Destroyed by the Ilians in the Hellenistic period.

site: Beşika Burnu, c. 2 km S of Yeniköy (Ezine, Çanakkale)
greek_from_text: Mytilenaean fortified base against Sigeion, c. 600 BC; walls first half of 6th c. BC
pre_detail: Beşik-Yassıtepe, at the Achilleion site on Beşika Burnu, has Troy I (EBA) occupation and Late Bronze Age (Troy VI late/VIIa) material (Korfmann's excavations); a 13th-c. BC cemetery of c. 100 graves lies c. 250 m away. The Greek fort's material begins in the 6th c. BC.
pre_sources: Korfmann, AA 1986, 1988 (Beşik-Tepe reports); Pavúk & Schubert 2014, Studia Troica Monogr. 5 (publikationen.uni-tuebingen.de handle 10900/73590); LuwianSiteAtlas site 80 (zenodo.org/records/17128262); vici.org/vici/57675
status_evidence: IACP 766; Athenian tribute lists 425/4 and 422/1 BC; possible coins c. 350-300 BC
note: Merged into Ilion by Lysimachus (306-281 BC); a hamlet by the 2nd c. BC.
sources: IACP 766; Hdt. 5.94; Strabo 13.1.39; Pleiades 550401; Wikipedia: Achilleion (Troad)

other_names: Antigoneia (Antigonus I, c. 311-306 BC); Alexandreia (Lysimachus, after 301 BC); Colonia Augusta Troas (Augustus); Troas (Late Roman)
greek_from_text: founded as Antigoneia by Antigonus I c. 311-306 BC by synoecism of Neandreia, Kebren, Kolonai, Hamaxitos, Larisa and others
founder: Antigonus I Monophthalmus; renamed by Lysimachus
pre_detail: Pliny (NH 5.124) gives an earlier name Sigia, but nothing shows it was a non-Greek town. The LuwianSiteAtlas lists a Bronze Age find-spot 'Dalyan' (after Cook 1973) c. 1.3 km N of the city centre, but its nature is unpublished online, and Feuser's harbour survey found no pre-Roman material. The new-ground status is also unproven.
pre_sources: Pliny NH 5.124; LuwianSiteAtlas site 115 (zenodo.org/records/17128262); Feuser 2011, harbour survey (ancientportsantiques.com AlexTroas-Feuser2011.pdf)
status_evidence: Cohen 1995; Hellenistic and Roman coins; Roman colony; Hierocles; bishops (Troas) 451 and later
note: Pliny (NH 5.124) says the site was earlier called Sigia; no pre-Greek settlement is attested archaeologically. Greek remained the main language despite the Roman colony.
sources: Strabo 13.1.26; 13.1.47; Cohen 1995; Pleiades 550434; Wikipedia: Alexandria Troas
refoundations: Antigoneia -> Alexandreia (Lysimachus, after 301 BC) -> Colonia Augusta Troas (Augustus)

site: Beşiktepe, south of Alexandria Troas (Ezine/Ayvacık, Çanakkale)
greek_from_text: first attested c. 477 BC as the seat of Pausanias (Thuc. 1.131); Archaic finds at the site (excavated by Akurgal)
pre_detail: Cook found prehistoric pottery on Beşiktepe, and the Bronze Age survey material from 'Beşik Tepe (Kolonai)' covers Troy VI early to VIIa (KP 2-5). Greek material begins in the 7th c. BC; continuity is unclear.
pre_sources: Cook 1973, The Troad, 216-220; Pavúk & Schubert 2014, Studia Troica Monogr. 5 (hdl.handle.net/10900/73590); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kolonai
status_evidence: IACP (Troas); Athenian tribute lists; Xen. Hell. 3.1.13
note: The Greek settlement is probably Archaic (6th c. BC or earlier), so the date given is a minimum. Synoecised into Antigoneia/Alexandria Troas c. 310 BC.

greek_from_text: first attested 399 BC, taken by Dercylidas (Xen. Hell. 3.1.13)
pre_detail: Surface pottery of Early Bronze Age III and Troy VI (Late Bronze Age) type at Limantepe shows a pre-Greek settlement from the mid-3rd millennium BC on the same hill.
pre_sources: Cook 1973, The Troad, 219; Akalın 1991, 'Larisa und der Liman-Tepe in der Troas', Asia Minor Studien 3, 65-66; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Larisa_(Troad)
status_evidence: IACP (Troas); Xen. Hell. 3.1.13
note: Strabo placed Homer's 'Pelasgian Larisa' here, but that is epic, not evidence of a native town. Possibly renamed Ptolemais (L. Robert); synoecised into Alexandria Troas.
sources: Xen. Hell. 3.1.13; Strabo 13.3.2; IACP (Troas); Robert 1987; Pleiades 550685

greek_from_text: first securely attested 399 BC (Xen. Hell. 3.1.13); coins 4th c. BC
pre_detail: Rejected the proposed 'yes'. The Late Neolithic/Chalcolithic village at Gülpınar is internationally published (Takaoğlu, Hesperia 75, 2006). But it lies under the Smintheion, c. 2.1 km from the city hill of Beşiktepe, which puts it at or beyond the 1–2 km limit, on a separate hill, and millennia before the Greek town (rule 8). No prehistoric finds are reported from Beşiktepe itself (Cook 1973, 231-5: the earliest material noted there is Classical). The Teucrian/Smintheus traditions are legendary.
pre_sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamaxitus (Cook, The Troad 1973, 231-5; Cook ABSA 83, 1988); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smintheion (coordinates); distance computed 2.1 km; knowledge: Takaoğlu, Hesperia 75 (2006) 289-315
status_evidence: IACP (Troas); coins (Apollo Smintheus) 4th c. BC
note: Controlled the sanctuary of Apollo Smintheus (Chrysa). Probably an older Aeolian foundation; date given is a minimum. Synoecised into Alexandria Troas.

greek_from_text: Methymnaean colony (Myrsilos ap. Strabo 13.1.58), Archaic, probably 7th c. BC; temple of Athena c. 530 BC
pre_detail: Ministry of Culture and UNESCO tentative-list texts say 'recent research' dates Assos to the Bronze Age (Assuwa/Lelegian Pedasos equations are speculative), but no stratified pre-Greek finds are published. The only find is a surface Chalcolithic stone axe from the necropolis, and the Troad Bronze Age site corpus does not list Assos.
pre_sources: whc.unesco.org/en/tentativelists/6242; turkishmuseums.kprod.kultur.gov.tr (Assos); cnnturk.com (2019 axe find); Pavúk & Schubert 2014, 'Die Troas in der Mittel- und Spätbronzezeit', Studia Troica Monogr. 5 (hdl.handle.net/10900/73590)
status_evidence: IACP (Troas); Athenian tribute lists; coins; Hierocles; bishops 431, 787
note: Some popular sources date the foundation to 1000-900 BC without support. Behramkale may continue the medieval Roman name Machramion (uncertain).

greek_from_text: first attested c. 511 BC, taken by Otanes (Hdt. 5.26)
pre_detail: Four Middle/Late Bronze Age sherds from Kozlu Dağ (Lamponeia) appear in the survey corpus, one of them analysed by NAA. The Greek circuit wall dates to the 6th c. BC.
pre_sources: Pavúk & Schubert 2014, Studia Troica Monogr. 5 (hdl.handle.net/10900/73590); Cook 1973; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lamponeia
status_evidence: IACP (Troas); Athenian tribute lists; coins
note: Herodotus calls it Lamponion; Strabo (13.1.58) says it was Aeolian.

site: near Arıklı, west of Küçükkuyu (Ayvacık, Çanakkale)
greek_from_text: first attested in the Athenian tribute lists (mid-5th c. BC); colony of Assos (Strabo 13.1.58), so Archaic in origin
pre_detail: At the original (upland) Gargara the earliest remains are 6th c. BC walls and temple foundations. The coastal site near Arıklı is a 4th c. BC relocation. Alcman's mention of Leleges at Gargara is an ethnographic or legendary tradition only, and no prehistoric finds are reported.
status_evidence: IACP (Troas); Athenian tribute lists; coins; Hierocles; bishops 553, 787
note: The city moved from Palaia Gargara (upland) to the coastal site; Strabo says the kings later added settlers from Miletopolis, making it 'half-barbarian'.

site: Devren hill, between Avcılar and Altınoluk (Edremit, Balıkesir)
greek_from_text: Greek pottery in the necropolis from the late 8th/early 7th c. BC (recent excavations); Aeolian city (Thucydides); first attested c. 511 BC (Hdt. 5.26)
status_evidence: IACP (Troas); coins; Hierocles; bishops 553, 787
note: Ancient traditions name Leleges (Alcaeus), Pelasgians (Hdt. 7.42), Edonian Thracians and Cimmerians as earlier inhabitants; the early material from the necropolis is reported as largely Greek. Later one of Mytilene's Aktaean cities.
sources: Hdt. 5.26; 7.42; Thuc. 4.52; 8.108; IACP (Troas); Pleiades 550433; Wikipedia: Antandrus

other_names: Astyra in the Adramyttene; sanctuary of Artemis Astyrene
site: coast between Antandros and Adramyttion, near Akçay (Edremit, Balıkesir)
greek_from_text: Astyrenoi in the Athenian tribute lists (mid-5th c. BC); coins c. 400 BC (some with the name of Tissaphernes)
status_evidence: IACP (Troas: Astyra); Athenian tribute lists (Astyrenoi, partly 'Astyrenoi Mysoi'); coins 4th c. BC; Strabo 13.1.51, 13.1.65 (sanctuary of Artemis Astyrene)
note: The tribute lists call the Astyrenoi partly 'Mysians', so a native community is implied. Attribution of the tribute entries and coins to this Astyra, rather than the Astyra above Abydos, is the usual view but not certain. Barrington offers two possible sites (550468 coastal, 550467 near Havran).
refoundations: Village dependent on Adramyttion by Strabo's time

other_names: Atramyttion; Adramytteion; Edremit (medieval Adramyttion, rebuilt inland)
site: Ören, c. 4 km W of Burhaniye (Burhaniye, Balıkesir)
greek_from_text: first attested 480 BC on Xerxes' route (Hdt. 7.42); traditions of a Lydian foundation by Adramys/Adramytes (6th c. BC) and of an Athenian colony (Strabo); Delian refugees settled 422 BC
founder: Adramys, son of Alyattes of Lydia (Aristotle ap. Steph. Byz.); 'Athenian colony' (Strabo 13.1.51)
status_evidence: IACP (Aiolis); coins; Roman assize centre (conventus); Hierocles; bishops 431-787 and to the 13th c.
note: Origin disputed: Lydian royal foundation or Athenian colony. The medieval Roman town was rebuilt c. 13 km NE at Edremit (date debated: 1109 or after 1197); Edremit preserves the name. Pre-Greek naming is Lydian by tradition only, with no native-script form.
sources: Hdt. 7.42; Thuc. 5.1; Strabo 13.1.51; Pleiades 550403; Wikipedia: Adramyttium
refoundations: Medieval city rebuilt inland at Edremit (12th c.)

greek_from_text: 4th c. BC: coins attributed to Kisthene; Strabo (13.1.51) calls it a deserted city (polis) with a harbour
status_evidence: Strabo 13.1.51; coins (4th c. BC, attributed)
note: Site proposed by Beksaç's survey (1997) at Kızçiftlik, with surface finds from the Early Bronze Age to Late medieval Roman. Not confirmed as an IACP polis.

greek_from_text: first attested 480 BC on Xerxes' route (Hdt. 7.42); Ephorus says Karene sent settlers to Ephesus
pre_detail: Site tentative (Asar Kaya/Taşağıl); no excavation and no recorded native predecessor.
status_evidence: IACP (Aiolis); Hdt. 7.42
note: Site tentative. Close to the İzmir (Dikili) border; check for a duplicate in the ION batch.

greek_from_text: silver and bronze coins inscribed ΒΙΡΥ, 4th-3rd c. BC; probably the Berysioi of the tribute lists (454/3-446/5 BC)
pre_detail: The site is unidentified: Barrington places it at Mersinoba (with '?'), while Cook and the LuwianSiteAtlas place it at Ada Tepe. Ada Tepe has a few weathered grey-ware sherds, probably Early Iron Age, which is not enough for a 'yes'.
pre_sources: Pleiades 550486; Pavúk & Schubert 2014, 'Die Troas in der Mittel- und Spätbronzezeit', Studia Troica Monogr. 5 (hdl.handle.net/10900/73590); LuwianSiteAtlas site 84
status_evidence: IACP (p. 1006); coins 4th-3rd c. BC; Athenian tribute lists (if = Berysioi)
note: Site not securely identified. If the Berysioi of the tribute lists are the same people, the date goes back to 454 BC. Origin unrecorded.
sources: IACP p. 1006; Steph. Byz. s.v.; Pleiades 550486; Wikipedia: Birytis

greek_from_text: first attested in the Athenian tribute lists 452/1 BC (to 444/3)
pre_detail: Late Bronze Age sherds from Ballı Dağ (Schliemann/Calvert trenches, published by Lamb) and clearer LBA surface finds on the east slope suggest occupation from middle Troy VI, though Pavúk & Schubert call it still questionable. The Gentinos identification is itself tentative.
pre_sources: Pavúk & Schubert 2014, Studia Troica Monogr. 5 (hdl.handle.net/10900/73590); Korfmann 1996; Hohfeld 2009; Pleiades 550546
status_evidence: IACP (p. 1008); Athenian tribute lists 452/1-444/3 BC; bronze coins ΓΕΝ / ΓΕΝΤΙ
note: Location at Ballı Dağ is tentative (Cook 1973; Barrington). Origin unrecorded.

greek_from_text: Pliny (NH 5.124) calls Scamandria a small city (civitas parva); listed by Hierocles (c. 527) as Skamandros
pre_detail: The Late Roman Skamandros site is unexcavated. At Ada Tepe (Barrington's Skamandreia, which Cook and the LuwianSiteAtlas call Birytis), a few weathered grey-ware sherds are 'probably Early Iron Age rather than LBA', which is too ambiguous to count.
pre_sources: Pavúk & Schubert 2014, 'Die Troas in der Mittel- und Spätbronzezeit', Studia Troica Monogr. 5 (hdl.handle.net/10900/73590); LuwianSiteAtlas site 84; Pleiades 550888, 550889
status_evidence: Pliny NH 5.124; Hierocles
note: Barrington gives separate sites for Hellenistic-Roman Skamandreia (Pleiades 550888, near Adatepe) and Late Roman Skamandros (550889), c. 4 km apart; treated here as one community. 4th c. BC bronzes are sometimes attributed to Skamandreia.
sources: Plin. NH 5.124; Hierocles, Synecdemus; Cook 1973; Pleiades 550889; 550888

greek_from_text: earliest remains on Çığrı Dağ 6th c. BC, with Aeolic inscriptions and an Aeolic temple
pre_detail: Excavation (Koldewey 1889) and the Münster survey/excavation of Çığrı Dağ found nothing earlier than the 6th c. BC and no 2nd-millennium occupation, so the Greek city appears to stand on new ground.
pre_sources: Schwertheim 1994; Schulz 2000; Wiegartz 1994 (Asia Minor Studien 11); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neandreia
status_evidence: IACP (Troas); Athenian tribute lists 454/3-410/9 BC; coins; Ps.-Skylax 96
note: No 2nd-millennium occupation found. Synoecised into Antigoneia/Alexandria Troas c. 310 BC.
sources: Strabo 13.1.47; IACP (Troas); Schulz 2000; Pleiades 550772; Wikipedia: Neandreia

greek_from_text: first attested 399 BC, joining Dercylidas with Ilion and Neandreia (Xen. Hell. 3.1.16)
pre_detail: Site not securely located (near Karaev?) and unexplored; no evidence either way.
status_evidence: IACP (Troas); Xen. Hell. 3.1.16
note: Site uncertain; Pliny (5.122) lists it among vanished Troad towns. Origin unrecorded.
sources: Xen. Hell. 3.1.16; Plin. NH 5.122; IACP (Troas); Pleiades 550658

greek_from_text: Greek city by c. 500 BC (earliest silver coins, ram's head); Athenian tribute lists; colony of Aeolian Kyme (Ephorus)
pre_detail: Jewell (1974) recorded 2nd-millennium BC surface material at Çal Dağ (Kebren) and judged it the largest Bronze Age site in the Troad; later surveys neither confirmed nor refuted this.
pre_sources: Jewell 1974 (diss.), cited in Pavúk & Schubert 2014, Studia Troica Monogr. 5 (hdl.handle.net/10900/73590); LuwianSiteAtlas site 39
status_evidence: IACP (Troas); coins from c. 500 BC; Athenian tribute lists; Xen. Hell. 3.1.17
note: Moved into Antigoneia c. 310 BC; probably refounded as Antiocheia under Antiochus I (coins ΑΝΤΙΟΧΕΩΝ with Kebren types; Cohen 1995). Metropolis per Ephorus.
refoundations: Synoecised into Antigoneia; refounded as Antiocheia? (Antiochus I)

greek_from_text: coins from c. 480 BC; Athenian tribute lists; Milesian settlers (Strabo 14.1.6) joined the community
founder: Milesians (joined an earlier community; local tradition: Skamandrios and Askanios)
pre_detail: The Kurşunlu Tepe site has no reported pre-Greek finds. Strabo's tradition that Skamandrios and Askanios moved the Skepsians down from Palaiskepsis is legendary, and the Milesian settlement is undated.
status_evidence: IACP (Troas); coins from c. 480 BC; Athenian tribute lists; home of Demetrius of Skepsis; bishop 431
note: Moved to Antigoneia by Antigonus and restored by Lysimachus. Local tradition makes Aeneas' descendants the founders; Strabo lists Skepsis among Milesian colonies.
refoundations: Palaiskepsis -> Skepsis; synoecised into Antigoneia and restored by Lysimachus

greek_from_text: Greek coin legends (ΓΕΡ, head of the Sibyl) from c. 400 BC; fortified town in 399 BC (Xen. Hell. 3.1.15)
status_evidence: IACP (Troas); coins c. 400 BC; Athenian tribute lists (Gergithioi); Hierocles
note: Herodotus (5.122; 7.43) calls the Gergithes a remnant of the ancient Teucrians, that is a non-Greek people. Attalus I moved part of the population to Gergitha near the Kaikos. Site location approximate.
sources: Hdt. 5.122; 7.43; Xen. Hell. 3.1.15; Strabo 13.1.70; IACP (Troas); Pleiades 550547

greek_from_text: first attested in the Athenian tribute lists 452/1 BC (to 415/4)
pre_detail: Unlocated; no archaeological evidence possible.
status_evidence: IACP (p. 1006); Athenian tribute lists 452/1-415/4 BC
note: Polis status is secure but the site is unknown; coordinates are the centre of the Troad. Province (il) assumed.
sources: IACP p. 1006; ATL; Steph. Byz. s.v. Ἀζεία; Wikipedia: Azeia

greek_from_text: walled place (teichos) in Strabo 13.1.45; named by Pliny (NH 5.122); city in Hierocles (c. 527)
pre_detail: Unlocated; no archaeological evidence possible.
status_evidence: Strabo 13.1.45; Pliny NH 5.122; Hierocles 662
note: If the classical Polichna that IACP lists for the Troad is this town, greek_from goes back to the 5th c. BC; not verified here. Site unknown; coordinates and province are guesses for the upper Aesepus valley.

greek_from_text: c. 470/460 BC: Arthmios son of Pythonax of Zeleia outlawed by Athens (Dem. 9.42); civic decree c. 334 BC (Syll.3 279)
status_evidence: IACP (Propontic coast); decree of boule and demos c. 334 BC (Syll.3 279); Arrian 1.12.8
note: Homer's Zeleia of the 'Lycians' under Pandaros (Il. 2.824-827) implies a pre-Greek town, but that is epic tradition only. Persian base before the Granicus (334 BC); disappears after Strabo.
sources: Dem. 9.42; Syll.3 279; Arrian, Anab. 1.12.8; IACP (Propontic coast); Pleiades 511461

greek_from_text: first bishop attested at Chalcedon 451 (Eutychianus); city in Hierocles
pre_detail: Baris is placed at Gönen only by the Barrington Atlas, and nothing pre-Roman is reported from the town. The LuwianSiteAtlas links Baris (Pleiades 511178) to Tütüncüyolu Üyücek, a höyük with Chalcolithic, EBA, LBA, Roman and Byzantine levels, but it lies c. 5 km SE of Gönen. If Baris was actually at that mound it would be a 'yes', but this is not established.
pre_sources: LuwianSiteAtlas (Zangger & Aşınmaz, Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.17128262) site 186 + pleiades.csv; Pleiades 511178; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gönen
status_evidence: Hierocles; bishops 451, 458; suffragan of Cyzicus (Notitia c. 640)
note: Barrington places Baris at Gönen; Pleiades periods suggest Hellenistic-Roman occupation, but civic status is attested only in Late Antiquity.
