sources: Price & Gaddis 2005 (Chalcedon); Hierocles; Pleiades 511178; Wikipedia: Baris in Hellesponto

greek_from_text: Poemaneni listed by Pliny (NH 5.123); earlier a fortified dependency of Cyzicus (Steph. Byz.)
pre_detail: Hasluck located Poimanenon at the Byzantine castle of Eski Manyas; the site is unexcavated and no pre-Greek settlement or name is recorded (Radet's link to the Macedonian Poemenii is only an etymology).
status_evidence: Pliny NH 5.123; Hierocles 662; bishops 451, 680, 787; medieval Roman fortress (battle of Poimanenon 1224)
note: In the territory of Cyzicus, with a noted Asklepieion. A link between the name Manyas and Poimanenon has been suggested but is not verified, so turkish_from is left as 'unrelated'.

greek_from_text: city in Hierocles (c. 527); later a bishopric
status_evidence: Hierocles; bishopric (Notitiae)
note: Probably a Mysian community. If Pliny's Erizii (5.123, conventus of Adramyttium) are the same people, it is attested in the 1st c. AD. Not in the seed.
sources: Hierocles; Plin. NH 5.123; RE II.1 721; Pleiades 550450

greek_from_text: civic coins ΠΙΟΝΙΤΩΝ of the early Imperial period (RPC I 1348); named by Strabo (p. 610 Cas.) and Pausanias (9.18.4)
status_evidence: coins (RPC I 1348 and later); Hierocles 663; bishop at Ephesus 431, Chalcedon 451
note: Site at Gömeniç (L. Robert; Barrington). Some coins may be Hellenistic; the earliest date is not fixed here.
sources: RPC I 1348; Paus. 9.18.4; Hierocles 663; Pleiades 550832; Wikipedia: Pionia (Mysia)

site: near Karaçam, east of Savaştepe (Savaştepe, Balıkesir)
greek_from_text: first attested as a city in the 2nd c. AD (Ptolemy 5.2.14)
status_evidence: Ptolemy 5.2.14; Hierocles 663; bishops at Ephesus 431, Chalcedon 451, Nicaea 787; suffragan of Cyzicus
note: Civic coins with ΓΕΡΜΗΝΩΝ (Domitian onward) may belong here or to another Germe; not used for the date. The seed puts the see at Savaştepe town, about 4 km west of the Barrington location.

greek_from_text: founded by Hadrian c. 124 AD to mark a successful hunt (Cass. Dio 69.10; HA Hadr. 20)
pre_detail: Cassius Dio 69.10 and HA Hadr. 20.13 say Hadrian founded the city where he had a successful (bear) hunt, which suggests a new foundation. But the site near Balıkesir is not fixed, and the LuwianSiteAtlas links Hadrianoutherai to two nearby Bronze Age mounds with later levels: Ovaköy Üyücek (EBA-LBA, Roman, Byzantine; c. 5 km E of Balıkesir) and Emre Mevkii. So there is no positive evidence of new ground; previously 'no known'.
pre_sources: Cass. Dio 69.10; HA Hadr. 20.13; LuwianSiteAtlas sites 183, 184 + pleiades.csv (Zenodo 17128262); acikbilim.yok.gov.tr/handle/20.500.12812/147588
status_evidence: coins from Hadrian onward (mention a boule); Hierocles 663; bishops 451, 553, 680, 787
note: Usually located at or just outside modern Balıkesir. The often-cited derivation of 'Balıkesir' from medieval Roman Palaiokastron is uncertain and does not continue the ancient name.
sources: Cass. Dio 69.10; HA Hadr. 20; Hierocles 663; Pleiades 550560; Robert 1962

site: Barrington: between Kepsut and Bigadiç (Balıkesir); RE: Ayazment near Altınova (Ayvalık, Balıkesir)
greek_from_text: civic coins (ΑΤΤΑΙΤΩΝ, ΑΤΤΕΑΤΩΝ) of the Severan period
status_evidence: Roman provincial coins; bishopric, suffragan of Ephesus (Notitiae)
note: Location disputed: Barrington puts the coin-issuing city inland (56 G2) and a separate 'Attea?' near Atarneus (Pleiades 550473), while RE (Bürchner) puts it at Ayazment near the coast. Both are in Balıkesir. The coins may begin before Caracalla.

greek_from_text: Hadrianic foundation, one of three Mysian cities named after Hadrian (c. 124 AD)
pre_detail: Hadrianic foundation inferred from the name; Dursunbey is unexcavated and no earlier settlement or new-site statement is known.
status_evidence: Hadrianic city name; bishop at Nicaea 787 (seed); Barrington 62 A2
note: The foundation is inferred from the name and Hadrian's 124 AD journey, not from an explicit text. The council list puts the see under Bithynia, while Hierocles' province is unverified. Not to be confused with Hadrianoi (Orhaneli, Bursa) or Hadrianoutherai.

greek_from_text: Classical-period town (Pleiades/BAtlas); securely a Greek city by the Hellenistic period (coins); renamed Theodosioupolis in Late Antiquity
status_evidence: Hellenistic & Roman coins; Strabo 13.1.51; Hierocles 661; bishop 451
note: Non-Greek name in inland Mysia; native origin is inferred, not documented (older literature calls it an Aeolian colony). Earliest dated civic evidence not verified here; the 4th-c. date is a rough estimate.

greek_from_text: Held by the Gongylid family (Greek dynasts under Persia) since Xerxes; first attested c. 399 BC (Xen. Hell. 3.1.6); coins 4th c. BC; famous sumptuary-law inscription (3rd c. BC)
status_evidence: IACP (Aiolis/SW Mysia); Xen. Hell. 3.1.6; coins 4th c. BC and Roman; civic decree on mourning (3rd c. BC)
note: Pleiades coordinates are a grid placeholder; the site is the Hisarlık hill at Poyracık in the Bakırçay valley. Neighbouring Palaigambreion (Xen.) is unlocated.

greek_from_text: Settlement from the late 8th c. BC (East Greek and Corinthian imports); first Greek coin legend ΠΕΡΓ c. 450 BC under the Gongylid dynasts; Xen. Anab. 7.8.8 (399 BC)
founder: (legend: Telephos' Arcadians; Pergamos son of Neoptolemos)
pre_detail: Changed from 'no known'. Bronze Age habitation on the acropolis is not demonstrated (Bronze Age stone tools only in the surroundings). The earliest settlement is late 8th-c. BC, with East Greek and Corinthian imports, but whether it was Aeolian or Mysian is unresolved. So there is no positive evidence either of new ground or of a native nucleus.
status_evidence: IACP (Aiolis/SW Mysia); coins c. 450 BC on; Attalid capital 281–133 BC; Hierocles; bishops from 1st/2nd c. AD; metropolis under Isaac II
note: Bronze Age habitation not demonstrated on the acropolis. Whether the Archaic settlement was Greek or Mysian is unclear. Refortified by Constans II (663/4) and Manuel I (c. 1170); taken by the Karasids soon after 1300.
sources: IACP (Aiolis); Xen. Anab. 7.8.8; Pleiades 550812; Wikipedia: Pergamon
refoundations: Attalid capital (Philetairos 281 BC on); rebuilt by Manuel I c. 1170

site: Kalarga Tepe, Kaikos plain SW of Bergama (Bergama, İzmir)
greek_from_text: Given by Darius/Xerxes to the exiled Spartan king Demaratos (c. 486 BC); held by his descendants, attested c. 399 BC (Xen. Hell. 3.1.6); 4th-c. coins
status_evidence: IACP (Aiolis/SW Mysia); Xen. Hell. 3.1.6, Anab. 7.8.17; coins 4th c. BC
note: Legendary seat of the Mysian king Teuthras; native (Mysian) origin follows the tradition. Identification with Kalarga Tepe from the DAI Pergamon micro-region survey.
sources: Xen. Hell. 3.1.6; Strabo 13.1.69; Pleiades 550916; Wikipedia: Teuthrania

site: Kaikos valley W of Bergama (Bergama, İzmir)
greek_from_text: Demaratid town attested c. 399 BC (Xen. Hell. 3.1.6); coins 4th c. BC
status_evidence: IACP (Aiolis/SW Mysia); Xen. Hell. 3.1.6; coins 4th c. BC
note: Non-Greek name; native origin inferred. Site placement follows BAtlas.

other_names: Nasos / Nesos (Aeolic Νᾶσος, the city); Poroselene (Late Roman see); Cunda / Moschonisi (island)
site: southern part of Cunda (Alibey) island (Ayvalık, Balıkesir)
greek_from_text: Classical Aeolian island town; civic decree of the Nasiotai for Thersippos c. 319 BC (OGIS 4)
pre_detail: Survey on Cunda (Alibey) island has published only Palaeolithic lithics. No Bronze Age or other pre-Greek settlement is reported at the city site.
status_evidence: IACP (Lesbos chapter: Nasos); Thersippos decree (OGIS 4); Strabo 13.2.5; see of Poroselene (Notitiae)
note: Pleiades notes there may have been two cities on the island. The date given is a minimum; Lesbian settlement is probably Archaic.

site: Kale Tepe (Kalemkaya), NE of Dikili (Dikili, İzmir)
greek_from_text: Given with its territory (Atarneitis) to Chios by the Persians c. 546 BC (Hdt. 1.160); Greek polis thereafter; coins 4th c. BC
status_evidence: IACP (Aiolis/SW Mysia); Hdt. 1.160, 8.106; Xen. Hell. 3.2.11; 4th-c. coins; seat of Hermias (4th c.)
note: Herodotus calls Atarneus a district of Mysia opposite Lesbos; whether it was Greek before the Chian grant is unknown. Deserted by Pliny's day (1st c. AD).

other_names: Autokane? (Αὐτοκάνη; IACP polis with 4th-c. coins ΑΥΤΟΚΑΝΑΙΩΝ, unlocated, named after Mt Kane)
site: Kane promontory (Kara Dağ peninsula), near Bademli (Dikili, İzmir)
greek_from_text: Lokrian foundation from Kynos (Strabo 13.1.68), undated; if = Autokane, coins c. 400–300 BC; town attested 191 BC (Livy 36.45); survey shows Hellenistic–early Roman town of c. 8 ha
pre_detail: The DAI Kane survey (Pirson et al.) and harbour geoarchaeology describe a c. 8 ha town with finds from the Hellenistic–early Roman period onward. No pre-Greek material is reported, but the publications do not say the site was virgin ground, and the Lokrian foundation is undated.
pre_sources: Fediuk et al. 2019, Kane harbour (ancientportsantiques.com/.../Kane-Fediuk2019.pdf); knowledge: Pirson, AA 2015–2017 (Kane survey)
status_evidence: Strabo 13.1.68 (polichnion); Livy 36.45; Pliny 5.122 (deserted); Autokane: IACP p. 1040, 4th-c. coins
note: City status rests on identifying Kane with the IACP polis Autokane (coins ΑΥΤΟΚΑΝΑ/ΑΥΤΟΚΑΝΑΙΩΝ), which is unlocated but named after Mt Kane; if they are different, Autokane is a separate unlocated polis in this area. Site located by DAI survey (Pirson) 2015.
sources: Strabo 13.1.68; IACP p. 1040 (Autokane); Wikipedia: Canae; Wikipedia: Autokane; DAI Pergamon micro-region survey (Pirson)

greek_from_text: one of the old Aeolian cities (Hdt. 1.149); settled in the Aeolian migration, by tradition soon after Kyme (c. 1050 BC); no individual foundation date, so c. 1000 BC
status_evidence: IACP (Aiolis); Hdt. 1.149; coins; Hierocles; bishops 451, 787
note: Late Bronze Age finds including Mycenaean-type (LH IIIC) pottery come from Çandarlı, but no Mycenaean settlement is shown; dated here from the Aeolian city.

greek_from_text: Athenian tribute lists from the 450s BC; silver coins later 5th c.; Strabo's foundation by Menestheus and Athenians after Troy is legend
pre_detail: The DAI Elaia team's geoarchaeological study concludes that the later acropolis, then a peninsula, was 'most probably uninhabited' in the Late Bronze Age (c. 1500 BC). It also finds that the settlement period was short (max. c. 1000 years), with intense activity from c. 300 BC. No pre-Greek material is reported from Pirson's survey. The Menestheus foundation story is legend.
pre_sources: Seeliger et al. 2018, Elaia harbour (ancientportsantiques.com/.../Elaia-Seeliger2018.pdf); Seeliger et al., 'Elaia, Pergamon's maritime satellite' (research.aber.ac.uk)
status_evidence: IACP (Aiolis); ATL; coins from later 5th c.; port of Pergamon; Hierocles; bishops 431, 451, 787
note: An Aeolic-speaking city not in Herodotus' Aeolian list; certainly older than its first attestation. Harbour of the Attalids.

greek_from_text: one of the old Aeolian cities (Hdt. 1.149); settled in the Aeolian migration, by tradition soon after Kyme (c. 1050 BC); no individual foundation date, so c. 1000 BC
pre_detail: Rejected 'yes': the claim rests on a CNN Türk news report (not evidence). In it M. Çekilmez says his survey from 2015 found only one body sherd datable to the 2nd millennium BC, inside the temple-like building, and that Özkan's unpublished or unseen 1992 rescue excavation 'mentions' 2nd-millennium pottery. That is a single unstratified survey sherd plus an uncheckable reference, and no non-Turkish scholarship reports pre-Aeolian levels. The French 1883 and Bergama Museum 1959 work found only later material.
pre_sources: cnnturk.com/turkiye/tarihe-yeni-bir-soluk-kazandiracak-kehanet-merkezi-gun-yuzune-cikiyor-1061539 (read: quotes Çekilmez on one 2nd-mill. BC sherd); en.wikipedia Gryneium; Pleiades 550555 (periods only Hellenistic/Roman)
status_evidence: IACP (Aiolis); Hdt. 1.149; ATL; Xen. Hell. 3.1.6; coins late 4th–3rd c.; oracle of Apollo
note: Sacked by Parmenion 335/4 BC; later a dependency of Myrina, mainly a sanctuary of Apollo Gryneios.

greek_from_text: one of the old Aeolian cities (Hdt. 1.149); settled in the Aeolian migration, by tradition soon after Kyme (c. 1050 BC); no individual foundation date, so c. 1000 BC
pre_detail: Rejected 'no known': the only basis is a Turkish survey and palaeogeographic paper saying no finds earlier than the Aeolian colonisation were encountered. That is absence of finds in an unexcavated acropolis, not positive evidence of new ground (rule 7). The French excavations of 1880–82 explored only the Hellenistic necropolis. The Myrinos/Amazon Myrina founder traditions are legendary. No non-Turkish source addresses pre-Greek occupation either way.
pre_sources: en.wikipedia Myrina (Aeolis) (necropolis excavations 1880–82; founder traditions in Strabo, Mela, Diodorus); Pleiades 550756 (IACP no. 822, BAtlas 56 D4); first-pass refs Vardar & Yavaşlı, CBÜ SBD 14.3 (2016) and Çekilmez 2011 survey (not re-read)
status_evidence: IACP (Aiolis); Hdt. 1.149; ATL; Hellenistic & Roman coins; Hierocles; bishops 431–787
note: Famous Hellenistic terracotta necropolis. The name Myrina is also that of an Amazon in legend.
refoundations: Myrina → Sebastopolis (after the AD 17 earthquake; honorific)

site: twin hills NW of Uzunhasanlar (Aliağa, İzmir)
greek_from_text: Settlement from the Early/Middle Geometric period (excavations, Erdan); coins of the city 4th–3rd c. BC
pre_detail: Downgraded from 'yes'. Gür (TÜBA-AR 27, 2020) reports only surface-survey finds from Sarıkale and Kocakale Tepe (2018–19): a bronze curved-knife fragment, pottery with parallels in Troy's LBA layers, local grey ware and a pendent-semicircle skyphos sherd. He frames them as LBA–EIA transition material and leaves confirmation to future excavation. The finds are unstratified, come from a Turkish academic report only, and the excavations (Erdan) date the earliest settlement to the Early/Middle Geometric. The lead is promising, but per rule 3 it is not enough for 'yes'.
pre_sources: B. Gür, TÜBA-AR 27 (2020) 113–127, doi:10.22520/tubaar2020.27.007 (abstract via trdizin); Arkhaia Anatolika 2021 (Lydian pottery at Tisna, late 7th–early 6th c., abstract via DOAJ); Pleiades 550933 (Erdan 2018: early- and middle-geometric)
status_evidence: own bronze coins 4th–3rd c. BC (ΤΙΣΝΑ); Pleiades
note: Not in Herodotus' Aeolian list; city status rests on its coinage. Whether the Geometric settlement was already Greek (Aeolian grey ware) is an inference.
sources: Pleiades 550933; Erdan 2018; CoinWeek: minor cities of Aiolis

greek_from_text: Tradition: founded by Aeolians from Phrikion in Lokris c. 1050 BC (Ps.-Hdt. Vita Homeri: 20 years after Lesbos); excavated Greek levels from Protogeometric/Geometric times
pre_detail: The earliest published excavated material is Geometric pottery on the south hill (Akurgal 1953). İdil's report on the Turkish excavations and the Italian work describe no Bronze Age settlement level. The traditions of 'Pelasgian' Larisa and of an Amazon eponym are legend. Stray Bronze Age finds have been mentioned but are not published as a settlement.
pre_sources: V. İdil, Belleten 53 (1989) 525–544 (belleten.gov.tr/tam-metin/2101/eng); en/de.wikipedia Cyme (Aeolis); Pleiades 550506
status_evidence: IACP (Aiolis); Hdt. 1.149; ATL; coins from c. 500 BC; Hierocles; bishops 431–787
note: Leading city of Aeolis and mother city of Cumae in Italy (tradition). Some Bronze Age material has been reported, but no pre-Greek settlement is established.

site: unlocated; perhaps between Larisa and Phokaia (Menemen/Foça, İzmir)

pre_detail: Known only from coins and unlocated, so no archaeological evidence either way.
status_evidence: own coins 4th–3rd c. BC
note: Name absent from literary sources; coins found mostly in the lower Hermos valley; Engelmann placed it between Larisa and Phokaia (BAtlas follows), but the reading behind this is disputed.

note: Unlocated; listed by Herodotus among the mainland Aeolian cities between Kyme and the Kaikos. Coordinates are only a regional centre; it may be identical with a site known by another name.

pre_detail: Excavations at Nemrut Kale (Manisa Museum/Ege Univ., from 2004) and the DAI necropolis survey conclude that the city was founded at the end of the 8th c. BC. No earlier (Bronze Age/native) levels are reported, so the earliest levels are those of the Greek city.
pre_sources: U. Kelp, e-Forschungsberichte DAI 2017/2, 168–172 ('dass die Stadt gegen Ende des 8. Jahrhunderts v. Chr. gegründet wurde'); Pleiades 550404

greek_from_text: one of the old Aeolian cities (Hdt. 1.149); settled in the Aeolian migration, by tradition soon after Kyme (c. 1050 BC); no individual foundation date, so c. 1000 BC
pre_detail: Unexcavated hill site near Emiralem, attested from 4th-c. BC coins and Hellenistic inscriptions. No survey reports earlier (pre-Greek) material, and none states that it was new ground.

Strabo instead makes it older than Kyme. The site near Yanıkköy is only tentatively identified and unexcavated, so there is no archaeological evidence either way.

greek_from_text: New walled town founded by the Genoese lords of Phokaia (Zaccaria), c. 1275–1304, for alum workers
founder: Genoese Zaccaria lords holding Phokaia by grant of Michael VIII (1275); walled c. 1300–1304
pre_detail: New Phocaea was built as a new stronghold, probably between 1286 and 1296, on a separate site north of Old Phocaea for the Genoese alum concession. No earlier non-Greek settlement is known at Yenifoça.

sources: Wikipedia: Yenifoça; Catholic Encyclopedia: Phocaea; Wikipedia: Metropolis of Ephesus; Doukas

greek_from_text: Aeolian (Kymaean) pottery into the 9th c. BC, Ionian from the end of the 9th c.; tradition: Phocians led by the Athenians Philogenes and Damon on land given by Kyme
founder: Phocians under the Athenians Philogenes and Damon (Paus. 7.3.10)
status_evidence: IACP (Ionia); Panionion member; electrum coins c. 600 BC; Hierocles; bishops 344–879
note: Late Bronze Age occupation with LH IIIC sherds and bathtubs (Özyiğit) but not a demonstrable Mycenaean settlement. Mother city of Massalia, Lampsakos, Alalia, Elea. Genoese from 1275, Ottoman 1455.
sources: IACP (Ionia); Paus. 7.3.10; Pleiades 550823; Wikipedia: Phocaea; Gür, Talanta

greek_from_text: Founded as a city on a coastal height by the Persian admiral Tachos (Diod. 15.18, under 383/2 BC; some modern accounts say 352 BC); coins 3rd c. BC
pre_detail: Kept 'no known' on the ancient source: Diodorus 15.18.1 says the Persian commander Tachos founded the city of Leuke on a coastal promontory that had a shrine of Apollo, as a new base. That is a city built from scratch, and the shrine, being Greek, does not count. Bean (PECS; Kleinasien I) and Der Neue Pauly treat it as Tachos' 4th-c. foundation. Anabolu's survey (Belleten 1990) found 4th-c. walls and undated sherds, with no prehistoric material. The site is unexcavated and the Bronze Age site of Panaztepe lies several km away in the Gediz delta, so confidence is low.
pre_sources: Diod. 15.18.1–4 (LacusCurtius, Loeb tr.); M. U. Anabolu, 'Su kuşları ve Leukai', Belleten 54/209 (1990) 29–32 (belleten.gov.tr/tam-metin/2124/tur); de.wikipedia Leukai (Ionien) (lit.: Bean, PECS s.v. Leukai; Bean, Kleinasien I 125–126); Pleiades 550697 (New Pauly s.v. Leucae 2; periods Classical onward)
status_evidence: Diod. 15.18; Strabo 14.1.38; own coins 3rd c. BC; Pliny 5.119
note: Disputed after Tachos' death between Klazomenai and Kyme; Klazomenai won. Base of Aristonikos (133–130 BC). Strabo calls it a polichnion.

other_names: Zmyrna; Eurydikeia (briefly, under Lysimachus); Naulochon (port, Old Smyrna?)
site: İzmir (Konak; Old Smyrna at Bayraklı, Bayraklı, İzmir)
greek_from_text: Greek (Aeolian) pottery at Old Smyrna (Bayraklı) from c. 1000 BC; taken by Kolophonian (Ionian) exiles c. 700 BC; refounded on Mt Pagos under Antigonus and Lysimachus c. 300 BC
founder: Aeolians from Kyme; Ionians from Kolophon took it c. 700 BC (Hdt. 1.150)
pre_greek_note: A place Ti-smurna occurs in Level II Kültepe (Kaneš) tablets (early 2nd millennium BC); its identification with Smyrna is not established. Bayraklı mound was settled from the 3rd millennium BC (Troy I-related), with LBA material showing Mycenaean influence.
status_evidence: IACP (Ionia); Hellenistic & Roman coins; neokoros; Hierocles; bishops from 2nd c. AD; metropolis 9th c.
note: Coordinates are for Hellenistic–Roman Smyrna (Kadifekale/agora); Old Smyrna lies at Bayraklı (38.464, 27.170, Pleiades 550771). Destroyed by Alyattes c. 600 BC, village-like until refoundation. medieval Roman to c. 1330 (Aydınids), Hospitallers 1344–1402.
sources: IACP (Ionia); Hdt. 1.149–150; Strabo 14.1.37; Pleiades 550893, 550771; Wikipedia: İzmir
refoundations: Old Smyrna (Bayraklı) → new city on Mt Pagos (Antigonus/Lysimachus c. 300 BC), briefly Eurydikeia; rebuilt by John III Vatatzes c. 1222

site: Liman Tepe and Karantina island, Urla İskele (Urla, İzmir)
greek_from_text: Ionian foundation (tradition: Parphoros/Paralos of Kolophon with settlers from Kleonai and Phleious); Early Iron Age (Protogeometric) Greek material at Liman Tepe
founder: Parphoros (Paus. 7.3.9) or Paralos (Strabo 14.1.3), from Kolophon, with Kleonaians and Phleiasians
status_evidence: IACP (Ionia); Panionion member; ATL; coins from 6th c.; Hierocles; bishops 431, 451
note: Liman Tepe was a major Chalcolithic–Late Bronze Age site; its LH IIIC phase has locally made Mycenaean-style pottery that some (Gür) read as Aegean newcomers, but it is not counted as a Mycenaean city. The city moved to Karantina island after c. 500 BC (coordinates).
refoundations: mainland site → island (Karantina) after the Ionian Revolt; linked to the mainland by Alexander's causeway

greek_from_text: Athenian tribute lists 450/49–430/29 BC
pre_detail: Small stronghold with a tentative, unexcavated site (Büyük Ada?). No evidence either way.
status_evidence: IACP (Ionia, pp. 1098–99); ATL
note: Small fortified dependency of Erythrai (Thuc. 8.24 calls it a stronghold); Pliny makes it an island. Site tentative (BAtlas).

greek_from_text: Athenian tribute lists 450/49–430/29 BC
pre_detail: Small fortified dependency of Erythrai with a tentative, unexcavated site. No evidence either way.
status_evidence: IACP (Ionia, p. 1093); ATL
note: Fortified dependency of Erythrai, Athenian base 412 BC (Thuc. 8.24, 31); counted only because it paid tribute separately.

greek_from_text: Ionian foundation by Knopos son of Kodros (tradition, c. 1000 BC); after an earlier settlement of Cretans under Erythros with Lycians, Carians and Pamphylians (Paus. 7.3.7)
status_evidence: IACP (Ionia); Panionion member; ATL; coins from 6th c.; Hierocles; bishops 431–1292
note: Early Bronze Age settlement on the acropolis; Archaic finds 7th–6th c. Ildır < Lythri < Erythrai.

greek_from_text: Athenian tribute lists 454/3–427/6 BC
pre_detail: The site is only approximately placed (BAtlas *Boutheia) near Çeşme. If it lay in Çeşme town, it would sit beside the excavated Bronze Age harbour settlement of Çeşme–Bağlararası (Şahoğlu), but the location is too uncertain to count.
pre_sources: Pleiades 550488 (BAtlas 56 C5 *Boutheia); luwianstudies.org/site/cesme-baglararasi; Şahoğlu et al., Çeşme–Bağlararası publications
status_evidence: IACP (Ionia, p. 1064); ATL
note: Dependency of Erythrai, sometimes listed under Erythrai in the tribute lists; site tentative.
sources: IACP (Ionia); Steph. Byz. s.v. Βούθεια; Wikipedia: Boutheia

greek_from_text: Athenian tribute lists 454/3–427/6 BC; own coins 4th c. BC (ΑΙΡΑΙΩΝ)
pre_detail: Site near Aşağı Demircili is unexcavated, and no survey of early material is published. No evidence either way.
status_evidence: IACP (Ionia, p. 1063); ATL; Thuc. 8.19–20; coins 4th c.
note: Later a small town subject to Teos (Strabo 14.1.32).

greek_from_text: Tradition: Minyans of Orchomenos under Athamas, then Ionians under Nauklos, Apoikos, Damasos and Geres (Paus. 7.3.6; Strabo 14.1.3); c. 1000 BC
founder: Athamas (Minyans); Ionians under Nauklos, Apoikos, Damasos and Geres
pre_detail: The excavators (Kadıoğlu) find the earliest settlement begins in the Protogeometric period, but the area of that settlement has not yet been located, and they list a possible Mycenaean settlement as a research aim. Vaessen notes that no Mycenaean finds have been reported. Pausanias' Carians living with the settlers (7.3.6) is tradition only.
pre_sources: Teos excavation page, KTB (bingol.ktb.gov.tr/Eklenti/9475,teos-kazisipdf.pdf); Vaessen 2014, Cultural Dynamics in Ionia (Sheffield PhD) p. 26; N. Tuna, AST 12 (1995)
status_evidence: IACP (Ionia); Panionion member; ATL; coins from c. 540 BC; Hierocles; bishop 431
note: Pausanias mentions Carians living with the settlers (tradition only). Teians founded Abdera (c. 545) and Phanagoria; Antigonus planned a synoecism with Lebedos (c. 303 BC).

greek_from_text: Ionian foundation by Andraimon son of Kodros (Paus. 7.3.5) or Andropompos (Strabo 14.1.3), tradition c. 1000 BC
pre_detail: Tradition only: Strabo 14.1.3 (Andropompus seized a place called Artis) and Pausanias 7.3.5 (Carians before the Ionians); no archaeological evidence of a pre-Greek settlement. Strabo (14.1.3) says Andropompos founded Lebedos after seizing 'a place called Artis', which is an attested pre-Greek name for the site. Pausanias (7.3.5) says Carians held it before the Ionians. Both belong to the Ionian migration tradition, and survey (Çevirici-Coşkun 2017–19) has found no pre-Greek material, so this rests on the literary name alone.
status_evidence: IACP (Ionia); Panionion member; ATL; Hellenistic coins; Hierocles
note: Pausanias says Carians held the site before (tradition only). Renamed Ptolemais under the Ptolemies; seat of the Ionian Dionysiac artists.

greek_from_text: Athenian tribute lists (Διοσιρῖται), mid-5th c. BC
pre_detail: The exact site on the coast near Gümüldür is uncertain and unexcavated. No evidence either way.
status_evidence: IACP (Ionia); ATL; Thuc. 8.19
note: Small coastal polis between Lebedos and Kolophon; not to be confused with Lydian Dios Hieron (Birgi) in the Kaystros valley. Exact site uncertain.

other_names: Kolophon by the sea (Colophon ad Mare)
greek_from_text: one of the old Aeolian cities (Hdt. 1.149); settled in the Aeolian migration, by tradition soon after Kyme (c. 1050 BC); no individual foundation date, so c. 1000 BC
pre_detail: The Michigan intensive survey finds that the present site was 'largely uninhabited before the 2nd century BCE', with intensive occupation only from the 3rd/2nd c. BC to the 1st c. AD. No prehistoric material is reported. However, the earlier Notion (attested from the 6th c. BC) probably lay nearer the harbour and is now buried by silt, so its antecedents are unknown.
pre_sources: Notion Archaeological Survey (sites.lsa.umich.edu/notionsurvey); Ratté et al., Archaeological Survey at Notion (Univ. of Michigan Press); ASCSA lecture abstract
status_evidence: IACP (Ionia); Hdt. 1.149; ATL; Thuc. 3.34; late-antique city
note: After Lysimachus moved Kolophonians to Ephesos (c. 294 BC), Notion became ‘Kolophon by the sea’; the Late Roman see of Kolophon may have been here.
refoundations: Notion → Kolophon by the Sea (after c. 294 BC)

greek_from_text: Ionian foundation by Andraimon of Pylos (Strabo 14.1.3, after Mimnermus) or by Damasichthon and Promethos, sons of Kodros (Paus. 7.3.3); tradition c. 1000 BC; Geometric houses on the acropolis
founder: Andraimon of Pylos (Strabo) / Damasichthon and Promethos (Paus.)
status_evidence: IACP (Ionia); Panionion member; ATL; coins; Hierocles; bishop 431
note: A tholos tomb of Mycenaean type (LH IIIB–C or Submycenaean) was found here, but no Mycenaean settlement; tradition puts Cretans under Rhakios and Carians here before the Ionians. Partly moved to Ephesos by Lysimachus c. 294 BC.

site: Efes ruins and Ayasuluk hill, Selçuk (Selçuk, İzmir)
greek_from_text: Ionian foundation by Androklos son of Kodros (tradition, c. 1050 BC); Protogeometric pottery at Ayasuluk and the Artemision, 10th c. BC
pre_greek_note: Apaša, capital of Arzawa, taken by Mursili II (late 14th c. BC); identification with Ephesos/Ayasuluk accepted by most scholars. Ayasuluk has a LBA settlement with Mycenaean pottery and a Mycenaean-type grave, not a Mycenaean city.
status_evidence: IACP (Ionia); Panionion member; electrum coins late 7th c.; capital of Roman Asia; Hierocles (metropolis); bishops 325–787
note: Medieval city moved to Ayasuluk (Hagios Theologos), Turkish 1304; modern Selçuk (named 1914; earlier Ayasluğ < Hagios Theologos) covers the medieval site, the Roman city (Efes) is ruins 3 km SW.
refoundations: moved by Lysimachus c. 294 BC to a new site as Arsinoeia (name soon dropped); medieval Hagios Theologos on Ayasuluk hill

greek_from_text: Greek settlement on the acropolis after the 9th c. BC; urban polis from the 3rd c. BC (theatre, bouleuterion 2nd c.); civic decrees 143 and 132 BC
pre_greek_note: Puranda, the Arzawan stronghold where refugees from Apaša fled and which Mursili II took, is placed at Bademgediği Tepe beside Metropolis by the excavators (Meriç); the identification is plausible but unproven.
status_evidence: Hellenistic decrees (SEG 53.1312); coins; Strabo 14.1.15; Hierocles; bishop 451
note: Early and Middle Bronze Age pottery on the acropolis; on adjacent Bademgediği Tepe a LBA fortified site with much locally made Mycenaean-style (LH IIIB–C) pottery, an Anatolian rather than Mycenaean settlement.
sources: Strabo 14.1.15; Meriç 2003 (Bademgediği Tepe); Pleiades 550741; Wikipedia: Metropolis (Anatolia)

greek_from_text: Delian League member (tribute lists from the 450s BC); coins with legend ΦΥΓ/ΦΥΓΑΛΕΩΝ c. 350–300 BC; legend of foundation by Agamemnon's veterans (Strabo 14.1.20)
pre_detail: Excavations at Kuştur north of Kuşadası (Gürçay, Akurgal, to 1975) exposed the Hellenistic agora and later remains. No pre-Greek level is reported, and the foundation by Agamemnon's veterans is legend. No statement that it was new ground.
pre_sources: grandsirkeci.com article on Pygela (summarising the excavations); Strabo 14.1.20; Pleiades 599887
status_evidence: IACP (Ionia); ATL; coins c. 350–300 BC
note: Ionian town outside the dodecapolis; exact site within Kuşadası not fixed.
sources: Strabo 14.1.20; IACP (Ionia): Pygela; Pleiades 599887; Wikipedia: Pygela

site: Ambar Tepe, south of Kuşadası (Kuşadası, Aydın)
greek_from_text: in the Athenian tribute lists 443/2–415/4 BC; dependent polis held by Samos, later exchanged to Ephesus (Strabo 14.1.20)
pre_detail: Site disputed (Ambar Tepe, largely destroyed, or under modern Kuşadası), with no excavated finds. The suggestion that the name is Greek (Linear B ma-ra-tu-wo) is irrelevant to pre-Greek settlement.
status_evidence: IACP (dependent polis); ATL 443/2–415/4
note: Site disputed: Ambar Tepe (Lohmann, followed by Pleiades) or the harbour of Kuşadası (Keil).
sources: IACP (Ionia): Marathesion; Strabo 14.1.20; Pleiades 599784; Wikipedia: Marathesium

greek_from_text: tradition: fortified by Samians expelled by Androklos of Ephesus during the Ionian settlement (Paus. 7.4.3); first historical mention 428 BC (Thuc. 3.19)
status_evidence: IACP (Ionia); Thuc. 3.19, 4.75; bishops 325–787; medieval Roman fortress town
note: Kadıkalesi mound has Chalcolithic to Late Bronze Age levels with Mycenaean pottery (not counted as a Mycenaean settlement); the Samian foundation date is only traditional.

other_names: Melia; Karion (Hellenistic fort on the site)
site: Kale Tepe (Çatallar Tepe) near Güzelçamlı (Kuşadası, Aydın)
greek_from_text: fortified Geometric settlement (8th c. BC) identified with Melie by H. Lohmann; early member of the Ionian League, destroyed by the other Ionians in the 'Meliac war' (c. 7th c. BC)
pre_detail: Lohmann's excavation on Çatallar Tepe (his site of Melie, not Kale Tepe/Karion) found an 8th-c. BC fortified settlement as the earliest occupation, with no Bronze Age level. But Lohmann, following Hecataeus ('polis of Caria'), takes Melie as a Carian town, while Vitruvius 4.1.4 counts it as Ionian. If Carian, it is a native town; if Ionian, new ground. Unresolved.
pre_sources: H. Lohmann 2012, 'Ionians and Carians in the Mycale: the discovery of Carian Melia and the Archaic Panionion' (Cifani & Stoddart eds., Oxbow); en.wikipedia Melia (Ionia); Vitr. 4.1.4
status_evidence: Vitruvius 4.1.4 (one of 13 Ionian cities); Lohmann's survey/excavation
note: Identification of Kale Tepe with Melie is Lohmann's; some think the Melians were Carians. The city ceased to exist in the 7th c. BC.

greek_from_text: Ionian dodecapolis; tradition: founded by Aipytos son of Neleus and Philotas of Thebes (Strabo 14.1.3; Paus. 7.2.10); refounded on the present site c. 350 BC
founder: Aipytos son of Neleus and Philotas of Thebes (tradition)
pre_detail: The excavated city (the coordinates given) was laid out on a fresh site c. 350 BC. Excavation reports find foundation-period buildings set in find-free soil, with no earlier occupation. The Archaic predecessor is unlocated (buried by Maeander silt). The older name Kadme (Strabo 14.1.12) is Boeotian, not native.
pre_sources: Prienebericht 2001, Univ. Frankfurt ('in fundfreiem Boden verlegt'); Forschung Frankfurt 2/2005 ('bis jetzt nicht lokalisierte Vorgängersiedlung'); Strabo 14.1.12
status_evidence: IACP (Ionia); Panionian League; coins; Hierocles; bishop 431
note: Coordinates are the 4th-c. BC city; the Archaic city, abandoned because of Maeander silting, has not been found.
refoundations: Archaic Priene (unlocated) → new city at Güllübahçe c. 350 BC

greek_from_text: Ionian dodecapolis; tradition: founded by Kydrelos (Kyaretos) son of Kodros (Strabo 14.1.3; Paus. 7.2.10)
pre_detail: Weber's excavations (1964–66) found the Archaic temples and a 6th–5th c. floruit as the earliest material, with no pre-Greek level. But the settlement was not explored, so new ground is not shown. The Carians expelled by the Ionians (Paus. 7.2.10) is tradition only.
pre_sources: H. Weber, 'Myus. Grabungen 1964 und 1966', TAD (taed.ktb.gov.tr/Eklenti/109181); en.wikipedia Myus; Paus. 7.2.10
status_evidence: IACP (Ionia); ATL; coins; sympoliteia with Miletus c. 200 BC
note: Pausanias says the Ionians expelled Carians here, but no pre-Greek levels are known. Silting emptied the town; it was merged into Miletus, with a small medieval Roman resettlement.

greek_from_text: Mycenaean settlement LH IIIA (c. 1400 BC), after a Minoan phase; Ionian city by tradition founded by Neleus c. 1050 BC
founder: Mycenaean Greeks; refounded by Ionians under Neleus (tradition)
pre_greek_note: Hittite Millawanda/Milawata, identified with Miletus by most scholars (Ahhiyawa texts)
status_evidence: IACP 854; coins; Hierocles; bishops 325–787
note: Earlier Minoan settlement (Miletus IV); Mycenaean levels V–VI.

other_names: Magnesia ad Maeandrum; Leukophrys (site of the later city)
greek_from_text: existing by the 7th c. BC (destroyed by the Cimmerians c. 650 BC; Archilochus fr. 20; Strabo 14.1.40); tradition: Magnetes from Thessaly (via Crete); moved to Leukophrys c. 400 BC
pre_detail: The c. 400 BC city at Leukophrys grew around an older (by the 6th c. BC) sanctuary of Artemis. No prehistoric or native settlement level is published from the excavations (Humann 1891–93; Bingöl from 1984). The story of Leukophryene betraying her father's city to the Magnetes is myth, and the Archaic city is unlocated.
pre_sources: turkisharchaeonews.net/node/104; en.wikipedia Magnesia on the Maeander; Xen. Hell. 3.2.19; Parthenius 5
status_evidence: IACP (Ionia); coins; Hierocles; bishops 431–680
note: Strabo calls it Aeolian. The Archaic city near the Maeander is unlocated; coordinates are the city refounded by Thibron at Leukophrys c. 400/399 BC.
sources: Strabo 14.1.39-40; IACP (Ionia): Magnesia; Pleiades 599778; Wikipedia: Magnesia on the Maeander
refoundations: Archaic Magnesia (unlocated) → Leukophrys site c. 400/399 BC (Thibron)

greek_from_text: medieval Roman town: first mentioned by Anna Komnene (base of Eumathios Philokales, 1108); bishopric 12th c., archbishopric 13th c.
pre_detail: No pre-Greek levels reported for the Kemalpaşa (Nif) town site; the nearest prehistoric site is Yenmiş Höyük (Neolithic), c. 5 km away, and the Archaic/Lydian-period sites of the Nif Dağı project lie on the mountain to the south, not at the town.
pre_sources: https://vici.org/vici/30373/ (Nif fortress, nearby Yenmiş Höyük); Pleiades 550778
status_evidence: bishopric 12th c.; archbishopric 13th c.; Laskarid winter residence; council of 1234; Treaty of Nymphaion 1261
note: A Hellenistic place of this name existed (BAtlas) but no ancient city. Fell to the Turks c. 1315. Ottoman Nif continued the Greek name; the town was renamed Kemalpaşa in the 20th c.
sources: Anna Komnene, Alexiad 14; byzantine-world.com: Nymphaion; Pleiades 550778

greek_from_text: Raised to a city as Arkadioupolis under Arcadius (395–408), to judge by the name; bishops 431–879; Hierocles
status_evidence: Hierocles; bishops 431–879
note: Teira/Thyaira appears in Roman times probably as a village of Ephesian territory; Greek tradition linked a Lydian town Tyrrha with Gyges. Identification of Arkadioupolis with Tire is standard but rests on location and continuity.
sources: Wikipedia: Arcadiopolis in Asia; Pleiades 599981; Hierocles

site: lower Kaystros plain between Bayındır and Tire (İzmir)
greek_from_text: Own bronze coins of the 2nd–1st c. BC (BMC Lydia 7–9)
status_evidence: Hellenistic civic coins
note: Known as an ethnic on coins; may have been a community (koinon) of the plain rather than one town; site unknown.

greek_from_text: Greek city by the late Hellenistic period: revolted against Mithridates (88 BC); civic coins from the 1st c. BC/Augustus
status_evidence: Strabo 13.4.7; coins to Gallienus; Hierocles; bishops 325–787; metropolis under Isaac II
note: Lydian town with a Persian cult of Artemis Anaitis (‘Persian Lydians’, Paus. 5.27.5). Earliest coin date not checked against RPC here.

other_names: Diospolis (Steph. Byz.); Christoupolis (7th c.); Pyrgion (from 12th c.)
greek_from_text: First civic coins under Augustus (RPC I 2556, ΔΙΟΣΙΕΡΙΤΩΝ)
status_evidence: Roman provincial coins; Hierocles; bishops 431–880; metropolis (Pyrgion) late 12th c.–1368
note: Upper Kaystros (Kilbian) town; the council seed ‘Christopolis’ is the same see. Exact relation of the ancient site to Birgi (Pyrgion, Aydınid capital from 1307) is approximate. Distinct from Ionian Dioshieron on the coast.
sources: RPC I 2556; Pleiades 550515; Wikipedia: Dios Hieron (Lydia)
refoundations: Dios Hieron → Christoupolis (7th c.) → Pyrgion (12th c.)

other_names: Kilbianoi around Nikaia (Κιλβιανοὶ οἱ περὶ Νείκαιαν); Cilbiani Inferiores?
site: upper Kaystros (Kilbian) plain SE of Ödemiş (İzmir)
greek_from_text: Roman provincial coins of the Kilbianoi around Nikaia, c. 138–140 under Antoninus Pius (RPC IV.2 1215)
status_evidence: Roman provincial coins (2nd c. AD)
note: Civic centre of the native Kilbianoi of the lower Kilbian plain; earlier issues may exist. Site not excavated.

greek_from_text: Civic coins of the Upper Kilbianoi under Nero (RPC I 2565–2566, AD 54–59)
status_evidence: Roman provincial coins Nero–Antoninus Pius; Hierocles 660; bishops 431, 692, 787
note: RPC attributes the Upper Kilbianoi coinage to Koloe. Leo the Deacon (born here) calls it a village in the 10th c.

greek_from_text: First bishop (Rhodon) at the Council of Ephesus 431; Hierocles 660.4
pre_detail: Unexcavated and only approximately located (Beydağ/Çaylı); known only as a late antique see. The name 'Old City' implies an older settlement but says nothing about a non-Greek one.
status_evidence: Hierocles; bishops 431–879; Notitiae to 13th c.
note: Secular history unknown; placed at or near Beydağ by BAtlas (council seed: near Çaylı).

site: unlocated, upper Kaystros valley (Ödemiş–Kiraz area?, İzmir)
greek_from_text: First bishop (Eutropius) at the Council of Ephesus 431; Hierocles
status_evidence: Hierocles; bishops 431–787; Notitiae
note: A small town in the hills behind Ephesus (case of Bassianos, Chalcedon 451); location unknown, coordinates a regional guess. Anatolian-looking name.

other_names: Magnesia Sipylou; Manisa (Turkish); residence and treasury of the Nicaean emperors (13th c.)
greek_from_text: first certain mention by Hellanicus (5th c. BC); polis with Seleucid military settlers in the sympoliteia with Smyrna (c. 245 BC, OGIS 229)
pre_detail: No pre-Greek settlement is known under Manisa. The Late Bronze Age Akpınar relief lies c. 7 km away on Sipylos, and the 'Tantalis' of Pliny and the Thessalian-Magnete origin are legend. Early Bronze Age (Yortan) material belongs to other places in the province.
pre_sources: en.wikipedia Manisa and Magnesia ad Sipylum; Plin. NH 5.117; Pleiades 550706
status_evidence: Hellanicus; OGIS 229; Hellenistic & Roman coins; AD 17 earthquake list (Tacitus Ann. 2.47); bishops 431–879
note: The Thessalian-Magnete founding tradition (cf. Magnesia on the Maeander) is late and cannot be dated, so the date is the first attestation. The Late Bronze Age rock relief at Akpınar on Sipylos is nearby, but no pre-Greek settlement is known under the town. Battle of Magnesia 190 BC; Nicaean imperial seat under John III Vatatzes; fell to the Turks (Saruhan) in 1313.
sources: Ihnken, IK 8 (1978); OGIS 229; Tacitus Ann. 2.47; Pleiades 550706; Wikipedia: Magnesia ad Sipylum
refoundations: Rebuilt with Tiberius' aid after the AD 17 earthquake

site: unlocated; BAtlas tentatively near Sancaklıbozköy (Manisa), at the E foot of Sipylos in the Hyrcanian plain
greek_from_text: Hellenistic civic bronze coins with legend ΜΟΣΤΗΝΩΝ (2nd c. BC); city in the AD 17 earthquake list
status_evidence: Hellenistic & Roman coins (to Gallienus); Tacitus Ann. 2.47; Ptolemy 5.2; see under Sardis (Notitiae)
note: Cohen (1995) treats it as a native Lydian community, not a Macedonian colony. Its site is not found, so certainty is probable rather than secure.
sources: Tacitus Ann. 2.47; Cohen 1995; Pleiades 550752; Wikipedia: Mostene

site: near Halitpaşa (Saruhanlı, Manisa), in the Hyrcanian plain
greek_from_text: Persian military colony of Hyrcanians (Strabo 13.4.13); Macedonian settlers added under the early Seleucids (3rd c. BC); polis by the Roman period
status_evidence: Roman coins (ΥΡΚΑΝΩΝ); Tacitus Ann. 2.47 ('Macedones Hyrcani'); Hierocles; bishop 787
note: The Persian colony is known only from Strabo. The date of the Macedonian settlement is inferred, not recorded. The site is placed only roughly (BAtlas).

other_names: Aureliopolis (on coins from the reign of Marcus Aurelius, c. AD 160s)
greek_from_text: first attested as a city in the AD 17 earthquake list (Tacitus Ann. 2.47); coins from Hadrian
status_evidence: Tacitus Ann. 2.47; Roman coins (Hadrian–Caracalla); Hierocles (Aureliopolis); bishops 325, 431, 680–81, 787
note: The council see 'Aureliopolis' (seed) is Tmolos. The site near Ahmetli is not precisely fixed.

other_names: Hyde? (Homer, Il. 20.385; identification disputed); Caesarea (title after the AD 17 earthquake, Tiberius); Sart (Turkish)
greek_from_text: Lydian capital; became a Greek polis under Antiochus I/II (c. 270s–250s BC): civic bronzes ΣΑΡΔΙΑΝΩΝ c. 240–220 BC; boule and demos addressed by Antiochus III in 213 BC
pre_greek_note: Lydian Sfard- in Lydian inscriptions (ethnic sfardẽtiś 'Sardian'); Old Persian Sparda; Aramaic SPRD in the Lydian–Aramaic bilingual. Secure.
status_evidence: Seleucid royal letters (213 BC); Hellenistic & Roman coins; Hierocles (metropolis of Lydia); bishops 325–787
note: Late Bronze Age occupation, then the Lydian royal city from the 7th c. BC. An older view (Hanfmann) dated the polis to Antiochus III's resettlement of 213 BC. Turkish c. 1310s.
sources: Berlin & Kosmin (eds.), Spear-Won Land (2019); Gauthier, Nouvelles inscriptions de Sardes II (1989); Pleiades 550867; Wikipedia: Sardis
refoundations: Rebuilt with Tiberius' aid after the AD 17 earthquake (styled Caesarea)

site: unlocated; probably on Mt Tmolos (Bozdağ) (the old placement at Takmak, Eşme, Uşak is doubtful)
greek_from_text: first attested in Hierocles' Synecdemus (c. 527); later a see under Sardis
pre_detail: Unlocated late-antique see on Mt Tmolos. No evidence either way.
status_evidence: Hierocles; Notitiae Episcopatuum (suffragan of Sardis)
note: The name means 'mid-Tmolos'. It may be a late-antique successor community on the mountain, but no site or earlier evidence is known. The coordinates are a regional guess.

other_names: Neocaesarea (after AD 17, Tiberius); Flavia Philadelphia (Vespasian); Alaşehir (Turkish)
greek_from_text: Attalid foundation named after Attalus II Philadelphus; founded by Eumenes II after 189 BC or by Attalus II himself (159–138 BC)
pre_detail: Rejected 'yes': every cited source is an excluded type (turkishmuseums, kureansiklopedi, LuwianSiteAtlas, TDV). TDV's 'probably on an older site' is a conjecture. No excavation report establishes that the Gevurtepe/Gavurtepe protohistoric mound is within 1–2 km of the Toptepe acropolis, or gives its stratified dates. PECS, Der Neue Pauly and de/en Wikipedia treat Philadelphia as an Attalid foundation and mention no earlier settlement. A Turkish or AJA report on Gevurtepe would be needed.
pre_sources: en.wikipedia Alaşehir; de.wikipedia Philadelphia (Lydien) (lit.: PECS s.v. Philadelphia, TAM V.3); Pleiades 550822 (periods Hellenistic onward); luwianstudies.org/sites/gavurtepe-alasehir (no usable content)
status_evidence: Hellenistic & Roman coins; Tacitus Ann. 2.47; Hierocles; bishops 325, 680–81, 787; medieval Roman city to 1390
note: One of the Seven Churches of Revelation. It was the last medieval Roman city in western Asia Minor and fell to Bayezid I in 1390.

site: between Sazoba and Kumkuyucak (Manisa), S of Akhisar
greek_from_text: Hellenistic sanctuary village of the Persian Artemis (Hiera Kome); a city under the name Hierocaesarea by AD 17 (Tacitus Ann. 2.47); Roman coins
status_evidence: Tacitus Ann. 2.47, 3.62; Roman coins; Hierocles; bishops 451, 787, 879
note: Tacitus (Ann. 3.62) says the temple of the 'Persian Diana' was dedicated under Cyrus. The name 'Caesarea' dates from Augustus or Tiberius, but the exact date of city status is unknown.

other_names: Pelopia, Euhippa (earlier names, Pliny NH 5.115); Akhisar (Turkish)
site: Akhisar (Manisa); Tepe Mezarlığı in the town centre
greek_from_text: Macedonian military colony founded by Seleucus I during his war with Lysimachus, 282/281 BC (Stephanus s.v.); dedication of 'the Macedonians in Thyateira' (OGIS 211)
status_evidence: OGIS 211; Hellenistic & Roman coins; Hierocles; bishops 325, 431
note: Pliny gives the earlier names Pelopia and Euhippa. The prehistoric mound at Tepe Mezarlığı and nearby Hastane Höyük show Bronze Age occupation. One of the Seven Churches of Revelation.
sources: Stephanus Byz. s.v. Θυάτειρα; OGIS 211; Cohen 1995; Pleiades 550924

greek_from_text: Attalid foundation named after Queen Apollonis (wife of Attalus I); founded by Eumenes II after 188 BC or by Attalus II (Strabo 13.4.4)
pre_detail: Schuchhardt (1888) read an inscription at Palamut naming 'Macedonians from Doidye' and dated the polygonal walls to c. 300 BC. He concluded that Doidye, a non-Greek name, was the pre-Attalid name of the place. Apollonis was thus a renaming/refoundation of an existing settlement with Seleucid Macedonian settlers. That the Doidye settlement was native rests on the name alone.
pre_sources: C. Schuchhardt, AM 13 (1888) 1–17 (archive.org/download/mitteilungen13deut); en.wikipedia Apollonis (Lydia); Hirschfeld, RE II.1 (1895) 163
status_evidence: Strabo 13.4.4; Hellenistic & Roman coins; Tacitus Ann. 2.47; Hierocles; see under Sardis
note: Strabo places it 300 stadia from both Pergamon and Sardis. A second Pleiades entry (550445) is only a regional label.

site: unlocated; BAtlas places it (with Thyessos?) near Zeytinliova (Akhisar, Manisa)
greek_from_text: first attested by its Roman provincial coins (late 1st–3rd c. AD)
pre_detail: Unlocated (Roman coins only). No evidence either way.
status_evidence: Roman coins (RPC: Hermocapelia); Hierocles; bishop 787
note: Greek name ('Hermes' market'). The site is not fixed, and the exact start of its coinage is not verified.
sources: RPC online: Hermocapelia; Pleiades 550574; Wikipedia: Hermocapelia

other_names: Nakrason / Nakrasos; often equated with Akrasos (disputed)
site: probably Maltepe near Bakır (Kırkağaç, Manisa); alternatives Bakır or İlyaslar
greek_from_text: Macedonian military settlement ('the Macedonians at Nakrasa') attested in a Hellenistic inscription of the Attalid period; probably a 3rd-c. Seleucid foundation; Roman coins ΝΑΚΡΑΣΕΙΤΩΝ
status_evidence: Hellenistic inscription of the Macedonians; Roman coins (RPC: Nacrasa); Ptolemy 5.2.16
note: The Maltepe mound has 3rd–2nd millennium BC occupation (Pleiades), if that identification is right. Whether the founders were Seleucid or Attalid is not known.
sources: Cohen 1995, 196–197; Ptolemy 5.2.16; RPC online: Nacrasa; Pleiades 550767

other_names: Akrassos; often equated with Nakrasa (Ptolemy 5.2.16), but the two mint separately
site: unlocated; upper Kaikos valley, perhaps near İlyaslar (Kırkağaç area, Manisa)
greek_from_text: first attested by Roman provincial coins ΑΚΡΑΣΙΩΤΩΝ (Imperial period, c. late 1st–3rd c. AD)
status_evidence: Roman coins (RPC: Acrasus, 87 types); Hierocles; Notitiae (suffragan of Sardis)
note: It is kept separate from Nakrasa because RPC lists Acrasus and Nacrasa as distinct mints. If they are one place, merge them. The site is unknown.
sources: RPC online: Acrasus; Wikipedia: Acrassus; Cohen 1995, 196–197

other_names: Agroeira or Alloeira (earlier names, Stephanus s.v.)
greek_from_text: Attalid refoundation of the native town Agroeira/Alloeira (3rd–2nd c. BC); Roman coins ΑΤΤΑΛΕΑΤΩΝ
status_evidence: Stephanus Byz.; Roman coins; Hierocles; bishops 451, 787
note: The former names come only from Stephanus and are recorded in Greek, so they are not counted as pre-Greek names. Which Attalus founded it is unknown.
sources: Stephanus Byz. s.v. Ἀττάλεια; Cohen 1995; Pleiades 550472; Wikipedia: Attaleia (Lydia)

other_names: Hadrianopolis (Hadrian, after his visit of 123/124); Stratonikeia-Hadrianopolis
greek_from_text: royal foundation named after a queen Stratonike: probably Attalid (Eumenes II, who married Stratonike c. 188 BC), possibly Seleucid (3rd c. BC)
pre_detail: Older accounts (Smith; Wikipedia) say the city was earlier called 'Indi', from coin ethnics of Trajan–Hadrian, and call it a Lydian village. But Robert explained the 'Indoi' as Indian (elephant-driver) settlers of the Seleucid era, so the name is not clearly pre-Greek. There is no archaeological evidence from Siledik.
pre_sources: en.wikipedia Stratonicea (Lydia); knowledge: L. Robert, Villes d'Asie Mineure; Cohen 1995 (Stratonikeia, Lydia); Pleiades 550898
status_evidence: Hellenistic & Roman coins; letter of Hadrian to Stratonikeia-Hadrianopolis (AD 127); Hierocles; bishop 431
note: Whether the founder was Attalid or Seleucid is debated (Robert 1962; Cohen 1995).
sources: Robert, Villes d'Asie Mineure (1962); Cohen 1995; Pleiades 550898

site: unlocated; RPC/Pleiades place it N of Gelenbe on the Manisa–Balıkesir border (BAtlas 'Kamai' at 38.96N 27.52E is an alternative)
greek_from_text: first attested by Roman provincial coins ΚΑΜΗΝΩΝ (Imperial period, probably 2nd–3rd c. AD)
status_evidence: Roman coins (RPC: Came, 14 types)
note: A small minting community. Its site and the exact dates of its coins are not verified. It sits on the Manisa/Balıkesir border, so it may also appear in the TRO batch.

site: Nardı/Narlı Kale, N of the Hermos (Salihli–Gölmarmara area, Manisa)
greek_from_text: a city by the Flavian period: coins with the title Flaviocaesarea (AD 69–96); Roman coins continue into the 3rd c.
status_evidence: Roman coins (RPC: Daldis); Hierocles; bishops 431, 680–81, 787
note: It may have received city status together with the Flavian name. Earlier pseudo-autonomous coins are possible but not verified here.
sources: RPC online: Daldis; Pleiades 550508; TAM V,1

greek_from_text: first attested as a city through its bishop Elpidius, deposed in 360; Hellenistic and Roman village remains; never minted coins
status_evidence: bishops c. 360, 451, 787, 879; Hierocles
note: A village of the Katakekaumene in the Roman period (with Ioudda in its territory), and a city only in late antiquity. That Adala continues the name Satala is likely but not proven.
sources: Socrates & Philostorgius (Elpidius); Wikipedia: Satala in Lydia; Ege Univ. thesis 'Lydia'daki Satala (Adala) antik kenti'; Pleiades 550869

greek_from_text: Roman-period community styling itself Charakipolis/Charakipolitai (2nd–3rd c. AD), which implies civic status
pre_detail: Location only approximate (near Karayakup) and unexcavated; the name suggests a Hellenistic fort. No evidence either way.
status_evidence: inscriptions (TAM V,1); BAtlas; city status implied by the -polis name
note: Its city status rests on the -polis name; it is not in Hierocles or the conciliar lists. The name Charax ('stockade') suggests a Hellenistic fort. Coins attributed to it are not verified here. Drop it if a stricter standard is used.

greek_from_text: Roman-period community named Flaviopolis after the Flavian emperors (AD 69–96), known from inscriptions
founder: Flavian emperors (grant of name and status)
status_evidence: inscriptions (BAtlas/DARE); imperial -polis name
note: It has no coins, no Hierocles entry and no known bishops, so city status rests only on the imperial name. Drop it if a stricter standard is used.

greek_from_text: first attested by Roman provincial coins ΤΟΜΑΡΗΝΩΝ (Imperial period, probably 2nd–3rd c. AD)
status_evidence: Roman coins (RPC: Tomara, 13 types)
note: A small minting community, not in Hierocles. The exact dates of its coins are not verified.
sources: RPC online: Tomara; Pleiades 550938; WildWinds: Tomaris

site: unlocated; N of the Hermos near Köprübaşı (council-list region); Wikipedia suggests Eliesler
greek_from_text: first attested as a city by its bishop Menecrates at Chalcedon (451); Hierocles
status_evidence: bishops 451, 553, 787, 879; Hierocles
note: This is the unnamed seed see (38.75N 28.35E; 451, 553, 787), whose councils match Kerassai exactly. The site is unknown.
sources: Wikipedia: Cerasa; Hierocles, Synecdemus (Lydia); Darrouzès, Notitiae

greek_from_text: a city with the title Iulia by the early Principate (Julio-Claudian); Roman coins ΙΟΥΛΙΕΩΝ ΓΟΡΔΗΝΩΝ
status_evidence: Roman coins (RPC: Iulia Gordus); TAM V,1 inscriptions; Hierocles; bishop 787
note: Pleiades lists Hellenistic material, and civic decrees may go back to the 1st c. BC (not verified). The title Iulia points to Augustus or his successors.
sources: TAM V,1 (Gordos); RPC online: Iulia Gordus; Pleiades 550601

greek_from_text: first coins under Nero (one issue dated AD 65); Roman-period city of the Katakekaumene
status_evidence: Roman coins (Nero–Decius); TAM V,1; Hierocles; bishop 787
note: The name continues the Homeric ethnic Maiones (Lydians), and the village name Menye preserves it. Pleiades also lists Hellenistic material, so city status may be earlier.

greek_from_text: first attested by Roman provincial coins from Hadrian (AD 117–138) and Ptolemy (5.2.21)
status_evidence: Roman coins (Hadrian–Gallienus); Ptolemy 5.2.21; Hierocles; bishops 431, 451, 680–81, 787
note: The local name Sidas preserves Saittai. Earlier inscriptions on site may show civic institutions in the 1st c. AD (not verified).
sources: Ptolemy 5.2.21; WildWinds: Saitta; TAM V,1; Pleiades 609517

greek_from_text: first attested by Roman provincial coins (from c. the late 1st c. AD)
status_evidence: Roman coins (RPC: Silandus, 72 types); Hierocles; bishops 451, 680–81, 787
note: The district town Selendi (c. 4 km E) also preserves the name. The start of the coinage is approximate.
sources: RPC online: Silandus; Pleiades 609528; Wikipedia: Silandus

greek_from_text: first attested by Roman provincial coins (late 1st–3rd c. AD)
status_evidence: Roman coins (RPC: Tabala); Hierocles; bishops 451, 787
note: The start of the coinage is approximate.
sources: RPC online: Tabala; TAM V,1; Pleiades 609540

site: unlocated; Lydian–Phrygian border, conventus of Sardis (Ramsay: Kepecik)
greek_from_text: coins as 'Domitianopolis Sala' under Domitian as Caesar (AD 71–81); coinage to Elagabalus
status_evidence: Roman coins AD 71–222 (RPC: Sala, 76 types); Ptolemy; bishop 787
note: Ramsay's Kepecik placement could not be verified. The site may lie in Kütahya rather than Manisa or Uşak; the coordinates are only a regional guess.
sources: RPC online: Sala; WildWinds: Sala; Ramsay, HGAM (1890); Wikipedia: Sala (Lydia)

greek_from_text: first attested by Roman provincial coins ΒΑΓΗΝΩΝ (1st–3rd c. AD)
status_evidence: Roman coins (RPC: Bagis, 91 types); TAM V,1; Hierocles; Notitiae (suffragan of Sardis)
note: The Lydian–Persian elite tumuli of Güre (İkiztepe, the 'Lydian Treasure', 6th c. BC) show an earlier native centre in the area. The start of the coinage is approximate.
sources: RPC online: Bagis; TAM V,1; Pleiades 609336; Wikipedia: Bagis

greek_from_text: early Hellenistic settlement of Macedonians (coins ΜΛΑΥΝΔΕΩΝ ΜΑΚΕΔΟΝΩΝ), late 4th/3rd c. BC, per excavations
founder: early Hellenistic kings (Macedonian settlers; Antigonid or Seleucid)
status_evidence: Hellenistic & Roman coins (RPC: Blaundus, 100 types); Hierocles; bishops 359, 451, 458
note: Cylinder seals point to a native settlement in the early 2nd millennium BC (Assyrian Colony period). It is unclear whether the Macedonian settlers came under Antigonus or the Seleucids.
sources: Filges, Blaundos (2006); Cohen 1995; Pleiades 609344; Wikipedia: Blaundus

other_names: Anthea, Euanthia (Pliny); Seleukeia and Antiocheia (Seleucid); Kaisareia (Augustus); Andronikopolis/Palaiologopolis (Andronikos II, c. 1280); Güzelhisar (Turkish)
site: plateau north of Aydın city centre (Efeler, Aydın)
greek_from_text: native town (tradition: founded by Argives and Thracian Trallians, Strabo 14.1.42); Greek city by the 4th c. BC; Seleucid refoundation as Seleukeia/Antiocheia
status_evidence: coins (incl. cistophori, 2nd c. BC); Strabo; Hierocles; bishops 431–787
note: Placed in Lydia or Caria by different authors. The Argive foundation story is late; the 4th-c. date is approximate.
refoundations: Tralleis → Seleukeia/Antiocheia (Seleucids) → Kaisareia (Augustus, after the 26 BC earthquake) → Andronikopolis/Palaiologopolis (Andronikos II, c. 1280)

greek_from_text: synoecism of Athymbra, Athymbrada and Hydrela, named after Nysa, wife of Antiochus I (c. 280–261 BC)
status_evidence: coins; Strabo 14.1.43-46; Hierocles; bishops 431–787
note: Legend: Athymbra was founded by three Spartan brothers (Strabo). Placed in Caria or Lydia by different sources.
sources: Strabo 14.1.46; Cohen 1995; Pleiades 599832; Wikipedia: Nysa on the Maeander

greek_from_text: city coinage of the early Imperial period (RPC, 81 types); Strabo 14.1.48; Pliny NH 5.120; bishops 431–787
status_evidence: RPC coins; Pliny NH 5.120; bishops 431, 680–81, 787
note: Non-Greek name; Stephanus links it to the goddess Ma.
sources: Strabo 14.1.48; RPC (city 123: Mastaura); Pleiades 599790; Wikipedia: Mastaura (Caria)

greek_from_text: first bishop at Ephesus (431); bishop again at Chalcedon (451)
status_evidence: bishops 431, 451; Notitiae (see of Ephesus)
note: Small Maeander-valley town; location from the Barrington Atlas. The name is probably non-Greek.

greek_from_text: Briulitae in Pliny NH 5.120 (c. AD 77); Imperial-period city coins (RPC); later a bishopric
status_evidence: RPC coins; Pliny NH 5.120; Strabo 14.1.48; Notitiae (see of Ephesus)
note: The exact site is uncertain. Not in the seed file; added.
sources: Strabo 14.1.48; RPC (city 343: Briula); Pleiades 638793; Wikipedia: Briula

greek_from_text: Hellenistic city (earlier name Apollonia); own coins from the 1st c. BC
pre_detail: The city itself has no reported pre-Hellenistic levels (excavators: history 'goes back to the Hellenistic period'). The Chalcolithic–Late Bronze Age pottery and stone tools come from a separate mound c. 2.5 km NW of the city, so outside the same-nucleus test.
status_evidence: coins; Pliny NH 5.111; Hierocles (Lydia); bishops 325–451
note: The name 'Apollonia' (Pliny) suggests an unrecorded Seleucid or Attalid foundation; the coinage date is approximate.
sources: Pleiades 639152; Pliny NH 5.111; Thonemann 2011; Wikipedia: Tripolis on the Meander

other_names: Latmos (earlier Carian city on the mountain); Pleistarcheia (c. 300 BC)
greek_from_text: Carian Latmos (tribute lists, 5th c.) taken by Mausolus and moved to the lakeside site as Herakleia; sympoliteia treaty of Latmos with Pidasa in Greek, c. 323–313 BC
founder: Carian Latmos; relocated and renamed under the Hecatomnids (Mausolus?), walled by Pleistarchos c. 300 BC
status_evidence: ATL (Latmioi); Greek treaty with Pidasa (late 4th c.); Hellenistic coins; Hierocles; bishops 431, 451
note: Old Latmos (Pleiades 599752) lies just above; who moved the city and named it Herakleia (Mausolus or Pleistarchos) is debated.
refoundations: Latmos → Herakleia (Hecatomnid relocation) → Pleistarcheia (Pleistarchos, c. 300 BC) → Herakleia

other_names: sometimes spelled Pedasa (not Lelegian Pedasa near Halikarnassos)
site: Mt Grion (İlbıra Dağı), south of Lake Bafa (Milas, Muğla)
greek_from_text: sympoliteia treaty with Latmos in Greek (c. 323–313 BC); later sympoliteia with Miletus (c. 187 BC)
status_evidence: IACP 925; Greek treaties with Latmos and Miletus
note: Absorbed by Miletus in the early 2nd c. BC.

greek_from_text: Protogeometric cemetery (10th–9th c. BC); tradition: Argive colony, reinforced by Milesians under a son of Neleus (Polyb. 16.12.2)
status_evidence: IACP (Caria); ATL; coins; Hierocles; bishops 431–787
note: Carian settlement from the Early Bronze Age, with Minoanizing levels and buildings with LH IIIA–C Mycenaean pottery. Whether it was a Mycenaean settlement proper is debated, so it is dated from the Protogeometric period.
sources: Polyb. 16.12.2; Momigliano 2012 (Bronze Age Carian Iasos); Pleiades 599664; Wikipedia: Iasos

other_names: Andanos (said to be its Carian name, Steph. Byz.); Varvıl (Ottoman name of the site)
greek_from_text: Carian member of the tribute lists (5th c.); Greek polis by the Hecatomnid period (4th c. BC); Hellenistic decrees and coins
status_evidence: IACP (Caria); ATL; Hellenistic decrees and coins; Hierocles; bishop 787
note: Absorbed neighbouring Kindye; the Ottoman name Varvıl continues Bargylia.
sources: IACP (Caria): Bargylia; Strabo 14.2.20; Pleiades 599550; Wikipedia: Bargylia

site: Gölköy/Türkbükü (Bodrum, Muğla) (later site); earlier site perhaps Salih Adası
greek_from_text: Carian community in the tribute lists (5th c.; home of Skylax, who wrote in Greek c. 500 BC); moved to a new mainland site (Neapolis), reportedly early 3rd c. BC
status_evidence: IACP (Caria); ATL; Strabo 14.2.20; Pliny NH 5.107
note: Both sites are uncertain (Pleiades 599693, Salih Adası?; 599694, Göl). There is no clear evidence of Greek civic institutions.
sources: IACP (Caria): Karyanda; Strabo 14.2.20; Pleiades 599694; Wikipedia: Caryanda
refoundations: Karyanda (island site) → Neapolis/Karyanda on the mainland (3rd c. BC?)

greek_from_text: Myndian ship in the Ionian revolt period, 499 BC (Hdt. 5.33); tradition: Troizenian colony (Paus. 2.30.9); refounded on the coast by Mausolus c. 360 BC
founder: Troizenians (tradition), at a Lelegian town; refounded by Mausolus
pre_greek_note: Carian ethnic mw[d]on- read as 'Myndian' (Adiego); a tentative reading of an ethnic, not a certain city name
status_evidence: IACP (Caria); ATL; coins; Hierocles; bishops 431–787
note: Strabo counts Myndos among the eight Lelegian towns, so the Troizenian tradition is doubtful. Coordinates are New Myndos; Palaia Myndos is Pleiades 599845.
refoundations: Palaia Myndos (Lelegian) → New Myndos at Gümüşlük (Mausolus, c. 360 BC)

greek_from_text: Lelegian/Carian town; counted from the Hecatomnid period (4th c. BC), when it survived Mausolus' synoecism; earlier the dynast Tymnes' coins had Greek legends (c. 500-480 BC) and it paid tribute from 454 BC, while Carian was probably still spoken; free town under Rome (Pliny NH 5.107)
status_evidence: IACP (Caria); ATL; dynastic coins; Pliny NH 5.107
note: One of Strabo's Lelegian towns. Greek-legend dynastic coins do not prove a Greek-speaking population, but it survived Mausolus' synoecism and was a free town under Rome.
sources: IACP (Caria): Termera; Strabo 13.1.59; Pliny NH 5.107; Pleiades 599965

other_names: Zephyria (Steph. Byz.); Petronion (castle of St Peter, 1404)
greek_from_text: Dorian city; tradition: founded by Troizenians under Anthes (Strabo 14.2.16; Paus. 2.30.9), in the Early Iron Age; Hecatomnid capital from c. 370 BC
pre_greek_note: Carian alosδ k̂arnosδ has been read as 'from/in Halikarnassos' (Adiego). The reading is tentative and the form is attested only in the 4th c. BC, long after the Greek city existed, so it is not entered as a pre-Greek name. The 5th-c. Salmakis inscription and Carian personal names show a mixed Greek–Carian population.
status_evidence: IACP (Caria); ATL; coins; Hierocles; bishops 451–787
note: Mycenaean chamber-tomb cemetery (LH IIIA–C) at nearby Müsgebi (Ortakent), but no Mycenaean settlement at Halikarnassos itself. Mausolus synoecized six Lelegian towns into it. Turkish Bodrum comes from Petronium, the Knights' name for their castle (1404), not from Halicarnassus.
sources: IACP (Caria): Halikarnassos; Strabo 14.2.16; Pleiades 599636; Wikipedia: Halicarnassus
refoundations: enlarged by Mausolus' synoecism (c. 370 BC) as Hecatomnid capital

greek_from_text: Carian Syangela (tribute lists, 5th c.; dynast Pigres) moved to a new fortified site as Theangela in the Hecatomnid period; Greek treaty with Eupolemos c. 310 BC; coins
founder: Carian Syangela, relocated under the Hecatomnids
status_evidence: IACP 931 (Syangela); Greek decrees and treaty (c. 310 BC); coins; historian Philippos of Theangela
note: Strabo says Mausolus kept Syangela when he merged the Lelegian towns into Halikarnassos; Theangela was later put under Halikarnassos (Pliny).

greek_from_text: Carian member of the tribute lists (5th c.); Greek polis by the Hecatomnid period (4th c. BC); Hellenistic decrees and coins
status_evidence: IACP 900; ATL; Chrysaoric League; coins; Hierocles; bishops 431, 787
note: Its membership of the Carian Chrysaoric League shows it was counted as Carian.

other_names: Old Knidos at Burgaz (Archaic–Classical seat, debated)
greek_from_text: Dorian city of the Hexapolis; tradition: Lacedaemonian colonists (Hdt. 1.174; Strabo 14.2.6), Early Iron Age; moved to Tekir in the mid-4th c. BC
pre_detail: At Tekir (the coordinates given), 'extensive habitation can be traced only from around the 4th century'. Decades of excavation (Love, Özgan, Doksanaltı) have reported no pre-Greek levels, only some earlier Greek sanctuary material. The probable Archaic city at Burgaz shows Geometric-to-Hellenistic occupation, with no Bronze Age level published.
pre_sources: Greene, Leidwanger & Özdaş 2013 (ancientportsantiques.com/.../Knidos-Greene2013.pdf); Burgaz Harbors Project (nauticalarch.org); Pleiades 599575
status_evidence: IACP (Caria); Dorian Hexapolis; coins; Hierocles; bishops 451, 553
note: Most scholars place the Archaic–Classical city at Burgaz near Datça (Pleiades 599576) and the move to Tekir in the 4th c. BC, but this is contested. Coordinates are Tekir.

greek_from_text: first bishop at the Second Council of Nicaea (787); Roman and late-antique town of the Knidian peninsula
pre_detail: Excavations at Burgaz (Old Knidos/Stadia) since 1993 (Tuna) show uninterrupted activity from the Geometric to the early Hellenistic period, and soundings find the earliest settlement activity directly on bedrock. No Bronze Age or native level is reported. The modern town of Datça itself is unexcavated. Pliny's earlier names for Knidos (Triopia, Pegusa, Stadia) are Greek.
pre_sources: Burgaz Harbors Project (nauticalarch.org: 'uninterrupted activity from the Geometric period'); N. Tuna et al. 2014 Burgaz report (ancientportsantiques.com/.../Knidos-Tuna2014.pdf); Sevimli 2016 METU thesis; Plin. NH 5.104
status_evidence: bishop at Nicaea II (787)
note: Successor town at or near Old Knidos (Burgaz). Datça < Dadya < Tadya < Stadia.

greek_from_text: Carian town; counted from the Hecatomnid period (4th c. BC); earlier coins of the dynast Paktyes with Greek legend ΙΔΥΜΙΟΝ (mid-5th c.) and tribute lists, with Carian probably still dominant; later in the Rhodian Peraia
status_evidence: IACP (Caria); ATL; 5th-c. coins
note: Later part of the Rhodian Peraia. Greek-legend dynastic coins do not prove Greek speech.

site: Şehir Adası (Sedir Island), Gulf of Gökova (Marmaris, Muğla)
greek_from_text: in the tribute lists c. 454–415 BC; taken by Lysander 405 BC, its people 'mixobarbaroi' (Xen. Hell. 2.1.15); later a Rhodian deme
status_evidence: IACP (Caria); ATL; Xen. Hell. 2.1.15
lang_later: half-Greek, half-Carian population in 405 BC
note: A polis only in the 5th c.; in the Hellenistic period a deme of Rhodes, with a theatre and an agora.
sources: IACP (Caria): Kedreai; Xen. Hell. 2.1.15; Pleiades 599702; Wikipedia: Cedreae

greek_from_text: Carian (Kaunian-speaking) city; Greek–Carian bilingual decree and Greek decrees of the Hecatomnid period (4th c. BC)
founder: Carian town (Kaunians claimed Cretan origin, Hdt. 1.172)
pre_greek_note: Carian kbid-/kbidn- 'Kaunos/Kaunians' in the Kaunos Greek–Carian bilingual (Frei & Marek 1997; Adiego); compare Lycian χbide-
status_evidence: IACP (Caria); ATL; coins; Hierocles; bishops (Notitiae)
note: Not in the seed file; added.
sources: IACP (Caria): Kaunos; Hdt. 1.172; Adiego 2007 (The Carian Language); Pleiades 638796

greek_from_text: city coinage from the early Empire (RPC, from Augustus); Pliny's Euhippini (NH 5.109)
pre_detail: Site near Dalama is uncertain and unexcavated, with only Hellenistic–Roman attestation. No evidence either way.
status_evidence: Roman provincial coins (RPC city 490, 15 types); Pliny NH 5.109
note: Coin legend ΕΥΙΠΠΕΩΝ. The Greek name may point to a Hellenistic settlement. Site uncertain, between the Marsyas and Harpasos rivers.

greek_from_text: Hellenistic town, attested in 167 BC (fighting with Mylasa and Alabanda near Orthosia); coins 2nd c. BC – 3rd c. AD
pre_detail: Never scientifically excavated (Donduran, Yenipazar), and heavily looted. No published survey of early material; the founder is unknown (Cohen suggests a Seleucid settlement).
status_evidence: coins (Delrieux 2008; RPC city 678); Hierocles; bishops
note: The Greek name (Artemis Orthosia) suggests a Hellenistic settlement, but no founder is recorded.
sources: Delrieux 2008 (coins of the lower Harpasos valley); Cohen 1995; Pleiades 599839; Wikipedia: Orthosia (Caria)

greek_from_text: city coinage of the Roman period (lower Harpasos valley series, to 3rd c. AD); Hierocles; bishops
status_evidence: RPC coins (city 96); Hierocles; bishops (Notitiae)
note: Named after the Harpasos river (Akçay); non-Greek name continued in Arpaz.

greek_from_text: coins (legend ΒΑΡΓΑΣΗΝΩΝ) from the late Hellenistic period(?) to the 3rd c. AD
status_evidence: coins (Delrieux 2008; RPC city 324)
note: Distinct from coastal Pargasa/Bargasa near Keramos (Strabo 14.2.15; rejected). Barrington and Delrieux give the coins to this inland Bargasa. Not in the seed file; added.
sources: Delrieux 2008; RPC (city 324: Bargasa); Pleiades 599548; Wikipedia: Bargasa (northern Caria)

greek_from_text: city coinage of the Roman Imperial period (lower Harpasos valley series); bishops 680–81, 787
pre_detail: The 'New City' implies a (re)foundation, but its date and predecessor are unknown. Pleiades' 'classical' tag concerns the Greek period, not pre-Greek occupation. No excavation or survey evidence for earlier settlement is known.
status_evidence: RPC coins (city 136); Hierocles; bishops 680–81, 787
note: The name 'New City' implies a foundation or refoundation of unknown date; Pleiades also records earlier occupation.
sources: Delrieux 2008; RPC (city 136: Neapolis ad Harpasum); Pleiades 599823

greek_from_text: founded by Antiochus I by synoecism of Symmaithos and Kranaos (Pliny NH 5.108; Steph. Byz.)
status_evidence: coins; Hierocles; bishops 325, 451
note: Stephanus says Antiochus son of Seleucus named it after his mother Antiochis.
sources: Pliny NH 5.108; Cohen 1995; Pleiades 638748; Wikipedia: Antioch on the Maeander

greek_from_text: Carian community; Greek polis in sympoliteia with Aphrodisias (joint coins; treaty with Kibyra and Tabai, 2nd c. BC)
status_evidence: joint Plarasa–Aphrodisias coins and decrees (2nd–1st c. BC); free status 39 BC
note: Merged into Aphrodisias by the late 1st c. BC.
sources: Robert 1962; Reynolds 1982 (Aphrodisias and Rome); Pleiades 639063; Wikipedia: Plarasa

other_names: Ninoe (Steph. Byz.); Lelegon polis; Stauropolis and Karia (medieval Roman)
greek_from_text: sanctuary settlement; Greek polis by the 2nd c. BC in sympoliteia with Plarasa (joint coins; treaty with Kibyra and Tabai)
founder: Carian settlement around the sanctuary of Aphrodite
status_evidence: coins; Roman free city (39 BC); metropolis of Caria; bishops 325–787
note: Prehistoric mounds (Pekmez, Acropolis) from the Late Chalcolithic and Bronze Age. Geyre village, on the site until the 1960s, takes its name from medieval Roman Karia.

other_names: Alexandria by the Latmos (c. 334 BC; modern identification)
greek_from_text: Carian city; residence of Queen Ada (c. 340–334 BC), who handed it to Alexander; Greek coins from the 3rd c. BC
pre_greek_note: Hittite Iyalanda/Ialanti (Tawagalawa letter) was identified with Alinda by Garstang & Gurney (1959); widely cited but unproven
status_evidence: coins 3rd c. BC–3rd c. AD; Hierocles; bishops 431, 451
note: Its identification with Alexandria by the Latmos is modern (L. Robert).
sources: Arrian Anab. 1.23.8; Garstang & Gurney 1959; Pleiades 599480; Wikipedia: Alinda
refoundations: Alinda → Alexandria by the Latmos (c. 334 BC?) → Alinda (by 81 BC)

greek_from_text: Greek decree dated under Philip III and the satrap Asander (c. 321 BC) (Robert, Fouilles d'Amyzon)
founder: Carian town around the sanctuary of Artemis
status_evidence: Greek decrees 4th–2nd c. BC; coins; Hierocles; bishops 431, 451
note: Strabo counts it as a dependency of Alabanda. The Turkish name Mazın preserves Amyzon.

other_names: Antiocheia of the Chrysaoreis (Seleucid, c. 197–190 BC)
greek_from_text: Carian city (tyrant Aridolis, Hdt. 7.195); Greek polis in the Hecatomnid period (4th c. BC); Hellenistic decrees and coins
pre_greek_note: Waliwanda, a place in the Tawagalawa letter, has been linked with Alabanda only on the sound of the name (e.g. vici.org); this is not an accepted identification, so it is not used. The pre-Greek settlement is the native Carian town (Hdt. 7.195).
status_evidence: coins; Chrysaoric League; Hierocles; bishops 451, 787
note: Stephanus explains the name as Carian ala 'horse' + banda 'victory'.
refoundations: Alabanda → Antiocheia of the Chrysaoreis (Antiochus III) → Alabanda

greek_from_text: Carian community (Kyromos in the 5th-c. tribute lists); Greek polis by the Hecatomnid period; Hellenistic decrees; coins 2nd c. BC – 2nd c. AD
status_evidence: IACP (Caria); ATL; Greek decrees; coins
note: Sanctuary of Zeus Lepsynos used from the 6th c. BC. Renamed Europos in the Hellenistic period.
sources: IACP (Caria): Euromos; Kızıl 2017; Pleiades 599616; Wikipedia: Euromus
refoundations: Euromos → Europos (Hellenistic, perhaps under Philip V) → Euromos

greek_from_text: Carian community in the tribute lists (5th c.); Hellenistic Greek decrees (3rd–2nd c. BC)
status_evidence: IACP (Caria); ATL; Hellenistic decrees (I.Mylasa)
note: Later absorbed by Mylasa.

greek_from_text: Carian community in the tribute lists (5th c.); many Hellenistic Greek decrees and leases (3rd–2nd c. BC)
status_evidence: IACP (Caria); ATL; Hellenistic decrees (I.Mylasa)
note: Later in sympoliteia with Mylasa.
sources: IACP (Caria): Olymos; I.Mylasa (Blümel); Pleiades 599658; Wikipedia: Olymos

greek_from_text: first Greek decree 367/6 BC (Mylasa decrees under Mausolus)
pre_greek_note: Carian city and Hecatomnid seat until c. 370 BC. No native-script form of the name is securely attested.
status_evidence: IACP (Caria); ATL; Greek decrees from 367 BC; coins; Hierocles; bishops 680–81, 787
note: Hecatomnid capital before the move to Halikarnassos.
sources: IACP (Caria): Mylasa; I.Mylasa 1–3; Pleiades 599809; Wikipedia: Mylasa

greek_from_text: Carian member of the tribute lists (5th c.); Hellenistic Greek decrees and coins; Roman provincial coins
status_evidence: IACP (Caria); ATL; coins (RPC city 100)
note: The Hellenistic start date is approximate.
sources: IACP (Caria): Hydisos; RPC (city 100: Hydisus); Pleiades 599653; Wikipedia: Hydisos

greek_from_text: founded by Antiochus I and named after Queen Stratonike (Strabo 14.2.25), c. 270s BC
status_evidence: coins; Chrysaoric League centre; Hierocles; bishops 451, 787
note: Built at or near the Carian town of Idrias/Chrysaoris, with earlier finds on the site. Under Rhodes 188–167 BC.

greek_from_text: Carian–Greek stele dated by Philip III (c. 320 BC); Greek polis institutions (eponymous archon, proxenies) by the 3rd c. BC
pre_greek_note: Carian yλarmi- is attested; Hittite Wallarima has been proposed as an earlier form (unproven)
status_evidence: Greek decrees; coins (RPC city 102); bishopric
lang_later: Carian still in use in the late 4th c. BC (bilingual stele)
note: The community moved from Asarcıktepe to Kapraklar in the 4th c. BC.
sources: Debord & Varinlioğlu 2018; RPC (city 102: Hyllarima); Pleiades 599659; Wikipedia: Hyllarima

greek_from_text: Carian town (king Damasithymos at Salamis 480 BC; Delian League); counted Greek from the Hecatomnid period, 4th c. BC
status_evidence: Hdt. 8.87; Athenian tribute lists; Hellenistic dependency of Kaunos, then Rhodes (Polybius); Roman coins; bishop Leontius 458 (Lycian bishops' letter)
note: Site east of the Dalaman river, on the Carian–Lycian border; also in the CAR seed (duplicate). Identification with Şerefler is the scholarly consensus but has been questioned.

site: Kapıdağ peninsula, west of Göcek (Fethiye/Dalaman, Muğla)
greek_from_text: Roman-period city (theatre, agora, mausolea; Lycian federal priests from the family of C. Iulius Heliodoros), 1st–2nd c. AD
pre_detail: Remains are Roman and Byzantine (identified by Bent 1888). No survey reports earlier or pre-Greek material, and none calls it new ground.
status_evidence: TAM II inscriptions (sympoliteia absorbing Arymaxa and the Kreneis as demes); Ptolemy 5.3.2
note: Within the Rhodian Peraea in the Hellenistic period; city status is documented only in the Roman period. Ancient sources disagree on Caria vs Lycia.
sources: Pleiades 638968; Wikipedia: Lydae; TAM II; Ptol. 5.3.2

greek_from_text: Carian/Lycian community of the 5th-c. tribute lists; as a town in Greek-speaking Roman Lycia, first in Pliny (NH 5.103, 'Crya fugitivorum') and Ptolemy 5.3.2
status_evidence: IACP (Karia); Athenian tribute lists; Pliny NH 5.103 ('Crya fugitivorum'); Ptolemy 5.3.2
note: Exact site unknown (near Taşyaka on the Gulf of Fethiye). Carian-Lycian border town; also in the CAR seed (duplicate).
sources: IACP (Karia); Pleiades 638947; Plin. NH 5.103; Wikipedia: Crya

greek_from_text: own coinage from the late Hellenistic period (1st c. BC) into the 3rd c. AD
pre_greek_note: Carian/Anatolian name; no native-script attestation
status_evidence: coins (ΚΙΔΡΑΜΗΝΩΝ) late Hellenistic–Roman
