note: BAtlas name reconstructed (*Kidrama); site identification approximate.
sources: Pleiades 638919; Robert, La Carie II (1954); Wikipedia: Cidramus

greek_from_text: Hellenistic polis: attested 189 BC (Livy 38.13); coins from 2nd c. BC; treaty with Rome 81 BC
pre_greek_note: Native name; no pre-Greek attestation
status_evidence: Livy 38.13; coins 2nd c. BC–3rd c. AD; SC de Tabenis (81 BC); Hierocles; bishops 431–787
note: Modern Tavas (15 km N) probably preserves the name, but the site itself is under Kale.
sources: Pleiades 639125; Robert, La Carie II (1954); Livy 38.13; Strabo 12.8.13

greek_from_text: name Sebastopolis implies an Augustan (re)naming of Saleia; Roman coins 2nd–3rd c. AD
pre_greek_note: Earlier name Saleia known only from Greek sources
status_evidence: Roman coins; titular see
note: Date only inferred from the imperial name; Hellenistic Saleia may already have been a community.
sources: Pleiades 639096; Robert, La Carie II (1954); Wikipedia: Sebastopolis (Caria)

greek_from_text: probably a Seleucid foundation (3rd c. BC); Hellenistic decrees and coins from the 2nd c. BC
pre_detail: Rejected 'yes': the 'Medet Höyük' and 'inhabited since the Bronze Age' claims come only from the Denizli culture directorate, the LuwianSiteAtlas and a Wikipedia page that cites government and municipal pages. All of these are excluded sources. No excavation report or international survey publication documenting a Bronze Age mound at the city site was found. The standard treatments (Robert, La Carie II 235–42; Cohen 1995, 253–55) were not checkable here, and I know of no prehistoric levels reported in them.
pre_sources: en.wikipedia Apollonia Salbace; en.wikipedia Medet, Tavas (claims uncited/government refs); luwianstudies.org/site/medet-hoyuk (no bibliography rendered); Pleiades 638757 (refs Robert 1954, Cohen 1995; periods Hellenistic–Late Antique)
status_evidence: Hellenistic inscriptions and coins; Hierocles; bishops 325, 451
note: Seleucid origin is inferred from the dynastic name (Robert; Cohen), not documented; the date given is that of the earliest civic evidence.
sources: Pleiades 638757; Cohen 1995; Robert, La Carie II (1954)

greek_from_text: Hellenistic polis (decrees, coins 2nd–1st c. BC)
pre_detail: Hellenistic polis at Vakıf with walls, a stadium and Roman remains. No höyük or pre-Greek finds are reported for the site, and no account calls it new ground. A renamed native community is possible but undocumented.
pre_sources: Denizli İl Kültür ve Turizm Müd., Herakleia Salbake page; en.wikipedia Heraclea Salbace; Pleiades 638857
status_evidence: Hellenistic & Roman inscriptions (Robert); coins; Hierocles; bishop 431, 451
note: Greek name with no recorded founder; may be a renamed native community or an unrecorded Hellenistic foundation.
sources: Pleiades 638857; Robert, La Carie II (1954); Strabo 12.8.13

greek_from_text: first coins under Augustus ('Ἱερὰ Βουλὴ Ἀττουδέων')
pre_greek_note: Anatolian name; no pre-Greek attestation
status_evidence: coins Augustus–3rd c.; Hierocles; bishops 431–879
note: Sanctuary of Men Karou in its territory; the settlement may be Hellenistic, but civic evidence starts under Augustus.

greek_from_text: first attested by Pliny (Trapezopolitae); Roman coins; bishops from c. 400
pre_detail: Surface remains at Boludüzü/Bekirler are Roman and Byzantine. No published evidence of earlier occupation and no statement that it was new ground.
pre_sources: Denizli İl Kültür ve Turizm Müd., Trapezopolis page; Pleiades 639149 (roman onward)
status_evidence: Pliny NH 5.109; Roman coins; Hierocles; bishops 431–879
note: Greek name, origin unknown (perhaps a late Hellenistic foundation).

other_names: Telmissos; Anastasiopolis (8th c., after Anastasios II); Makre/Makri (medieval Roman, from 879; Turkish Meğri)
greek_from_text: Lycian town (Telebehi); Greek replaces Lycian in public use c. 300 BC; Greek decrees under the Ptolemies (OGIS 55, 240 BC)
pre_greek_note: Telebehi is the Lycian name (Lycian inscriptions and coins; Lebrun 1992, Melchert). Identification with Hittite Kuwalapašša (Annals of Hattusili III, Lukka) is speculative.
status_evidence: IACP (Lykia); Arrian 1.24.4; Ptolemaic and Attalid decrees; Lycian League; Hierocles; bishops 370?, 451; Notitiae (Telmessos, later Makre)
note: Fethiye was named in 1934 after the aviator Fethi Bey; the older Turkish name Meğri continues medieval Roman Makri. Lycian rock tombs (Amyntas tomb) with Lycian inscriptions.

greek_from_text: Lycian town (Xadawãti); Greek city from the early Hellenistic period (Ptolemaic rule, Greek decrees), c. 300 BC
pre_greek_note: Lycian Xadawãti (Lycian inscriptions incl. TL 35 at the site; standard identification, Melchert).
status_evidence: Lycian tombs and inscriptions; Hellenistic and Roman Greek inscriptions; Lycian League; Pliny NH 5.101
note: Not attested as a bishopric.
sources: Pleiades 638885; TAM II; Wikipedia: Cadyanda; Bean 1978

greek_from_text: Lycian town; Greek replaces Lycian in public use c. 300 BC; one of the six three-vote cities of the Lycian League
pre_greek_note: Lycian Tlawa (ethnic tlãñna). Hittite Dalawa (Annals, Madduwatta text) and Luwian Talawa (Yalburt inscription of Tudhaliya IV), generally identified with Tlos.
status_evidence: Strabo 14.3.3 (three votes); Hellenistic & Roman inscriptions; Lycian League coins; Hierocles; bishops 451, 787
note: Bronze Age finds at the site; Ottoman fortress on the acropolis.

greek_from_text: Lycian town (Pilleñni); Greek city from c. 300 BC; three-vote member of the Lycian League
pre_greek_note: Lycian Pilleñni (coin legends, inscriptions). Pinali of the Yalburt inscription (Tudhaliya IV) is generally identified with Pinara.
status_evidence: Strabo 14.3.3; Lycian rock tombs; Hellenistic & Roman inscriptions; Hierocles; bishop 787

greek_from_text: first attested as a city of the Lycian League in the 2nd–1st c. BC; most documents are Roman imperial
status_evidence: Hellenistic & Roman inscriptions (TAM II); Lycian League; Hierocles; bishops 680–81, 787
note: A few Lycian-type tombs but no Lycian inscriptions; probably a minor Lycian community before the Hellenistic period.
sources: Pleiades 639108; TAM II; Bean 1978; Wikipedia: Sidyma

greek_from_text: Greek polis by the early 2nd c. BC (decree for Orthagoras, SEG 18.570, c. 180–160 BC)
status_evidence: SEG 18.570 (Orthagoras decree); Alexander Polyhistor, Lyciaca; Lycian League; Hierocles; bishops 381, 451, 692, 787
note: Lycian coin legend sometimes ascribed to Araxa is not secure, so no pre-Greek name is given.

other_names: Termessos Minor / Termessos by Oinoanda (Τερμησσὸς ἡ πρὸς Οἰνοάνδοις)
greek_from_text: colony of Termessos (Pisidia) c. 200–190 BC; member of the Kibyratic tetrapolis, Lycian League after 84 BC
pre_greek_note: Hittite/Luwian Wiyanawanda ('wine-town', Yalburt inscription and Hittite texts on Lukka) is generally identified with Oinoanda.
status_evidence: Hellenistic & Roman inscriptions (Demostheneia dossier AD 124; Diogenes' Epicurean inscription); coins; Hierocles; bishops 381, 680–81, 787
note: Hellenistic colony of a Pisidian (but Greek-speaking) city, so 'colony' is used loosely.

greek_from_text: Lycian dynastic city (Arñna); Greek civic decree in the Letoon trilingual (337 BC) beside Lycian and Aramaic; Greek sole public language by c. 300 BC
pre_greek_note: Arñna is certain (Letoon trilingual; Xanthos stele; coins). Luwian Awarna (Yalburt inscription) is generally identified with Xanthos.
status_evidence: IACP (Lykia); Hdt. 1.176; Letoon trilingual; three votes in the Lycian League; Hierocles; bishop 381
note: Occupation from the 8th c. BC; Inscribed Pillar (c. 400 BC) with Lycian A, Lycian B and Greek texts.

greek_from_text: Lycian town (Pttara); Greek city from c. 300 BC; renamed Arsinoe under Ptolemy II
pre_greek_note: Lycian Pttara is certain. A Hittite/Luwian Patar(a) in Lukka texts has been proposed; uncertain. Bronze Age occupation at Tepecik.
status_evidence: Hdt. 1.182 (oracle); Lycian League (three votes, federal meeting place); Stadiasmus Patarensis (AD 45/46); Hierocles; bishops 325, 381, 451

greek_from_text: Lycian town (Wehñti); polis in Ps.-Skylax (4th c. BC); Greek city from c. 300 BC
pre_greek_note: Lycian Wehñti/Wehñte-, with adjective wehñteze/i- 'of Phellos' in TL 56 (Antiphellos) (eDiAna; Laroche, Neumann).
status_evidence: Ps.-Skylax 100; Lycian tombs and inscriptions; Lycian League coins; Hierocles; bishop 553
sources: Ps.-Skylax 100; Pleiades 639052; eDiAna s.v. wedre/i-; Wikipedia: Phellos

greek_from_text: Lycian harbour town (port of Phellos); Greek city from c. 300 BC; Hellenistic theatre
pre_greek_note: Habesos (Pliny) is known only in Greek/Latin, so it is not given as a pre-Greek name; Lycian and Milyan (Lycian B) inscriptions at the site.
status_evidence: Lycian League coins; Hellenistic & Roman inscriptions; Hierocles; bishop 451
note: The town was called Andifli until the 20th century (< Antiphellos); Kaş is a separate Turkish name.
sources: Plin. NH 5.100; Pleiades 638749; Bean 1978; Wikipedia: Antiphellos

greek_from_text: member polis of the sympoliteia headed by Aperlai (late Hellenistic–Roman inscriptions)
status_evidence: Aperlai sympoliteia inscriptions; Lycian rock tombs with Lycian inscriptions
note: Minor member of the sympolity of Aperlai, Simena, Apollonia and Isinda (one vote in the League). Not to be confused with Pisidian Isinda (Korkuteli). Exact site disputed (above Belenli or 2–3 km south).

greek_from_text: Lycian town (dynastic coins 'Aprlla'); Greek city from c. 300 BC; head of a sympoliteia with Simena, Apollonia and Isinda
pre_greek_note: Lycian dynastic coin legend Aprlla/prl, usually attributed to Aperlai; some assign it to Apollonia.
status_evidence: Lycian League coins (ΑΠΕ); sympoliteia inscriptions; Notitiae (see of Aperlai)
note: Purple-dye harbour town; partly submerged.
sources: Pleiades 638752; Hohlfelder 2005; lycianmonuments.com: Apollonia; Wikipedia: Aperlae

greek_from_text: member polis of the sympoliteia headed by Aperlai (late Hellenistic–Roman)
status_evidence: Aperlai sympoliteia inscriptions; walled acropolis, theatre, churches
note: Pillar tombs of c. 500 BC show a Lycian settlement; no ancient author names it, and its city status rests on its membership in the sympolity.

greek_from_text: member polis of the sympoliteia headed by Aperlai (late Hellenistic–Roman)
status_evidence: Aperlai sympoliteia inscriptions; small theatre; Lycian tombs
note: Medieval castle above the village.

greek_from_text: Lycian settlement; Greek city from the Hellenistic period (first named 2nd c. BC); Roman council and demos
pre_greek_note: A Lycian name Xbane- is sometimes given but is not secure, so it is omitted.
status_evidence: Lycian League coins; Roman inscriptions (Jason of Kyaneai); Hierocles; Notitia c. 640
note: Central place of a large territory (Kolb's Kyaneai survey) that absorbed Trysa, Tyberissos, Istlada and Teimiussa.

greek_from_text: Lycian town (rock tombs with Lycian inscriptions); Hellenized by the 3rd c. BC; three-vote city of the Lycian League
pre_greek_note: No Lycian name known; equation with Mira of Arzawa is rejected.
status_evidence: Strabo 14.3.3; Lycian League coins; metropolis of Lycia; Hierocles; bishops 325 (St Nicholas)–787
note: Seljuk capture under Alexios I; later medieval Roman recovery; Turkish town Kale, renamed Demre 2005.

greek_from_text: first attested as a see in the Notitia of Ps.-Epiphanius (c. 640)
pre_greek_note: Native (Anatolian) place-name only; no pre-Greek-script attestation.
status_evidence: Notitiae (7th and 10th c., first suffragan of Myra); possibly bishop Baanes 879
note: Site proposed at Dereağzı (large domed medieval Roman church, possibly the cathedral; Henning 2007, Şahin & Adak 2007); not certain. The Anatolian name suggests a native community, but there is no evidence.

greek_from_text: Roman-period city (inscriptions 1st–2nd c. AD); Hierocles
status_evidence: Roman inscriptions; Hierocles; Notitiae (see of Arneai)
note: Lycian-type rock tombs; the village name Ernes continues Arneai. Probably a Greek city already in the Hellenistic period, but undated.

greek_from_text: Lycian town (Xãkbi); Greek city from c. 300 BC; voting polis of the Lycian League
pre_greek_note: Lycian Xãkbi is the standard identification (Melchert). Hittite Hinduwa (Lukka) has been proposed; uncertain.
status_evidence: Lycian inscription; coins (ΚΑΝΔ); Lycian League; Pliny NH 5.101; bishops 451, 787, 879
note: The older village name Gendova continues Kandyba.

greek_from_text: city in the Milyas known from Roman inscriptions (Opramoas dossier) and Ptolemy
status_evidence: Roman inscriptions; Ptolemy 5.3.7; Notitiae; bishop 787
note: Pleiades also lists Hellenistic occupation; city status may be older than the Roman evidence.

greek_from_text: Roman-period city (inscriptions; Ptolemy)
status_evidence: Ptolemy 5.3.7; Roman inscriptions; Notitiae; bishops 692, 787, 879 (the seed list also gives 381)
note: The town name Gömbe continues Komba. Site identification near Gömbe is accepted but the ruins are scanty.

greek_from_text: first named as a town by Pliny (NH 5.101) in the 1st c. AD; Roman inscriptions
pre_greek_note: Settlement mound occupied from the Early Bronze Age (also Middle Bronze and Iron Age layers); no Hittite name securely attached.
status_evidence: Pliny NH 5.101; Ptolemy; inscriptions from Hacımusalar; Notitiae; bishops 381, 431, 451, 879
note: Identification with Hacımusalar Höyük rests on inscriptions found there (Özgen).

greek_from_text: first named as a town by Pliny (NH 5.101), 1st c. AD; coins of Gordian III
status_evidence: Pliny NH 5.101; Opramoas dossier; coins of Gordian III; Hierocles; bishops 381, 458, 536, 879
note: Site at Söğle is 'almost certain' (PECS); other sites have been proposed. Pleiades also lists Hellenistic occupation.
sources: Pleiades 639065; PECS s.v. Podalia; Wikipedia: Podalia (Lycia)

greek_from_text: Lycian dynastic capital (Zẽmuri) under Pericle c. 380–360 BC; Greek city from c. 300 BC (Ptolemaic Ptolemaieia)
pre_greek_note: Lycian Zẽmu/Zẽmuri (Lycian inscriptions and coin legends); standard identification.
status_evidence: Lycian inscriptions; Hellenistic & Roman Greek inscriptions; Lycian League coins; Hierocles; bishops 381, 451, 553, 787
note: Gaius Caesar died here in AD 4 (cenotaph).

greek_from_text: Lycian settlement (Archaic–Classical finds); Greek city from the Hellenistic period (Lycian League coins)
pre_greek_note: No Lycian name securely attested (forms like 'Arykawanda' in modern lists are reconstructions).
status_evidence: Lycian League coins; Hellenistic & Roman inscriptions; Hierocles; Notitiae (see of Arykanda)
note: Pleiades has two records (638769, 638770) for the same site.

greek_from_text: Lycian town (Lycian inscriptions TL 149–150); Greek city from c. 300 BC, though small before the Roman period
pre_greek_note: Lycian coin legends wedrẽi/wedrewi and the epithet wedrẽñni (TL 149–150, at Rhodiapolis) are often linked to Rhodiapolis. eDiAna treats wedre/i- as 'city-state' and the link as only a hypothesis.
status_evidence: coins; Opramoas inscriptions (2nd c. AD); Hierocles; bishop 518
note: Ancient tradition of a Rhodian foundation (Theopompus ap. Steph. Byz.) is not supported by finds, so it is treated as a Hellenized Lycian town.
sources: Pleiades 639078; eDiAna s.v. wedrẽñne/i-; Wikipedia: Rhodiapolis

greek_from_text: called a 'city of the Rhodians' by Hecataeus (c. 500 BC, ap. Steph. Byz.); certainly a Greek polis in the Hellenistic and Roman periods
pre_detail: Hecataeus calls Korydalla Rhodian, and the name looks Greek (korydallos, 'lark'). Against that, a Lycian–Greek bilingual from Kumluca shows a Lycian community in the Classical period (PECS: 'a genuine Lycian city'), and other Lycian inscriptions exist (N 302). There is no excavation, so nothing shows a non-Greek settlement before a Greek foundation. If the Rhodian claim is rejected, this becomes a Hellenized Lycian town ('yes').
pre_sources: Hecataeus ap. Steph. Byz. s.v.; lycianmonuments.com/korydalla; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hacıveliler (citing PECS); Pleiades 638937
status_evidence: Hecataeus ap. Steph. Byz.; imperial coins (ΚΟΡΥΔΑΛΛΕΩΝ); boule and demos under Marcus Aurelius; Hierocles; bishops 431, 458, 787, 879
note: The Rhodian origin rests only on Hecataeus and is doubted; if rejected, date it to the Hellenistic period (c. 300 BC) as a Hellenized Lycian town.
sources: Steph. Byz. s.v. Κορύδαλλα; Pleiades 638937; Wikipedia: Korydalla

greek_from_text: Rhodian settlement of the Classical period (Doric funerary epigrams; tradition of Rhodian founders); Greek polis in the Hellenistic and Roman periods
pre_detail: Rejected the proposed 'yes'. The 'Gaχe' Lycian coin legend and the EBA vessel come from the Turkish survey publication (Çevik & Bulut, Adalya 11, 2008), via kureansiklopedi, which does not count. The vessel is a single find from a cave of unclear context, not a settlement level. I could not confirm the attribution of 'Gaχe' coins to Gagai in non-Turkish numismatic literature. If that attribution holds, it would be a pre-Greek name in a non-Greek document and justify 'yes'. The Rhodian 'gā gā' foundation story is aetiological.
pre_sources: de./en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gagai, Gagae (citing Çevik & Bulut, Adalya 11, 2008, 63-98; Ruge, RE VII.1, 465f.; Ps.-Skylax 100); Pleiades 638842 (Barrington: Gagai/Palaion Teichos, Yenice); Onur, Adalya 14 (2011) abstract
status_evidence: Lycian League coins; Roman inscriptions and coins; Pliny NH 5.100; Notitiae (see of Gagai)
note: Rhodian colonisation supported by Doric epigrams (GRBS) and a later aetiological tale ('gā gā'); the foundation date is unknown. Gagates stone named after the town.
sources: GRBS: Rhodian Funerary Epigrams at Gagai; Pleiades 638842; Wikipedia: Gagae

greek_from_text: first possible bishop (Nicetas 'of Mela') at Nicaea II, 787
pre_detail: Unlocated, and even its existence as a Lycian see is uncertain (Mela/Meloë).
status_evidence: bishops 787?, 869, 879 (Le Quien; attribution disputed)
note: Le Quien assumes Mela = Meloë. Some of these bishops may belong to a Mela in Bithynia (Darrouzès). Origin unknown.
sources: Wikipedia: Meloë (Lycia); Le Quien, Oriens Christianus I

greek_from_text: Roman-period city (coins; inscriptions incl. Opramoas dossier, 2nd c. AD)
status_evidence: coins; Roman inscriptions; sympoliteia with Idebessos and Kormoi; Hierocles; Notitia c. 640

greek_from_text: Roman-period city (inscriptions, 2nd c. AD)
status_evidence: Roman inscriptions; sympoliteia with Akalissos; Notitiae (see of Idebessos)

greek_from_text: named on the Stadiasmus Patarensis (AD 45/46); city coins; walls from the Hellenistic period
status_evidence: Stadiasmus Patarensis; coins (identified 1998); bath-gymnasium; five churches
note: Not named by any ancient author; the name was identified from coins and the Patara road monument. Hellenistic walls suggest an older town.

greek_from_text: first attested in the 2nd c. BC (Lycian League coinage); one of the six three-vote cities
pre_detail: The excavations (since 1998/2006) report only Hellenistic, Roman and Byzantine remains, with about 5% of the city exposed. Whether the coastal site is the Hellenistic league city is still debated. There is no evidence either way on pre-Hellenistic occupation.
pre_sources: cumhuriyet.com.tr Olimpos 16 yıllık kazılar; avesis.marmara.edu.tr 'Olympos in Lycia: a novel assessment…'
status_evidence: Strabo 14.3.3; Lycian League coins; taken from the pirate Zeniketes by Servilius Isauricus 78/77 BC; Hierocles; bishops 431, 451
note: No pre-Hellenistic or Lycian evidence at the site. Genoese/Venetian fort in the Middle Ages.

greek_from_text: founded c. 690 BC by Lindians under Lakios (tradition); archaeological finds from the 7th c. BC
pre_detail: Rejected the proposed 'no known'. The Kylabras story (Lindians buying the land from a shepherd for salt fish; Heropythos and Philostephanos ap. Athen. 7.297e–298a) is a foundation legend, which is not enough on its own (rule 5). That the excavations since 2012 found nothing before the 7th-c. BC sanctuary is absence of evidence from partial digging, not positive proof of new ground (rule 7). I know of no reliable modern account (e.g. Schäfer 1981, IACP, Bean) that explicitly calls it an unoccupied site, and kureansiklopedi does not count.
pre_sources: Athen. 7.297e–298a; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phaselis; Pleiades 639051; knowledge: J. Schäfer, Phaselis (IstMitt Beih. 24, 1981); IACP s.v. Phaselis
pre_greek_note: Tradition (Heropythos ap. Athen. 7.297e–f): Lakios bought the land from a local shepherd, Kylabras.
status_evidence: IACP (Lykia); Hdt. 2.178 (Hellenion at Naukratis); Athenian tribute lists; coins from c. 500 BC; Hierocles; bishops 381, 451, 787
note: Greek city in Lycian territory, often counted to Pamphylia; joined the Lycian League in the 2nd–1st c. BC.

greek_from_text: listed as a town north of Phaselis by Pseudo-Skylax (mid-4th c. BC); Classical–Hellenistic remains at Kemer
pre_detail: Trial trenches and finds at Kemer show Classical, Hellenistic, Roman and Byzantine settlement only. Little excavation or publication exists (Türkmen 2025), and no pre-Greek level or name is known.
pre_sources: cumhuriyet.com.tr 'İdyros'ta otel projesine bilimsel itiraz' (B. Türkmen); kemer.bel.tr Idyros; Pleiades 638866
status_evidence: Ps.-Skylax 100 (as cited); Pliny NH 5.96?; BAtlas 65 E4
note: Site uncertain (BAtlas places it at Kemer with a query) and polis status rests on one periplus entry; not checked against IACP.

greek_from_text: first attested on the Stadiasmus Patarensis (AD 45/46); coins of Gordian III
status_evidence: Stadiasmus Patarensis; inscriptions naming Trebenna; coins of Gordian III; Lycian League member
note: No evidence for a Hellenistic city (Çevik 2005). Also relevant to the PAM batch.

greek_from_text: city founded late 3rd/early 2nd c. BC (earliest finds); member of the Kibyratic tetrapolis; Hellenistic coins
pre_greek_note: Kabalian (Pisidian-speaking) community; the urban site itself starts c. 200 BC, perhaps settled by Pisidians like Oinoanda.
status_evidence: Hellenistic coins and coins of Caligula; tetrapolis; Lycian League after 84 BC; Hierocles; bishops 381, 451, 458, 879

greek_from_text: Hellenistic city of the Kibyratic tetrapolis (2nd c. BC); Hellenistic coins
pre_greek_note: Kabalian native community; no pre-Greek-script name.
status_evidence: Hellenistic & Roman coins; tetrapolis (Strabo 13.4.17); Lycian League after 84 BC; Sebasteion; Hierocles; bishops 381, 451

other_names: Kibyra (Megale); Caesarea Kibyra (after the AD 23 earthquake)
greek_from_text: Hellenistic city ruled by tyrants (Moagetes, 189 BC); Greek inscriptions and coins from the 2nd c. BC
pre_greek_note: Strabo 13.4.17: founded by Lydians who subdued the Pisidians and later moved the city. The Early Iron Age site at Uylupınar (c. 18 km away) is taken to be the earlier settlement.
status_evidence: Strabo 13.4.17; Livy 38.14; coins 2nd c. BC–3rd c. AD; head of the tetrapolis; conventus seat; Hierocles (Caria); bishops 325, 381, 431, 553, 787
lang_later: Strabo says Pisidian, Solymian, Greek and Lydian were spoken (Hellenistic period)
refoundations: Kibyra → Caesarea Kibyra (after the AD 23 earthquake, Tiberius/Claudius)

greek_from_text: first bishop (Januarius) at the Synod of Constantinople, 448
pre_detail: Unlocated. Known only from one bishop in 448.
pre_sources: ACO (Synod of Constantinople 448); no Pleiades entry
status_evidence: bishops 448, 459, 518; Notitiae 6th–12th/13th c. (suffragan of Myra)
note: Site unknown and not named by any ancient author; il and coordinates are placeholders for Lycia. The name may honour Trajan's sister Marciana, but no foundation is recorded.
sources: Wikipedia: Marciana (Lycia); Le Quien, Oriens Christianus I 983

greek_from_text: Pisidian town on Manlius Vulso's route (Livy 38.15, 189 BC); listed among Pisidian towns by Strabo
status_evidence: Livy 38.15; Strabo 12.7.2, 13.4.17; Polybius 21.35?
note: Little more than a name; Greek-speaking civic status is not documented and the site location (Hall 1994) is approximate. Probably absorbed by Kibyra.

greek_from_text: Hellenistic: Strabo 14.4.1 (from Artemidorus, c. 100 BC) calls it a great fortress whose people colonised Kadrema in Lycia
pre_detail: The site near Arapsuyu is not excavated beyond walls. Stephanus puts Olbia in Solymian territory, and local accounts call it a Solymian (Termessian) port. Those are territorial or traditional claims, not evidence of an earlier settlement on the site.
pre_sources: Strabo 14.4.1; Steph. Byz. s.v. Olbia; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olbia_(Pamphylia); konyaalti.bel.tr/en/history
status_evidence: Strabo 14.4.1 (founded a colony, Kadrema); Ptolemy (between Phaselis and Attaleia); Stephanus s.v.
note: Greek name ('prosperous') suggests a Greek foundation, but founder and date are unknown; a Classical date is possible. Westernmost town of Pamphylia; also in the LYC seeds.

site: Kaleiçi, old town of Antalya (Muratpaşa, Antalya)
greek_from_text: founded by Attalos II Philadelphos (159–138 BC), c. 150 BC
pre_detail: The Doğu Garajı necropolis was in use from the late 4th c. BC, so a town preceded Attalos II's foundation. That town may be Pamphylian Korykos or an Olbian/Greek settlement, and nothing marks it as non-Greek. No Bronze or Iron Age level is reported in Kaleiçi; Pleiades' Bronze Age tags come from TAVO name indexing and are noise.
pre_sources: turkishmuseums.com Antalya Necropolis Museum; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antalya (Doğu Garajı 2008); Strabo 14.4.1
status_evidence: Strabo 14.4.1; Hellenistic and Roman coins; Hierocles; bishops from 431; medieval Roman metropolis and naval base
note: Strabo says Attalos also settled colonists at neighbouring Korykos; whether an earlier town lay at the harbour is debated. medieval Roman until the Seljuk conquest of 1207.

greek_from_text: listed among the towns of Pamphylia by Ps.-Skylax 100 (c. 340s BC)
pre_detail: The site at Lara is probable, not proven, and unexcavated. The name is non-Greek, but no earlier name or pre-Greek level is attested.
status_evidence: Ps.-Skylax 100; Roman imperial coins; Hierocles; bishops 325–787
note: Site at Lara (small artificial harbour) is probable rather than proven. Origin unknown: a Pamphylian (Greek-speaking) coastal town with a non-Greek name.

site: Aksu, 15 km E of Antalya (Aksu, Antalya)
greek_from_text: Tradition: founded after the Trojan War by Achaeans under Kalchas and Mopsos (founder statues at Perge; Strabo 14.4.3), and the Pamphylian dialect points to Greek settlers c. 1200–1000 BC; archaeology on the acropolis shows a native Iron Age town with Greek (Rhodian/Cypriot) influence from the 7th c. BC and a polis from the Classical period
pre_greek_note: Parha is named with the Kaštaraya river (Kestros) as Tarhuntassa's western border in the Bronze Tablet of Tudhaliya IV (c. 1235 BC); the identification with Perge is generally accepted. The acropolis was settled from the Late Chalcolithic/Early Bronze Age.
status_evidence: IACP (Pamphylia); coins from 3rd/2nd c. BC; Hierocles; bishops 431–787; metropolis of Pamphylia II
note: Date choice: the brief prefers the archaeological date (7th c. BC); tradition and dialect would give c. 1100 BC. 'Mycenaeans' stands for the post-Trojan-War Achaean settlers of the Pamphylian tradition.
sources: IACP (Pamphylia); Otten 1988 (Bronze Tablet); Strabo 14.4.3; Pleiades 639048; Wikipedia: Perga

site: Yanköy Hisarı / Asar köy, near Kumköy (Serik, Antalya)
greek_from_text: Tradition: founded by Mopsos, Kalchas and Amphilochos after the Trojan War (or by Argives); Pamphylian Greek town; longest Pamphylian-dialect inscription (4th c. BC); coins from early 3rd c. BC. Date set with Perge (7th c. BC, earliest Greek material in Pamphylia)
pre_detail: The earliest finds are 8th–7th c. BC Geometric-decorated sherds, with no architecture from that phase. The Pamukkale excavation team equates Sillyon with 'Šalluša' in Hittite texts, but the identification is conjectural. The Mopsos/Argive foundation stories are legend. No pre-Greek level has been shown.
pre_greek_note: A derivation of the Pamphylian name Selywiys from Hittite Šalawašša has been suggested (Wikipedia: Sillyon, as 'Sallawassi'), but this is only an etymology and the same Hittite name is also linked to Sagalassos, so no pre-Greek name is entered. No pre-Greek levels are known at the site.
status_evidence: IACP (Pamphylia); Pamphylian dialect decree (4th c. BC); coins c. 280 BC–AD 270s; Hierocles; bishops 381–787
note: Resisted Alexander in 333 BC (Arrian 1.26.5). In the medieval Roman period the metropolitan see moved here from Perge (late 8th–9th c.); fell to the Seljuks in 1207.

other_names: Estwedys (Pamphylian, coin legend ΕΣΤϜΕΔΙΙΥΣ); Primoupolis (medieval Roman); Belkıs (Turkish name of the site)
greek_from_text: Tradition: an Argive foundation (Strabo 14.4.2; Mela 1.78) or founded by Trojan War heroes (Mopsos, or Polypoites and Leonteus); Pamphylian Greek legends on coins from c. 500 BC. Date set with Perge (7th c. BC, earliest Greek material in Pamphylia)
pre_detail: Rejected the proposed 'yes'. The Late Chalcolithic (c. 4000–3500 BC) finds under the acropolis shops were only announced in the press in September 2026 (Hürriyet Daily News, Daily Sabah, Greek Reporter). They are unpublished (rule 4: the brief's own example). The native name Estwediiys is attested only in Pamphylian Greek coin legends, not in a pre-Greek document, and its link to Luwian Azatiwada is disputed (rule 6). The Argive and Mopsos foundations are legendary. No pre-Iron Age level is reported in non-Turkish scholarship.
pre_sources: proposal's press sources (not evidence); Pleiades 638776; knowledge: Brixhe, Le dialecte grec de Pamphylie (1976) on ΕΣΤϜΕΔΙΙΥΣ coin legend
status_evidence: IACP (Pamphylia); coins from c. 500 BC (Pamphylian Greek legends); Hierocles; bishops 325–431 and later
note: Could be classed as an Argive colony (metropolis Argos), but the Argive claim is probably a later kinship myth. Tradition and dialect would give c. 1100 BC.

site: unlocated, near the coast between the Eurymedon and Side (Manavgat or Serik, Antalya)
greek_from_text: Seleucid foundation, 3rd/early 2nd c. BC (founder and date unknown)
pre_detail: Unlocated; the Şıhlar ruins are now attributed to Lyrbe.
status_evidence: Hellenistic honorific decree for Asklepiades of Perge; Ptolemy?; bishop at Nicaea 325 (per seed list)
note: The ruins at Şıhlar/Bucakşeyhler long called 'Seleukeia' are now usually taken to be Lyrbe (Nollé); Seleukeia was probably a separate coastal town. Position here is the Barrington/Pleiades estimate.
sources: Cohen 1995; Nollé 1993 (Side im Altertum); Pleiades 639099; Wikipedia: Seleucia (Pamphylia)

other_names: Eski Antalya ('Old Antalya', Ottoman); Selimiye (village name before 20th-c. revival of 'Side')
greek_from_text: colony of Aeolian Kyme (Ps.-Skylax 100; Strabo 14.4.2; Arrian 1.26.4), usually dated to the 7th c. BC
pre_greek_note: Arrian says the Kymaean settlers took up the local tongue, so a native (Sidetic-speaking) community existed. Pleiades lists a native form 'Sibdē', which I could not verify; not used.
status_evidence: IACP (Pamphylia); coins from 5th c. BC (Sidetic legends, Greek from the Hellenistic period); Hierocles; bishops 431–787; metropolis of Pamphylia I
lang_later: Sidetic (native Anatolian) was the main language: Arrian 1.26.4 says the colonists forgot Greek; Sidetic coin legends 5th–3rd c. BC and bilinguals to the 2nd c. BC; Greek dominant from the Hellenistic period
note: The name means 'pomegranate' (the city's emblem); the modern name Side is a revival of the ancient name. The village on the site was called Selimiye (founded 1895); the name Side is a modern revival.
sources: IACP (Pamphylia); Arrian 1.26.4; Strabo 14.4.2; Pleiades 639105; Wikipedia: Sidetic language

other_names: Lyrba; the site was formerly identified as Seleukeia; Scandalor (portolans, if the site is Seleukeia)
site: Şıhlar, 1 km N of Bucakşeyhler, 15 km NE of Side (Manavgat, Antalya)
greek_from_text: Hellenistic town: agora 2nd c. BC; Roman imperial coins (ΛΥΡΒΙΤΩΝ)
pre_greek_note: Sidetic inscriptions and graffiti from the site show a Sidetic-speaking population; the name may be Luwian, but there is no pre-Greek attestation.
status_evidence: Roman imperial coins; Ptolemy 5.5.8; Hierocles; bishops 381, 431
lang_later: Sidetic in use alongside Greek in the Hellenistic period (Sidetic texts found on the site)
note: Identification of the Şıhlar ruins as Lyrbe rather than Seleukeia (Nollé) is likely but not proven.
sources: Nollé 1993; Pleiades 638970; Wikipedia: Lyrbe; turkisharchaeonews.net: Lyrbe

site: Fığla Burnu, on the coast W of Alanya (Alanya, Antalya)
greek_from_text: Ptolemaic foundation of the 3rd c. BC (Ptolemaic control of the coast c. 280–197 BC); named as a polis by Strabo 14.4.2
founder: a Ptolemaic king (probably Ptolemy II or III)
pre_detail: A short-lived Ptolemaic town at Fığla Burnu, known only from surface remains. No pre-Hellenistic finds or earlier name are reported.
status_evidence: Strabo 14.4.2 (polis between the Melas and Korakesion)
note: Short-lived Hellenistic town, not in Hierocles. Border case: Alanya district, may duplicate the CIL batch.

greek_from_text: first bishop at Ephesus 431; Roman-period town
status_evidence: Hierocles (Karalia); bishops 431, 451, 680
note: Hill town in the hinterland of Korakesion; native name. Border case (Alanya district), possibly also in the CIL batch.

site: 250–500 m N of Sırtköy, N of Manavgat (Manavgat, Antalya)
greek_from_text: silver coins from the late 4th–3rd c. BC; the Etenneis sent 8,000 hoplites to Achaios in 218 BC (Polybius 5.73)
pre_greek_note: Classical-period sherds on the site
status_evidence: coins 4th/3rd c. BC–3rd c. AD; Polybius 5.73; Hierocles; bishops 381–879
note: Site at Sırtköy chosen on coin finds; Gölcük near Sarraçlı is the weaker alternative. Some equate the Etenneis with the Kotenneis, but the Notitiae list them as separate sees.

greek_from_text: Roman-period civic inscriptions of the Kotenneis; first bishop 381
pre_greek_note: The Katenneis appear as a Pisidian people in Strabo 12.7.1.
status_evidence: Roman inscriptions; Hierocles (Kotana); bishops 381–879
note: Possibly the same community as, or split from, the Etenneis. No coins of its own unless the Etenna coins belong to it.

greek_from_text: Roman-period civic inscriptions (no coinage); first bishop 431
pre_greek_note: Named as 'Erymnai' in Alexander Polyhistor's Lyciaca (1st c. BC, via Stephanus).
status_evidence: inscriptions; Hierocles (Orymna); bishops 431, 680/692, 787, 879
note: The village of Ormana keeps the ancient name (Orymna).

other_names: Estlegiys (Pamphylian-script coin legend ΕΣΤΛΕΓΙΙΥΣ); acropolis Kesbedion
site: Altınkaya (formerly Zerk), above the Köprülü Kanyon (Manavgat, Antalya)
greek_from_text: 4th c. BC: coins with the Pamphylian-Greek legend ΕΣΤΛΕΓΙΙΥΣ; embassy to Alexander 333 BC (Arrian 1.28.1); claimed Spartan kinship (Polybius 5.76)
pre_greek_note: Strabo calls the Selgeis the leading Pisidians; no pre-Greek attestation of the name.
status_evidence: coins from 4th c. BC; Polybius 5.72–76; Strabo 12.7.3; Hierocles; bishops 431 and later (into the 14th c.)
note: The Spartan-colony claim is a Hellenistic kinship tradition; treated as a native Pisidian town.

site: near Kozan, N of Gebiz (Serik, Antalya)
greek_from_text: attested as a city besieged by Selge in 218 BC (Polybius 5.72); listed by Artemidorus c. 100 BC; coins from Trajan
status_evidence: Polybius 5.72; Strabo 12.7.2; coins Trajan–3rd c. AD; Hierocles; Notitiae
note: Site near Kozan identified by survey (Vandeput & Köse); sometimes called uncertain.

greek_from_text: Hellenistic polis: Greek decrees from c. 200 BC, war with Isinda 189 BC, treaty with Adada (2nd c. BC); coins from 71 BC
pre_greek_note: Solymian/Pisidian town that held out against Alexander in 333 BC (Arrian 1.27–28).
status_evidence: Arrian 1.27; Polybius 21.35; treaty with Adada; lex Antonia de Termessibus 71 BC; coins; Hierocles; bishops 325, 431, 448
note: Declined in late antiquity (bishops 'of Termessos and Eudokias' combined later).

site: near Evdir Han, on the Antalya–Korkuteli road (Döşemealtı, Antalya)
greek_from_text: named after Empress Eudocia (married Theodosius II in 421); first bishop at Ephesus 431
pre_detail: Located only approximately near Evdir Han. Reportedly a renamed earlier town (Anydros?), whose date and origin are unknown. No excavation.
status_evidence: Hierocles; bishops 431, 448, 458, 787; Notitiae
note: Lowland successor of Termessos; the Seljuk Evdir Han probably preserves the name. Said to have been an earlier town (Anydros?) rebuilt and renamed.

greek_from_text: first attested 189 BC, besieged by Termessos (Polybius 21.35; Livy 38.15); Hellenistic coins (claiming Ionian origin)
status_evidence: Polybius 21.35; Hellenistic and Roman coins; Hierocles; bishops 325–879
note: Coins call the citizens Ionians, a claim of Greek descent; the -nda name is native Anatolian. Not to be confused with Lycian Isinda (Belenli, LYC batch).

greek_from_text: listed as a Pisidian city by Artemidorus c. 100 BC (Strabo 12.7.2, as Aarassos); Hellenistic remains (3rd–2nd c. BC); Roman coins
status_evidence: Strabo 12.7.2; Ptolemy 5.5.6; Roman imperial coins; Hierocles; bishops 381, 451, 458
note: Survey (Mitchell) dates the first town to the Hellenistic period; most visible remains Roman.

greek_from_text: Roman imperial coins (ΟΥΕΡΒΙΑΝΩΝ, 2nd–3rd c. AD)
status_evidence: Roman imperial coins; Hierocles; bishop at Nicaea 325 (per seed list); Notitiae
note: Location approximate (Barrington '*Ouerbe').

greek_from_text: Roman imperial coins (ΑΝΔΗΔΕΩΝ, 2nd–3rd c. AD)
status_evidence: Roman imperial coins; Notitiae (Pamphylia II)
note: Pleiades also records Hellenistic occupation; no earlier civic evidence known to me.

greek_from_text: Roman imperial coins (ΠΟΓΛΕΩΝ, 2nd–3rd c. AD); Ptolemy 5.5.6
status_evidence: Roman imperial coins; Ptolemy; Hierocles (?); bishops 451, 787

other_names: Colonia Iulia Augusta Prima Fida Comama
greek_from_text: Augustan veteran colony, founded after 27 BC (probably by the Via Sebaste milestones of 6 BC)
pre_greek_note: The Augustan colony kept the native name of the place (Komama), implying an existing native Pisidian community; the name is known only from Greek and Latin sources.
status_evidence: colonial coins (Antoninus Pius, Marcus Aurelius); bishops 381, 458
lang_later: Latin was the colony's official language in the 1st–2nd c. AD; Greek took over in the 3rd c.
note: Counted under the brief's rule for Pisidian coloniae that became Greek-speaking.

greek_from_text: attested 319 BC (battle of Kretopolis, Diodorus 18.44–47)
founder: unknown; the name ('city of the Cretans') implies Cretan settlers, probably early Hellenistic
pre_detail: The site at Buğdüz/Yüreğil is a probable identification (Mitchell) and is unexcavated. No pre-Hellenistic level or earlier name is known.
status_evidence: Diodorus 18.44, 18.47; Polybius 5.72; Ptolemy 5.5; Cohen 1995
note: Founder and founder_group are conjecture from the name; it may be a settlement of Cretan mercenaries under Alexander or Antigonos. Site identification (Mitchell) probable.
sources: Diodorus 18.44; Cohen 1995; Mitchell 1994; Pleiades 638946; Wikipedia: Cretopolis

greek_from_text: Roman imperial coins (2nd–3rd c. AD); bishop at Nicaea 325
pre_greek_note: Iron Age fortified settlement (Panemoteichos I) next to the Roman town.
status_evidence: Roman imperial coins; Hierocles 681.3; bishops 325, 451?, 536; Constantine Porph. De them. 1.38
sources: Aydal et al. 1997; Mitchell 1994; Pleiades 639036; Wikipedia: Panemoteichos

greek_from_text: Hellenistic polis known only from the site: temple inscription 'ho demos ho Sienōn'
status_evidence: dedication by the demos of Sia; Hellenistic and Roman public buildings
note: Not named in any ancient author; date from the Hellenistic remains. Under excavation (Ü. Işın).

greek_from_text: Augustan veteran colony (after 27 BC) at a native town
pre_greek_note: The Augustan colony took the name of the native Pisidian town of Olbasa (Colonia Iulia Augusta Olbasenorum), which has Hellenistic occupation (Pleiades); the name is known only from Greek and Latin sources.
status_evidence: colonial coins (2nd–3rd c. AD); Ptolemy
lang_later: Latin was the colony's official language in the 1st–2nd c. AD; Greek took over in the 3rd c.
note: Pleiades records Hellenistic occupation; the native name (-asa) suggests an earlier Pisidian town, but there is no direct evidence.

greek_from_text: Roman imperial coins (ΚΟΛΒΑΣΕΩΝ, 2nd–3rd c. AD)
status_evidence: Roman imperial coins; Hierocles; bishop at Ephesus 431; Notitiae (Pamphylia II)
note: Exact site uncertain (Hall survey; Barrington position).

site: unexcavated site SW of Bucak (Bucak/Çeltikçi, Burdur)
greek_from_text: Roman imperial coins (2nd–3rd c. AD)
status_evidence: Roman imperial coins; Hierocles; bishops 451, 787
note: Location from the Barrington Atlas; Pleiades also records Hellenistic occupation.

greek_from_text: late Hellenistic coins of the Keraeitai (ΚΕΡΑΕΙΤΩΝ)
status_evidence: coins (late Hellenistic and Roman)
note: Known mainly from its coinage; location and coin dating need checking (Barrington '*Keraia').

greek_from_text: Pisidian city in Artemidorus' list, c. 100 BC (Strabo 12.7.2); taken by Amyntas; Augustan colony c. 25 BC
status_evidence: Strabo 12.6.4, 12.7.2; colonial coins from Hadrian; Hierocles; bishop 787
lang_later: Latin official in the colony (1st–3rd c. AD)
note: Besieged and taken from the brigand Lydius in 276/278 AD. Population moved to Çamlık in the Middle Ages.
sources: Strabo 12.6.4; Mitchell 1995 (Cremna in Pisidia); Pleiades 638814; Wikipedia: Cremna
refoundations: Kremna → Colonia Iulia Augusta Felix Cremnensium (Augustus, c. 25 BC)

site: Gâvur Ören, SW of Lake Burdur (Burdur)
greek_from_text: first attested 189 BC on Manlius Vulso's march (Polybius 21.36; Livy 38.15)
status_evidence: Polybius 21.36; Livy 38.15; coins (Kormasa; and Palaiopolis, if the same); Notitiae (Palaiopolis)
note: Pleiades joins Kormasa and Palaiopolis at the Gâvur Ören site (from von Aulock 1977); the identification and the date of city status are uncertain.

site: Karakent, W end of Lake Burdur (Burdur)
greek_from_text: first attested 189 BC (Polybius 21.36; Livy 38.15); Roman imperial coins
status_evidence: Polybius 21.36; Livy 38.15; Roman imperial coins; Hierocles (Lysenara); bishop 451
note: The 189 BC mention shows a town, not necessarily Greek civic institutions; secure civic evidence (coins) is Roman.

greek_from_text: Pisidian town taken by Alexander in 333 BC (Arrian 1.28); Hellenistic civic buildings and Greek inscriptions from the 2nd c. BC; coins from the 1st c. BC
pre_greek_note: Salawassa, a mountain place in 14th-c. BC Hittite texts, has been suggested as Sagalassos; uncertain, and the same Hittite name has been linked to Sillyon. Achaemenid-period settlement at nearby Düzen Tepe and on the site.
status_evidence: Arrian 1.28; Strabo 12.6.5; Hellenistic and Roman coins; Hierocles; bishops 381, 451 and later
note: The modern town of Ağlasun, below the site, keeps the name; the ancient city was largely abandoned after 7th-c. earthquakes.
sources: Arrian 1.28; Waelkens & Poblome (Sagalassos reports); Pleiades 639087; Wikipedia: Sagalassos

other_names: Adadare, Odada (variants); Karabavlu (Turkish name of the ruins)
greek_from_text: Greek treaty of friendship and alliance with Termessos (2nd c. BC); listed by Artemidorus c. 100 BC; coins from the 1st c. BC
status_evidence: treaty with Termessos; Strabo 12.7.2; coins 1st c. BC and Trajan–Gallienus; Hierocles; bishops 381, 451

greek_from_text: probably the 'Pityassos' of Artemidorus' list of Pisidian cities, c. 100 BC (Strabo 12.7.2); Roman imperial coins
status_evidence: Strabo 12.7.2 (if = Pityassos); Roman imperial coins; bishopric (Notitiae)
note: The Artemidorus identification (Pityassos = Tityassos) is a common emendation; secure evidence is Roman.

site: near Mirahor / Akçaşar, at the source of the Köprüçay (Aksu, Isparta)
greek_from_text: listed among Pisidian cities by Artemidorus c. 100 BC (Strabo 12.7.2); coins 2nd–3rd c. AD
status_evidence: Strabo 12.7.2; Roman imperial coins (river-god Eurymedon); bishops 680/81, 787

greek_from_text: listed as a city by Hierocles (c. 527); Roman-period remains
status_evidence: Hierocles; bishopric (Notitiae; titular see)
note: Pleiades and DARE give positions some 8 km apart; site uncertain.

greek_from_text: Roman imperial coins (ΒΑΡΗΝΩΝ, 2nd–3rd c. AD); first bishop 325
status_evidence: Roman imperial coins; Hierocles; bishops 325, 381
note: Formerly placed at Isparta (Pleiades 638790 coordinates are Isparta's); modern scholars (TIB 7) put it near Kılıç. Isparta's name comes from medieval Roman Sparta/Saporda, not from Baris.
sources: TIB 7; Pleiades 638790; Wikipedia: Baris (Pisidia); Wikipedia: Isparta

greek_from_text: founded by Seleucus I or Antiochus I to guard the northern Pisidian road, early 3rd c. BC
pre_detail: Kept 'yes' at low confidence. The excavation volume Seleukeia Sidera I (eds. Hürmüzlü, Talloen, Sönmez, Togan, 2022/23) is bilingual and co-edited by P. Talloen of the Sagalassos school, so it counts as an international-team publication. It states that 'the original settlement, dating back to the 8th century BC, was located on top of Hisar Tepe', based on 8th-c. BC Iron Age pottery from surveys on the hill (pp. 8, 21). These are surface finds, not stratified, and the volume calls early evidence 'limited'. Chalcolithic–Iron Age mounds in the territory are separate sites and were not used. kureansiklopedi was disregarded.
status_evidence: Cohen 1995; coins as Claudioseleucia (Claudius–Claudius II); Hierocles; bishops 325, 451
note: The village's former name, Selef, preserved 'Seleukeia'.
sources: Cohen 1995; Robert 1939; Pleiades 639098; Wikipedia: Seleucia Sidera

site: saddle of Sivri Tepe / Davraz, 4 km SW of Eğirdir (Eğirdir, Isparta)
greek_from_text: Roman imperial coins (ΠΡΟΣΤΑΝΝΕΩΝ); boundary stone with Parlais; Ptolemy 5.5.7
status_evidence: Roman imperial coins; Ptolemy 5.5.7; bishop at Constantinople 381

site: W of Lake Eğirdir, between Isparta and Eğirdir (Isparta)
greek_from_text: listed as a city by Hierocles (c. 527); later see of Pisidia
status_evidence: Hierocles; Notitiae (suffragan of Antioch); titular see
note: Status from Hierocles/Notitiae, from memory and TIB 7 via Pleiades; not checked against the text.

greek_from_text: Roman imperial coins (ΚΟΝΑΝΕΩΝ, 2nd–3rd c. AD)
status_evidence: Roman imperial coins; Hierocles; bishop 431; Notitiae
note: Gönen continues the native name Konana. Pleiades also records Hellenistic occupation.

other_names: Colonia Iulia Augusta Hadriana Parlais; Paralais (Ptolemy)
site: Barla, on the W shore of Lake Eğirdir (Eğirdir, Isparta)
greek_from_text: Augustan veteran colony (Colonia Iulia Augusta), late 1st c. BC; 'Hadriana' added under Hadrian
pre_greek_note: The Augustan colony kept the native name of the place (Parlais/Paralais, modern Barla), implying an existing native Pisidian community; the name is known only from Greek and Latin sources.
status_evidence: colonial coins; Ptolemy 5.4.12; boundary stone with Prostanna; bishops 381, 451, 692, 879
lang_later: Latin official in the colony (1st–3rd c. AD)
note: The native name Parlais survives in Barla; site identification (Kiepert) generally accepted, against Ramsay's Uzumla Monastir.

greek_from_text: listed among Pisidian cities by Artemidorus c. 100 BC (Strabo 12.7.2)
status_evidence: Strabo 12.7.2; Hellenistic–medieval Roman remains
note: Only literary evidence for civic status is Artemidorus' list; no coins or see known to me.

site: near Kıyakdede, on the Isparta–Konya border (Şarkikaraağaç, Isparta)
greek_from_text: first attested by Pliny (NH book 5, list of Galatia, 1st c. AD); Ptolemy; bishops from 325
pre_detail: An unexcavated site near Kıyakdede. Its Greek name 'new city' says nothing about earlier occupation, and no prehistoric level or earlier name is reported.
status_evidence: Pliny NH 5 (Galatia); Ptolemy 5.4.11; Hierocles; bishops 325, 381, 451
note: The Greek name ('new city') suggests a late Hellenistic or early Roman foundation, but no founder is recorded. Border case: also in the GAL seeds (placed in Hüyük, Konya).

greek_from_text: raised to city status by an imperial rescript (probably Diocletian, late 3rd c. AD), with council of 50 decurions and magistrates
pre_greek_note: The rescript raises an existing village community to a city.
status_evidence: imperial rescript in Latin (ILS 6090); Hierocles; bishops at Constantinople 381
note: Date of the rescript disputed (late 3rd to 4th c.).

greek_from_text: Seleucid foundation (3rd c. BC) at the native town of Mordiaion; Roman-period coins name Alexander as founder
pre_greek_note: Mordiaion is known only from Stephanus (a Greek source), so it is not a pre-Greek attestation.
status_evidence: Cohen 1995; coins; inscriptions of the 'Apolloniatai Lykioi Thrakes kolonoi'; Hierocles; bishops 381–680
note: Settlers included Lycians and Thracians (inscriptions). medieval Roman Sozopolis fell to the Seljuks c. 1074 and was retaken by John II in 1120.

site: Gaziri, near Kumdanlı on Lake Hoyran (Yalvaç, Isparta)
greek_from_text: first bishop at Nicaea 325
pre_detail: Known only from church sources and located only approximately at Gaziri on Lake Hoyran. No excavation, and no earlier name or prehistoric level is reported for the site.
status_evidence: bishops 325, 381; Hierocles; Notitiae (suffragan of Antioch)
note: Known only from church sources; coordinates from the council-sees seed list. Island ruins (Limenia) in Lake Hoyran nearby.

greek_from_text: Seleucid foundation, probably by Antiochus I (281–261 BC), with settlers from Magnesia on the Maeander (Strabo 12.8.14); Augustan colony 25 BC
pre_detail: Rejected the proposed 'no known'. That no Proto-Hittite, Hittite, Phrygian or Lydian finds have come from the city is absence of evidence. Its source is unclear (Wikipedia, apparently relaying Demirer 2002, a Turkish museum guide). Most excavation (Robinson 1924; Özhanlı) exposed Roman levels, and the Hellenistic and earlier strata are barely reached (rule 7). Strabo 12.8.14 says only that Magnesians settled it, not that the site was new. I could not confirm that Mitchell & Waelkens 1998 explicitly call it virgin ground. The 3rd-millennium mounds in the plain and the Men sanctuary (4th c. BC finds, c. 3.5 km away) are not the city site.
pre_sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antioch_of_Pisidia (citing Mitchell & Waelkens 1998; Demirer 2002; Blanco-Pérez 2016); Strabo 12.8.14; Pleiades 609307
pre_greek_note: No pre-Seleucid levels known on the city hill; the sanctuary of Men Askaenos nearby has 4th-c. BC finds.
status_evidence: Strabo 12.8.14; Hellenistic and colonial coins; capital of Pisidia (Diocletian); bishops 381–787
lang_later: Latin official in the colony (1st–3rd c. AD)
note: Settlers came from Magnesia on the Maeander (Strabo 12.8.14). Sacked by the Arabs in 713 and declined.
sources: Strabo 12.8.14; Cohen 1995; Levick 1967; Pleiades 609307; Wikipedia: Antioch of Pisidia

greek_from_text: Roman provincial coins (2nd–3rd c. AD); bishops 381–553
pre_greek_note: Native name; no pre-Greek attestation.
status_evidence: Roman provincial coins (ΚΑΣΑΤΩΝ); bishops 381, 431, 553
note: Site lies in Gündoğmuş district, just outside the Alanya/Gazipaşa area; included because it is in this batch's seed (may duplicate PAM). Location is the 'modern view'.

greek_from_text: listed among the Pisidian poleis in Artemidorus' list, c. 100 BC (Strabo 12.7.2); civic coins Commodus–Philip I
status_evidence: Strabo 12.7.2; coins Commodus–Philip I (RPC IV.3–VIII); bishops 325, 381, 787; Hierocles
note: Pleiades also records Hellenistic occupation.
sources: Pleiades 638741; Strabo 12.7.2; RPC IV.3 (Amblada); Wikipedia: Amblada

other_names: Tiberiopolis (Τιβεριεῖς Παππηνοί on coins); Pappa Orondikos (Ptolemy)
greek_from_text: title Tiberiopolis implies civic status under Tiberius (AD 14–37); Greek civic coins under Antoninus Pius
status_evidence: coins Antoninus Pius (RPC IV.3 7693–94, 7785); Ptolemy; Notitiae; bishop 787
note: Town of the Orondeis; the Tiberian dating rests on the city title only.

other_names: Korakesion; Kalon Oros (medieval Roman); Candelore (medieval Latin); Alaiye (Seljuk, after 1221)
greek_from_text: Ptolemaic possession in the 3rd c. BC; first named as a town resisting Antiochus III in 197 BC (Livy 33.20); stronghold of Diodotos Tryphon c. 140 BC; Roman provincial coins
pre_detail: The castle rock was first fortified in the Hellenistic period. The claimed Luwian etymology (*Korakassa) and 'probable' Hittite/Achaemenid occupation are unsupported speculation. The 7th c. BC Phoenician inscription often cited for Alanya comes from Laertes (Cebel Ires Dağı), not from the castle.
status_evidence: Strabo 14.5.2 (first city of Cilicia); Roman provincial coins; bishops 431–692
note: Greek-named fortress town; Ptolemaic control in the 3rd c. BC is inferred from Bagnall's list of Ptolemaic possessions. Taken by the Seljuks in 1221 (renamed Alaiye > Alanya).

greek_from_text: Strabo (c. AD 20) calls it a katoikia with an anchorage; Roman-period civic inscriptions (1st–2nd c. AD)
pre_detail: Sinek Kalesi has Hellenistic-Roman remains only (Bean & Mitford; Rough Cilicia survey). No pre-Hellenistic evidence, and no proof of new ground.
pre_sources: Bean & Mitford 1970; Pleiades 638853; Rough Cilicia Archaeological Survey reports (Rauh et al.)
status_evidence: Strabo 14.5.3; Roman-period inscriptions (Bean & Mitford 1970)
note: Identification of Sinek Kalesi with Hamaxia (Bean & Mitford) is generally accepted but marked '?' in Barrington. By c. AD 200 apparently dependent on Coracesium; no coins or bishops known, so civic status rests on inscriptions.

greek_from_text: Roman provincial coins (2nd–3rd c. AD); bishops 381 and 431
pre_greek_note: Anatolian (-assos) place name of a native hill community; no pre-Greek attestation.
status_evidence: Roman provincial coins; Notitiae; bishops 381, 431
note: Hill city in the hinterland of Alanya; Hellenistic remains reported (Pleiades periods).

greek_from_text: Strabo (c. AD 20) calls it a phrourion on a hill; civic inscriptions and Roman provincial coins of the 1st–3rd c. AD
pre_detail: A Phoenician judicial inscription of the second half of the 7th c. BC was found (in secondary context) within the ruins of Laertes on Cebel Ires Dağı. It records land dealings among people with Luwian names under King Warika (of Hiyawa/Adana), showing a native community there long before the Greek town.
status_evidence: Strabo 14.5.3; inscriptions; Roman provincial coins
note: Hellenistic occupation reported (Pleiades); not a bishopric. Diogenes Laertius' connection to the town is unproven.

greek_from_text: Town where Pompey stopped after Pharsalus, 48 BC (Lucan 8.259; Florus); Roman provincial coins; bishops 325, 451
pre_greek_note: Non-Greek name; no pre-Greek attestation.
status_evidence: Roman provincial coins; Hierocles; bishops 325, 451
note: Probably a polis already in the Hellenistic period, but the first datable mention is 48 BC.

greek_from_text: Founded by Antiochus IV of Commagene (client ruler of Rough Cilicia AD 38/41–72), named after his wife Iotape; coins Trajan–Valerian
pre_detail: Changed from 'no known': no source states that Antiochus IV of Commagene built Iotape on virgin ground, and Pleiades records Hellenistic attestation. The site has no published stratigraphy before the 1st c. AD.
status_evidence: Roman provincial coins; Hierocles; bishops (Isauria)
note: Exact foundation year unknown (c. AD 52 often cited). The modern locality name Aytap preserves Iotape.
sources: Pleiades 648650; TIB 5 (Kilikien und Isaurien); Wikipedia: Iotape (city)

site: coastal acropolis and plain at the mouth of the Hacımusa Çayı, c. 3 km WSW of Gazipaşa centre (Gazipaşa, Antalya)
greek_from_text: Listed as a polis by Ps.-Skylax 102 (c. 340 BC); taken by Antiochus III 197 BC (Livy 33.20); Trajan died here 117 → Traianopolis
pre_greek_note: Sallunê, burned by Neriglissar in 557/6 BC 'at the border of Lydia' (Babylonian Chronicle ABC 6), is often identified with Selinous; uncertain.
status_evidence: Ps.-Skylax 102 (polis); Roman provincial coins; Hierocles; bishops 381, 451
note: Ps.-Skylax calls it a polis but not 'Hellenic', so it may have been a native community with a Greek name in the 4th c. BC. Older Turkish name Selinti continued Selinous; the town was renamed Gazipaşa in the 20th c.

greek_from_text: Roman-period civic inscriptions and buildings (1st–3rd c. AD); bishop at Chalcedon 451
pre_detail: Macar Kalesi has only Roman-period remains recorded. No pre-Greek evidence and no proof of new ground.
status_evidence: Roman inscriptions (Bean & Mitford 1965); Hierocles; bishop 451
note: Earlier scholars (Le Quien) put the see in Pamphylia by the river Kestros; the Macar site follows Bean & Mitford and TIB 5.
sources: Bean & Mitford 1965; Pleiades 648665; TIB 5; Wikipedia: Cestrus

greek_from_text: Roman-period city, 'metropolis of the Lamotis' on Roman provincial coins (3rd c. AD); bishops 451/458 (with Charadros) and 787
pre_greek_note: Native name; no pre-Greek attestation.
status_evidence: Roman provincial coins; Hierocles; bishops 451/458, 787
note: The council seed placed the see 'Lamus' at the mouth of the Lamos river (Limonlu, Erdemli), but that Lamos was only a village (Strabo 14.5.6); the coin-issuing city and see is this Lamos above Adanda, whose port was Charadros (bishop Nunechius of 'Lamus and Charadrus').
sources: Bean & Mitford 1970; TIB 5; Pleiades 648690; Wikipedia: Lamus (see)

other_names: Antiocheia epi Krago; Antioch in Isauria
greek_from_text: Founded by Antiochus IV of Commagene (ruled Rough Cilicia AD 38/41–72); coins from Trajan; bishops from 325
pre_detail: Changed from 'no known': the excavators (Hoff, Townsend, Erdoğmuş) attribute the city to Antiochus IV of Commagene but think the harbour may earlier have been a Cilician pirate haven ('From Pirate Base to Roman City'). They report no pre-Roman remains, yet nothing shows the site was virgin ground.
pre_sources: archaeological.org/fieldwork/antiochia-ad-cragum-excavations; 'From Pirate Base to Roman City: The Excavations of Antiochia ad Cragum in Rough Cilicia' (excavation volume); Pleiades 648560
status_evidence: Roman provincial coins; Hierocles; bishops 325, 381, 451
note: Pleiades dates the foundation to 170 BC (Antiochus IV Epiphanes), but the excavators (Hoff et al.) and most scholars attribute it to Antiochus IV of Commagene.

greek_from_text: Attested as a city only as a bishopric of Isauria in the Notitiae episcopatuum (6th c. onward)
pre_detail: Site only tentatively identified near Muzkent; no relevant archaeology.
status_evidence: Notitiae episcopatuum (Isauria); Catholic titular see
note: Cape Nephelis appears in Livy 33.20 (197 BC); site of the town identified only tentatively (Barrington 'Nephelis?').

greek_from_text: name implies a Julio-Claudian foundation or renaming (1st c. AD, perhaps by Antiochus IV of Commagene); attested only as a see (Heliosebaste) in the Notitiae
founder: unknown; name honours the Julio-Claudian house (perhaps a foundation of Antiochus IV of Commagene)
pre_detail: Location tentative (Asar Tepe); no archaeology of early levels.
status_evidence: Notitiae episcopatuum; Catholic titular see
note: Origin and founder are inferred only from the name; location tentative (Barrington 'Iuliosebaste/Heliosebaste?').

greek_from_text: Listed as a polis with harbour by Ps.-Skylax 102 (c. 340 BC); later the port of Lamos; bishop 451
pre_detail: Kaledran has visible Roman and later remains. The Ps.-Skylax polis (c. 340 BC) shows a pre-Hellenistic town but not its character, and no excavation exists.
status_evidence: Ps.-Skylax 102 (polis); bishop 451 (Nunechius 'of Lamus and Charadrus')
note: Not labelled 'Hellenic' by Ps.-Skylax. The local name Kaledran preserves Charadros.

site: Eski Anamur / Ören, 6 km W of Anamur (Anamur, Mersin)
greek_from_text: Listed as cape and polis by Ps.-Skylax 102 (c. 340 BC); taken by Antiochus III 197 BC (Livy 33.20); coins under Antiochus IV of Commagene and Roman emperors
pre_detail: The Russell excavations recovered mainly Roman-Byzantine levels with only Hellenistic elements in the citadel walls. The popular claim that Anemurium 'began as a Phoenician city' is unsupported, and the 4th c. BC town of Ps.-Skylax is archaeologically unknown.
pre_sources: Russell, Anemurium excavation reports; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anemurium; turkisharchaeonews.net/site/anemurium
status_evidence: Ps.-Skylax 102 (polis); coins; Hierocles; bishops 381–692
note: Greek name ('windy'); not labelled 'Hellenic' by Ps.-Skylax. The nearby town of Anamur preserves the name, but the ruins lie outside it.

greek_from_text: name (Titioupolis) implies a Flavian foundation or renaming (Titus, 79–81); first bishop (Artemius) at Constantinople 381; Isaurian Decapolis
founder: unknown; name probably honours Titus (Flavian period)
pre_detail: Unlocated; no archaeological evidence possible.
status_evidence: Hierocles; Notitiae; bishops 381, 451, 692
note: City status is secure (see), but the site is unknown: Barrington marks 'Titioupolis?' near Anamur, while its listing in the inland Isaurian Decapolis suggests an interior site.

site: Paşabeleni hill at the mouth of the Sini Çay, Bozyazı (Bozyazı, Mersin)
greek_from_text: Samian colony (Mela 1.77), date unknown; excavated graves from the 5th c. BC; Greek-legend silver coins from c. 400 BC
pre_detail: Changed from 'no known'. The Mersin University excavations (1997-2003) and the 1986 necropolis dig found nothing earlier than 5th c. BC graves and Classical pottery. However, the 1930s Swedish survey (Gjerstad) reported Iron Age (Cypro-Archaic-type) sherds, which may belong to a native or Cypriot settlement before or alongside the Samian colony. Neither new ground nor a pre-Greek settlement is demonstrated.
pre_sources: Durugönül (ed.), Nagidos (2007); turkisharchaeonews.net/site/nagidos; Gjerstad, Revue archéologique 1934; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nagidus
status_evidence: IACP (Kilikia); Ps.-Skylax 102 (polis); coins from c. 400 BC
note: Lost land to the Ptolemaic foundation Arsinoe (c. 260s BC) and was its nominal mother city; abandoned c. mid-2nd c. BC. Foundation date uncertain: 6th c. BC is a guess bracketed by the 5th-c. graves.

site: near Softa Kalesi, E of Bozyazı (Bozyazı, Mersin)
greek_from_text: Founded by Aetos son of Apollonios, Ptolemaic strategos of Cilicia, on land taken from Nagidos, between 279 and 253 BC (probably 260s)
founder: Aetos son of Apollonios, for Ptolemy II
pre_detail: Changed from 'no known'. The Nagidos decree (SEG 39.1426) says Aetos occupied a strong position, expelled the 'barbarians' encroaching on Nagidian land, and founded and settled the city. That may mean natives were living on or near the spot, so new ground is not proven. The site is not securely located and has not been excavated.
status_evidence: Arsinoe–Nagidos inscription (SEG 39.1426); Strabo 14.5.3; Cohen 1995
note: Shared citizenship with Nagidos according to the inscription. Exact site uncertain.

greek_from_text: Attested as a city only as a bishopric of Isauria (Notitiae)
pre_detail: Known only as a late bishopric. The site near Softa Kalesi is tentative and unexcavated, and no earlier name or prehistoric site is reported.
status_evidence: Notitiae episcopatuum; Catholic titular see
note: Possibly Ps.-Skylax's harbour 'Seton'; site tentative.

greek_from_text: Samian colony (Mela 1.77); excavated Greek material from the late 8th/7th c. BC; coins from c. 450 BC
founder: Samians; legend of Sandokos from Syria (Apollod. 3.14.3)
pre_detail: Excavations at Aydıncık (Zoroğlu) give Greek-style material and local East-Greek-style pottery workshops from c. 700 BC. No Bronze Age or earlier Iron Age level is reported. The Syrian founder Sandokos (Apollod. 3.14.3) is legend only.
pre_sources: levantineceramics.org/kilns/118; Lehmann et al., Levant 2020 (doi 10.1080/00758914.2020.1772633); knowledge: Zoroğlu, Kelenderis I (1994)
pre_greek_note: Hittite Ura has occasionally been placed near Gilindire, but most locate it at Silifke or Olba.
status_evidence: IACP (Kilikia); Ps.-Skylax 102 (polis); coins; Hierocles; bishops 381, 451, 787
note: A Phoenician/Syrian element is suggested by the Sandokos legend. The older Turkish name Gilindire continued Kelenderis; renamed Aydıncık in the 20th c.

greek_from_text: Harbour in Ps.-Skylax 102; town in 315 BC (Diodorus 19.64) and 197 BC (Livy 33.20); called a polis by Stephanus
pre_detail: Known as a harbour and Hellenistic town (Ps.-Skylax, Diodorus, Livy). The headland remains are not excavated, and no pre-Greek name or prehistoric level is reported.
status_evidence: Diodorus 19.64; Livy 33.20; Steph. Byz.
note: Civic status is weakly attested: no coins or bishops are certain, and Ps.-Skylax lists it only as a harbour. It was a Ptolemaic port in the late 4th–3rd c. BC.

greek_from_text: Called a 'Hellenic polis' by Ps.-Skylax 102 (c. 340 BC); its people were moved to Seleukeia c. 295–280 BC (Strabo 14.5.4)
pre_detail: Ps.-Skylax calls it a Hellenic polis. There is no excavation at Taşucu, and no pre-Greek name or prehistoric level is reported.
status_evidence: IACP (Kilikia); Ps.-Skylax 102 ('Hellenic polis')
note: Mother city unrecorded. After the synoecism into Seleukeia it survived as Seleukeia's harbour.
refoundations: Synoecized into Seleukeia on the Kalykadnos (Seleucus I)

other_names: Seleukeia Tracheia; Olbia and Hyria (earlier names, Steph. Byz.); Seleucia Isauriae
greek_from_text: Founded by Seleucus I between c. 296 and 280 BC, with settlers from Holmoi
pre_greek_note: Hittite/Ugaritic port Ura placed at Silifke by Beal 1992; alternatives are Olba (modern village Ura), the Gilindire area or Soloi. Stephanus' earlier name 'Hyria' may echo it. Doubtful.
status_evidence: Strabo 14.5.4; coins; Hierocles (metropolis of Isauria); bishops 325–787
note: Metropolis of Isauria and pilgrimage centre of St Thecla (Meriamlik). In Armenian and Crusader hands in the 13th c., then Karamanid.

greek_from_text: Taken by Antiochus III in 197 BC (Livy 33.20); autonomous coins in the 1st c. BC; Roman provincial coins
pre_detail: Aşkın (2010) says the written and archaeological evidence for Korykos goes back only to the early Hellenistic period: Livy 33.20 for 197 BC and a polygonal wall. Nothing earlier is known, but the site is not excavated deeply enough to show new ground.
status_evidence: Livy 33.20; coins; Hierocles; bishops 381–692
note: Under Armenian rule c. 1200–1360 and Cypriot (Lusignan) 1361–1448; the population was then mixed.

greek_from_text: Hellenistic settlement of the 2nd c. BC on the former island (excavations); capital of Archelaus I of Cappadocia as Sebaste from c. 25–20 BC; coins
founder: no recorded founder; refounded by Archelaus I of Cappadocia
pre_detail: The Rome–La Sapienza excavations (since 1995) show settlement on the former island running continuously from the 2nd c. BC to the 7th c. AD. No earlier levels are reported, so this was a new Hellenistic settlement.
pre_sources: italiana.esteri.it 'Scavi e ricerche a Elaiussa Sebaste'; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaiussa_Sebaste; knowledge: Equini Schneider (ed.), Elaiussa Sebaste I–III
status_evidence: Strabo 14.5.6; coins of Elaiussa and Sebaste; Hierocles; bishops (Sebaste in Cilicia)
note: Excavated by the Rome-La Sapienza mission (Equini Schneider).
refoundations: Elaiussa → Sebaste (Archelaus I of Cappadocia, c. 25–20 BC)

greek_from_text: Hellenistic settlement of the Olban priest-dynasts; reportedly renamed Neapolis by Theodosius II (408–450)
pre_detail: The visible settlement grew up around a Hellenistic tower of the Olban priest-dynasts and the sinkhole. No pre-Hellenistic finds or earlier name are reported.
status_evidence: Neapolis of the Isaurian Decapolis/Notitiae (identification unproven); five churches
note: The Neapolis renaming appears in modern site literature; Barrington leaves Isaurian Neapolis unlocated, so the identification is doubtful. If it is wrong, Kanytelis was a large village of the territory of Elaiussa/Olba.

greek_from_text: Colony of Lindos (Rhodes) and Achaeans/Argives by tradition; excavations at Soli Höyük show the Greek settlement c. 700–690 BC; 'Hellenic polis' in Ps.-Skylax; coins from the 5th c. BC
founder: Rhodians from Lindos with Achaeans/Argives (Strabo 14.5.8; Polybius 21.24)
pre_greek_note: Late Bronze Age (Luwian/Hittite) occupation on Soli Höyük from the 15th c. BC. Identifications with Ellipra, Pitura (Šunaššura treaty) or Sallusa are speculative.
status_evidence: IACP (Kilikia); Ps.-Skylax 102 ('Hellenic polis'); coins; Hierocles; bishops
note: Mycenaean (LH IIIA–B) imports at Soli Höyük show only trade. 'Soloikismos' (solecism) was proverbially attributed to the Greek spoken here. Refounded by Pompey with pirates as Pompeiopolis; largely abandoned after the 525 earthquake.
sources: IACP (Kilikia); Strabo 14.5.8; Yağcı (Soli Höyük excavations); Pleiades 648781

greek_from_text: Listed as a polis by Ps.-Skylax 102 (c. 340 BC); taken by Antiochus III 197 BC (Livy 33.20); coins Hellenistic and Roman (Hadrianopolis)
pre_detail: Zephyrion's exact site under modern Mersin is unexcavated. The great Neolithic-Iron Age mound of Yumuktepe lies c. 3 km NW of the centre, too far to count as the same nucleus unless Zephyrion lay beside it, which is unproven. Pleiades' Bronze/Iron Age tags come only from Mersin/Yumuktepe toponyms.
pre_sources: Pleiades 648810 (TAVO names for Mersin/Yumuktepe); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yumuktepe; Barrington 66 F3
status_evidence: Ps.-Skylax 102 (polis); coins; Hierocles; bishops 381, 451
note: The exact site lies under modern Mersin. Not to be confused with Cape Zephyrion near Korykos.

greek_from_text: Called a polis (founded by Sardanapalos) when Alexander passed in 333 BC (Arrian, Anab. 2.5.2–4)
pre_greek_note: Ingirâ, taken by Sennacherib's army in 696 BC, is generally equated with Anchiale; the location of Anchiale (Yumuktepe or Karaduvar) is itself uncertain. Yumuktepe has Neolithic to Iron Age levels.
status_evidence: Arrian 2.5; Strabo 14.5.9; no secure coins or bishop
note: Whether it was ever a Greek polis rather than a native town that declined (Strabo calls it a small place) is uncertain. Beaufort placed it at Karaduvar.

other_names: Antiocheia on the Kydnos (Antiochus IV); imperial titles Hadriana, Severiana, Antoniniana etc.
greek_from_text: Greek coin legend ΤΕΡΣΙΚΟΝ c. 420–400 BC; 'large and prosperous polis' in Xenophon (401 BC); refounded as Antiocheia on the Kydnos under Antiochus IV (175–164 BC)
founder: Argives with Triptolemos (Greek legend, Strabo 14.5.12); Sennacherib (Berossus)
pre_greek_note: Hittite Tarša (Kizzuwatna) and Neo-Assyrian Tarzi/Tarzu (Shalmaneser III, Sennacherib) are secure. Gözlükule has Neolithic to Iron Age levels.
status_evidence: IACP (Kilikia); coins from c. 420 BC; Hierocles (metropolis of Cilicia I); bishops 325–692
lang_later: Cilician (Luwian) and Aramaic used alongside Greek in the Achaemenid period; Arabic-speaking Muslim frontier city c. 700–965; under Armenian rule 12th–14th c.
note: Early coins also carry Aramaic legends, so Greek was one language among several before the Hellenistic period.
sources: IACP (Kilikia); Xenophon Anab. 1.2.23; Goldman, Gözlükule; Pleiades 648789
refoundations: Tarsos → Antiocheia on the Kydnos (Antiochus IV) → Tarsos

site: Adana city centre, Tepebağ mound (Seyhan, Adana)
greek_from_text: Refounded as the polis Antiocheia on the Saros under Antiochus IV (175–164 BC), with civic coins
founder: Antiochus IV (refoundation of the native town)
pre_greek_note: Hittite Adaniya (Kizzuwatna); Hieroglyphic Luwian Adanawa and Phoenician ʾDN in the Karatepe and Çineköy inscriptions (8th c. BC); Tepebağ mound occupied from the Bronze Age.
status_evidence: Seleucid civic coins; Roman provincial coins; Hierocles; bishops 325–680
lang_later: Arabic-speaking Muslim frontier city c. 700–965; Armenian rule 12th–14th c.; Ramadanid Turkish from the mid-14th c.
note: Ps.-Skylax 102 lists an 'Adane' emporion with harbour, perhaps this place.
sources: Cohen 2006; Karatepe bilingual; Pleiades 648548; Wikipedia: Adana
refoundations: Adana → Antiocheia on the Saros (Antiochus IV) → Adana

other_names: Magarsa; Antiocheia on the Pyramos (Antiochus IV)
site: Dörtdirek, c. 3.5 km SW of Karataş town (Karataş, Adana)
greek_from_text: Sanctuary town of Athena Magarsia (Alexander sacrificed there, 333 BC); refounded as Antiocheia on the Pyramos under Antiochus IV (175–164 BC), with coins
pre_greek_note: Magarsos is a non-Greek name; a sanctuary and town existed before the Seleucid refoundation (Arrian 2.5.9).
status_evidence: Coins of Antiocheia on the Pyramos; inscriptions at Karataş (Robert 1951)
note: Port and sanctuary of Mallos. Robert placed Antiocheia on the Pyramos here; others think Mallos itself was renamed, so this entry may overlap with Mallos.
refoundations: Magarsos → Antiocheia on the Pyramos (Antiochus IV)

greek_from_text: Silver coins with Greek legends from the later 5th c. BC; polis in Ps.-Skylax 102; treated as an Argive colony by Alexander (333 BC)
pre_greek_note: Native Cilician town in the 'House of Mopsos' milieu (Luwian Muksa-, Phoenician MPŠ); no pre-Greek attestation of the name.
status_evidence: IACP (Kilikia); coins; Ps.-Skylax 102; Roman colony (3rd c.); Hierocles; bishops 377–553
note: Argos claimed it as a colony (Arrian 2.5.9), but the founding legend is mythical; Schürr 2019 argues there was no Greek settlement in Cilicia before the Hellenistic period. The site at Kızıltahta is inferred from ancient distances.

greek_from_text: Hellenistic polis: autonomous civic coins from the later 2nd/1st c. BC; civic era from 47 BC (Caesar); Strabo calls it a small town
pre_detail: A Syro-Hittite (Neo-Hittite) basalt funerary stele of the 9th c. BC was found in 1994 during building work in Yumurtalık itself, showing an Iron Age native community at the site. Hittite pottery of the 17th c. BC also comes from Zeytinbeli Höyük, c. 7 km away, too far to count.
pre_sources: Bonatz 2000, Das syro-hethitische Grabdenkmal, C 58; hittitemonuments.com/yumurtalik; vici.org/vici/73930; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aegeae_(Cilicia)
pre_greek_note: Bronze Age (Hittite-period) pottery comes from Zeytinbeli Höyük nearby, not from the city site.
status_evidence: Coins; Hierocles; bishops 325–553; Asklepieion
lang_later: Armenian port (Ayas/Laiazzo) under the Armenian Kingdom of Cilicia, 12th–14th c.; Mamluk from 1347
note: The medieval name Ayas continues Aigai.

greek_from_text: 'Last city of Cilicia, large and prosperous' (Xenophon, 401 BC); coins with Greek legend ΙΣΣΙΚΟΝ c. 400–380 BC
pre_greek_note: Kinet Höyük was occupied from the Neolithic onward; the excavator (Gates) proposed Late Bronze Age Izziya, which is not certain.
status_evidence: IACP (Kilikia); Xenophon Anab. 1.2.24; coins
note: The site was abandoned c. 50 BC and eclipsed by Alexandreia and Nikopolis; whether Nikopolis was Issos renamed or a separate town is disputed.
sources: Xenophon Anab. 1.2.24; Gates 2013; Pleiades 658490; Livius: Issus

greek_from_text: Native Oiniandos refounded as Epiphaneia under Antiochus IV (175–164 BC); Pompey settled pirates there (civic era 67/66 BC)
pre_greek_note: The earlier name Oiniandos survives only in Greek sources (Pliny, Steph. Byz.).
status_evidence: Coins; Hierocles; bishops 325–553
refoundations: Oiniandos → Epiphaneia (Antiochus IV); pirates settled by Pompey (67 BC)

greek_from_text: Founded according to tradition by Alexander after Issos (333 BC); more likely a foundation of one of the Successors
founder: Alexander the Great (tradition) or a Successor
pre_detail: The ancient site is not securely located (Barrington: Esentepe in İskenderun). Phoenician Myriandos (Xen. Anab. 1.4.6) lay c. 6 km to the SW and was superseded, not built over. No archaeology of earlier levels.
pre_greek_note: The Phoenician emporion Myriandos lay nearby but on a different site.
status_evidence: Strabo 14.5.19; coins; Hierocles; bishops 325–518
lang_later: Arab-held c. 640–969; Crusader, Armenian and Mamluk control 12th–15th c.
note: The ancient city is probably, but not certainly, under modern İskenderun.

greek_from_text: native harbour town where Harpalus set up a statue of Glykera c. 325 BC (Theopompus); first civic evidence: city coins of the 2nd–1st c. BC; polis with archons, boule and demos in Octavian's dossier of Seleukos of Rhosos (42–31 BC)
pre_greek_note: Pleiades lists an Akkadian form 'Urrus', but no attestation could be traced, so it is not used. Malalas makes Rhosos a foundation of Kilix (legend); the native town is known only from Greek sources.
status_evidence: Coins ('sacred, inviolable and autonomous'); Hierocles; bishops 363–600
note: Arsuz continues Rhosos. 'Pre-Greek name' assumes Rhosos is not Greek, which is likely but unproven.

greek_from_text: Founded by Seleucus I in 300 BC as his first capital and the port of Antioch
pre_detail: An earlier place stood here. Strabo 16.2.8 says the site was formerly called Hydatos Potamoi, and Malalas (and Pausanias) mention a 'Palaiopolis'. Both names are Greek, though, and no pre-Hellenistic level has been published, so the earlier place cannot be shown to be non-Greek. Iron Age Al Mina is c. 6 km away at the Orontes mouth.
pre_greek_note: Pleiades notes a possible earlier village (Hydatos Potamoi). The Archaic emporion al-Mina is nearby but on a different site.
status_evidence: Strabo 16.2.8; coins; Hierocles; bishops 325–553
lang_later: Aramaic (Syriac) widespread in the hinterland; Arab rule 637–969
note: Settlers from Antigonia were transferred here in part. The city declined after the 6th century.

site: unlocated, on the Orontes c. 7 km NE of Antakya (Antakya, Hatay)
greek_from_text: Founded by Antigonus I in 307 BC; its population was moved to Antioch (and Seleukeia) by Seleucus I in 300 BC
pre_detail: Unlocated; the city existed only from 307 to 300 BC.
status_evidence: Diodorus 20.47; Strabo 16.2.4; Malalas
note: A short-lived city (307–300 BC); its exact site is unknown.
refoundations: Abandoned; inhabitants moved to Antioch (300 BC)

greek_from_text: Founded by Seleucus I on 22 Artemisios (May) 300 BC
pre_detail: The Amuq tells (Atchana, Tayinat) lie well away, and most had been abandoned before Alexander. No pre-Seleucid level is published from Antakya. Libanius' and Malalas' predecessors (Iopolis, Kasiotis, Herakleia, Alexander's Emathia/Bottia) are legendary or Greek. Pleiades' Bronze Age tags come from TAVO name indexing.
pre_greek_note: Native villages such as Bottia and Meroe are mentioned by late sources (Libanius, Malalas); Neo-Hittite Kunulua (Tell Tayinat) is a different site c. 25 km away.
status_evidence: Coins; Hierocles (metropolis of Syria I); patriarchal see; bishops 325–787
lang_later: Bilingual with Syriac (Aramaic) in Late Antiquity; Arabic increasingly dominant after 637 (Roman again 969–1084; Seljuk 1084; Crusader 1098–1268; Mamluk from 1268)
note: Malalas reports a legendary Argive settlement (Iopolis) on Mt Silpius; it has no archaeological confirmation.

greek_from_text: Named after Domitian (Malalas) or L. Domitius Ahenobarbus; Roman-period town; bishops from 451
founder: Domitian (Malalas); alternatively named for L. Domitius Ahenobarbus
pre_detail: An unexcavated Roman-period town at Katranlı (Dindebol); no earlier settlement or native name is known.
status_evidence: Isaurian Decapolis; Notitiae; bishops 451–879 (Le Quien)
