note: Karaman province (GAL batch); border duplicate. The former village name Dindebol may continue Dometiopolis.

site: uncertain; Barrington places it W of Mut (Mut, Mersin)
greek_from_text: Known as a city only as a bishopric of Isauria (Notitiae)
pre_detail: The site is unlocated (W of Mut, or Ağalimanı) and known only from church lists.
status_evidence: Notitiae episcopatuum; Catholic titular see
note: Location disputed: Barrington 'Meloe?' W of Mut; GCatholic gives Ağalimanı on the coast near Taşucu.
sources: Pleiades 648707; Wikipedia: Meloe (Isauria); GCatholic: Meloë in Isauria

other_names: Ninica, Colonia Iulia Augusta Felix (Augustan colony, if the same place)
greek_from_text: Augustan veteran colony Ninica (Colonia Iulia Augusta Felix, after 27 BC), if the same place; colony of Claudius as Claudiopolis (Ammianus 14.8.2); bishops from 325
pre_detail: The colony title 'Ninica' looks native and may preserve a pre-colonial place name, but it is attested only with the Roman colony. No pre-Roman finds are reported under Mut or its castle. Bronze–Iron Age sites in the Göksu valley (e.g. Kilise Tepe) lie well away.
status_evidence: Colonial coins (Latin legends, 2nd–3rd c.); Hierocles; Isaurian Decapolis; bishops 325, 381, 451
lang_later: Latin was used officially by the colony (coin legends) before Greek prevailed
note: Pleiades and Mitford equate Ninica with Claudiopolis; if they are separate, the date is AD 41–54 (Claudius).

greek_from_text: Roman provincial coins as 'metropolis of the Ketis' (2nd–3rd c. AD); bishop 325
pre_greek_note: Anatolian (-issos) place name of the native Ketis; no pre-Greek attestation.
status_evidence: Coins; Notitiae; bishop 325
note: Identification with Dağpazarı follows Hild & Hellenkemper (TIB 5); Pleiades also has a separate Koropissos entry (652347) further west. Not to be confused with Koropassos in Lycaonia.

site: Ura (Ören), 4 km E of Uzuncaburç (Silifke, Mersin)
greek_from_text: Seat of the Teukrid priest-dynasts of Zeus Olbios, with Greek inscriptions from the 3rd/2nd c. BC; coins of the dynasts (Ajax son of Teukros, AD 10–15) and civic coins of Olba
founder: Ajax son of Teukros (Greek legend, Strabo 14.5.10)
pre_greek_note: The priest-dynasts bore Luwian names (Tarkyaris, Teukros < Tarku-?). The modern village name Ura has been linked to Hittite Ura (see Seleukeia), which is doubtful.
status_evidence: Strabo 14.5.10; coins; Hierocles; bishops 381, 680
note: The cult centre at Uzuncaburç became the separate city Diokaisareia under Vespasian.

other_names: Uzuncaburç; earlier the sanctuary of Zeus Olbios at Olba
greek_from_text: The Hellenistic sanctuary of Zeus Olbios (temple c. 300 BC) was made a city with coinage under Vespasian (AD 69–79)
pre_detail: Changed from 'no known'. Vespasian's city replaced an existing Hellenistic sanctuary settlement of Zeus Olbios, so it was not new ground. That sanctuary was run by Hellenized native (Luwian-named) priest-dynasts, e.g. Teukros son of Tarkyaris, which may make it a native community. Still, the Corinthian temple and the remains are Hellenistic Greek, and no pre-Hellenistic level is reported.
pre_sources: Strabo 14.5.10; dergipark.org.tr/en/pub/olba/article/1269054; knowledge: Wannagat; Trampedach on the Olba temple state
status_evidence: Coins from Vespasian; Hierocles; Isaurian Decapolis; bishops 381, 451
note: Before city status it was the temple precinct of Olba (Hellenistic tower of Teukros son of Tarkyaris).

other_names: Mopsouhestia; Seleukeia on the Pyramos (Antiochus IV); Hadriana, Decia (imperial titles); al-Massisa (Arabic); Mamistra (Crusader)
greek_from_text: Native town refounded as Seleukeia on the Pyramos under Antiochus IV (175–164 BC), with coins; earlier Greek name Mopsou hestia ('hearth of Mopsos')
pre_greek_note: Neo-Assyrian Pahri (and Phoenician/Luwian Pʿr/Pahar at Karatepe) is identified with Misis by Pleiades and others; uncertain. The Misis mound has Bronze and Iron Age levels.
status_evidence: Coins; free city (Pliny); Hierocles; bishops 325–553
lang_later: Arabic-speaking Muslim frontier city (al-Massisa) c. 700–965; Armenian rule 12th–14th c.
note: Its traditional Turkish name Misis continues Mopsuestia (officially Yakapınar since the 1960s).
refoundations: Mopsou hestia → Seleukeia on the Pyramos (Antiochus IV) → Mopsuestia

site: Gübe, now under the Seyhan reservoir near Çatalan (Adana)
greek_from_text: Founded in AD 20 and named after Livia (Julia Augusta); civic era from AD 20; coins
founder: Tiberius, in honour of Livia (Julia Augusta)
pre_detail: Gough's 1952 survey before the flooding describes only the Roman city and reports a höyük (Ortatepe) c. 5 km to the south, not at the site. No evidence of earlier occupation or of new ground.
pre_sources: M. Gough, 'Augusta Ciliciae', Anatolian Studies 2 (1952), n. 20 (cambridge.org abstract); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augusta_(Cilicia)
status_evidence: Coins (era AD 20); Hierocles; bishops 431, 451
note: Surveyed by Gough before the Seyhan dam flooded the site in 1955.

other_names: Caesarea by Anazarbos (Augustus); Iustinopolis/Iustinianopolis (Justin I/Justinian); ʿAyn Zarba (Arabic)
greek_from_text: Made a polis as Caesarea by Anazarbos, civic era 19 BC (Augustus); coins
founder: eponym Anazarbos (legend); city status under Augustus
pre_greek_note: Native (non-Greek) name; within the dynasty of Tarkondimotos in the 1st c. BC.
status_evidence: Coins (era 19 BC); Hierocles (metropolis of Cilicia II); bishops 325–680
lang_later: Arab frontier city (ʿAyn Zarba) 8th–10th c.; Armenian royal city 12th–14th c.; destroyed by the Mamluks 1374
note: The traditional name Anavarza continues Anazarbos.

greek_from_text: Native Kastabala refounded as Hieropolis on the Pyramos under Antiochus IV (175–164 BC), with coins
pre_greek_note: Kastabala is probably a Luwian name and the cult of Perasia continues an Anatolian goddess, but no pre-Greek attestation of the town is known.
status_evidence: Coins; capital of Tarkondimotos (1st c. BC); Hierocles; bishop 325

greek_from_text: Founded under Vespasian; civic era AD 73/74; coins
pre_detail: No pre-Roman remains are reported at Kadirli itself. Neo-Hittite Karatepe lies c. 20 km away, which is irrelevant. Whether Flaviopolis was a refoundation or a new site is not stated.
status_evidence: Coins (era 73/74); Hierocles; bishops 325, 451, 680
note: The seed gives the province as Adana, but Kadirli belongs to Osmaniye.

greek_from_text: Civic era AD 51/52; named Neronias under Nero, later Eirenopolis; coins
pre_detail: Rescue excavations at Düziçi report Roman and later remains only. No pre-Roman occupation is reported, and nothing shows a fresh site either.
status_evidence: Coins (era 51/52); Hierocles; bishops 325, 451 (as Neronias)
note: Identification of the site with Düziçi is the modern view. Not to be confused with Eirenopolis in Isauria (Kazancı, Karaman).

other_names: Cotrada; Kotrades/Kotradeis (Notitiae); Ano Kotradis, Klima Kotradon (Barrington)
site: Ano Kotradis, near Göktepe on the Karaman–Antalya border (Gazipaşa, Antalya)
greek_from_text: first attested bishop at Constantinople 680–81 (also Nicaea 787)
status_evidence: see of Isauria in the Notitiae; bishops 680–81, 787
note: Native Isaurian name; Barrington locates 'Ano Kotradis' on the Karaman–Antalya border (seed coordinates fall just inside Antalya). Border case, included because seeded here.

greek_from_text: first attested bishop at Nicaea II (787); probably a see earlier (Isaurian Notitiae)
status_evidence: see of Isauria (Notitiae); bishop 787
note: Small Isaurian highland see; native name.

greek_from_text: first bishop (John) at Nicaea 325; Hierocles; Isaurian Decapolis
founder: unknown (Greek name suggests a Roman-period foundation or renaming)
pre_detail: An unexcavated Isaurian town known from church lists; no earlier name or settlement is recorded.
status_evidence: Hierocles; Notitia of Anastasius of Antioch; George of Cyprus; bishops 325, 451, 458, 692, 878
note: Not to be confused with Eirenopolis-Neronias in Cilicia Pedias (Antiochus IV). Founder and date of the Isaurian city unknown.

other_names: Philadelpheia tes Kietidos (coins); Philadelphia Minor (titular see)
site: İmşi Ören near Gökçeseki (Ermenek, Karaman), tentative
greek_from_text: dynastic name: probably founded or renamed by Antiochus IV of Commagene, king of Cilicia Tracheia (AD 38–72); coins from Trajan ('Philadelpheis of the Kietis')
pre_detail: The site (İmşi Ören) is tentative and unexcavated. The coin legend 'of the Kietis' names a native district, not an earlier town on the site.
status_evidence: coins Trajan–Maximinus (RPC III, IV.3, VI); Hierocles; bishops 381, 451, 787
note: Attribution to Antiochus IV is inferred from the dynastic name (cf. Germanikopolis, Iotape); site identification at İmşi Ören tentative.
sources: Pleiades 648736; RPC III 3211–14; TIB 5; Wikipedia: Philadelphia (Cilicia)

other_names: Hadriane Germanikopolis (coins under Hadrian); Klibanos?; Germanig/Ermenak (medieval)
greek_from_text: named after Germanicus, most likely under Caligula when Antiochus IV of Commagene received Cilicia Tracheia (AD 38); coins from Hadrian
founder: Antiochus IV of Commagene (probable), honouring Germanicus
pre_detail: No archaeology at Ermenek earlier than Roman. Local claims of Hittite origins rest on place-name etymology only; the equation with Klibanos is uncertain and would not show a pre-Greek town anyway.
pre_sources: Pleiades 648635; en.wikipedia Ermenek; ermenek tarihi (meb.k12.tr school page, unreliable)
status_evidence: coins Hadrian–Marcus/Verus (RPC III 3207–10, IV.3); Hierocles; bishops 451, 787, 879
note: Ermenek derives from Germanik(opolis). Identification with Klibanos uncertain.
sources: Pleiades 648635; RPC III 3207–10; TIB 5; Wikipedia: Ermenek

site: near Balabolu (Mut, Mersin), on the Karaman border
greek_from_text: first attested bishop at Constantinople 553
status_evidence: see of Isauria (Notitiae); bishop 553
note: Native (-ssos) name. Site just across the Karaman border in Mersin; border case included from seed.

other_names: Rousoumblada (native village, birthplace of Zeno); Zenopolis
greek_from_text: Zeno's native place raised to city and renamed after him (474–491)
status_evidence: Isaurian Decapolis (George of Cyprus, Const. Porph.); bishops 553?, 680–81, 787
note: Equation with Rousoumblada (Ramsay) and the exact site are uncertain (Pleiades marks the identification with ?).

greek_from_text: listed as a see of Isauria in the Notitiae (Antiochene list c. 570 and later)
status_evidence: see of Isauria (Notitiae); titular see
note: Native name; few data. Date is the earliest certain episcopal listing.

greek_from_text: listed as a see of Isauria in the Notitiae (6th–7th c.)
status_evidence: see of Isauria (Notitiae); titular see
note: Native name; minimal evidence beyond episcopal lists.

greek_from_text: Greek civic coins (Lycaonian koinon issues) under Marcus Aurelius and Lucius Verus (c. 163–169)
status_evidence: coins Marcus/Verus and Philip I (RPC IV.3, VIII); see in the Notitiae under Side
note: Commonly identified with Belören (Bozkır); Fasıllar and the Seydişehir area have also been proposed. A homonymous Isaurian Dalisandos (Hierocles) is unlocated and not included.
sources: Pleiades 652334; RPC IV.3 (Dalisandus); Wikipedia: Dalisandus in Pamphylia

other_names: Isaura Nea; Isauropolis (see merged with it); Leontopolis (medieval Roman)
site: Zengibar Kalesi near Hacılar, c. 19 km E of Bozkır (Bozkır, Konya)
greek_from_text: native Isaurian town (sacked by Perdiccas 322 BC and by Servilius Isauricus 75 BC); rebuilt with new walls by Amyntas of Galatia (c. 36–25 BC, Strabo 12.6.3); Greek civic coins from Antoninus Pius
founder: Amyntas of Galatia (refounded the native town as Isaura Nea)
status_evidence: Strabo 12.6.3; Greek civic inscriptions; coins Antoninus Pius–Severus Alexander (RPC IV.3, V.3, VI); bishops 325, 381, 451; Hierocles
note: Old vs New Isaura is disputed: most place the Roman city (Amyntas' Isaura Nea) at Zengibar Kalesi, with Old Isaura nearby (Pleiades 648652, 'Isaura Vetus/Isauropolis?'); Ramsay put Isaura Nea at Dorla (Aydoğmuş).
sources: Pleiades 648651; Strabo 12.6.3; Diodorus 18.22; RPC IV.3 5730; Wikipedia: Isaura Nea
refoundations: Isaura (Palaia) → Isaura Nea (Amyntas, c. 30 BC) → Leontopolis (medieval Roman)

other_names: Homonada; Homona; Homonanda (capital of the Homonadeis)
site: SW of Lake Suğla (Trogitis), near Yalıhüyük (Seydişehir, Konya)
greek_from_text: first bishop at Nicaea 325 (also 381); Hierocles (Umanada)
status_evidence: Pliny NH 5.94; Hierocles; bishops 325, 381
note: Chief place of the Homonadeis, subdued by Quirinius c. 5–3 BC; site located only approximately (seed 'modern view').
sources: Pliny NH 5.94; Strabo 12.6.5; Wikipedia: Homana; TIB 4

greek_from_text: Hellenistic foundation; Roman-period civic coins of Nikopolis Seleukidos show Seleucus I crowning the city's Tyche, i.e. claim him as founder (c. 300 BC)
founder: Seleucus I (claimed on civic coins); a link with Alexander's victory at Issus has also been suggested
pre_detail: No pre-Hellenistic level is reported at the Nikopolis ruins by İslahiye. A Late Hittite storm-god stele (Kazdağı/İslahiye stele) comes from Kazdağı Tepe c. 1 km away. Hamaç Höyük in İslahiye district has Middle Iron Age to Hellenistic levels. Neolithic–MBA Tilmen Höyük is 7 km away. None is shown to be the city site.
pre_sources: vici.org/vici/29229 (Kazdağı stele); dha.com.tr Hamaç Höyük 2022; Pleiades 658547
status_evidence: Cohen 2006 (Nikopolis); civic coins Commodus–Philip (ΝΙΚΟΠΟΛΕΙΤΩΝ ΣΕΛΕΥΚΙΔΟΣ); late Roman see
lang_later: Aramaic/Syriac probably widespread by late antiquity
note: Attribution of the 'Nikopolis Seleukidos' coins to the İslahiye site is the usual one but not certain; distinct from Nicopolis near Issus on the Cilician coast if that was a separate town.
sources: Cohen 2006, 120–21; Pleiades 658547; RPC online: Nicopolis Seleucidis; Wikipedia: Nicopolis (Cilicia)

site: Karkamış (Karkamış, Gaziantep): acropolis and inner town in Turkey, outer town in Syria (Jarabulus)
greek_from_text: Seleucid refoundation as Europos (after Europos in Macedonia), probably under Seleucus I c. 300 BC; Hellenistic rebuilding found in excavation
pre_greek_note: Kargamiš/Karkamiš in Ebla, Mari, Hittite and Assyrian texts; Hittite viceregal seat and Neo-Hittite capital; identification certain.
status_evidence: Cohen 2006, 169; Pliny 5.87; Ptolemy; walls rebuilt by Justinian (Procopius, Aed. 2.9)
lang_later: Aramaic/Syriac majority in Roman and late antique times
note: About 55 of the site's 90 ha, including the acropolis and inner town, are in Turkey; the modern Karkamış district town beside the site is named after it. Abandoned after the Abbasid period.
sources: Cohen 2006, 169; Pliny NH 5.87; Pleiades 658465; Wikipedia: Carchemish

greek_from_text: first attested by Roman provincial coins (1st–3rd c. AD), some with the founder-hero Temenos
status_evidence: Roman coins; Ptolemy; Hierocles; bishops 451, 787
note: It lies on the Lydian–Phrygian border (Ptolemy calls it Mysian). The start of the coinage is approximate.

other_names: Grimenothyrai (the earlier community; ethnic Τραιανοπολεῖται Γριμενοθυρεῖς)
greek_from_text: city founded in Trajan's name for the Grimenothyritai with Hadrian's permission, c. AD 117–125; coins
status_evidence: Hadrian's letter to the Grimenothyritai; Roman coins; Ptolemy; Hierocles; bishops 459–879 (553, 787 in seed)
note: The site has been placed at Çarıkköy (Radet), Giaurören (Ramsay) or Ortaköy (most recent). Grimenothyrai was a native community. Some sources date the foundation c. 109, which conflicts with Hadrian's role.
sources: Ptolemy 5.2; MAMA XI (Sebaste/Traianopolis); Pleiades 609559; Wikipedia: Traianopolis (Phrygia)

greek_from_text: Hellenistic civic coinage and decrees (2nd–1st c. BC); Cicero (Pro Flacco) cites an Akmonian civic decree (59 BC)
status_evidence: Hellenistic & Roman coins; Cicero, Pro Flacco; Hierocles; bishops 451, 459, 787, 869, 879
note: A Phrygian town on the Dorylaion–Philadelphia road. Notable Jewish community (synagogue of Iulia Severa under Nero). The exact start of polis institutions is not fixed.
sources: Cicero, Pro Flacco; MAMA VI; Thonemann (ed.), Roman Phrygia (2013); Pleiades 609293; Wikipedia: Acmonia

site: near Yeşilhisar / Doğla, SW flank of Ahır Dağı (Afyonkarahisar–Uşak border)
greek_from_text: first attested by Roman provincial coins (Severan, early 3rd c. AD); bishop Constantius 431/451
status_evidence: Roman coins (Elagabalus); bishops 431/451, 11th c.; Notitiae
note: Border case: the Pleiades point lies about 1 km inside Afyonkarahisar on coarse province boundaries.

greek_from_text: founded by Augustus through a synoecism of local villages (27 BC–AD 14); Roman coins
pre_detail: Downgraded from 'yes', pending the primary report. Asgari's TAD article notes only that Fıratlı's Selçikler excavation report (TAD 19.2, 1970) 'gives information' on the prehistoric period, the 5th c. BC, and the Roman and Byzantine periods. It gives no findspot or stratigraphy, and I could not access Fıratlı's report. The 5th-c. BC tumuli (İzmirligil, TAD 22.1, 1975) are burials near, not a settlement on, the city site. A Turkish history-journal article (Toruk 2013) claiming EBA/Chalcolithic 'tumuli' and Hittites is muddled and was rejected. Strong lead: check Fıratlı TAD 19.2 and Mellink's AJA summaries.
pre_sources: N. Asgari, 'Uşak Selçikler ve çevresinden Roma çağı lahitleri ve mermer ocakları', TAD (taed.ktb.gov.tr/Eklenti/109260,59nusinpdf.pdf; cites Fıratlı TAD 19.2 and İzmirligil TAD 22.1); F. Toruk 2013 (erdem.gov.tr/tam-metin-pdf/116/tur; rejected); en.wikipedia Selçikler; Pleiades 609521 (Roman/Late Antique only)
status_evidence: Roman coins; MAMA XI 65–89; Hierocles; bishop 451
note: Villages in its territory included Eibeos (Payamalanı) and Dioskome. Excavations 1966–78 at Selçikler. The district town Sivaslı (Turkish 'from Sebaste') preserves the name.

site: unlocated, Phrygia Pacatiana south of Akmonia (Uşak)
greek_from_text: Roman provincial coins under the Severans (c. 200); bishop Macedonius 536
pre_greek_note: The name is the Thraco-Phrygian word for "town".
status_evidence: Severan coins; bishop 536; Notitiae (suffragan of Laodicea)
note: Site not located.

greek_from_text: Roman imperial coins (ΚΕΡΕΤΑΠΕΩΝ, with the spring Aulindenos)
status_evidence: Roman imperial coins; bishops 431, 787
note: Phrygian town near Lake Salda; site 'Keretapa?' in Barrington. Also called Diokaisareia (date of the name unknown).

site: near Acıpayam, in the Acıpayam (Karayük) plain (Acıpayam, Denizli)
greek_from_text: Hellenistic town; own coinage from the 2nd/1st c. BC (Aulock: 200–10 BC) to Geta
pre_greek_note: Native (Kabalian/Pisidian-Phrygian) community; no pre-Greek attestation of the name
status_evidence: coins Hellenistic–Severan; Hierocles (Caria); bishops 451, 680/81
note: BAtlas left Eriza unlocated ('Karayük plain'); modern view (Malay) places it near Acıpayam. Coordinates from the council-sees seed.
sources: Pleiades 642521; Aulock, Münzen und Städte Phrygiens; Malay, Antik devirde Acıpayam vadisi; Hierocles, Synecdemus

site: Acıpayam (Karayük) plain, site not fixed (Acıpayam area, Denizli)
greek_from_text: probably named after Themison, favourite of Antiochus II (c. 261–246 BC); mentioned by Pausanias for the Gallic invasion (3rd c. BC); Roman coins
founder: probably Antiochus II (named after his favourite Themison)
pre_detail: Unlocated in the Karayük/Acıpayam plain. Pausanias (10.32.4) mentions the Themisonians' refuge cave during the Galatian invasion, but there is no evidence about the earlier occupation of the city site.
status_evidence: Strabo 12.8.13; Pausanias 10.32.4; Roman coins; Hierocles; see of Phrygia Pacatiana
note: Seleucid origin inferred from the name (Cohen); site unlocated in the Karayük (Acıpayam) plain per BAtlas directory, so could lie just across the Burdur border.

greek_from_text: late Roman city named after an emperor (Valens or Valentinian?), 4th c.; see in Phrygia Pacatiana
pre_detail: Unlocated; known only as a late Roman bishopric.
status_evidence: see in Notitiae (Phrygia Pacatiana)
note: Only known as a bishopric; founder inferred from the name. Region from BAtlas directory ('Themisonion region').

site: unlocated; south (left) bank of the Maeander opposite Tripolis, between Lykos and Maeander (Sarayköy area, Denizli)
greek_from_text: coins from c. 133–100 BC into the 3rd c. AD
pre_greek_note: Native name; no pre-Greek attestation
status_evidence: coins late Hellenistic–Roman; Strabo 14.1.46; Pliny (Hydrelitae)
note: Ramsay placed it on the left bank of the Maeander opposite Tripolis; may lie in Aydın (Buharkent) rather than Denizli.
sources: Pleiades 642528; Strabo 14.1.46; Ramsay, CBP I; Wildwinds: Hydrela

other_names: Diospolis, Rhoas (earlier names, Pliny); Lādik (medieval Turkish)
site: Eskihisar/Goncalı, 6 km N of Denizli (Pamukkale/Merkezefendi, Denizli)
greek_from_text: founded by Antiochus II (261–253 BC), named after his wife Laodike
pre_greek_note: Pliny's earlier names Diospolis/Rhoas are known only from Greek/Latin sources; prehistoric (Chalcolithic) occupation on the Asopos hill
status_evidence: Hellenistic & Roman coins; metropolis of Phrygia Pacatiana; bishops 325–787 and later
note: The medieval town (Turkish Lādik) shifted to modern Denizli after the Turkish conquest (late 12th–13th c.).

greek_from_text: Seleucid foundation under Antiochus I (281–261 BC) per excavators; polis status confirmed by Eumenes II after 188 BC
founder: Antiochus I (Seleucid); refounded/privileged by Eumenes II
pre_greek_note: Phrygian sanctuary of the Mother (Plutonion) and Iron Age structures found 2016
status_evidence: coins from 2nd c. BC; Hierocles; metropolis from 531; bishops 325–787
note: Foundation date disputed (3rd c. BC Seleucid vs early 2nd c. BC Attalid); abandoned c. 1220 after the Seljuk takeover.

greek_from_text: Phrygian city (Hdt. 7.30, 480 BC; Xen. Anab. 1.2.6); Greek civic coinage from the 2nd/1st c. BC
pre_greek_note: Called 'a great city of Phrygia' by Herodotus; no native-script attestation of the name
status_evidence: Hellenistic & Roman coins; Paul's Letter to the Colossians; bishops to 451, then see moved to Chonai
note: Unexcavated mound; replaced by Chonai (Honaz) in the early Middle Ages.
sources: Pleiades 638811; Herodotus 7.30; Xenophon, Anabasis 1.2.6; Wikipedia: Colossae

greek_from_text: see of Chonai attested at Nicaea II (787); metropolis 858
pre_detail: No pre-Greek finds reported at Honaz itself. Chonai succeeded Colossae, a native Phrygian city (Hdt. 7.30; Xen. Anab. 1.2.6) with a prehistoric mound, but the Colossae höyük lies c. 3 km north of Honaz, outside the 1–2 km test.
pre_sources: Hdt. 7.30; Xen. Anab. 1.2.6; knowledge: Colossae höyük c. 3 km N of Honaz
status_evidence: bishop 787; metropolitan see from 858; medieval Roman city (Niketas Choniates)
note: Medieval successor of Colossae around the pilgrimage church of St Michael; sacked by Seljuks 1070, Turkish from the early 13th c.
sources: Wikipedia: Chonae; TIB 7 (Belke & Mersich 1990); Council-sees seed (Nicaea 787)

site: c. 6 km NE of Çal (Çal, Denizli)
greek_from_text: first attested as a see: bishop at Chalcedon (451); Hierocles
pre_greek_note: Native name
status_evidence: Hierocles; bishops 451, 787
note: Roman-period community of the Mossyneis known from inscriptions; civic status certain only from the 5th c.

greek_from_text: city in Hierocles (c. 527); see in the Notitiae
pre_greek_note: Native name
status_evidence: Hierocles; Notitiae (titular see Lunda)
note: Probably a polis earlier (Roman period) but no earlier civic evidence checked.

site: Asar Tepe, just S of Bekilli (Bekilli, Denizli)
greek_from_text: founded by Eumenes II and Attalus (Steph. Byz.), between 188 and 159 BC
founder: Eumenes II and his brother Attalus (II)
pre_detail: Steph. Byz. says Eumenes II and Attalus founded it where a xoanon of Dionysus had been found, which suggests a pre-existing cult place but not a settlement. The site (Asar Tepe, Bekilli) is not firmly fixed and is unexcavated.
pre_sources: Steph. Byz. s.v. Dionysopolis; knowledge: Cohen 1995; Pleiades 609363
status_evidence: Steph. Byz.; coins 2nd c. BC–3rd c. AD; Pliny; Hierocles; bishop 451
note: Exact site not firmly fixed (MAMA XI: Asar Tepe near Bekilli is the best candidate).
sources: Pleiades 609363; Cohen 1995; MAMA XI: Dionysopolis; Stephanus of Byzantium s.v.

site: plain N of the Maeander between Dionysopolis and Peltai (near Bekilli/Akkent, Denizli)
greek_from_text: own coinage from Antoninus Pius (138–141) to Severus Alexander
pre_greek_note: Native ethnic name
status_evidence: Roman coins (ΥΡΓΑΛΕΩΝ) 138–235
note: A federation (koinon) of villages that minted coins rather than a single urban polis; included because it was self-governing.
sources: Pleiades 609410; SNG von Aulock 3677; Wildwinds: Hyrgaleis

greek_from_text: raised to a city as Pulcherianopolis, named after the empress Pulcheria (c. 450); bishops 6th–9th c.
pre_greek_note: Phrygian village name Motella in Roman inscriptions
status_evidence: Hierocles (as Pulcherianopolis); Notitiae (Metellopolis); bishops 556–879
note: Identification of Hierocles' Pulcherianopolis with Motella/Metellopolis follows Ramsay; the equation is not certain.
sources: Pleiades 609478; Pleiades 614816 (Pulcherianopolis); Ramsay, CBP I; Wikipedia: Motella

site: unlocated; between Apamea and Laodikeia (upper Maeander, Denizli)
greek_from_text: own coins from AD 4 (Gaius Caesar) to Caracalla
pre_greek_note: Native name
status_evidence: coins AD 4–217; Pliny NH 5.106; Hierocles; see in Notitiae
note: Site unknown (BAtlas: 'Apamea and Laodikeia region'); province attribution is a guess.

site: unlocated; Peltaean plain, probably SW of Eumeneia (Çivril plain, Denizli)
greek_from_text: Phrygian town in 401 BC (Xenophon); Macedonian settlers in the Hellenistic period; coins from the 2nd c. BC
pre_greek_note: Xenophon (Anab. 1.2.10) calls it a populous city of Phrygia
status_evidence: Xenophon Anab. 1.2.10; Hellenistic & Roman coins; Pliny; see in Phrygia Pacatiana
note: Site unknown (Cohen: probably SW of Eumeneia). A Macedonian katoikia planted in an existing Phrygian town; Seleucid founder inferred, not documented.

greek_from_text: founded by Attalus II (159–138 BC), named after his brother Eumenes II
pre_detail: MAMA XI calls it an Attalid foundation of the 160s/150s BC at the foot of Sarıbaba Tepesi. No pre-Hellenistic levels or mound are reported at Işıklı, and there is no positive evidence of new ground either.
status_evidence: coins 2nd c. BC–3rd c. AD; Pliny; Hierocles; bishops 381, 787
note: Briefly renamed Fulvia after Antony's wife (41–40 BC).
sources: Pleiades 609382; Cohen 1995; Stephanus of Byzantium s.v.

greek_from_text: Phrygian town (Herodotus' Anaua, 480 BC); Greek city with Roman imperial coins (ΣΑΝΑΗΝΩΝ); bishop 325
pre_greek_note: Anaua is known only from Herodotus (Greek)
status_evidence: Herodotus 7.30 (Anaua); Roman coins; Hierocles; bishop 325
note: Anaua = Sanaos is the usual identification (Lake Sanaos = Acıgöl); start of coinage not checked.

greek_from_text: founded by Antiochus I (c. 270s BC) next to Kelainai, named after his mother Apama
pre_greek_note: Kelainai: Phrygian town and Achaemenid satrapal seat (Hdt. 7.26, Xen. Anab. 1.2.7), excavated by the Kelainai project; no pre-Greek-script name attested
status_evidence: Strabo 12.8.15; coins 2nd c. BC–3rd c. AD; Peace of Apamea 188 BC; bishops 325–553
note: Kelainai was Antigonus' capital 333–301 BC; the Greek city dates from the Seleucid refoundation.

greek_from_text: named on the Apamea–Philomelion road by Artemidorus (c. 100 BC, in Strabo 14.2.29); civic coins and Pliny's Metropolitae in the early Empire
pre_detail: Not excavated. The only pre-Greek site recorded nearby is an Early Bronze Age II surface site at Tatarlı (Mellaart survey), c. 3 km away. The famous Achaemenid-period painted tumulus is also at Tatarlı, but there is no evidence for the city site itself.
status_evidence: Strabo 14.2.29; Pliny NH 5.106; coins; bishops 325, 381, 451
note: Greek name ('Mother-city', perhaps of the Mother goddess); origin unknown. Not to be confused with Metropolis near Kırka (Eskişehir).

greek_from_text: Roman imperial coins (1st–3rd c. AD); member of the Phrygian Pentapolis
pre_greek_note: Native name
status_evidence: Roman coins; Hierocles; bishop 553
note: Start of coinage not verified; date is a cautious estimate.
sources: Pleiades 609535; Ramsay, CBP II; Hierocles, Synecdemus

greek_from_text: named by Strabo (12.8.13); coins in the Roman imperial period
pre_detail: The site itself is uncertain (a plateau NW of Emirhisar, supported by one inscription). MAMA XI calls it a Graeco-Macedonian Hellenistic foundation. No pre-Greek finds are reported.
status_evidence: Strabo 12.8.13; Roman coins; Hierocles; bishops 325–787
note: Greek name ('fruitful'); origin unknown.

greek_from_text: Roman imperial coins (Ἱεροπολειτῶν); epitaph of Abercius (late 2nd c.)
pre_greek_note: Temple-community ('holy city') of a native cult; no native name attested
status_evidence: Roman coins; Abercius inscription; Hierocles; bishops 451, 787
note: Distinct from Hierapolis/Pamukkale. Start of coinage not verified.
sources: Pleiades 609403; Ramsay, CBP II; Wikipedia: Hierapolis (Phrygia)

greek_from_text: Roman imperial coins
pre_greek_note: Native name
status_evidence: Roman coins; Hierocles; bishops 325?–787
sources: Pleiades 609489; Ramsay, CBP II; Hierocles, Synecdemus

greek_from_text: Roman imperial coins (2nd–3rd c. AD)
pre_greek_note: Native name
status_evidence: Roman coins; Hierocles; bishops

site: unlocated, near the Pentapolis (Sandıklı plain, Afyonkarahisar)
greek_from_text: Roman imperial coins only
pre_greek_note: Native name
status_evidence: Roman coins (Wildwinds: Okokleia)
note: Known only from coins; site unknown (BAtlas: 'near Pentapolis').

site: unlocated; near the Pentapolis, plain of Oinan (Ramsay) (Afyonkarahisar)
greek_from_text: founded by and named after Lysias, probably a Phrygian dynast of the Philomelid house (3rd c. BC); Hellenistic & Roman coins
pre_detail: Unlocated. MAMA XI notes that the large site at Yanıkören may be either Otrous or Lysias, with nothing decisive. There is no archaeological evidence of earlier occupation.
status_evidence: Strabo 12.8.13; coins; Hierocles; bishops 344, 451, 879
note: Founder and date are inferences (Cohen; Catholic Encyclopedia gives Antiochus III c. 200 BC); site unknown, could lie across the Isparta border.
sources: Pleiades 614738; Cohen 1995; Strabo 12.8.13; Catholic Encyclopedia: Lysias

greek_from_text: see listed in the 7th-c. Notitia
pre_detail: Unlocated; known only as a bishopric.
status_evidence: Notitiae (titular see Aristium)
note: Known only as a bishopric; date is the earliest Notitia, perhaps later than its actual elevation.

greek_from_text: Roman imperial coins (from c. Domitian?) and civic inscriptions
pre_greek_note: Native name
status_evidence: Roman coins (ΚΙΔΥΗΣΣΕΩΝ); inscriptions
note: Start of coinage not verified.

greek_from_text: Antigonid stronghold with a royal treasury in 302 BC (Diod. 20.107); Greek polis by 189 BC (Livy 38.15); coins call the citizens 'Dorians and Ionians'
founder: Greek/Macedonian settlers of the early Hellenistic period (founder unknown; legend: Akamas)
pre_greek_note: Name looks Anatolian; no pre-Greek attestation
status_evidence: Livy 38.15; coins (ΣΥΝΝΑΔΕΩΝ ΔΩΡΙΕΩΝ ΙΩΝΩΝ); conventus capital; metropolis of Phrygia Salutaris; bishops 325–787
note: Founder undocumented: a Greek/Macedonian settlement is inferred from the coin legends and Steph. Byz.; dated here by the first clear civic evidence.

greek_from_text: known only as a medieval Roman see (Notitiae)
pre_greek_note: Native name
status_evidence: Notitiae (titular see Amadassa)

greek_from_text: civic coins from the early Imperial period (Midas types); Pliny (Prymnesii)
pre_greek_note: Phrygian town (Midas on its coins); no pre-Greek attestation of the name
status_evidence: Roman coins; Pliny NH 5.105; Hierocles; bishops 381–680
note: Start of coinage not verified.

greek_from_text: medieval Roman fortress-town (Arab sieges 716, 740; renamed Nikopolis 740); bishopric of Phrygia Salutaris from the 10th c.
pre_detail: No excavation evidence. Local accounts link the castle rock to Hittite Hapanuwa (Mursili II's Arzawa campaign) and report Phrygian rock-cut features (niche, stepped altar, offering pits), but these are unverified popular claims and the Hapanuwa identification is a hypothesis.
pre_greek_note: A Hittite name 'Hapanuwa' and a Late Bronze Age fortress are claimed for the Afyon castle rock in popular, uncited sources (e.g. Wikipedia: Afyonkarahisar); there is no scholarly identification or published pre-Greek level, so nothing is entered.
status_evidence: medieval Roman chronicles (battle of Akroinon 740); middle Roman (medieval) Notitiae
note: Medieval city that succeeded nearby Prymnessos; Turkish c. 1210. A 'pre-settlement' rests only on the Hapanuwa proposal.

greek_from_text: village at the battle of 301 BC; city and see by the 5th c. (bishop at Chalcedon 451); earlier if = Julia (Augustan coins)
pre_greek_note: Native (Phrygian) place-name; village before it became a city
status_evidence: Hierocles; bishops 451, 787
note: Ramsay identified Ipsos with the Augustan city Julia; BAtlas keeps Iulia separate (unlocated, near Polybotos?). The village's former name Sipsin preserves Ipsos.

greek_from_text: founded by Dokimos, Macedonian general of Antigonus who went over to Lysimachus (302 BC); coins of the 'Dokimeis Makedones'
pre_detail: Founded by Dokimos (coins of the 'Dokimeis Makedones'); Strabo calls it a village (kome) near Synnada. No archaeological evidence for a pre-Hellenistic settlement at İscehisar has been reported.
status_evidence: Steph. Byz.; coins (ΔΟΚΙΜΕΩΝ ΜΑΚΕΔΟΝΩΝ); Hierocles; bishops 431–787
note: Famous for its marble quarries (Docimian/Synnadic marble).
sources: Pleiades 609366; Cohen 1995; Robert, À travers l'Asie Mineure

site: unlocated; middle Akar Çay (Kaystros) plain between Akroinos and Polybotos (Afyonkarahisar)
greek_from_text: first bishop 359 (synod of Seleucia); later bishops 553, 787, 869
pre_detail: Unlocated; known only from bishop lists.
status_evidence: bishops 359, 553, 787, 869; Hierocles
note: Imperial name implies a Roman foundation or renaming, but neither founder nor date is known; Annuario Pontificio's 'Surmene' is not a firm identification.
sources: Pleiades 614619; Wikipedia: Augustopolis in Phrygia; Anna Komnene 15.6

greek_from_text: bishop at Chalcedon (451); Hierocles (c. 527)
pre_detail: No pre-Roman remains are reported at Bolvadin. The ancient visible history is Roman, small finds are Byzantine (Drew-Bear), and one study places Polybotos at 'Dura Yeri' c. 5 km from the town.
status_evidence: bishops 451, 787; Hierocles; Notitiae
note: Bolvadin < Polybotos; the name looks Greek ('rich in pasture') but may be a folk-etymology of a native name.

greek_from_text: bishop at Chalcedon (451)
pre_greek_note: Native name
status_evidence: bishop 451 (council list)
note: Known only from the council list; province assignment follows the council-sees seed.

greek_from_text: bishop at Nicaea II (787)
pre_detail: Known from one council attestation; the location is approximate and the site is unexcavated.
status_evidence: bishop 787 (council list)
note: Only a single council attestation; location from BAtlas.

greek_from_text: Phrygian town; own coins from the 2nd c. BC
pre_greek_note: Large höyük; pre-Hellenistic (Phrygian and earlier) occupation reported by the excavators; no pre-Greek name attested
status_evidence: coins 2nd c. BC–3rd c. AD; Strabo 12.5.3; Hierocles; bishops 431–; capital of the Anatolikon theme; metropolis 9th c.
note: Sacked by al-Mu'tasim 838; Turkish after 1071.

greek_from_text: civic status granted by Constantine (rescript c. 324–331), freeing it from Nakoleia
pre_greek_note: Earlier community (vicus of Nakoleia) with native name
status_evidence: Orcistus inscription (MAMA VII 305); bishops 431, 451
note: Petitioners claimed former city status; the Constantinian grant is the first secure civic date. Near the Eskişehir border.

greek_from_text: first attested by Pliny (Conium); later see of Phrygia Salutaris
pre_greek_note: Native name
status_evidence: Pliny; Ptolemy; Tabula Peutingeriana; Notitiae (see under Synnada)
note: Pleiades leaves it unlocated (BAtlas: between Nakoleia and Eukarpia); the coordinates follow Wikipedia/DARE. The alternative name Demetriopolis may point to a Hellenistic refoundation.

greek_from_text: Roman imperial coins
pre_greek_note: Native name
status_evidence: Roman coins (Wildwinds: Alia); bishops 553, 787
note: BAtlas name reconstructed (*Alia); start of coinage not verified.

site: near Pınarcık, SE of Altıntaş (Altıntaş, Kütahya)
greek_from_text: Pliny (Appiani, conventus of Synnada); Roman imperial coins
pre_greek_note: Native community; no pre-Greek name attested
status_evidence: Pliny NH 5.105; Roman coins; bishops 381–787
note: Start of coinage not verified; the date is a cautious estimate.

greek_from_text: city named after the empress Eudokia (wife of Theodosius II, 421–460); a see
pre_detail: Unlocated (BAtlas: between Appia and Aizanoi); known only as a see.
status_evidence: Hierocles; Notitiae
note: Founder inferred from the name; site unknown (BAtlas: 'between Appia and Aizanoi').

greek_from_text: listed among the cities of Phrygia Epiktetos by Strabo (12.8.12); Roman coins
pre_greek_note: Name derived from the Thraco-Phrygian personal name Kotys; no pre-Greek attestation
status_evidence: Strabo 12.8.12; Roman coins; Hierocles; bishops 431–879; later metropolis
note: Fortified by Justinian; Seljuk raids 1071, Turkish (Germiyanid) by c. 1300, Ottoman 1428.

greek_from_text: Hellenistic city contested by the Attalids and Bithynian kings (late 3rd–2nd c. BC); civic coinage from the 2nd/1st c. BC
pre_greek_note: Early Bronze Age settlement (3rd millennium BC) under the temple hill; Phrygian door-stones
status_evidence: coins; Strabo 12.8.12; Hierocles; bishops 325–879
note: Temple of Zeus (Domitianic/Hadrianic); declined after the 7th c.
sources: Pleiades 609292; Rheidt, Aizanoi; Strabo 12.8.12; Wikipedia: Aizanoi

site: Hisarardı Kale, immediately E of Eskigediz (old Gediz) (Gediz, Kütahya)
greek_from_text: late Hellenistic civic coinage; listed by Strabo (12.8.12)
pre_greek_note: Native name, continued in Gediz
status_evidence: coins late Hellenistic–3rd c.; Strabo 12.8.12; Hierocles; bishops 451, 787
note: Gediz town was moved after the 1970 earthquake. Hellenistic coin date approximate.

greek_from_text: Roman imperial coins
pre_greek_note: Native name, continued in Simav
status_evidence: Roman coins; Hierocles; bishops 553, 787
note: Start of coinage not verified.

other_names: Ankyra Sidera ('Iron Ankyra'); Ankyra of the Abbaitis
greek_from_text: Roman imperial coins (Ἀγκυρανῶν); Strabo, Pliny
pre_greek_note: Native community; no pre-Greek name attested
status_evidence: Roman coins; Hierocles; bishops 325–787
note: 'Sidera' rests on a Latin/Syriac council list entry (Price 2010 doubts it). Start of coinage not verified.

greek_from_text: name implies foundation or renaming under Tiberius (14–37); coins from Trajan; bishops 536–879
pre_detail: The site is doubtful (Pleiades 'Tiberioupolis?') and unexcavated, and there are no reports of earlier occupation.
status_evidence: coins from Trajan; Hierocles; bishops 536, 553, 692, 787, 879
note: Site doubtful (Pleiades 'Tiberioupolis?'). Not to be confused with Pappa-Tiberiopolis in Pisidia.

site: near Kırka (Seyitgazi, Eskişehir), near the Afyon/Kütahya border
greek_from_text: see of Phrygia Salutaris in the Notitiae (from the 7th c.)
pre_greek_note: Native name
status_evidence: Notitiae (titular see Merus)
note: Province uncertain (Eskişehir/Afyon/Kütahya border). Possibly a city earlier than its first Notitia listing.

greek_from_text: Pliny's Metropolitae (conventus of Synnada); Ptolemy
pre_detail: No excavation at Oynaş. Phrygian monuments of the Highlands (Kümbet, Midas City) lie c. 5-9 km away, outside the settlement test. The 19th-c. equation with Pişmiş Kale (a Phrygian site) is outdated.
pre_sources: Pleiades 609470; TIB 7, 340-41; Haspels, Highlands of Phrygia (1971); en.wikipedia Metropolis (northern Phrygia)
status_evidence: Pliny NH 5.105; Ptolemy; inscriptions
note: Near Midas City (Yazılıkaya); its civic status and separation from the southern Metropolis rest on Pliny/Ptolemy and the BAtlas location.

greek_from_text: listed among the cities of Phrygia Epiktetos by Strabo (12.8.12)
pre_greek_note: Native (Phrygian) name; no pre-Greek attestation
status_evidence: Strabo 12.8.12; coins; Hierocles; bishops 451–787
note: Home of the iconoclast bishop Constantine of Nakoleia; Seyitgazi is named after Battal Gazi.

greek_from_text: medieval Roman fortress-town; bishopric in the Notitiae of the 9th–10th c. (to be verified)
pre_detail: The location (Bardakçı?) is unverified; no archaeology.
status_evidence: medieval Roman sources (Theodore Santabarenos); Notitiae (to be verified)
note: Status as a bishopric and the Bardakçı location (Ramsay) are not verified here; check TIB 7.

greek_from_text: attested as a place in 302 BC; listed among the cities of Phrygia Epiktetos by Strabo (12.8.12); Roman coins
pre_greek_note: Şarhöyük mound: Early Bronze Age, Hittite-period and Phrygian (Iron Age) levels; no pre-Greek name attested
status_evidence: Strabo 12.8.12; coins; Hierocles; bishops 325–787
note: Crusader battles 1097 and 1147; refortified by Manuel I 1175; Turkish thereafter.
sources: Pleiades 609367; Strabo 12.8.12; Darga, Şarhöyük excavations; Wikipedia: Dorylaeum

greek_from_text: listed among the cities of Phrygia Epiktetos by Strabo (12.8.12); Roman coins
pre_greek_note: Named after the Phrygian king Midas (Greek tradition); höyük site
status_evidence: Strabo 12.8.12; coins; Hierocles; bishops 451–787

greek_from_text: bishop at Chalcedon (451)
pre_greek_note: Native name
status_evidence: bishops 451, 787
note: Probably a village community raised to a see in Late Antiquity.

greek_from_text: named after Hadrian (117–138); Greek civic coins from Hadrian onwards
pre_detail: No archaeology. The suggested identification with Xenophon's inhabited city Thymbrion (Anab. 1.2.13) is unproven, so it cannot support a 'yes'.
status_evidence: coins Hadrian–Geta (RPC III, IV.3, V.3; ΑΔΡΙΑΝΟΠΟΛΕΙΤΩΝ); bishops 325, 381, 451, 553; Hierocles
note: Probably a renamed older settlement of Phrygia Paroreios; earlier name unknown (Xenophon's Thymbrion has been suggested). Not the Hadrianopolis near Eğnes (Burdur).
sources: Pleiades 609397; RPC city 93 (Hadrianopolis, Phrygia); TIB 7 (Belke & Mersich 1990)

greek_from_text: Hellenistic foundation named after Philomelos (3rd–2nd c. BC); Cicero passed through in 51 BC; civic coins from Augustus
founder: probably the dynast Philomelos (Lysias dynasty, 3rd c. BC); an Attalid foundation is also proposed
pre_detail: No höyük or pre-Hellenistic level is reported at Akşehir; accounts begin with the 3rd-c. BC foundation.
status_evidence: Strabo 14.2.29; Cicero; Martyrdom of Polycarp addressed to the church of Philomelion (c. 155); coins Augustus–Geta (RPC I 3243 ff.); bishops 381–787; Hierocles
note: Founder and date inferred from the dynastic name (Cohen 1995); Wikipedia calls it 'probably a Pergamene foundation'.
sources: Pleiades 609501; Cohen 1995; RPC I 3243; Wikipedia: Philomelium

site: Ilgın (Konya); royal letters found at Mahmuthisar, S of Ilgın
greek_from_text: native town where Cyrus reviewed his army in 401 BC (Xenophon Anab. 1.2.14); granted polis status, laws, council and gymnasium by Eumenes II shortly after 188 BC (royal letters from Mahmuthisar)
founder: Eumenes II (grant of a polis constitution)
status_evidence: Xenophon Anab. 1.2.14; letters of Eumenes II (Jonnes & Ricl 1997); bishop 451; Hierocles
note: Site at or near Ilgın (Pleiades: Tyr(i)aion?).
sources: Pleiades 609564; Jonnes & Ricl, EA 29 (1997); Xenophon Anab. 1.2.14; Wikipedia: Tyriaion

greek_from_text: Roman colony founded under Augustus (after the annexation of Galatia, 25 BC)
pre_detail: No pre-Roman finds are reported at Babadat, and Niewöhner et al. 2013 question whether Babadat is the colony at all. The native-looking name Germa ('Germeni') hints at an older community but is not attested before the colony. Regionally, Roman sites lie near but never on Bronze Age höyüks.
pre_sources: Niewöhner et al., Anatolian Studies 63 (2013) 97-136; Pleiades 609351; en.wikipedia Germa (Galatia)
status_evidence: colonial coins; Hierocles; see of Galatia Salutaris (bishop 451?)
lang_later: Latin colony initially; Galatian and Phrygian spoken in the territory; Greek dominant by Late Antiquity
note: Not the same as Germia (Myriangeloi) at Gümüşkonak. The unnamed Galatia II seed row near Sivrihisar (Chalcedon 451) is probably this see.

greek_from_text: Phrygian temple-state of the Mother (Greek-language Attalid letters, 160s BC); organised as a polis (Sebastenoi Tolistobogioi Pessinuntioi) under Augustus
pre_greek_note: Phrygian sanctuary of Kybele/Agdistis; no pre-Greek name attested
status_evidence: Attalid letters (RC 55–61); Strabo 12.5.3; coins; metropolis of Galatia Salutaris; bishops 431–787
lang_later: Galatian (Celtic) and Phrygian spoken in the territory into Late Antiquity
note: Could be dated to the 2nd c. BC (Greek-speaking priestly administration), but polis status is Augustan.

greek_from_text: see (Myriangeloi) attested 451; pilgrimage town of St Michael, later autocephalous archbishopric
pre_detail: Survey and geophysics at Gümüşkonak found no Roman, let alone prehistoric, material: Germia was 'apparently a late foundation' as a pilgrimage centre. In this area Roman and Byzantine sites lie near but never on Bronze Age höyüks.
pre_sources: Niewöhner et al., 'Bronze Age höyüks, Iron Age hilltop forts, Roman poleis and Byzantine pilgrimage in Germia and its vicinity', Anatolian Studies 63 (2013) 97-136
status_evidence: bishops 451, 553, 787; autocephalous archbishopric
note: Late antique spa and pilgrimage centre (Church of the Archangel).

greek_from_text: named after the empress Eudoxia (d. 404), wife of Arcadius; bishop 451
pre_detail: The site is doubtful. If Eudoxias = Roman Mantalos at Ayvalı (Niewöhner et al. 2013), an MBA/LBA mound (Ayvalı Höyük) lies c. 1.5 km south of it, but the authors treat it as a separate, discontinuous settlement.
pre_sources: Niewöhner et al., Anatolian Studies 63 (2013) 97-136; Pleiades 609377
status_evidence: bishop 451; Notitiae
note: Founder inferred from the name; Pleiades location marked doubtful ('Eudoxias?').

greek_from_text: native town stormed by Perdiccas in 322 BC (Diodorus 18.22); first Greek civic coins AD 163–165
pre_greek_note: Landa, a Lower Land town in the Telipinu Proclamation (with Ḫupišna, Tuwanuwa, Lušna), is equated with Laranda on phonetic grounds only; doubtful.
status_evidence: Diodorus 18.22; coins 163–249 (RPC IV.3, VIII); bishop Neon early 3rd c. (Eusebius HE 6.19); bishops 325, 451; Hierocles
note: Probably Greek-speaking earlier than the first coins; the town was renamed Karaman after Karaman Bey (1256).
sources: Pleiades 648693; RPC IV.3 7249–51; Diodorus 18.22; Wikipedia: Laranda (Lycaonia); TIB 4

greek_from_text: Greek civic coins under Marcus Aurelius and Lucius Verus (c. 163–169)
status_evidence: coins Antonines–Philip I (RPC IV.3 7245–48, VIII); bishop 325; Hierocles
note: Village was officially renamed Yollarbaşı; the older name Ilisra continues Ilistra.

site: Kerti Hüyük near Ekinözü (Karaman merkez, Karaman)
greek_from_text: seat of the dynast Antipater (1st c. BC); honorific title Klaudioderbe under Claudius (AD 41–54); 'city of Lycaonia' in Acts 14:6; coins 163–169
status_evidence: Acts 14; coins ΚΛΑΥ ΔΕΡΒ (RPC IV.3 7238–41); bishops 381–672
note: Site at Kerti Hüyük (Ballance 1957, from an inscription of AD 157) is generally preferred; Devri Şehri (findspot of a bishop's epitaph) is the alternative.
sources: Pleiades 648620; Ballance 1957; RPC IV.3 7238–41; Wikipedia: Derbe

site: Kızılkale on Kara Dağ (Karaman merkez, Karaman)
greek_from_text: Greek civic coins under Marcus Aurelius (c. 164–169)
status_evidence: coins Marcus Aurelius & Philip I (RPC IV.3 7225–34, VIII); bishops 325, 381, 680; Hierocles
note: Barrington places Barata at Kızılkale; Ramsay and Bell identified it with Maden Şehri (Binbirkilise) on Kara Dağ.
sources: Pleiades 648582; RPC IV.3 7225–34; TIB 4; Wikipedia: Barate

greek_from_text: Greek civic coins under Marcus Aurelius and Lucius Verus (163–165)
pre_greek_note: Pleiades lists Hittite Ḫapalla as a name of this place; the equation is not generally accepted and is not used here.
status_evidence: coins 163–165 (RPC IV.3 7242–44); Pliny NH 5.95; bishops 381, 451; Hierocles
note: Site identification marked uncertain in Barrington (Hyde?).

greek_from_text: first bishop (Theodorus) at Nicaea 325
status_evidence: Ptolemy; Hierocles; bishops from 325
note: Roman-period Greek inscriptions from the site suggest civic life well before 325; date kept at first firm attestation.

site: Beyşehir or its immediate vicinity (Beyşehir, Konya)
greek_from_text: Claudian title Klaudiokaisareia shows civic status under Claudius (AD 41–54); bishop 381
status_evidence: Claudian title (Barrington/Pleiades); Hierocles; bishop 381; later archbishopric
note: Site identification with Beyşehir (Barrington) versus Fasıllar is debated.

greek_from_text: first attested bishop at Constantinople 381
status_evidence: Hierocles; bishops 381, 451
note: Site uncertain (Barrington: Korna?).

other_names: Colonia Iulia Felix Gemina Lustra (Augustus, 6 BC)
site: Zoldera Höyük, N of Hatunsaray (Meram, Konya)
greek_from_text: native Lycaonian town made an Augustan veteran colony (Colonia Iulia Felix Gemina Lustra) in 6 BC; Latin official until the later 2nd c. AD, Greek-speaking city by c. AD 200; bishops from 381
founder: Augustus (veteran colony, 6 BC) on a native Lycaonian town
pre_greek_note: Lušna, a Lower Land town in the Telipinu Proclamation, is often equated with Lystra on phonetic and regional grounds; unproven.
status_evidence: Latin colonial coins Augustus–Marcus Aurelius (RPC I 3538–40, IV.3); Acts 14, 16; bishops 381, 431, 451; Hierocles
lang_later: Latin official in the colony (coin legends to Marcus Aurelius); Lycaonian vernacular in AD 47 (Acts 14:11); Greek prevailed by c. AD 200
note: Counted as a colony that became Greek-speaking; the c. 200 date is an estimate from the end of Latin coinage and the Greek epigraphy of the area.
sources: Pleiades 648699; RPC I 3538–40; Acts 14:6–20; Levick 1967; Wikipedia: Lystra
refoundations: Lystra → Col. Iulia Felix Gemina Lustra (Augustus, 6 BC)

other_names: Klaudeikonion (Claudius); Col. Iulia Augusta (Augustan colony beside the polis); Col. Aelia Hadriana Augusta Iconiensium (Hadrian); Konya (Seljuk capital)
greek_from_text: native town ('last city of Phrygia', Xenophon 401 BC); autonomous Greek bronze coins (ΕΙΚΟΝΙΕΩΝ) 1st c. BC; Klaudeikonion under Claudius; Roman colony under Hadrian
pre_greek_note: Ikkuwaniya appears in the Bronze Tablet treaty of Tudḫaliya IV with Kurunta as a border town of Tarḫuntašša; identification with Ikonion generally accepted. Alaeddin Tepe has Bronze Age and Phrygian levels.
status_evidence: Xenophon Anab. 1.2.19; autonomous coins 1st c. BC (SNG vA 5285); coins Tiberius–3rd c. (RPC I 3540A ff.); Acts 13–14; metropolis of Lycaonia; bishops 325–787
note: The Greek polis coexisted with an Augustan Roman colony (Latin legends from Vespasian) until Hadrian made the whole city a colony. Seljuk capital from 1097.
sources: Pleiades 648647; Xenophon Anab. 1.2.19; RPC I 3540A–3545; Belke & Restle, TIB 4
refoundations: Ikonion → Klaudeikonion (Claudius) → Col. Aelia Hadriana Augusta Iconiensium (Hadrian)

greek_from_text: first attested bishop at Constantinople 381
status_evidence: Hierocles; bishops 381, 451

greek_from_text: a waterless village-town in Strabo (12.6.1); Greek civic coins under Antoninus Pius (138–161)
status_evidence: coins Antoninus Pius–Marcus (RPC IV.3 7252–57); Ptolemy; Hierocles; bishops 381, 451
note: Placement near Yağlıbayat is the modern consensus; Ramsay proposed other sites.
sources: Pleiades 648780; RPC IV.3 7252–57; Strabo 12.6.1; Wikipedia: Savatra

greek_from_text: see of Lycaonia in the Notitiae (6th–7th c.)
status_evidence: Tabula Peutingeriana; Notitiae (Lycaonia); titular see
note: Episcopal status rests on the Notitiae and titular lists; no earlier civic evidence was found.

greek_from_text: renamed Verinopolis after Empress Verina (457–479), implying city status; see in the Notitiae
founder: renamed under Leo I or Zeno (Verina)
status_evidence: Notitiae (Lycaonia); titular see
note: Unlocated; Ramsay compared Sibyla (Yıldızköy, Mut). Not the Galatian Verinopolis. One of the unnamed region-only Lycaonian council seeds may be this see.

greek_from_text: Seleucid foundation named after a Laodike; Appian credits Seleucus I, but Antiochus I or II (c. 281–246 BC) is as likely; Claudiolaodicea under Claudius
pre_detail: MAMA XI and local reports trace the town only from its Seleucid foundation. No höyük or pre-Hellenistic level is reported at Ladik (Halıcı).
pre_sources: MAMA XI (mama.csad.ox.ac.uk/monuments/Laodikeia.html); Pleiades 619197; Aydınlık report on Ladik archaeopark
status_evidence: Strabo 14.2.29; coins Vespasian–Domitian (RPC II 1612–13); epitaph of bishop M. Julius Eugenius (early 4th c.); bishops 451, 553, 692; Hierocles
note: 'Burnt' after the volcanic landscape. Hierocles lists it in Pisidia; other authors place it in Lycaonia or Galatia.
sources: Pleiades 619197; Cohen 1995; RPC II 1612–13; Wikipedia: Laodicea Combusta

greek_from_text: bishop at Nicaea 325 (Honigmann)
status_evidence: Ptolemy 5.4; bishop 325
note: Only one attested bishop; later lists do not show it.

greek_from_text: listed by Hierocles (c. 527); bishops 680–81, 787
status_evidence: Hierocles; Notitiae (under Pessinous); bishops 680–81, 692, 787
note: Site tentatively placed near Turgut (Barrington: Klaneos?).

site: unlocated: W of Lake Tatta (Tuz Gölü), perhaps near Piribeyli (Kulu, Konya)
greek_from_text: made a bishopric by Theodosius I (386–395); bishop Pius at Chalcedon 451; Hierocles
status_evidence: Strabo; Ptolemy; Hierocles; Notitiae (under Pessinous); bishop 451
note: Location only regional (Strabo: in the salt steppe west of Lake Tatta; Ramsay: near Piribeyli).

greek_from_text: first attested bishop at Ephesus 431
pre_greek_note: Wikipedia equates Kinna with Hittite Zallara; the identification is unsupported and not used.
status_evidence: Ptolemy; Hierocles; bishops 431, 451, 680–81, 787
note: Site only approximately located (alternatives near Cihanbeyli or Kulu).

site: Sarıhüyük (formerly Şedithüyük), Bala (Ankara), near the Kırıkkale border
greek_from_text: road station (itineraries); bishop Catherius at Serdica 343; 'municipium' of Galatia in Ammianus (364)
status_evidence: Itin. Ant.; Itin. Burdig.; Ammianus 25.10; Hierocles; bishops 343, 431, 451, 680–81, 787

greek_from_text: Phrygian town (Midas foundation legend, Pausanias 1.4.5) and seat of the Galatian Tectosages; constituted a polis (Sebaste Tektosagon) after Galatia became a province in 25 BC
founder: Augustus (polis constitution for the tribal centre)
status_evidence: Monumentum Ancyranum; coins Augustus–3rd c. (RPC); koinon of Galatia; Council of Ancyra 314; bishops 325–787; Hierocles
note: The name may be a Hellenized native name (folk-etymologised as 'anchor'). Galatian Celtic survived in the countryside into the 4th c. (Jerome). Hittite Ankuwa is Alişar Hüyük, not Ankara.
sources: Pleiades 619103; Mitchell, Anatolia I (1993); Pausanias 1.4.5; RPC (Ancyra, Galatia)

greek_from_text: first bishop at Chalcedon 451
status_evidence: Hierocles (as Rhegemnezos); imperial constitutions issued there (Anastasius); bishops 451, 680–81, 787
note: Listed by Hierocles with the 'Rhege-' (regio) prefix, i.e. as an estate district, yet a see from 451.

site: S of Beypazarı (Beypazarı, Ankara); traditionally equated with Beypazarı town
greek_from_text: first bishop at Chalcedon 451; renamed Anastasiopolis by Anastasius I
status_evidence: itineraries; bishops 451, 680–81, 787; Theodore of Sykeon bishop (late 6th c.)
note: Barrington/Pleiades put the site c. 15 km S of Beypazarı; Wikipedia equates it with Beypazarı itself.
sources: Pleiades 609447; TIB 4; Life of Theodore of Sykeon; Wikipedia: Lagania

site: near Çayırhan (Nallıhan, Ankara), partly under the Sarıyar Dam reservoir
greek_from_text: the village Gordiou Kome was made a city and renamed Juliopolis (after Octavian) by the local dynast Cleon (Strabo 12.8.9), c. 30s BC
founder: Cleon of Gordiou Kome, dynast under Antony and Octavian
status_evidence: Strabo 12.8.9; Pliny NH 5; coins (Bithynian series); bishop Philadelphus at Ancyra 314 and Nicaea 325; Hierocles
note: In Bithynia in the early empire, in Galatia I in Late Antiquity (border with the BIT batch). Milestones confirm the site; necropolis excavated before the dam.
refoundations: Gordiou Kome → Juliopolis (Cleon/Octavian) → Basileion (Basil I, c. 880)

site: unlocated in Galatia I (region centre given); old equation with Euagina near Büyük Köhne (Sorgun, Yozgat) probably wrong
greek_from_text: named after Empress Verina (wife of Leo I, 457–474), implying city status; bishops from 680–81
founder: named after Empress Verina (reign of Leo I)
pre_detail: Unlocated see.
status_evidence: Notitiae (under Ankyra); bishops 680–81, 692, 787, 869–80
note: Unlocated; the unnamed region-only Galatia I council seed (680–81, 787) matches this see. Under Leo VI part of the tourma of Saniana (Charsianon), so perhaps E of Ankara toward the Halys.

greek_from_text: emporion of the Galatian Trocmi (Strabo 12.5.2); constituted a polis (Sebaste Trokmon) in the Augustan organisation of Galatia; coins from the mid-1st c. AD
pre_greek_note: Hittite Tawiniya is equated with Tavium on phonetic and regional grounds (listed by Pleiades); not proven. The mound has occupation from the 4th millennium BC.
status_evidence: Strabo 12.5.2; coins mid-1st c.–Severus (RPC I 3568–70, II 1624–26); bishops 325, 451, 553; Hierocles
note: Polis status may postdate Ankyra slightly; Galatian Celtic long spoken in the countryside.
sources: Pleiades 619267; Strabo 12.5.2; RPC II 1624; Strobel & Gerber, Tavium survey

other_names: Tios, Teion (Ps.-Scylax); Phileios (medieval Roman, after the river Billaios/Phileios)
greek_from_text: Milesian colony (Steph. Byz.); excavators date the earliest acropolis settlement to the 6th c. BC (some 7th-c. material reported in the region); Ps.-Scylax 90 'Hellenic city with harbour' (c. 340 BC)
pre_detail: Rejected 'no known'. Sönmez & Öztürk report only one acropolis sounding (Kale Tepesi), whose earliest sherds are black-figure pieces 'thought possibly Archaic'. They give no depth and do not say virgin soil or bedrock was reached, so this is absence of finds in a limited sounding (rule 7). No author calls the site new ground. Strabo (12.3.5) places the native Kaukones around Tieion, so a native presence nearby is possible but unproven.
pre_sources: İ. F. Sönmez & B. Öztürk, 'Batı Karadeniz'de bir antik kent kazısı: Tios (Filyos)', 133–146 (ancientportsantiques.com/.../Tios-Sonmez2008.pdf); en.wikipedia Tium (Gorman, Miletos 70: 7th-c. Milesian colony); Strabo 12.3.5
status_evidence: IACP (Pontos); Ps.-Scylax 90; coins Hellenistic to Gallienus; Hierocles; bishops 431–869
note: Ancient writers disagree whether it belonged to Bithynia or Paphlagonia. Birthplace of Philetairos of Pergamon. The Turkish Filyos comes from the medieval Roman name of the river and town.
sources: IACP (Pontos); Strabo 12.3.8; Atasoy, Filyos-Tios excavations (2006–); Pleiades 845084; Wikipedia: Tium
refoundations: Joined Amastris' synoecism c. 300 BC but soon seceded and became independent again

other_names: Sesamos (Σήσαμος, the earlier Greek city on the site); Samastro (Genoese)
greek_from_text: Sesamos: Ionian (probably Milesian) settlement of unknown date, probably Archaic; first firm evidence is Ps.-Scylax 90 'Hellenic city' (c. 340 BC); synoecised as Amastris by Queen Amastris c. 300 BC
founder: Ionian (probably Milesian) settlers at Sesamos; synoecism by Queen Amastris c. 300 BC
pre_greek_note: Sesamos is named among Paphlagonian places in Homer (Il. 2.853); surveys at Tekketepe report possible Bronze Age material. No native-script name.
status_evidence: IACP (Pontos) for Sesamos; Ps.-Scylax 90; coins of Queen Amastris and the city; Roman 'metropolis' title; Hierocles; bishops from 2nd c. (Palmas) to 787; later metropolis
note: Mother city not attested; the founding date of Sesamos is probably Archaic but undocumented. Genoese 1261–1460, then Ottoman.
sources: Strabo 12.3.10; IACP (Pontos), Sesamos; Pleiades 844856; Wikipedia: Amasra
refoundations: Sesamos → Amastris (synoecism of Sesamos, Kytoros, Kromna and Tieion by Queen Amastris, c. 300 BC); Sesamos became its acropolis

greek_from_text: Homeric Paphlagonian place (Il. 2.855); a Greek polis striking its own silver in the 4th c. BC; probably an Archaic Ionian foundation of unknown date
pre_greek_note: Named as a Paphlagonian place in Homer's Trojan Catalogue; no pre-Greek-script attestation.
status_evidence: IACP (Pontos); civic silver coins 4th c. BC; absorbed into Amastris c. 300 BC
note: Steph. Byz. says Amastris was first called Kromna, so some place Kromna at Amasra; Barrington puts it at Tekkeönü near Kurucaşile. A village dependent on Amastris after c. 300 BC.

greek_from_text: Emporion of Sinope (Strabo 12.3.10), founding date unknown; first called a 'Hellenic city' by Ps.-Scylax 90 (c. 340 BC)
pre_greek_note: Named as a Paphlagonian place in Homer (Il. 2.853); Greek myth makes Kytoros son of Phrixos the eponym.
status_evidence: IACP (Pontos); Ps.-Scylax 90; absorbed into Amastris c. 300 BC
note: Famous for boxwood. Turkish Gideros keeps the name, which is probably Paphlagonian (Homeric). A village of Amastris after the synoecism.
sources: Strabo 12.3.10; Ps.-Scylax 90; Homer Il. 2.853; Pleiades 844997; Wikipedia: Cytorus

greek_from_text: called a 'Hellenic city' by Ps.-Scylax 90 (c. 340 BC); founding date unknown
pre_detail: Known only from Ps.-Scylax; the site near Cape Kerempe is tentative and unexcavated.
status_evidence: Ps.-Scylax 90 'Hellenic city'; Pliny, Strabo (cape)
note: The only evidence that it was a city is Ps.-Scylax. The site near Cape Kerempe is a tentative placement.

other_names: Ionopolis (Ἰωνόπολις, renamed c. AD 160s at the request of Alexander of Abonouteichos); Inepolis (medieval Roman)
greek_from_text: first attested as a minting community: Pontic civic bronzes 'ΑΒΩΝΟΥ ΤΕΙΧΟΥΣ' under Mithridates VI (c. 120–63 BC); Strabo 12.3.10 calls it a polisma
pre_detail: The İnebolu–Bozkurt–Abana survey found Hellenistic pottery, Roman blocks and a necropolis, with no pre-Greek levels reported. The origin of the name 'Abonos' is unknown.
status_evidence: Pontic civic bronzes c. 120–63 BC; Strabo 12.3.10; Roman provincial coins (Abonouteichos, then Ionopolis); Hierocles; bishops 325–787
note: Home of the prophet Alexander and the Glykon cult (Lucian). The origin of the name 'Abonos' is unknown. It may have been a Greek coastal settlement long before the coins.
sources: Strabo 12.3.10; Lucian, Alexander; Pleiades 844847; Wikipedia: Abonoteichos

site: Ginolu Kalesi, on the coast c. 4.5 km W of Çatalzeytin (Çatalzeytin, Kastamonu)
greek_from_text: called a 'Hellenic city' by Ps.-Scylax 90 (c. 340 BC); founding date unknown
pre_detail: Known from Ps.-Scylax and later periploi; the only visible remains are a 9th/10th-c. castle at Ginolu Kalesi. No early levels are known.
status_evidence: Ps.-Scylax 90 'Hellenic city'; later only an anchorage/emporion (Strabo 12.3.10, Arrian, Periplus)
note: Its city status rests only on Ps.-Scylax. Later a small emporion, with a 9th/10th-c. medieval Roman castle at Ginolu Kalesi.
sources: Ps.-Scylax 90; Arrian, Periplus; Pleiades 844984; Wikipedia: Cinolis

greek_from_text: called a 'Hellenic city' by Ps.-Scylax 90 (c. 340 BC); founding date unknown
pre_detail: Known only from Ps.-Scylax; the location is a Barrington placement and the site is unexcavated.
status_evidence: Ps.-Scylax 90 'Hellenic city' only
note: Known only from Ps.-Scylax. The site is Barrington's placement and lies near the Kastamonu–Sinop boundary.
sources: Ps.-Scylax 90; Barrington 86 E2; Pleiades 844989; Wikipedia: Colussa

site: unlocated, Sinop coast between Stephane and Armene (Ayancık–Erfelek area?)
greek_from_text: called a 'Hellenic city' by Ps.-Scylax 89 (c. 340 BC), listed after Armene
pre_detail: Unlocated; known only from Ps.-Scylax.
status_evidence: Ps.-Scylax 89 'Hellenic city' only
note: Known only from Ps.-Scylax. Its position comes from his east-to-west order (Sinope, Kerasous, Harmene, Tetrakis, then Stephane in Paphlagonia).

greek_from_text: harbour of Sinope where the Ten Thousand stayed in 400 BC (Xen. Anab. 6.1.15); 'Hellenic city with harbour' in Ps.-Scylax 89 (c. 340 BC)
pre_detail: No excavation at Akliman, and no report of a pre-Greek settlement at the site. Strabo's 'who walled Armene' proverb is not evidence of earlier occupation.
status_evidence: IACP (Pontos); Xen. Anab. 6.1.15; Ps.-Scylax 89; Strabo 12.3.10
note: A dependency of Sinope 50 stadia to its west. Strabo quotes a proverb about the man 'who walled Armene'.
sources: Xen. Anab. 6.1.15; Ps.-Scylax 89; Strabo 12.3.10; Pleiades 844865; Wikipedia: Armene

greek_from_text: refounded by the Milesians Kous and Kretines after the Cimmerian raids, 631 BC (Eusebius), matching the earliest Greek pottery (late 7th c.); tradition of an earlier Milesian foundation (Habrondas) before the Cimmerians, which Trapezous' date (756) would put before 756
founder: Miletus (oikists Kous and Kretines; earlier Habrondas by tradition; mythical Autolykos)
pre_greek_note: Sinop Kale excavations (2000, 2015) found Early Bronze Age pottery and Early–Middle Iron Age (c. 1000–700 BC) structures, probably a seasonal fishing settlement, beneath the colony. No pre-Greek name is attested; claims of a Hittite-era port are unsupported.
status_evidence: IACP (Pontos); coins from 5th c. BC; Pontic royal capital 183–70 BC; Roman colony 45 BC; Hierocles; bishops 451–; medieval Roman autocephalous archbishopric
note: Mother city of Kotyora, Kerasous, Trapezous and (in part) Amisos. Trapezuntine 1204–14; Seljuk from 1214 (briefly retaken by Trebizond in the mid-13th c.); Ottoman 1461.
sources: IACP (Pontos), Sinope; Ps.-Scymnus (Sinope); Doonan et al. 2017, Sinop Kale excavations; Pleiades 857321; Wikipedia: Sinop, Turkey
refoundations: Refounded after the Cimmerian destruction (631 BC); Roman colony Colonia Iulia Felix (45 BC)

greek_from_text: assessed for tribute in the Athenian Pontic assessment of 425/4 BC; 'Hellenic city' in Ps.-Scylax 89 (c. 340 BC)
pre_detail: No archaeological evidence for occupation at Gerze before the Greek town is reported.
status_evidence: IACP p. 958; Athenian tribute assessment 425/4 BC; Ps.-Scylax 89
note: 150 stadia south-east of Sinope; later a small emporion (Arrian).
sources: IACP p. 958; Ps.-Scylax 89; Arrian, Periplus; Pleiades 857181; Wikipedia: Carussa

other_names: Zaliches/Zalichos (Ζάλιχος); Saltus Zalichenus, an imperial estate (Hierocles: Σάλτον Ζαλίχην)
greek_from_text: an imperial estate (saltus) made a city and renamed Leontopolis, presumably by Leo I (457–474); listed by Hierocles (c. 527); later a see under Amaseia ('Leontopolis or Zaliches')
pre_detail: The site is not securely located (Alaçam?). 'Zaliches' is a native-looking alternative name, but it is attested only from late antiquity (Hierocles 'saltus Zaliches', Nicaea II) and is tied to an imperial estate, not to an earlier town. No archaeology is reported.
status_evidence: Hierocles; Notitiae (Leontopolis/Zaliches, suffragan of Amaseia); bishops 6th–9th c.
note: The site is not securely located; Barrington places it near Alaçam. The name points to Leo I, but no text names him as founder.

other_names: Peiraieus (Athenian refoundation, c. 437 BC); Eupatoria (adjoining foundation of Mithridates VI); Samsoun (medieval)
site: Baruthane / Toraman Tepe headland NW of the modern centre (İlkadım, Samsun)
greek_from_text: Phocaean foundation four years before Herakleia, i.e. c. 564 BC (Ps.-Scymnus/Anon. Periplus); Theopompus: first founded by Milesians; earliest Greek pottery 6th c. BC; Athenian refoundation as Peiraieus c. 437 BC
founder: Milesians (Theopompus) or Phocaeans (Ps.-Scymnus); Athenian settlers under Athenokles c. 437 BC
pre_detail: No pre-Greek levels are reported at Baruthane/Toraman Tepe, where the surveyed remains are Hellenistic–Roman. Bronze/Iron Age sites (Dündartepe, Tekkeköy) lie several km away. The name Amisos is probably non-Greek, but that is not an attested earlier name. Samsun excavators place Archaic Amisos at Çakalca-Karadoğan Höyük (Atakum), a mound said to have finds from the earliest Iron Age onward. If confirmed, that would make the first Amisos a 'yes'.
pre_greek_note: Bronze Age and Hittite-period mounds (Dündartepe, Tekkeköy) lie nearby, but not on the Greek city site; no pre-Greek name is attested.
status_evidence: IACP (Pontos); coins from 5th c. BC (as Peiraieus) to 3rd c. AD; free city under Rome; Hierocles; bishops 451–879; medieval Roman metropolis
note: The mother city is disputed: Milesian (Theopompus in Strabo 12.3.14) or Phocaean (Ps.-Scymnus); Sinopean involvement is also suggested. Ottoman from 1420.
sources: IACP (Pontos), Amisos; Strabo 12.3.14; Anon. Periplus Ponti Euxini (Ps.-Scymnus fragment); Pleiades 857024; Wikipedia: Amisos
refoundations: Amisos → Peiraieus (Athenians, c. 437 BC) → Amisos again; Eupatoria founded beside it by Mithridates VI and later merged

site: unlocated, near the Mert Irmağı east of Samsun (Samsun)
greek_from_text: 'Hellenic city' on the river Lykastos in Ps.-Scylax 89 (c. 340 BC); founding date unknown
founder: unknown Greek settlers (perhaps from Amisos or Sinope)
pre_detail: Unlocated; known only from Ps.-Scylax and periploi.
status_evidence: Ps.-Scylax 89 'Hellenic city'; Mela 1.19; Pliny 6.3
note: It lay about 20 stadia beyond Amisos on the river of the same name (probably the Mert Irmağı); the town site is unlocated and was probably absorbed by Amisos.

site: unlocated castle-town and see in the Yeşilırmak delta (Çarşamba–Terme plain, Samsun); point placed near Çarşamba
greek_from_text: a see from 1317 (the metropolitan of Amaseia told to reside at Limnia); a Trapezuntine town and lordship from 1297 at the latest (John II of Trebizond died there), perhaps already Kinte in 1139–40 (Bryer & Winfield pp. 100–01); lost to the Turkmen 1384–86
status_evidence: Panaretos; synodal acts of 1317 and 1384 (Vryonis 1971; Bryer 1975): a Trapezuntine kastron and lordship with a see and thirteen imperial forts
lang_later: Turkmen settlement of the delta from the 14th c.; the emirate of Limnia from the 1380s
note: City status from its see (1317).
sources: Bryer & Winfield, The Byzantine Monuments and Topography of the Pontos (1985) pp. 100–01 (opened, archive.org); Bryer, "Greeks and Türkmens: the Pontic Exception", DOP 29 (1975) p. 128; Panaretos, Chronicle (via Bryer & Winfield)

greek_from_text: Herodotus 4.86 names Themiskyra on the Thermodon (c. 430 BC); first called a 'Hellenic city' by Ps.-Scylax 89 (c. 340 BC); a walled town besieged by Lucullus in 71 BC (Appian, Mith. 78)
founder: unknown Greek settlers (perhaps from Amisos or Sinope)
pre_detail: The city site is unidentified on the Terme plain. The Amazon traditions are legendary and do not count, and no archaeological evidence exists for the town itself.
pre_greek_note: The legendary city of the Amazons; there is no historical pre-Greek attestation.
status_evidence: Herodotus 4.86; Ps.-Scylax 89 'Hellenic city'; Appian, Mith. 78
note: The city site is not identified on the Terme plain. The Turkish name Terme comes from the river Thermodon, not from Themiskyra.

greek_from_text: ancient Oinoe was only a coastal place; possible see of Oinaion known from 8th- and 11th-c. seals (attribution queried) and one MS of Notitia 10; a major town of the Empire of Trebizond
pre_detail: No pre-Greek settlement is reported at the town site. The district's earliest finds are Palaeolithic, from caves in the Cevizdere valley, and the Kaska/Hittite claims are general regional history, not site evidence.
status_evidence: medieval Roman seals of bishops 'of Oinaion (?)' (8th and 11th c., Dumbarton Oaks); Notitia 10 (one MS); Trapezuntine kastron/town
note: Its city status is doubtful: the see may be the see of Polemonion moved here. The castle was built by the emperors of Trebizond; under Turkish (Hacıemiroğlu) rule from 1346.
sources: Dumbarton Oaks seals BZS.1955.1.2057 and 1.4681; Bryer & Winfield 1985; Pleiades 857254; Wikipedia: Ünye

other_names: Side (Σίδη), the earlier fort of the Sidene district; Pouleman (medieval)
greek_from_text: founded at Side by a Polemonid king of Pontus; Strabo (c. AD 20) names only Side as a fort, so probably Polemon II (AD 38–64); some credit Polemon I (37–8 BC)
founder: Polemon II (or Polemon I) of Pontus
pre_detail: Founded at the pre-existing Pontic fortress Side, which gave its name to the district Sidene (Strabo 12.3.16). Nothing shows whether Side was a native settlement or a royal (Hellenized) stronghold, and no pre-Roman levels are reported at Fatsa or Bolaman.
pre_sources: Strabo 12.3.16; Pleiades 857285; kulturenvanteri.com/en/yer/polemonion; Buyruk, Bolaman Kalesi (akmb.gov.tr 2026)
status_evidence: Pliny 6.11; Ptolemy; gave its name to the province Pontus Polemoniacus; Hierocles; bishops 451–787
note: The Polemonids were Roman client kings of Pontus, not Mithridatids. The name survives in nearby Bolaman; Barrington places the site at Fatsa (Phadisane).
sources: Strabo 12.3.16; Pliny NH 6.11; Pleiades 857285; Wikipedia: Polemonium

site: unlocated, coast between Fatsa and Ordu (Ordu)
greek_from_text: 'Hellenic city' among the Chalybes in Ps.-Scylax 88 (c. 340 BC); founding date unknown
pre_detail: Known only from Ps.-Scylax 88; the site is unlocated and unexplored.
status_evidence: Ps.-Scylax 88 'Hellenic city' only
note: Known only from Ps.-Scylax. It lay between the Genetes harbour and Cape Iasonion; Barrington tentatively places 'Stamene/Ameneia?' near Perşembe.

greek_from_text: 'Greek city, colonists of Sinope', paying tribute to it, where the Ten Thousand stayed in 400 BC (Xen. Anab. 5.5.3–10); founding date unknown (probably 5th c. BC)
pre_detail: No excavation; only harbour remains have been noted near Bozukkale/Kirazlimanı. No pre-Greek settlement or name is recorded.
status_evidence: IACP (Pontos); Xen. Anab. 5.5
note: Its people were moved to Pharnakeia c. 183 BC; Arrian (AD 131) calls it 'a village, and not a large one'. Harbour remains have been noted near Bozukkale/Kirazlimanı.
sources: Xen. Anab. 5.5.3–10; Strabo 12.3.17; Arrian, Periplus; Pleiades 857200
refoundations: Population moved to Pharnakeia c. 183 BC

greek_from_text: c. 340 BC: probably the "Hellenic city" Choirades of Ps.-Scylax 86, between Zephyrion and the island of Ares; refounded as Pharnakeia by Pharnakes I c. 183 BC with settlers from Kotyora; later Kerasous
founder: unknown (Choirades); refounded by Pharnakes I of Pontus c. 183 BC
pre_detail: Giresun castle and Giresun Island have yielded only Classical and later material. Any earlier occupation would be Greek (Kerasous/Choirades), which does not count, and no native settlement is attested.
status_evidence: Strabo 12.3.17; Cohen; Pontic and Roman coins; Hierocles (Kerasous); bishops 431–879; later metropolis; second city of the Empire of Trebizond
note: Many identify Giresun with Xenophon's Sinopean colony Kerasous; if so, greek_from is c. 400 BC. Barrington puts that Kerasous further east (next entry), and Ps.-Scylax's 'Hellenic city' Choirades near Ares Island may have stood here. Held out briefly after Trebizond fell in 1461. Dated by Choirades (eastern review, 11 Oct 2026): the identification with Giresun is probable, not certain; if it is wrong, the date is c. 183 BC.
sources: Strabo 12.3.17; Cohen 1995; Bryer & Winfield 1985; Pleiades 857185; Wikipedia: Giresun
refoundations: Choirades? (c. 340 BC) → Pharnakeia (Pharnakes I, c. 183 BC) → Kerasous (Roman/medieval)

greek_from_text: 'Greek city by the sea, colonists of Sinope' where the Ten Thousand stayed in 400 BC (Xen. Anab. 5.3.2); founding date unknown
pre_detail: The site is unlocated or disputed (Kerasus Dere vs Giresun) and unexcavated.
status_evidence: IACP (Pontos); Xen. Anab. 5.3.2
note: The site is disputed. Barrington, following Bryer & Winfield, places Xenophon's Kerasous here, three days' march west of Trapezous; others put it at Giresun (merge with Pharnakeia if so). Ps.-Scylax 89 also lists a 'Kerasous' between Sinope and Armene, probably a textual displacement.
sources: Xen. Anab. 5.3.2; Bryer & Winfield 1985; Barrington 87 E3; Pleiades 857183

greek_from_text: 756 BC (Eusebius); 'Greek city, colonists of Sinope' (Xen. Anab. 4.8.22); no Archaic finds, and modern scholars mostly prefer the late 7th or 6th c. BC, after Sinope's (re)foundation c. 631
pre_detail: No pre-Classical finds from Trabzon; the İçkale excavations report Roman to Ottoman levels. Protohistoric surveys of the province (TYAP) have published no site on the city hill.
pre_sources: Pleiades 857359; Hürriyet Daily News 'Excavations begin in Trabzon' (İçkale); KTÜ TYAP survey page
status_evidence: IACP (Pontos); Xenophon; Ps.-Scylax 85 'Hellenic city'; coins; Roman free city and fleet base; Hierocles; bishops 325–; metropolis; capital of the Empire of Trebizond 1204–1461
note: The ancient date of 756 depends on the tradition of a pre-Cimmerian Sinope; archaeology gives nothing earlier than Classical. Fell to Mehmed II in 1461.
sources: IACP (Pontos), Trapezous; Xen. Anab. 4.8.22; Eusebius, Chronicle; Bryer & Winfield 1985; Pleiades 857359

greek_from_text: Roman harbour and fort (Arrian names the river Rhizios); walled by Justinian (Procopius); a see under Neocaesarea in the earliest Notitiae (7th c.); bishop at Nicaea 787
pre_detail: A Roman harbour and fort, walled by Justinian; no archaeology or pre-Greek name is known for the town site.
status_evidence: Procopius, Buildings 3.7; Notitiae (suffragan of Neocaesarea, later Trapezous); bishop 787; town of the Empire of Trebizond
note: On the edge of Laz (Kartvelian) country; the countryside east of it was largely Laz-speaking, but the town was Greek in medieval Roman and Trapezuntine times. The 650 date reflects the Notitia; the town may have had civic status under Justinian.
sources: Arrian, Periplus; Procopius, Buildings 3.7; Bryer & Winfield 1985; Pleiades 857297

site: unlocated, on the coast of Rize province (land of the Becheires)
greek_from_text: c. 340 BC: a "Hellenic city" (πόλις Ἑλληνίς) in Ps.-Scylax 84
founder: unknown Greek settlers (perhaps from Sinope or Trapezus)
status_evidence: Ps.-Scylax 84 ("Hellenic city")
note: Added in the eastern review (11 Oct 2026): Ps.-Scylax lists the peoples west of the Apsaros in order (Byzeres, Ekecheirieis, Becheires), so the town lay on the Turkish side, like Stameneia. Earlier rejected as possibly in Georgia.
sources: Ps.-Scylax 81-89 (Shipley 2011/2019) [from knowledge and the PON batch notes]; PON batch entry (out/PON.json); editor's rejection note (rejected_v2.json); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byzeres (fetched: Byzeres 'south of the Chorokhi')

site: unlocated, on the coast of Rize/Artvin (land of the Ekecheirieis)
