greek_from_text: c. 340 BC: a "Hellenic city" in Ps.-Scylax 83
status_evidence: Ps.-Scylax 83 ("Hellenic city")
note: Added in the eastern review (11 Oct 2026); see Becheirias.
sources: Ps.-Scylax 81-89 (Shipley 2011/2019) [from knowledge and the PON batch notes]; Arrian, Periplus Ponti Euxini [from knowledge]; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byzeres (fetched: the Byzeres lived 'south of the Chorokhi', i.e. on the Turkish side, so the Ekecheirieis further west are in Turkey); PON batch entry; editor's rejection note

other_names: Kabaköy; Kabakilise (the church of Hagia Sophia, now Ayasofya Camii)
site: The Leri valley east of Gümüşhane; the church of Hagia Sophia at Kabaköy, 'probably the oldest surviving church in the Pontos' (6th c.; Bryer & Winfield pp. 313–16)
greek_from_text: a see of Trebizond by the reign of Leo VI (886–912), in the lists down to c. 1054 (Bryer & Winfield p. 313)
status_evidence: suffragan see of Trebizond in the Nea Taktika of Leo VI and in lists of c. 980–1054 (Bryer & Winfield p. 313)
lang_later: On the edge of Greek and Armenian settlement (Bryer & Winfield p. 313)
note: Added in the second look at the inland Pontus and the east (11 Oct 2026). The see lay among 'the Leri villages'; no town is described.
sources: Bryer & Winfield, The Byzantine Monuments and Topography of the Pontos (1985) pp. 49, 311–16 (opened, archive.org)

other_names: Şiran (the Ottoman town, about 6 km SSW)
site: Probably the walled mound at Uluşiran, 6 km NNE of Şiran, 'walled in Byzantine times' (Bryer & Winfield p. 171)
greek_from_text: 10th c.: a new see of the metropolis of Trebizond in the 10th-c. episcopal lists (Bryer & Winfield p. 167); 'a chora' to Lazaropoulos; in Turkish hands by 1355
pre_detail: The Uluşiran mound is a prehistoric site with a Roman phase (perhaps Cunissa) (B&W p. 171).
status_evidence: a see of Trebizond in the 10th-c. lists (no bishop named); Lazaropoulos calls it a chora; walled hill site (Bryer & Winfield 1985 pp. 165–72)
lang_later: Armenian settlement along the Lykos from the 10th c.; Turkish (Türkmen) by 1355
note: Added in the second look at the inland Pontus and the east (11 Oct 2026). 'Clearly a Greek enclave with its own bishop, until this century the most southerly outpost of Pontic Greek settlement' (Bryer & Winfield p. 171); its town is inferred from the see, not described.
sources: Bryer & Winfield, The Byzantine Monuments and Topography of the Pontos (1985) pp. 165–75 (opened, archive.org); Bryer, "Greeks and Türkmens: the Pontic Exception", DOP 29 (1975) pp. 125, 133 (opened); Panaretos and Lazaropoulos (via Bryer & Winfield)

site: Devrek (Devrek, Zonguldak), per Barrington; alternatively Safranbolu (Karabük)
greek_from_text: first bishop at Chalcedon 451; city in Hierocles (c. 527)
pre_greek_note: A non-Greek (Paphlagonian) place name, listed by Ptolemy; no pre-Greek-script attestation.
status_evidence: Ptolemy 5.4; Hierocles; bishops 451–681; Notitiae; 10th–11th-c. episcopal seals
note: Site disputed: Barrington puts it at Devrek, while a study of seals naming St Stephen argues for Safranbolu (Karabük).
sources: Hierocles, Synekdemos; Belke, TIB 9 Paphlagonien (1996); Pleiades 844903; Deltio KMS (Safranbolu study)

other_names: Kaisareia (Καισάρεια); Proseilemmene/Proseilemmenitai district; Hadrianopolis in Honoriade
site: ruins 3 km W of Eskipazar (Eskipazar, Karabük)
greek_from_text: settlement from the 1st c. BC; earlier city name Kaisareia (probably Julio-Claudian); named Hadrianopolis under Hadrian (117–138); Hierocles; bishops from the 4th–5th c.
founder: Hadrian (as Hadrianopolis); earlier Kaisareia, under an unknown Julio-Claudian emperor
pre_detail: Kept 'yes' only on the excavators' own academic report (Daily Sabah rejected). Kalkan & Çelikbaş 2022 report handmade red-clay pottery in a pit in the city's necropolis, which was partly destroyed by the Roman rock-cut graves, plus dry-stone walls that predate the Roman city. They date this short-lived prehistoric occupation to at least 5,000 years ago (Late Chalcolithic), long before the 1st-c. BC town. These are concrete finds in a sealed feature on the site, but they are dated only typologically and have no non-Turkish corroboration, so confidence is low.
pre_sources: E. Kalkan & E. Çelikbaş, 'New findings from prehistoric period in Western Black Sea Region: Hadrianopolis (Karabük-Eskipazar) prehistoric pottery', Karadeniz Araştırmaları Enstitüsü Dergisi 8/16 (2022) 417–431 (abstract, ceeol.com article 1088014); en.wikipedia Hadrianopolis (Paphlagonia); Pleiades 844959
status_evidence: Hierocles (Honorias); bishops 325 (Honigmann) and 451–787; excavations since 2003 (theatre, baths, churches with mosaics)
note: Its city status probably began as Kaisareia before Hadrian, but the date is not documented, so the Hadrianic date is used. Excavations show occupation to the 8th c.
sources: Çelikbaş, Hadrianopolis excavations; Hierocles, Synekdemos; Pleiades 844959; Wikipedia: Hadrianopolis (Paphlagonia)

greek_from_text: first bishop at Chalcedon 451; city in Hierocles (c. 527)
pre_greek_note: A non-Greek place name; no pre-Greek-script attestation.
status_evidence: Hierocles; bishops 451–787; Notitiae (suffragan of Gangra)
note: The site is only approximately known (Barrington 86 C2, near Karabük).
sources: Hierocles, Synekdemos; Belke, TIB 9 Paphlagonien (1996); Pleiades 845067; Wikipedia: Sora (Anatolia)

other_names: Germanikopolis (Γερμανικόπολις, Roman city name); Kangırı (medieval Turkish)
greek_from_text: royal seat of the Paphlagonian kings (Strabo 12.3.41: 'small town and fortress'); organised as the city Germanikopolis on the annexation of Paphlagonia, 6/5 BC (civic era); oath to Augustus sworn at Gangra in 3 BC
pre_greek_note: A Paphlagonian royal residence (Morzeus, Deiotaros Philadelphos) before the Roman city; no secure Hittite identification of the name.
status_evidence: Strabo 12.3.41; Paphlagonian oath of 3 BC (OGIS 532); coins of Germanikopolis; Hierocles (metropolis of Paphlagonia); Council of Gangra (c. 340); bishops from 325 (Hypatius, by tradition) to 787
note: Some scholars question whether Germanikopolis and Gangra were exactly the same site, but most equate them.
sources: Strabo 12.3.41; OGIS 532; Belke, TIB 9 Paphlagonien (1996); Pleiades 844926
refoundations: Gangra → Germanikopolis (Augustus); Gangra again in Late Antiquity

greek_from_text: founded by Pompey in 65/64 BC after the Third Mithridatic War
pre_detail: Excavations on Zımbıllı Tepe show Roman walls set into sterile subsoil. The hill's earliest pottery is late 1st c. BC/1st c. AD (Summerer: first occupied c. 1st–2nd c. AD), so its earliest levels are those of the Roman city. Note: Pompey's 64 BC city may first have stood elsewhere.
pre_sources: https://bmcr.brynmawr.edu/?p=37724 ; J. Koch in Summerer (ed.), Pompeiopolis (fis.uni-bamberg.de)
pre_greek_note: The site is a mound (Zımbıllı Tepe höyüğü), but the excavators have not yet found pre-Roman architecture; the Amnias valley has Iron Age rock tombs and tumuli.
status_evidence: Strabo 12.3.40; coins; 'metropolis of Paphlagonia' (Antoninus Pius–Gallienus); Hierocles; bishops 325–787; medieval Roman metropolis to the 14th c.
note: It may have taken over from the Mithridatic fortress of Pimolisa. Excavated since 2006 (Summerer).
sources: Strabo 12.3.40; Summerer (ed.) 2011, Pompeiopolis I; Pleiades 845041; Wikipedia: Pompeiopolis

site: Osmancık castle (Osmancık, Çorum), per Barrington; others put it near Boyabat (Sinop)
greek_from_text: civic bronze coins 'ΠΙΜΩΛΙΣΩΝ' struck under Mithridates VI (c. 111–90 BC); destroyed by Strabo's time
pre_greek_note: A native Paphlagonian fortress (non-Greek name) on the Halys before the Mithridatic coinage.
status_evidence: Pontic civic bronzes c. 111–90 BC; Strabo 12.3.40 (royal fortress, destroyed); a see 'Pimolissa' in medieval Roman Notitiae (to be checked)
note: Mithridatic 'civic' bronzes were also struck at fortresses, so its polis status is uncertain. The site is disputed (Osmancık vs Boyabat).
sources: Strabo 12.3.40; Künker: Pimolisa Æ 111/90 BC; Belke, TIB 9 Paphlagonien (1996); Pleiades 845039

other_names: Avkat (Ottoman); linked with Theodoroupolis (John I Tzimiskes, 972)
greek_from_text: village and pilgrimage centre of St Theodore (4th c.); after a Hunnic raid in 515 Anastasius I walled it and raised it to city status
pre_detail: Avkat Project: the village is dominated by a Bronze Age mound next to the Roman lower town. Survey ceramics show occupation from the Early Bronze Age, including Late Bronze Age burnished wares (Hittite Şapinuwa is c. 20 km away). The site was 'occupied since prehistoric, and certainly since Hittite times'.
pre_sources: Haldon, Elton & Newhard, Archaeology and Urban Settlement in Late Roman and Byzantine Anatolia (CUP 2018), excerpt; BIAA PRJ100 summary
status_evidence: raised to a city by Anastasius I; bishops 680–787; autocephalous archbishopric (7th c.), then metropolis
note: Wikipedia says the renaming as Theodoroupolis in 972 applied to neighbouring Euchaneia; some sources apply it to Euchaita itself. Records end after Manzikert (1071). Excavated by the Avkat Project (2006–12).
sources: Haldon et al. 2018, The Euchaita/Avkat Project; Pleiades 857120; Wikipedia: Euchaita

greek_from_text: Pompey made the village of Phazemon into the city Neapolis, 64 BC (Strabo 12.3.38); renamed Neoklaudiopolis under Claudius; Andrapa in late antiquity
pre_greek_note: The native village of Phazemon (Strabo). Hittite Nerik lies at nearby Oymaağaç Höyük, a different site, so no pre-Greek name is claimed.
status_evidence: Strabo 12.3.38; Paphlagonian oath of 3 BC found here; city coins (Neoklaudiopolis); Hierocles (Andrapa); bishops 431–681
note: Older scholarship placed Phazemon/Neapolis at Merzifon; the city territory centred on Vezirköprü is now generally accepted.

greek_from_text: known from civic bronzes 'ΛΑΟΔΙΚΕΙΑΣ' of the Mithridatic period (c. 120–63 BC); presumably named after a Pontic queen Laodike
founder: a Mithridatid king of Pontus (named after a queen Laodike)
pre_detail: The location at Ladik is itself uncertain, and no pre-Hellenistic finds are reported at the town.
status_evidence: Pontic civic bronzes; Ptolemy
note: Barrington leaves it unlocated (87 A4, 'Laodikeia', region of Amasya); the link to Ladik rests on the modern name. Barrington puts the fortress Kizari at Ladik.
sources: Cohen 1995 (Laodikeia in Pontos); Barrington 87 A4; Pleiades 857208; Wikipedia: Ladik

other_names: Amaseia; Ḫaraşna/Harşena (Ottoman name of the citadel)
greek_from_text: royal residence of the Pontic kings from c. 281 BC; first Greek civic coins (ΑΜΑΣΕΙΑΣ) under Mithridates VI, c. 110–63 BC; city era from 3/2 BC
founder: native town; capital of the Mithridatid kings
pre_greek_note: A Hittite name (Ḫakmiš/Ḫakpiš) has been suggested for Amasya, but the identification is speculative and not adopted here.
status_evidence: Mithridatic civic bronze coins (c. 110–63 BC); Roman provincial coins (era 3/2 BC); Strabo 12.3.39; Hierocles; bishops 325–787
note: Strabo's home town and the early Pontic royal capital (royal rock tombs). The name is native, not Greek.
sources: Strabo 12.3.39; Pleiades 857018; Wikipedia: Pontic coinage; Wikipedia: Amasya

greek_from_text: Mithridatic civic bronze coins (ΓΑΖΙΟΥΡΩΝ), c. 110–63 BC; earlier satrapal mint with Aramaic legends (c. 333–322 BC)
pre_greek_note: Aramaic legend B‘L GZWR/GZYR ('Baal of Gazur') on coins of the satrap Ariarathes (c. 333–322 BC) struck at Gaziura.
status_evidence: Mithridatic civic bronze coins (c. 110–63 BC); Strabo 12.3.15 ('ancient royal residence, now deserted'); Greek inscription of Mithridates VI's time on the castle rock
note: Civic status is short-lived: Strabo calls it deserted in his day, and it does not reappear as a city.
sources: Strabo 12.3.15; Pleiades 857134; Wikipedia: Pontic coinage; Numista 427294 (Ariarathes, Gaziura)

site: Zile town and castle mound (Zile, Tokat)
greek_from_text: temple-state of Anaitis made a polis by Pompey, 64 BC; city era from 3/2 BC
founder: Pompey (raised the temple-state to city status)
pre_greek_note: Strabo says the temple stood on the 'mound of Semiramis'; no pre-Greek name is attested.
status_evidence: Strabo 12.3.37; Roman provincial coins (era 3/2 BC); Hierocles; bishops 325–451 and later
note: Site of Caesar's 'veni, vidi, vici' victory (47 BC). Persian cult of Anaitis before Pompey.

site: Gümenek, c. 9 km NE of Tokat (Merkez, Tokat)
greek_from_text: Mithridatic civic bronze coins (ΚΟΜΑΝΩΝ), c. 110–63 BC; temple-state of Ma enlarged by Pompey; city era AD 34/35
pre_greek_note: Native temple-state of Ma (Enyo); no pre-Greek attestation of the name for this Pontic site.
status_evidence: Mithridatic civic bronze coins (c. 110–63 BC); Strabo 12.3.32–36; Roman provincial coins (era 34/35); Hierocles; bishops 325–787
note: Strabo describes over 6,000 temple slaves. medieval Roman Tokat (Dazimon/Dokeia) grew 9 km to the SW.
sources: Strabo 12.3.32–36; Pleiades 857095; Wikipedia: Pontic coinage; Olshausen & Biller 1984

site: probably near Çevresu, at the Iris (Yeşilırmak)–Lycus (Kelkit) confluence (Erbaa, Tokat)
greek_from_text: founded by Mithridates VI Eupator (120–63 BC; exact date unknown), left unfinished; completed by Pompey as Magnopolis, 64 BC
founder: Mithridates VI Eupator; completed by Pompey
pre_detail: Kept. Strabo 12.3.30 says Mithridates VI founded it at the Iris–Lycus confluence and Pompey found it half-finished, which describes a city built from scratch. The site is unlocated and unexcavated, so the evidence is textual only.
status_evidence: Strabo 12.3.30; Appian Mith. 115
note: Coordinates are an estimate for the confluence at the west end of the Phanaroia plain; Pleiades has only a rough point (40.5, 36.5). The city disappears after the 1st c. AD (perhaps absorbed by Neocaesarea).

greek_from_text: first bishop at the Council of Constantinople, 381; city in Hierocles (c. 527)
pre_greek_note: Native place-name; no pre-Greek attestation.
status_evidence: Hierocles; bishops 381, 451, 680–81; Basil's letters
note: Near Annisa, the family estate of Basil of Caesarea. Home town of Evagrius Ponticus.

other_names: Kabeira (Mithridatic royal residence); Diospolis (Pompey, 64 BC); Sebaste (Pythodoris); Hadriane (2nd c. title)
greek_from_text: Mithridatic civic bronze coins of Kabeira (c. 110–63 BC); made a polis as Diospolis by Pompey 64 BC; Neocaesarea from the 1st c. AD (era AD 64)
founder: Mithridatic royal residence Kabeira; refounded by Pompey as Diospolis
pre_greek_note: Kabeira was a royal residence (palace, water-mill, park) of Mithridates VI before Pompey; no pre-Greek name attested.
status_evidence: Mithridatic civic bronze coins (c. 110–63 BC); Strabo 12.3.30–31; Roman provincial coins (era 64); metropolis of Pontus Polemoniacus; Hierocles; bishops from the 3rd c. (Gregory Thaumaturgus)
note: Pleiades puts Kabeira c. 6 km E of Niksar; Neocaesarea is under Niksar. Turkish Niksar < Neokaisareia (a Greek–Latin hybrid name).
sources: Strabo 12.3.30–31; Pleiades 857177; Wikipedia: Pontic coinage; Wikipedia: Niksar
refoundations: Kabeira → Diospolis (Pompey) → Sebaste (Pythodoris) → Neocaesarea (1st c. AD)

greek_from_text: Mithridatic civic bronze coins (ΧΑΒΑΚΤΩΝ), c. 100–85 BC
pre_greek_note: Non-Greek place-name, known only from coins.
status_evidence: Mithridatic civic bronze coins only
note: Known only from coins of Mithridates VI's reign. The site and province are unknown; coordinates are a placeholder for inland Pontus.
sources: Wikipedia: Pontic coinage; Künker: Pontus, Chabakta Æ 100/85 BC

site: unlocated; Pleiades point near Doğanşar (Sivas), Olshausen proposes the area between Tokat and Horoztepe
greek_from_text: Mithridatic civic bronze coins (ΤΑΥΛΑΡΩΝ), c. 110–63 BC
pre_greek_note: Non-Greek place-name.
status_evidence: Mithridatic civic bronze coins only
note: Perhaps the Talaura where Mithridates kept treasure (Appian, Plutarch). Some link it to Sebasteia (Pleiades: Sebasteia/Megalopolis?/Talaura?).
sources: Pleiades 857345; Wikipedia: Pontic coinage; Olshausen & Biller 1984

site: Bolus, c. 25 km SW of Tokat, near Çamlıbel (Yeşilyurt?, Tokat)
greek_from_text: first known bishop (Maxentius) signs the letter of the Armenia I bishops to Leo I, 458
pre_greek_note: Native place-name; no pre-Greek attestation.
status_evidence: bishops 458, 553, 680–81; Justinian Nov. 31; Notitiae (suffragan, later archbishopric, under Sebasteia)
note: Under Basil it belonged to the see of Ibora; it is not in Hierocles. The site was identified by Kiepert and Ramsay. The current official name of the village is not verified.
sources: Pleiades 857369; Wikipedia: Berissa; Catholic Encyclopedia: Berissa

greek_from_text: the village of Karana became the city of Sebastopolis when Pontus Galaticus was annexed (city era 3/2 BC)
founder: Augustus (city status with the annexation of 3/2 BC)
pre_greek_note: Karana/Karanitis (Strabo 12.3.37) was a native settlement; no pre-Greek attestation.
status_evidence: Roman provincial coins (Trajan onward, era 3/2 BC); Pliny NH 6.8; Hierocles; bishops 4th c., 451, 458, 692
note: Some of the council signatures for 'Herakleopolis' (e.g. 680–81) belong to Pedachthoe-Herakleoupolis, not to Sebastopolis.
sources: Strabo 12.3.37; Pleiades 629076; Catholic Encyclopedia: Sebastopolis; Hierocles, Synecdemus

site: Ereğli (Konya); Bronze/Iron Age mound probably Ereğli Karahöyük c. 15 km NE
greek_from_text: Neo-Hittite Ḫubišna; Cappadocian royal town where Cicero camped (51 BC); first Greek civic coins dated year 8 of Trajan (AD 104/5)
pre_greek_note: Old Assyrian Ḫabušna, Hittite Ḫupišna/Ḫapušna, Neo-Assyrian Ḫubišna (capital of a Luwian kingdom of Tabal); equation with Kybistra secure, exact Bronze Age site (Karahöyük or Tont Kalesi) unresolved.
status_evidence: Strabo 12.2.7; Cicero Fam. 15.2, 15.4; coins Trajan (RPC III 3178–80); bishops 325, 451; Hierocles
note: Coordinates are for Ereğli (the medieval Roman Herakleia); Pleiades places Kybistra at 37.59, 34.15 near Karahöyük. Turkish Ereğli continues Herakleia.
sources: Pleiades 648614; RPC III 3178–80; Cicero Fam. 15.2; Wikipedia: Cybistra

greek_from_text: Cappadocian town on the Ankyra–Archelais road (Polybius 25.4); first bishop (Pancratius) at Serdica/Philippopolis 343
status_evidence: Polybius 25.4; Basil, Letters; bishops 343, 381, 431, 451; Hierocles
note: Native (-assos) name; the village name Parlasan probably preserves it.
sources: Pleiades 619235; Polybius 25.4; Wikipedia: Parnassus (Cappadocia); TIB 2 (Hild & Restle 1981)

greek_from_text: first attested bishop at Chalcedon 451; Hierocles (Therma)
pre_detail: The 2nd-c. AD Roman bath (Aquae Saravenae, Ptolemy's Sarouena) is the earliest documented phase. No Hittite, Phrygian or höyük occupation is reported at Sarıkaya.
status_evidence: Hierocles; bishops 451, 680–81, 787; Roman baths
note: A spa settlement on (former) royal/imperial land that became a city and see; date is first firm attestation.

site: Güneykaya, formerly Bedohtun, N of Sivas (Yıldızeli?, Sivas)
greek_from_text: the village of the martyr Athenogenes became the city and see Herakleoupolis, probably under Heraclius (610–641); first bishop (Ioannes) at Constantinople 680–81
pre_greek_note: Native village name; no pre-Greek attestation.
status_evidence: bishop 680–81 (Ioannes, 'Herakleioupolis or Pidachthoe'); 7th-c. seal of an archbishop of Pidachthoe; Notitiae (autocephalous archbishopric)
note: The founder Heraclius is inferred only from the name. The Ottoman village name Bedohtun preserves Pedachthoe.
sources: Pleiades 857266; Wikipedia: Pedachtoë; PBE Ioannes 46; Martyrdom of Athenogenes

greek_from_text: probably Pompey's Megalopolis (64 BC); Sebasteia under Augustus (city era 2 BC); coins from Trajan
founder: Pompey (Megalopolis, if identical); renamed Sebasteia under Augustus
pre_greek_note: Pleiades lists Hittite Šamuḫa and Šanaḫwitta, but Šamuḫa is now placed at Kayalıpınar and Šanaḫwitta is unlocated; there is no secure pre-Greek name. The Topraktepe mound in the city shows earlier occupation.
status_evidence: Roman provincial coins (Trajan onward); metropolis of Armenia I; Hierocles; bishops 325–787
lang_later: Large Armenian population from 1021 (Senekerim Artsruni's resettlement); mixed Greek–Armenian until the Turkish conquest
note: That Sebasteia is Pompey's Megalopolis (Strabo 12.3.37) is the common view but unproven. If they are different, the date becomes c. 2 BC.
sources: Strabo 12.3.37; Pleiades 629075; Catholic Encyclopedia: Sebaste; Hierocles, Synecdemus

greek_from_text: founded by Pompey on the field of his victory over Mithridates (66 BC), with veterans and locals; city era 64 BC
pre_detail: Pompey founded the city on the battlefield where he defeated Mithridates (66 BC), with wounded and aged veterans, and neighbouring natives joined it (Dio 36.50.3). It was a new foundation, not a refoundation of a native town. The site itself is unexcavated.
pre_sources: Dio Cass. 36.50.3; Strabo 12.3.28; Appian Mithr. 105; Pleiades 857248
status_evidence: Strabo 12.3.28; Roman provincial coins (era 64 BC); metropolis of Armenia I; Hierocles; bishops from the 4th c.
note: Armenia Minor had a mixed Greek–Armenian population. The city itself used Greek (coins, inscriptions, metropolitan see).
sources: Strabo 12.3.28; Cassius Dio 36.50; Pleiades 857248; Wikipedia: Nicopolis (Armenia)

greek_from_text: ancient fortress said to have been built/renamed by Pompey c. 64 BC (Procopius); first attested as a city and see c. 375 (Basil's letters to the clergy and magistrates of Colonia; bishop Euphronius); Hierocles c. 527; rebuilt by Justinian
pre_greek_note: Procopius calls it an ancient fortress before Pompey; no name is recorded.
status_evidence: Procopius Aed. 3.4.6; Hierocles; bishops; seat of the theme of Koloneia (by 863); Greek inscription of the 9th–10th c. in the fortress
note: Site in Giresun, just across the Sivas border, so it also appears in the Pontic seeds. Strabo does not list it among Pompey's foundations; the Pompeian origin rests on Procopius. Held by Trebizond and the Turks in turn; taken by Mehmed II in 1461.
sources: Procopius, Aed. 3.4.6; Pleiades 857194; Hierocles, Synecdemus; Wikipedia: Şebinkarahisar

other_names: Satala in Armenia (to distinguish it from Satala in Lydia)
site: Sadak village, Kelkit (Gümüşhane): the legionary fortress and the late Roman city
greek_from_text: bishop at Nicaea in 325; the people of Satala wrote to Basil for a bishop c. 372 (Basil, Ep. 99, 102, 103); city of Armenia I in Hierocles
founder: Roman legionary base (legio XV Apollinaris, c. AD 75–117), which grew into a city
status_evidence: Hierocles (Armenia I); Procopius, Aed. 3.4.1–4 ("the city of Satala"); bishops 325–879; Notitiae into the 13th c.
lang_later: Mixed: a Greek-speaking civic and church community (Basil writes in Greek "to the citizens of Satala") among an Armenian-speaking countryside; Latin in the legion
note: Added in the eastern review (11 Oct 2026); earlier left out as "Armenian". Its four sister cities of Armenia I (Sebasteia, Sebastopolis, Nikopolis, Koloneia) were already in the set.
sources: Basil, Epp. 99, 102, 103 (newadvent.org/fathers/3202099, 3202102, 3202103, fetched); Procopius, Buildings 3.4-3.7 (LacusCurtius, Dewing transl., fetched); Hierocles, Synekdemos 703 [from knowledge]; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satala (fetched: bishops after Le Quien, 2017 Greek epitaph, Lightfoot 1998); CAP seed row 'Satala, Nicaea 325 (Honigmann)'; Mitford, East of Asia Minor (2018) and JRS 64 (1974) on the Satala inscriptions [from knowledge]

other_names: Eriza (Ptolemy); Erēz, Erznka (Armenian); Arzinjan (Arabic, Persian); Arzinga (Marco Polo, Clavijo); Erzincan
site: Old Erzincan, just south of the present city, which was rebuilt further north after the 1939 earthquake; the medieval walled town is not precisely located
province_late: Keltzene (tourma of Chaldia, then the theme of Mesopotamia, 899–911)
greek_from_text: c. 900: a see of the Constantinopolitan church (first under Kamachos, a metropolis by c. 1000); Greeks beside Armenians in the city still in 1404 (Clavijo)
pre_detail: Armenian Erēz, cult centre of Anahit in Acilisene (Strabo 11.14.16; Agathangelos)
pre_greek_note: The Armenian town Erēz, cult centre of Anahit in Acilisene.
status_evidence: see from c. 900, metropolis by c. 1000 (Honigmann; ODB); metropolitans at the synods of 1029 and 1031/2; metropolitan Basil 1071–72 (Dumbarton Oaks seal); the metropolis last filled 1318/19; Clavijo (1404): a walled, populous city
lang_later: Mixed: Armenians the majority (Marco Polo, Ibn Battuta, ODB). Clavijo (1404) found 'many Christians, Armenians and Greeks', with a Greek priest at the head of the city's clergy (Le Strange tr. pp. 160–61).
note: Added in the second look at the inland Pontus and the east (11 Oct 2026). Under Turkish rule from c. 1071 (Mengujekid, Seljuk, Ilkhanid, then the emir Mutahharten, who married a Trapezuntine princess).
sources: Clavijo, Embassy to Tamerlane, tr. Le Strange (1928) pp. 160–61; Historia del gran Tamorlan (Madrid 1782) pp. 109–10 (opened, archive.org); Clavijo, tr. Markham (1859) ch. IV; Marco Polo, tr. Yule, bk 1 ch. 4; Ibn Battuta via Bosworth, Encyclopaedia Iranica s.v. Arzenjan; Oxford Dictionary of Byzantium (1991) s.v. Keltzene p. 1173 (opened); Honigmann, Die Ostgrenze des byzantinischen Reiches (1935) pp. 198–213; Dumbarton Oaks seal BZS.1947.2.51 (Basil, metropolitan of Keltzene); Charanis, The Armenians in the Byzantine Empire (1963)

site: Erzurum city: the citadel and old town (Yakutiye, Erzurum)
province_late: Armenia I (Justinian); theme of Theodosiopolis, then Iberia
greek_from_text: 949: taken by John Kourkouas's successor Theophilos Kourkouas; its Muslim population was replaced by Greek and Armenian settlers; Roman until c. 1071–80
founder: Theodosius II (c. 415–421, as Theodosiopolis); resettled under Constantine VII (949)
pre_greek_note: The Armenian town Karin, fortified as Theodosiopolis c. 415–421.
status_evidence: late Roman fortress-city and see; theme capital after 949 (theme of Iberia from 1000/1022)
lang_later: Mixed: Greek and Armenian settlers after 949 (Runciman, Whittow, Holmes); Armenians probably the majority. Before 949 Greek was only the language of the garrison and administration.
note: Added in the eastern review (11 Oct 2026) for 949–c. 1071 only. The Turkish name comes from Arabic Arzan al-Rum, "Arzan of the Romans".
sources: Wikipedia 'Erzurum' (consulted; cites Whittow, The Making of Byzantium 600-1025 (1996) p. 322; Garsoian, 'The Foundation of Theodosiopolis-Karin' (2003); Arakelyan 1976; Inalcik, EI2 s.v. Erzurum; Gelzer 1901 pp. 536, 551 for the Notitiae; Meyendorff 1989 for the council of 593); Wikipedia 'John Kourkouas' (consulted

site: Battalgazi / Eski Malatya, within the medieval Roman walls (Battalgazi, Malatya)
greek_from_text: base of legio XII Fulminata from c. AD 70; raised to city rank by Trajan (98–117) according to Procopius
founder: Trajan (city status at the legionary base)
pre_detail: The legionary fortress of XII Fulminata (c. AD 70) was built on level ground on a site different from Hittite/Neo-Hittite Melid, which is at Arslantepe c. 3 km south of the Battalgazi walls. The Roman city took the district name Melitene, and no pre-Roman level is known inside Battalgazi.
pre_sources: Procop. Aed. 3.4.15-20; en.wikipedia Melitene ('re-established ... on a different site'); Pleiades 629040
pre_greek_note: The Bronze and Iron Age city (Melid) is the Arslantepe mound, c. 4–5 km SW of the Roman city. The name passed to the Roman site, but the site is new.
status_evidence: Procopius Aed. 3.4.15–20; metropolis of Armenia II; Hierocles; bishops 381–787
lang_later: After the Roman reconquest (934) the population was largely Syriac (Jacobite) and Armenian
note: Late antique Melitene was a Greek-speaking Christian city (Euthymius the Great, Acacius, Otreius), with a mixed Cappadocian/Armenian/Syriac hinterland. Pleiades' point (38.382, 38.361) is on Arslantepe, so the coordinates here are moved to Battalgazi.
sources: Procopius, Aed. 3.4.15–20; Pleiades 629040; TIB 2 (Kappadokien); Wikipedia: Melitene

greek_from_text: first bishop at the Council of Ephesus, 431; city in Hierocles (c. 527)
pre_greek_note: Native place-name; no pre-Greek attestation.
status_evidence: Hierocles; bishops 431, 451, 553, 680–81
note: The old Turkish name Arga preserves Arka. The Greek-speaking character is inferred from the province's church life.

greek_from_text: small town of John Chrysostom's exile (404–407), described in his Greek letters; city in Hierocles (c. 527)
pre_greek_note: Native place-name; no pre-Greek attestation.
status_evidence: Hierocles; Chrysostom's letters; bishops (5th c. onward)
note: Border case: the site is in Kahramanmaraş (EAST batch), included here as a Cappadocian city of Armenia II.
sources: Pleiades 629013; Hierocles, Synecdemus; John Chrysostom, Letters to Olympias

greek_from_text: Hellenistic temple-city of Ma under the name Hierapolis (Greek inscriptions, 2nd–1st c. BC); Strabo 12.2.3
pre_greek_note: Kummanni, the Kizzuwatnean cult centre of Ḫebat, is traditionally equated with Comana; several scholars now locate Kummanni in the Cilician plain instead.
status_evidence: Strabo 12.2.3; Greek civic inscriptions of the Hieropolitai; Hierocles; bishops (5th c. onward)
note: Border case: the site is in Adana (CIL batch). Included because it is the main Cappadocian temple-city of Cataonia. The Hellenistic date of the name Hierapolis is not closely fixed.

greek_from_text: founded by Ariarathes IV (220–163 BC) according to most modern accounts (Stephanus: by an Ariarathes)
pre_detail: No excavation or recorded höyük at Pınarbaşı. A regional article asserts the town's 'history goes back to Tabal' and notes Hittite works in the district (Karakuyu dam), but cites no settlement evidence at the site.
pre_sources: Pleiades 628934; DergiPark article-file 3538252 (Ariaratheia/Pınarbaşı); en.wikipedia Pınarbaşı, Kayseri
status_evidence: Cohen 1995; Ptolemy; Hierocles; bishops 431, 449, 451
note: Which Ariarathes founded it is uncertain (III, IV and V have all been proposed). The city disappeared in the Arab frontier wars (8th–9th c.). Ramsay's equation with Tzamandos is rejected; Tzamandos lies c. 15 km away.

site: near Yaylacık, SE of Develi (Kayseri; district not verified)
greek_from_text: first known bishop (Plato) at the Council in Trullo, 692; bishop at Nicaea 787
pre_greek_note: Native place-name (also in Ptolemy); no pre-Greek attestation.
status_evidence: bishops 692, 787; Notitiae (suffragan of Caesarea)
note: The Barrington Atlas brackets the name, so the location is tentative.

greek_from_text: dynastic foundation named after Ariaramnes (c. 280–230 BC); attested in the Greek–Aramaic Farasa bilingual inscription (2nd c. BC)
pre_detail: Known only from the Greek-Aramaic Farasa inscription. The site is not excavated, and the Barrington alternative name [Rodandos] is a Byzantine fortress name, not a pre-Greek one.
status_evidence: Farasa bilingual inscription (a strategos 'of Ariaramneia')
lang_later: Iranian/Aramaic-using elite (Mithra cult) beside Greek in the 2nd c. BC
note: Known only from one inscription, which names it as the seat of a strategos. Polis status is not proven, and the location is only that of the inscription.
sources: Pleiades 648569; Encyclopaedia Iranica: Ariaramneia; Wikipedia: Farasa bilingual inscription

site: Kültepe (Karahöyük) mound, NE of Kayseri (Kocasinan, Kayseri)
greek_from_text: Greek decree of the Anisenoi (boule, demos, prytaneis, archons), dated 'year 7' of a Cappadocian king, c. 157–90 BC
pre_greek_note: Kültepe is securely Kaneš (Old Assyrian archives). Anisa is placed there from the decree's findspot and Hellenistic–Roman levels on the mound; the name may continue Kaneš.
status_evidence: Anisa decree (bronze tablet); Hellenistic–Roman occupation at Kültepe
note: The decree refers to a lawsuit at Eusebeia (Mazaka). Anisa was not a city in Roman imperial times and was absorbed by Caesarea.
sources: Attalus.org inscr. 162 (Anisa decree); Pleiades 628923; Wikipedia: Anisa; Robert, Noms indigènes 1963

other_names: Mazaka (native); Eusebeia by the Argaios (Ariarathes V); Caesarea (Archelaus, before AD 14)
greek_from_text: the royal residence Mazaka was refounded as the polis Eusebeia by Ariarathes V Eusebes Philopator (163–130 BC), with laws of Charondas (Strabo 12.2.9)
founder: Ariarathes V (refoundation of native Mazaka as Eusebeia)
pre_greek_note: Mazaka is a native name known only in Greek. The Hittite Kuššara has been suggested for the Kayseri area but is unlocated, so it is not used. Kaneš/Kültepe is a separate site 20 km NE.
status_evidence: Strabo 12.2.7–9; royal and Roman provincial coins (Eusebeia, Caesarea); metropolis of Cappadocia I; Hierocles; bishops 314–787
note: Pleiades also has a separate 'Mazaka' point (629034) c. 13 km W; the city is under modern Kayseri. Which king renamed it is sometimes given as Ariarathes IV, since both bore the epithet Eusebes.
refoundations: Mazaka → Eusebeia by the Argaios (Ariarathes V) → Caesarea (Archelaus)

site: tentatively near Emmiler, NW of Kayseri, near the Çokgöz bridge over the Halys (Kocasinan, Kayseri)
greek_from_text: village of the 'acheiropoietos' image of Christ, made a polis (Iustinianoupolis) by Justinian (527–565); first bishop 553
pre_detail: Unlocated village-see; no archaeology.
status_evidence: bishops 553, 680, 692, 787, 879; Notitiae (suffragan of Caesarea)
note: The seed row 'region only 38.95, 35.2 (Cappadocia I, 553–787)' is this see. The name is often called Celtic.

site: Tilköy (formerly Kaysar), N of Derinkuyu (Derinkuyu, Nevşehir)
greek_from_text: first named by Pliny (NH 6.8, AD 77) among Cappadocian towns; Ptolemy 5.6
founder: unknown (the name honours Zeus and Caesar; perhaps Archelaus or an early emperor)
pre_detail: The town is known only from Pliny and Ptolemy and has not been excavated. No earlier name or prehistoric site is reported at Tilköy.
status_evidence: Pliny NH 6.8; Ptolemy 5.6
note: Sometimes wrongly identified with Nazianzos. Civic status is inferred only from the dynastic name and its listing by Pliny and Ptolemy; there are no coins or bishops. The old village name Kaysar may echo (Dio)caesarea.

site: Büyükkale and Küçükkale tells, 1–2 km N of Harmandalı (Ortaköy, Aksaray)
greek_from_text: see of Gregory of Nyssa from 372; town in Ptolemy and the Itineraries earlier
pre_greek_note: Hittite Nenašša, on the Maraššantiya (Halys) route, has been equated with Nyssa because the names and locations are similar. This is an unproven proposal.
status_evidence: Hierocles; bishops 372–879; Notitiae (suffragan of Caesarea)
note: An older identification with Nevşehir is now rejected. The site is near the Halys.
sources: Pleiades 619222; Wikipedia: Nyssa (Cappadocia); TIB 2 (Kappadokien); Hierocles, Synecdemus

other_names: Garsaura (native); Colonia Claudia Archelais (Claudius); Koloneia (late antique)
greek_from_text: refounded as Archelais by Archelaus, king of Cappadocia (36 BC–AD 17); Roman colony under Claudius
founder: Archelaus of Cappadocia; colony of Claudius
pre_greek_note: Garsaura, chief place of the strategia Garsauritis (Strabo 12.2.6), is a native name known only in Greek.
status_evidence: Strabo 12.2.6; Pliny NH 6.8; coins; Hierocles (Koloneia); bishops from 325
note: The seed 'Colonia' see (325–451) is this city. The foundation year under Archelaus is not known.
refoundations: Garsaura → Archelais (Archelaus) → Colonia Claudia Archelais (Claudius) → Koloneia

site: Viranşehir ruins near Helvadere, below Hasandağ (Merkez, Aksaray)
province_late: Cappadocia II; metropolis of Cappadocia III from 536
greek_from_text: Justinian rebuilt the hill-fort on a new site as Iustinianoupolis and made it the metropolis of Cappadocia III (536); listed earlier by Hierocles as Rhegemoukisos
pre_greek_note: An earlier fortress/regio Mokissos (native name) existed before Justinian.
status_evidence: Procopius Aed. 5.4.15–18; Hierocles (Rhegemoukisos); metropolis of Cappadocia III; bishops 553–879
note: Earlier literature placed Mokissos at Kırşehir; TIB places it at Viranşehir. The seed council see 'Justinianopolis' is this city.
sources: Procopius, Aed. 5.4.15–18; Pleiades 619174; Wikipedia: Mokissos; TIB 2 (Kappadokien)

greek_from_text: bishopric under Gregory the Elder (bishop c. 328/9–374); city in Hierocles (c. 527)
pre_greek_note: Native place-name; no pre-Greek attestation.
status_evidence: Hierocles; bishops from c. 329 (Gregory the Elder, Gregory of Nazianzus); later a metropolis
note: Gregory of Nazianzus calls it a small town. The old village name Nenezi preserves Nazianzos.
sources: Pleiades 619218; Wikipedia: Nazianzus; Hierocles, Synecdemus; TIB 2 (Kappadokien)

greek_from_text: post-station village made a see by Basil, with Gregory of Nazianzus as bishop (372); city in Hierocles
pre_greek_note: Native place-name; no pre-Greek attestation.
status_evidence: Hierocles; bishops from 372 (Gregory of Nazianzus) to 787
note: Gregory describes it as a dreary, dusty post-station.
sources: Pleiades 619256; Gregory of Nazianzus, Carm. 2.1.11; Hierocles, Synecdemus

site: near Çiftlik (Niğde); exact site not verified
greek_from_text: see with a (Homoian) bishop in Basil's letters (c. 375); 'Rhegedoara' in Hierocles
pre_greek_note: Native place-name; no pre-Greek attestation.
status_evidence: Basil, Ep. 239; Hierocles; bishops to 680–81 and later
note: The prefix rhege- in Hierocles suggests an imperial estate (regio). The location follows the Barrington Atlas.
sources: Pleiades 619151; Basil, Ep. 239; Hierocles, Synecdemus; TIB 2 (Kappadokien)

other_names: Dana (Xenophon); Eusebeia by the Taurus (Cappadocian kings); Colonia Aurelia Antoniniana (Caracalla)
greek_from_text: Neo-Hittite capital and 'great and prosperous city' Dana (Xenophon, 401 BC); refounded as the polis Eusebeia by the Taurus under Ariarathes IV or V (2nd c. BC)
founder: Ariarathes IV or V Eusebes (refoundation as Eusebeia)
pre_greek_note: Tuwanuwa/Tuwana was the capital of King Warpalawa (8th c. BC; inscriptions from Tyana and nearby Bor). The identification is secure.
status_evidence: Strabo 12.2.7; royal and Roman provincial coins; Roman colony under Caracalla; metropolis of Cappadocia II from 371; Hierocles; bishops 325–787
note: Home of Apollonius of Tyana. Which of the two Eusebes kings refounded it is uncertain, so the date is approximate.
refoundations: Tyana → Eusebeia by the Taurus (Ariarathid) → Col. Aurelia Antoniniana (Caracalla)

site: near Başmakçı / Çiftehan, at the northern approach to the Cilician Gates (Ulukışla, Niğde)
greek_from_text: the village Halala was made a colony named Faustinopolis by Marcus Aurelius after Empress Faustina the Younger died there (175/6)
pre_greek_note: Halala was a native village (Historia Augusta, Marcus 26.9).
status_evidence: Historia Augusta, Marcus 26.9; Hierocles; bishops 4th c.–680–81
note: The modern Turkish name of the locality is not settled in the sources used (Başmakçı is the usual identification).
sources: Historia Augusta, Marcus 26.9; Pleiades 648608; Hierocles, Synecdemus; TIB 2 (Kappadokien)

greek_from_text: first certain bishop Adolius at Chalcedon 451 (Otreius, 381, sometimes listed here, was bishop of Melitene); city in Hierocles (Armenia II)
pre_greek_note: Native Anatolian toponym (-issos); no pre-Greek attestation.
status_evidence: Hierocles (Armenia II); bishops 381, 451, 458, 692; birthplace of emperor Maurice (539), who embellished it
note: Jacobite (Syriac) bishops are known for the 7th–10th c.; ravaged by Sayf al-Dawla (944, 951) and replaced as local centre by Plasta (Elbistan).
sources: Pleiades 628925; TIB 2 (Kappadokien); Hierocles, Synecdemus; Wikipedia: Arabissus

site: Kahramanmaraş city: the citadel mound and old town (Dulkadiroğlu, Kahramanmaraş)
greek_from_text: refounded as Germanikeia Kaisareia by Antiochus IV of Commagene (AD 38–72); bishops from 325; city of Euphratensis in Hierocles
pre_greek_note: Capital of the Neo-Hittite kingdom of Gurgum.
status_evidence: Greek civic name; one of the four cities of Commagene c. AD 200; bishops 325–451; Hierocles; Roman-period civic coins reported (to be checked in RPC)
lang_later: Mixed: Greek alongside Aramaic (Syriac); Eudoxius was bishop here and Nestorius was born here. Arab frontier city from the 640s; Armenian in the 11th–12th c.
note: Added in the eastern review (11 Oct 2026). The Turkish name comes from the native name (Marqas) through Arabic, not from the Greek.
sources: Wikipedia en 'Kahramanmaraş', 'Germanikeia', de 'Germanikeia' (consulted); Wikipedia 'Commagene' (Germanicea 'declared itself a Commagenian city'); Socrates, HE 7.29 (Nestorius); Theophanes on Leo III; Head, HN² (Commagene, from memory); Facella 2006; Honigmann, Ostgrenze (962 reconquest).

greek_from_text: founded in the 3rd c. BC, urban from the 2nd c. BC (Münster excavations); the name of Thessalian Doliche suggests Greek/Macedonian settlers under the Seleucids
founder: Seleucids (probable; settlers named after Doliche in Perrhaebia)
pre_detail: The Münster survey of the urban area on Keber Tepe shows the city site was inhabited before the Hellenistic period, with numerous Stone Age finds. The Iron Age storm-god (Dolichenus) sanctuary stands c. 1 km away on Dülük Baba Tepesi. The input note says the city site had no pre-Greek occupation, which is wrong.
status_evidence: Cohen 2006, 155; civic coins Marcus Aurelius–Caracalla; city archive of c. 2,000 sealings; Hierocles; bishops 325, 381, 451
lang_later: Aramaic/Syriac probably the majority language in Roman and late antique times (Jacobite see 8th–9th c.)
note: The Iron Age storm-god sanctuary (later Jupiter Dolichenus) lies c. 1 km away on Dülük Baba Tepesi, not on the city site. Whether 'Doliche' is a Greek colonists' name or a Hellenized native one is debated; Dülük continues it either way.
sources: Cohen 2006, 155; Pleiades 658455; Blömer & Winter (Doliche excavations, Univ. Münster); Wikipedia: Doliche (Commagene)

site: unlocated; most often placed at or near Gaziantep (Aintab)
greek_from_text: Hellenistic foundation named after a king Antiochus (Seleucid, or possibly Antiochus I of Commagene); listed by Ptolemy in Commagene
founder: a king Antiochus (Seleucid or Commagenian; uncertain)
pre_detail: Unlocated. If it was at Gaziantep, the castle mound (with prehistoric levels) would make it 'yes', but the identification is a guess.
status_evidence: Ptolemy (Commagene); Cohen 2006, 150
lang_later: Aramaic probably dominant (Commagene)
note: Location unknown; Gaziantep is the commonest guess, Perrhe has also been proposed. Coordinates are a regional placeholder (Gaziantep).
sources: Cohen 2006, 150; Ptolemy, Geography 5 (Commagene); Wikipedia: Antiochia ad Taurum

site: Örenli (formerly Pirin), north of Adıyaman: rock-cut necropolis and town site
greek_from_text: by AD 198–200, when it was one of the four cities of Commagene on the Cendere bridge; Greek epitaphs of residents in the Roman imperial period
pre_greek_note: A native Commagenian town (by definition an earlier settlement); no pre-Greek name attested.
status_evidence: one of the four cities of Commagene (CIL III 6709–6710); bishops 381, 451; Hierocles
lang_later: Mixed: Greek epitaphs of its own residents (Crowther & Facella 2011) beside an Aramaic-speaking majority
note: Added in the eastern review (11 Oct 2026). Some identify it with Antioch near the Taurus (C586); here they are kept apart. The former Turkish name Pirin continued the ancient one.
sources: Wikipedia en/de 'Perrhe' (consulted 11 Oct 2026); Crowther & Facella, 'Inscriptions from the Necropolis of Perrhe', in Winter (ed.), Von Kummuh nach Telouch (AMS 64, 2011) 367–394; Blömer & Facella 2008 (AMS 60) 189–200; Eraslan & Winter 2008; Erarslan 2012 in Wagner (ed.), Gottkönige am Euphrat; Wikipedia 'Severan Bridge' (CIL III 6709–6710).

other_names: Flavia Samosata, metropolis of Commagene; Šamšaṭ (Syriac); Sumaysat (Arabic)
site: Samsat Höyük, under the Atatürk Dam lake since 1989 (Samsat, Adıyaman); the modern town was moved
greek_from_text: AD 72: annexed and made "Flavia Samosata, metropolis of Commagene", with civic coins in Greek (Hadrian to Philip); before that the royal capital of Commagene with a Greek-using court
pre_greek_note: Capital of the Neo-Hittite kingdom of Kummuḫ (Assyrian sources); the identification of the city with the kingdom's capital is usual but not certain.
status_evidence: civic Greek coinage (ΦΛ ΣΑΜΟΣΑΤΕΩΝ ΜΗΤΡΟ ΚΟΜ); one of the four cities of Commagene on the Cendere bridge (c. AD 200); bishops 325–451; Hierocles
lang_later: Mixed: Greek alongside Aramaic (Syriac). Lucian, Paul of Samosata and Eusebius of Samosata came from the city; Lucian says he was "still barbarian in speech" as a boy
note: Added in the eastern review (11 Oct 2026); earlier left out as Aramaic-speaking. The mound was excavated before the dam flooded it.
sources: Wikipedia en/de 'Samosata' (consulted 11 Oct 2026); Wikipedia 'Commagene' (Millar on language), 'Severan Bridge' (CIL III 6709–6710); Lucian, Bis Acc. 27 and De Dea Syria 1; Strabo 16.2.3; Basil, Letters to Eusebius of Samosata; Head, HN² (Commagene); IGLS I (Jalabert & Mouterde 1929); Facella 2006

other_names: Seleukeia epi tou Zeugmatos / Seleucia on the Euphrates (Seleucus I); Zeugma ('the bridge'), twin city with Apamea
site: Belkıs (Kavunlu) (Nizip, Gaziantep); lower town under the Birecik Dam lake
greek_from_text: founded by Seleucus I c. 300 BC as Seleucia, with Apamea opposite (Pliny 5.86)
pre_detail: Excavators report little evidence before Alexander and no sealed pre-Hellenistic deposits. The earliest closed deposits are Hellenistic. Pleiades lists 'Zuqarri' in Shalmaneser III's inscriptions as only possibly Zeugma.
pre_sources: Zeugma final report vol. 1 ch. 1 (zeugma.packhum.org/pdfs/v1ch01.pdf); Pleiades 658636 (Zuqarri)
pre_greek_note: Pleiades lists an Akkadian name 'Zuqarri'; not verified, so not used.
status_evidence: Cohen 2006, 190–96; Polybius 5.43 (Antiochus III's wedding, 221 BC); civic coins Antoninus Pius–Philip; base of legio IIII Scythica; Hierocles; bishops 325, 451, 553
lang_later: Greek–Aramaic bilingual in Roman times; abandoned after 7th-c. Persian and Arab raids
note: Given to Commagene by Pompey (64 BC), Roman province of Syria later; Greek funerary stelae and mosaics are abundant. Seleukeia 'epi tou Zeugmatos' (Polybius) is usually taken to be this city.
sources: Pliny NH 5.86; Cohen 2006, 190–96; Pleiades 658636; Wikipedia: Zeugma, Commagene
refoundations: Seleucia (Seleucus I) → Zeugma (common name from the Roman period)

other_names: Antiochia ad Euphratem (Pliny); Ourima/Urima (late Roman see); Arulis (Tabula Peutingeriana)
site: Horum Höyük, north of Zeugma (Nizip, Gaziantep); flooded by the Birecik Dam
greek_from_text: Hellenistic foundation named after a king Antiochus, attested as a river town by Pliny 5.86
founder: a king Antiochus (Seleucid, or Antiochus I of Commagene; uncertain)
pre_greek_note: Horum Höyük, where BAtlas places Ourima/Antioch, is a settlement mound excavated in the Birecik-dam salvage work (French–Turkish team, late 1990s), with Early Bronze Age and later pre-Hellenistic levels. No pre-Greek name is attested.
status_evidence: Pliny 5.86 (oppidum); Cohen 2006, 151; late Roman see of Urima
lang_later: Aramaic/Syriac in late antiquity (Syriac Urim)
note: Identification of Pliny's Antiochia with Urima/Arulis at Horum Höyük follows the Barrington Atlas and is not certain; the Turkish name Horum may continue Urima.
sources: Pliny NH 5.86; Cohen 2006, 151; Pleiades 658562; Wikipedia: Urima

site: conjecturally near Keskince (Tilmusa) (Birecik, Şanlıurfa); under the Birecik Dam lake
greek_from_text: name implies foundation or renaming by Antiochus IV Epiphanes (175–164 BC); known only from Pliny 5.86
founder: Antiochus IV Epiphanes (inferred from the name)
pre_detail: Known only from Pliny 5.86. The site is conjectural and flooded by the Birecik dam.
status_evidence: Pliny 5.86 (oppidum); Cohen 2006, 169
lang_later: Aramaic probably dominant in the Roman period
note: A Seleucid dynastic name only; the Barrington Atlas location next to Apamea is conjectural.

site: Tilmusa Höyük at Keskince (Birecik, Şanlıurfa); under the Birecik Dam lake
greek_from_text: founded by Seleucus I c. 300 BC opposite Seleucia-Zeugma, named after his wife Apama (Pliny 5.86)
pre_detail: Rejected the proposed 'yes', pending confirmation. Tilmusa Höyük, a 9 m conical tell of 0.45 ha on the riverbank at Keskince/Tilmusa, was excavated in 1999 by the Spanish-Czech salvage team (Gil Fuensanta, Charvát, Bucak, Orient-Express 2001/1). It is a non-Turkish source and very probably pre-Hellenistic. But neither the proposal nor any source I could read gives its dated periods, or its position relative to Apamea's walls (Wikipedia: 'not fully clear' which Apamea is meant). This becomes 'yes' if that report or the French Apamea publications (Abadie-Reynal & Gaborit 2003) confirm Bronze/Iron Age levels at the city site.
pre_sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tilbeş_Höyük (citing Gil Fuensanta, Charvát & Bucak 2001; Pascual, DHA 48.2, 2022); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apamea_(Euphrates); Pleiades 658385 (Barrington: Keskince, formerly Tilmusa); Pascual 2022 not accessible
status_evidence: Pliny 5.86; Isidore of Charax 1 (polis); Hellenistic fortifications excavated 1996–2000 (Abadie-Reynal)
lang_later: Aramaic (Osrhoene) in the Roman period; the town declined and merged into greater Zeugma
note: Fortified Hellenistic city on the east bank; occupation was slight after the Hellenistic period.
sources: Pliny NH 5.86; Cohen 2013 (Apameia on the Euphrates); Pleiades 658385; Wikipedia: Apamea (Euphrates)

site: unlocated, between Apamea and Batnai on the road to Edessa (Birecik–Suruç plain, Şanlıurfa)
greek_from_text: Macedonian foundation with a Greek name (Tacitus, Ann. 6.41), named after Anthemous in Macedonia; early Seleucid
pre_detail: Unlocated. Pleiades merges it with Batnai (Suruç, an older town), but that identification is not accepted here.
pre_sources: Tacitus Ann. 6.41; Isidore of Charax 1; Ammianus 14.3.3
status_evidence: Isidore of Charax 1 (polis); Strabo 16.1.27; Pliny 5.86 (oppidum); Tacitus Ann. 6.41; Cohen 2013
lang_later: Aramaic-speaking by the Roman period (Osrhoene; local dynasts of Anthemusia)
note: Gave its name to the district Anthemusia in which Batnai lay (Ammianus 14.3.3); Pleiades merges it with Batnae. Isidore puts it c. 5 schoinoi beyond Apamea and 3 before Koraia in Batane.
sources: Tacitus, Ann. 6.41; Isidore of Charax, Parthian Stations 1; Cohen 2013 (Anthemousias); Pleiades 658405 (merged)

greek_from_text: founded by 'the ancient Macedonians' (Ammianus 14.3.3), i.e. early Seleucid period
pre_greek_note: Neo-Assyrian Sarugi is usually identified with Suruç (Syriac Serugh, Arabic Sarūj); whether it lay at the Greek town itself is uncertain, and the attestation was not re-checked here.
status_evidence: Ammianus 14.3.3 (municipium); Hierocles (Osrhoene); bishops 381, 451, 553 (Jacob of Serugh, bishop 519–521)
lang_later: Syriac-speaking in late antiquity (Jacob of Serugh)
note: Ammianus' statement is late (4th c. AD) but explicit; the town lay in the district Anthemusia.

other_names: Antioch on the Callirhoe (Antiochus IV); Colonia Marcia Aurelia Antoniniana (213/14); Justinopolis (Justin I); Urhay/Orhay (Syriac); al-Ruha (Arabic)
greek_from_text: refounded by Seleucus I c. 303 BC as a Macedonian military settlement named after Edessa in Macedonia; Antioch on the Callirhoe on coins of Antiochus IV
pre_greek_note: Harrak (1992) argued that Assyrian Adme/Admu, preserved in the Syriac name Adme, was the old name of Edessa; plausible but not proven. The Aramaic name Urhay is attested only after the Greek foundation.
status_evidence: Seleucid civic coins (Antiochus IV); capital of Abgarid Osrhoene c. 132 BC–AD 214/248; Roman colony 213/14; bishops 325, 381, 451, 553; metropolis of Osrhoene
lang_later: Aramaic/Syriac-dominant from the Abgarid period (2nd c. BC); the centre of Syriac literature
note: medieval Roman again 1031–1087; Urfa continues the native name, not the Greek one.
sources: Pliny NH 5.86; Cohen 2013 (Edessa); Pleiades 658457; Wikipedia: Edessa
refoundations: Urhay → Edessa (Seleucus I) → Antioch on the Callirhoe (Antiochus IV) → Edessa; Colonia M. Aurelia Antoniniana (Caracalla); Justinopolis (Justin I, 525)

other_names: Harran (Akkadian/Aramaic); Hellenopolis ('city of pagans', late antique Christian epithet)
greek_from_text: Macedonian military settlers there by 312 BC (Diodorus 19.91.1), presumably settled under Alexander or the early Successors
founder: Macedonian settlers (katoikia) under Alexander or the early Successors
pre_greek_note: Ḫarrān(u), attested from the early 2nd millennium BC (Mari, Old Assyrian) and the seat of the moon-god Sîn; last Assyrian capital 610 BC. Identification certain.
status_evidence: Diodorus 19.91.1; Cohen 2013 (Karrhai); Roman provincial coins and colonia (Severans); bishops 381, 451
lang_later: Aramaic/Syriac; pagan Harranians ('Sabians') until the 11th c., Arabic after the 7th c.
note: Crassus was defeated nearby in 53 BC.

site: the walled city of Diyarbakır (Sur, Diyarbakır)
greek_from_text: capital of the province of Mesopotamia from 363; first bishop at Constantinople in 381; Greek writers born there c. 470–500
pre_greek_note: Capital of the Aramaean state of Bit-Zamani in Assyrian sources.
status_evidence: metropolis of Mesopotamia (bishops 381, 451, 553); Hierocles; fortified by Constantius II c. 349
lang_later: Mixed: Syriac majority with a Greek-educated community: the physician Aetius of Amida and the patriarch Ephraem of Amida wrote in Greek; a Chalcedonian party in the 6th c.
note: Added in the eastern review (11 Oct 2026) as a mixed city, with low confidence: the evidence for Greek speakers beyond officials rests on its writers and the Chalcedonian community.
sources: Wikipedia 'Amida (Mesopotamia)', 'Diyarbakır', 'Aëtius of Amida', 'Ephraim of Antioch', 'Mesopotamia (Roman province)' (consulted 11 Oct 2026); Ammianus 18–19; Procopius, Aed. 2.3; Photius, Bibl. cod. 228–229; Palmer 1990; Greatrex & Lieu 2002; van Berchem & Strzygowski, Amida (1910).

other_names: Antiocheia en Mygdonia (Seleucid); Septimia Colonia Nesibi (Septimius Severus); Nṣibin (Syriac)
greek_from_text: Seleucid refoundation as Antioch in Mygdonia, attested 221/220 BC (Polybius 5.51); founder probably Seleucus I or Antiochus I
pre_greek_note: Aramaean Naṣibina, taken by Adad-nirari II in 896 BC and a Neo-Assyrian provincial capital; identification certain.
status_evidence: Polybius 5.51; Seleucid civic coins of the Antiochenes in Mygdonia; Plutarch, Lucullus 32; Roman colony (Septimius Severus); bishop Jacob at Nicaea 325
lang_later: Aramaic/Syriac-dominant by the Roman period (Ephrem, School of Nisibis); ceded to Persia in 363
note: Not in Hierocles because it was Persian from 363; its Roman citizens were moved to Amida under the treaty of 363.
refoundations: Naṣibina → Antioch in Mygdonia (Seleucid) → Nisibis; Septimia Colonia (Septimius Severus)
